This game is amazing, it's a metroidvania game and unlike most indie games of this genre it doesn't suck. I got it day of and after only a day i have 10 hours longed, it's incredibly addicting and I can tell it has hours more of game play (considering I've only beaten 8 of the 30 bosses).
Pros:
-Beautiful (and adorable) art
-great score (favorite song is "Hornet")
-great atmosphere
-platforming is solid with controls that feel responsive and controlable
-the SOUL mechanic is extremely cool and gives the players options of how to fight in game (for instance a player can use soul power to heal or shoot a powerful attack)
-a multiiitude of powers and skills to make the game dynamic and strategic with customization and upgradability
-most of the enemies are unique making fights not feel repetitive or stale
-Bosses are creativite and interesting and event pose a challenge at times
-a unique mapping system that makes exploring easier
Cons:
-the first hour or two starts slow and is fairly linear, after the first boss is defeated you get a new power which unlocks one path to the next section and it's a somewhat slow process of traveling from one room to the next waiting for the fun to come back. the game more-or-less requires you to grind enemies for money so you can buy certain items in the shop (like keys); this is one major complaint i hear a lot but personally i didn't find it to bad, after traveling around the expansive map trying to find the next boss i killed enough enemies to get what i needed in a decent amount of time
-the only other complaint i've heard is frame stutter issues, but i personally haven't had any issue so it may just come down to computer specs
all-in-all it's a greart buy that;s totally worth the money

While I've barely scratched the surface, this game has been a real treat. Beautiful visuals and diverse area design lead to a desire to explore to the fullest depths; and well placed rewards continue to encourage such exploration. The combat starts simple, but grows in complexity steadily, providing an even paced challenge as one grasps the mechanics needed to succeed.
Enemy variance and boss design are fantastic and each present a new puzzle to overcome. Death is punishing, but fair, and so far has not served to discourage me from continuing. Movement is fluid, though marred by the occasional dropped input (or locked input - I would frequently remain running in one direction as if my control stick were stuck) and there are also rare instances of the game "tripping" over itself and skipping several frames (this did not strike me as a performance problem with my PC, but may very well be), but despite these infrequent annoyances, it is still very satisfying to travel around. I also hold grievance with the design of the mapping system, which does not update as you progress through areas, rather it updates once you are able to sit at a bench/save-point. It's not a major complaint, just feels odd when exploring a new area over several rooms and just being "in the void."
Overall, it's a fantastic "Metroidvania" with a very rich sense of exploration, engaging combat, and over all else, absolutely stunning visuals. Easily worth the price of admission, as well, with a lengthy and satisfying campaign.

What a great game! It has a very Dark Souls'ish feeling to it:
- If you die you drop your Geo (the name of the currency). To reclaim it venture back to the place where you died, but beware of the evil spirit that lingers around (similar to Salt and Sanctuary).
- NPCs are scattered throughout the world and can will talk to you, always exhaust their dialogue just as in DkS. Often they will then head back to town to offer their services to you.
- Speaking of dialogue, a lot of it is very cryptic and you will have to piece it all together by yourself.
- Benches are like Bonfires
- "Illusory" walls!
Pros and Cons after roughly 2 hours of gameplay:
Pros:
- It is a metroidvania style game, meaning you are free to explore the world as much as you want, but sometimes your road is blocked by a door ("Does not open from this side ;) ) or by an un-traversable hurdle. It is very likely that you also have to come from the other side or need a power-up.
- You can never travel too far though and "get lost" because there is a comfortable way to get around the world.
- Nice music.
- Controls feel very precise, (except for the aerial down slash, but that may just be me).
- Collectable secrets.
Cons:
- NPCs don't have a human voice and their soundbites seem rather limited. In my opinion this gets rather annoying if you talk to the same NPC more often to exhaust their dialogue.
I will update this review whenever I have something more to add.

I'm a little torn when I try to rate The Stanley Parable. It is not really a game I would say. I mean, in a way it is: you control a character move, press buttons, but that's pretty much it, in terms of 'playing' the game. It is more of an experience, a little bit pleasant, a little bit masochistic. One worth going through, for sure.
Stanley Parable leaves one confused. You will never know, if you have gotten to the ending yet. Actually, there really is no ending at all. Or maybe there is, I don't know.
I will tell you what it will do to you though. It WILL make you change your mind often. It WILL make you notice tiny, little details change, when entering the same room for the 50th time and it WILL leave you trying to figure out, if that change will eventually lead to another part of the game. It WILL leave you in a janitor's closet for at least 10 minutes and it WILL make you listen to the narrator mock you for sitting there for the whole time. It WILL try to kill you. It WILL make you kill yourself. It WILL kill you. It WON'T kill you. It WILL lead you to heaven. It WILL make you push buttons, or not...
The only real problem with Stanley Parable is that it's too short.  Because who wouldn't like to walk through empty corridors for a tiny bit longer, while being mocked of and insulted by someone who controls you?
Some people say they would like to have Morgan Freeman as a narrator of their life, I would prefer to leave this job to the narrator of The Stanley Parable.

Let's begin on this review (anyone get the joke?).

Of the first twelve hours after release for Hollow Knight, I spent eight of them playing it. Taking breaks so as not to burn myself out. The guys at Team Cherry did an outstanding job with this game and I'd easily recommend it to anyone who likes metroidvanias and/or games with rewarding combat. I can't speak for replay value or if it has a NG+ option because I haven't beaten the game (I don't think I've even gotten half way), but even if it has none, the game has so much content in it that I imagine I'll be satisfied even if I only finish it once.
Luckily, I haven't had any problems running the game or streaming it, I've only had a handful of stutters and fps drops that were quickly over. There are a few things I don't like about combat, but it's mostly because I'm more used to Dark Souls combat with blocking and i-frame dodging, neither of which are in HK (to my knowledge). The map is great and the fact that you have to buy the components to make it more complete is novel, but I definitely wished it was more detailed (to the point where I might just take screenshots and photoshop the extra details in myself); I sometimes find myself wondering if I've already found everything and the maze-like areas are a real pain to work through without a detailed map.
Ultimately, this is a fantastic game with an enormous amount of content. The combat is very enjoyable once you get into the rhythm for each enemy. The art style looks great and is consistant throughout the game and the boss designs (both artistic and mechanical) are easily memorable. One of the things about the game that I really enjoy discovering is the NPC's. Almost all of them have such unique personalities and the way some of them interact or talk about each other is amusing.
Long and short of it is that you should buy this game, it's great and the amount of content you get for the price is certainly worth it.

All of your typical Metroidvania troupes are here, but with a lot of it's own flavour too. I won't go into too much detail as these are things we come to expect from these games, but collecting power up's to be able to access new areas and such, secret rooms and shortcuts, challenging yet responsive platforming and a mix of classic mega man or metroid enemies that just follow tracked paths and castlevania style enemies with sophisticated attack patterns.
The game has been quite tame so far though with a gradual learning curve (this a good thing, the game doesn't start off hard as nails, but it gets there) I know the game gets a lot tougher later on though, with sections akin to more modern games like super meat boy and how crazy some of the end game maps can be and bosses from japanese bullet hell games spring to mind as well.

Dispite all of that however, the game has a few game breaking AI glitches (like enemies hiding behind cover forever in a place the player can't reach) that make it impossible to advance due to the "kill everything to advance" system that only works if it's well placed in games like castle crashers. Also as i mentoned earlier the abilities are hard to use at first due to minor control issues and the exploration can get pretty boring when you just want to kill everything in sight but there's nothing for you to kill. Another thing to note is the unbareable load times, it's worse than dead rising 2 in this respect.
Overall i'd reccomend this game to anyone who likes good stories, mindless killing, non-serious games and good humour but can tolerate a few downsides that prevent this game being perfect

Well, this one shocked me to say the least.
I was one of the few people it seems that actually thought AC3 was a good game, yes Connor had the personality of a cardboard box and the most epic parts of the game were scripted to death and the side missions felt rather pointless. But it made good choices like foliage as cover and a few missions where you could control a ship. The entire story of Desmond though was all over the place and the game just kinda... ended. And I never played it again.
Enter AC4, the newest AC game released only about a year after AC3, and I gotta say they made a TON of good choices this time around. The game starts out with full action, no tutorial just instant action, your ship is attacked and you end up on shore with an Assassin, you kill the Assassin, take his out fit and of course loot him. Quite the entrance for our main character Edward Kenway.
You then wake up in the modern world to find out YOU (not desmond or another character just you) are being welcomed to Abstergo Entertainment, a company focused on taking the Ancestors of Sample 17 (Desmond's DNA) and others to create interactive experiences with their stories. You are a worker there and your goal is to visit the memories of Edward Kenway, a Pirate during the golden age of piracy in the West Indies. That's all I'm going to reveal about the story for now, I'll dip into it again later but it will contain spoliers.
So to kick things off let's focus on the PC port. How is it? Well, I played it on a 3rd gen i5 and a GTX 660 with the newest drivers and I'm pleased to say the game ran very well. Good luck getting 60 fps constant, but since this is a 3rd person game 60 fps isn't a requirement in my book. For the brief time I ran FRAPs I was getting the upper 40s and 50s at sea, and lower 40s in the cities. The lowest it ever got was in the mid to low 30s and that happened during a intense rainstorm in the forest, so it is definitley playable. I was running the game on all High, FXAA, god rays at high, The fog setting (I can't remember the name) on, and the only thing off was Physx (which adds more smoke when you fire a gun and other than that is rather pointless besides killing framerate). I played the entire game on M&K and never felt at a disadvantage or felt I needed a controller to win or be better. Controls can be changed to your liking and the options menu is very good. I have to say, this is a really good port so props to Ubisoft.
So this game is the first "next gen" Assassins Creed game, and many regard it as one of the best launch titles for the PS4 and XB1. And let me tell you, on PC at least, THIS GAME IS BEAUTIFUL! The enviroment is easily the most beautiful in any game. The way the foliage moves when a rainstorm hits, how plants will move when you walk by them, such little touches that just make the game feel amazing. The sea is the best looking sea to date in any game. Huge massive waves come swooshing by, harpooning near the shores of Jamaica in the bright blue water is gorgeous, and the sea is very dynamic, while boarding ships it's not the same experience over and over again, the sea can send you above a Man O War while boarding or keep you below it. It's just beautiful, as somebody who plays BF4 quite a lot I must say, this is up there with that quality of visuals.
Now we can move on to the game play, and to keep it rather short I'll make a list.
Postitives:
Most fluid Assassins Creed game to date
All the awesome equipment from past games return and are just as fun
Missions where you must tail somebody seems much more fun and less stressful now that there is more foliage to hide in
Negatives:
Pretty much the exact same combat system as before, so it starts to get repetive over time
VERY EASY! After you upgrade to about the halfway point nobody can take you on, not even Man O Wars.
So, the gameplay on land is pretty much the exact same as your normal Assassins Creed. The good news? You won't be on land very often besides some of the main missions, and there are only 3 major cities.
Now lets talk about the new features in the game. So of course the biggest new feature in the game is the naval combat, and it's AMAZING. The most fluid naval combat I've ever played in a game, it's just fantastic and so much fun. WIll you take on a fort? Or maybe attack a convoy to get 10,000 Reales? Get into it with a few Man O Wars? Swoop in on a Spanish fleet taking on a few British Frigates, and take advantage of both sides to loot the ships? The possibilties are endless, and always fresh. I never grew tired of naval combat. Yes, boarding does get a little repetive, but the battle is always a heck of a time. I wish for every Pirate game to use this system and keep imroving on it from now on, it's great.
The world is huge! The biggest world in AC to date. That island there in the distance? Yep, you can visit it. That Mayan temple? You can visit it too! You can visit anywhere you like in the West Indies, the world spands from southern Florida to Jamaica and then some. And without giving too much away, you will be going to other areas of the world later on in the game. The only down side is some areas will be blocked off until you advance the story, and a few side missions such as diving to the remains of a boat and some upgrades are blocked off until you progress further. Side missions range from harpooning, to hunting templars, to attacking forts, to diving into ship remeains, hunting treasure, assassin contracts, and, well you get the point. There is a lot to do!
Another rather large edition to the game is that money now has more use. You can use money to upgrade the Jackdaw (your ship) to be a powerful demon, instead of buying a new couch for that elderly couple you took into your homestead in AC3. Also hunting is no longer a patience game, you literally just shoot a monkey now instead of waiting for a rabbit to take the bait and try to catch it like you would do in AC3. Crafting works just like Far Cry 3, you hunt a certain animal twice (sometimes more), skin it, and then use it to upgrade your health, or get a new ammo pouch, or a new holster, etc...
And finally the story, it's great in my opinion
*SPOLIER ALRET*
*SPOLIER ALRET*
*SPOLIER ALRET*
Edward was the most relateable character in the series to me. He is out for his own personal reward, and questions the Assassins and Templars equally. He even joins the Templars briefly, and the only reason he leaves them is becasue they payed him a small amount of money for protecting them from a Assassin assault. Yep, that's right, the main reason you attack the templars is because of money, no deeper reason just...money. Which is great in my opinion, of course the story does develop and there beocmes a deeper reason for why Edward kills the templars, many of his fellow pirates betray him, a few go crazy, and it's all just a crazy ride. Several famous pirates show up along the way. Mary Read (who pretends to be James Kidd, the son of William Kidd) and Anne Bond, the two most famous female pirates, and Mary Read beocmes a love interest for Edward. Blackbeard (Thatch), who was my favorite character in the game, is a ally of Edward and you are even there to see his last stand on the shore of North Carolina, which was the best and most dramatic part of the game in my opinion. Several others come along the way to, even famous traitors like Benjamin Hornigold. If you know your history of pirates, than a lot of what happens is to be expected, many deaths of characters happened in real life at the same time. The game manages to make you like such pirates like Blackbeard as friends, and even find them funny and warm hearted, even though history tells them as beast with no mercy. That alone is something I feel is worth mentioning, the game makes you like characters and see where they are coming from that you normally wouldn't.
Overall: Great Game

This game is absolutely the spiritual successor to Bloodline Champions, but with just the right balance of intelligent additions and sticking true to the original formula.   This is hands down the height of competitive arena pvp and even in early access feels impeccibly balanced.
My favorite change from the old formula is each champion having a choice of "talents".  You get to pick one out of three each tier, and the tiers are per round.  These choices are static and not random, sticking true to the "no RNG" policy, as well as something you will learn to track and pay attention to with time, i.e. "okay, (xyz support champion) just took his offensive talent, watch out for the damage on (xyz ability)"  There seems to be a healthy balance of defensive, offensive, control and mixed options to allow you to tailor your build based on how the rounds are going vs your opponents.  Also prevents matchups from becoming stale.  This is also much better than the old system where you'd pick raw stats as that really messed with balance.
Update more than one year later: IT'S STILL GOOD.  EVEN BETTER.  PLAY NOW.

I played this masterpiece of a game with no knowledge of either the original or hard reset, and when i actually started playing i fell in love with the game by the first level. The combat is as satisfying as it is responsive and the katana's hit detection is probably the best i've ever seen in a video game (however special abilities are difficult to use at first), there is no weapon that you feel you won't like simply due to the fact that all of them have niche roles. The plot is interesting as well making mindless killing actually seem like your doing something meaningful however i won't talk too much about it due to spoilers. The game also has a surprisingly good sense of (especially considering the fact that the main character's name is essentially a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥joke). Lastly the world is absolutely beautiful (albeit it's no columbia from bioshock infinite)
Dispite all of that however, the game has a few game breaking AI glitches (like enemies hiding behind cover forever in a place the player can't reach) that make it impossible to advance due to the "kill everything to advance" system that only works if it's well placed in games like castle crashers. Also as i mentoned earlier the abilities are hard to use at first due to minor control issues and the exploration can get pretty boring when you just want to kill everything in sight but there's nothing for you to kill. Another thing to note is the unbareable load times, it's worse than dead rising 2 in this respect.
Overall i'd reccomend this game to anyone who likes good stories, mindless killing, non-serious games and good humour but can tolerate a few downsides that prevent this game being perfect

Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag is one of the most innovative of the franchise. Nothing quite compares to the first time the game hands you control of your ship and allows you to traverse the world map in search of your next mission. While access to all the features available on the world map only comes after certain milestones in the main storyline are reached, it nonetheless provides a steadfast timesink for those interested in the plundering of other ships. The scale of the game is far beyond its predecessors, and this is, perhaps, both its biggest strength and its biggest flaw.
Black Flag makes the player feel as if they are in a living, breathing world, and then punishes them by restricting certain areas and activities until they chase the carrot at the end of the stick a certain distance. Equally as negative is Assassin's Creed ever-present fetch meta. Finding all the fragments, musical notes, chests, synchronization points, and secrets on a world map of this scale is daunting and, at first, overwhelming. Players who are completionists will find multiple hurdles assailing their path in achieving a true 100% in the game.
This isn't just because of all the items to find, however. Black Flag provides a mission-rating system that allows players to provide feedback concerning how much or how little they enjoyed the mission they are playing. Some of the game's missions are truly frustrating in the type of optional objectives they demand for 100% synchronization. The missions that take place in a naval setting can be the most demanding, and the player is thrust into situations where optional objectives are only feasible--the first time around--with an upgraded ship. The franchise doesn't deviate from their trademark follow or eavesdrop missions either, and this time the game will punish the player with failure if there are too many interruptions to overhearing conversations or otherwise.
Despite some of the glaring flaws, such as random stutters during the fluidity of the freerunning or any of the aforementioned issues, Black Flag stands above those that came before in gameplay. The story is very solid, and overlooking the annoyance of being yanked out of the animus to complete "real world" missions the player may or may not care about, the game delivers on multiple levels. It is an experience worth having.

How do you screw up a game about pirates? You try to smash it into a game about assassins, that's how. Then, you take your jumbled mess of a storyline, squeeze in all the horrible controls that made the previous titles in the series infuriating, and finish it off with botching the ship combat.
Maybe I'm just old school (which is a cowardly way of admitting that I'm just plain old), but I can't stand this current generation of "sticky" gameplay. Yes, I realize that all this parkour assisted "free running" stuff is there to make the game look more cinematic, but I can't stand it. You try to run down the street and you can't get three steps before the invisible collision of a barrel reaches out and grabs you, launching you into some absurd Jackie Chan acrobatic maneuver at a 90 degree angle. Before you can stop yourself, you've vaulted over a building, spun around a clothesline, and ended up perched on a chimney. What the hell?
But even if you could avoid the handicap of Assassin's Creed's controls and just focus on the ship combat (this is a pirate game, remember?), you'd be even more disappointed. It's probably due to console constraints, but there's hardly any room. You spot another ship on the ocean and close in for a battle. Yeah, awesome, right? Nope. The ocean is so clogged with other stuff, you can't even have a decent battle. Seriously. You do one circle around an enemy ship at medium cannon range and you'll probably run into half a dozen other ships and twice that many tiny little islands. It's more like bumper cars than a ship battle.
It goes without saying that the interface is horrible, as with all PC ports of console titles. Why do I have to install another game service to play a game I bought off of Steam? Terrible. It's just more corporate upper management nonsense; greedy halfwits trying to force something unnecessary on customers, sabotaging their product's quality in the hopes of milking a few extra bucks out of a tiny fraction of their players.
And, since we've already established that I'm apparently old fashioned, here's my (at least) one positive comment: The music is good. Love the modern take on old timey sea songs. I'm sure the person responsible for that aspect of the game is one of your underpaid, crunch-time addled wage slaves, while the jackass who invented that piece of crap "UPlay" has a posh corner office. Anyway, kudos to the audio team. Them and the art team. The game looks fantastic.

You're 10 years old. Your parents finally give in after your constant whining and begging whittles down their sanity, and take you to go see that awesome action movie you saw commercials about after you assure them it won't be too violent or adult for you. They're sitting through it rolling their eyes, because it's nothing new to them and they think it's dumb. But, it's new and fresh to you, so you're glued to the screen. The movie isn't based on their reality of working a boring desk job with petty problems for a living. It's based on being macho, solving all your problems with violence, and caters to the base, testosterone-laced, primal instinct welling up in you as a young boy ... a feeling that has long-since flamed out in your parents. Your parents saw an action movie. You saw a training documentary on how to become a bad-***.
The fountain of youth is anything you experience that makes you feel young again. This is what my inner 10-year-old remembers of the 80's, and being able to recapture that feeling is an amazing feeling. I laughed, I cried, and my chest swelled with machismo pride. The 80's were never this awesome, but living through it as a kid ... this is what a 10-year-old thought they saw while growing up.

I only have 40 minutes in the game, so I can only speak for those minutes played.
The game has fantastic atmosphere, with a moving soundtrack that fits the theme of emptiness. The characters are fantastically designed, and have unique personalities. There is voice acting, but I can't tell if it's gibberish or an actual language; however, the voice acted lines do not encompass the entirety of what is shown in the text dialogue box. Not much has developed so far for me in story, but it looks like it has the potential to be great.
The controls are absolutely fantastic. The response on the Hollow Knight (I'm assuming that this is the name of the player character) is tight and quick. You are a bit floaty, but it's made up for in the fact that the millesecond you let go of your jump button you stop ascending. So far, there are 3 basic attacks, side, up, and aerial down. Aerial down can be used to bounce off of things, classic platformer style. Some examples of this are the down aerial in shovel knight and rogue legacy.
Again, I've only played for 40 minutes, but what I've seen so far impresses me so much. I've been waiting for an atmospheric platformer/metroidvania game like this for a while.
With an incredibly modest price tag, there is no reason that you shouldn't pick this up if you enjoy metroidvania style games, or platformers for that matter.

+ The gameplay is a lot of fun. To put things simply, you are a warrior in an insect world. You journey underground to fight creatures, find treasure, and to discover the mysteries about the world you live in.  The combat and platforming is fast, fluid, and feels great.
+ Visually the game looks fantastic with amazing hand-drawn graphics. Great use of lighting and color with very diverse environements.
+ Great controls (at least with a XB1 Controller), very responsive and precise jumping which is needed through many of the challenging platforming sections.
+ The world itself is huge. The game takes place almost entirely underground, but the caverns you travel through are expansive and have so many paths to take. It's like jumping down a rabbit hole, and traveling so deep that you end up wondering how you are going to get back to the surface...or if you even want to return.
+ Many skills / abilities that you unlock as you progress including platforming favorites like dashing and wall jumping.
+ The bosses are challenging and very exciting to face.
+ Very emersive sounds with a fantastic soundtrack

A highly amusing experience; the narratives appear to change with every playthrough I have, even if I repeat the same route over and over again at least one piece of dialgue will change.
There are numerous outcomes to each choice you make, even if they don't appear to be present before you when the time comes; just remember to touch everything, stand still for no reason in certain places, disobey the narrator, walk through closed doors and windows to break the game, or maybe you can just do as you're told...do as Stanley would do; question nothing, go insane and then die a slow and horrible death only for the cycle to repeat.
It got 3 hours out of me before I called it quits because my arm got tired, but then I popped on it again the next day and gave it a quick whirl for 10 minutes. It's a good little time killer and a barrel of laughs if sarcasm, dry or dark humour is your thing.
10/10 worth the money, just for the amount of laughs it gave me and the unusual experiences I had playing it...and I didn't need to take narcotics or drink booze to experience them, so no headaches or waking up in the middle of a field again. Hurray!

AC4 was my introduction to the Assassin's Creed series, and I'm hooked. The single-player mode is fun, but the multiplayer mode is even better. You play through a story in single-player mode, which seems pretty standard to me, and you can really benefit from being sneaky and assassin-like instead of just running in and killing everyone, which is neat. In multiplayer, you get to choose characters, level up by playing various modes (both co-op and adversarial), and customize abilities and appearances. Wolfpack mode lets you play through a number of sequences with different objectives, all of which involve assassinations, of course, either solo or with friends or strangers online. The other modes are PvP, some in teams and some free-for-all. You can choose the game mode that is most appealing to you, and get a bunch of friends to play with you or just wait for a lobby online. The levels system is a bit misleading, since being a high level or prestige doesn't necessarily mean you're good, it just means you play too much (very true in my case...I find it a great deal of fun even though I am not good), but when you're in the middle of a game that's hardly the first thing on your mind anyway.
Overall, it's a pretty diverse game, with game modes to appeal to many different types of gamers. The graphics are gorgeous even with everything on super low, though some of the more graphic kills may be disturbing to more squeamish folk (you can always tell when a kill animation will happen though, so you can look away if need be, and blood can be turned off). It's a good option for people who tend not to have fast reactions but still like action games, because there is some subtlety involved in the gameplay. I definitely recomend this to anyone remotely interested, particularly if you can find it discounted somewhere, as it is a bit pricey (but worth it!).

The Stanley Parable is a deconstruction of video games, storytelling, and the question of free will.  The only gameplay is walking around some rooms listening to an almost wizardly voice guide you.  But you'll be just delighted to walk around those rooms.  You will learn to hate yellow lines and enjoy letting babies die in fires.
Most games that attempt to be such a
are doomed to wallow in their own artiness.  While The Stanely Parable certainly qualifies as interactive art, it pulls it off with panache thanks to its shining sense of humor and the countless new rewards (more story) for exploration.
Now, if you'll excuse me, I need to get back to not playing this game for five years, maybe finish that novel I've been working on, meet a nice girl, and then get the "Go Outside" achievement.

I cannot recommend this game honestly, I want to like it but I couldn't. The main flaws in this game start small then become larger as you progress further in the game, and it's honestly just personal nitpicks of mine that really discouraged me from playing any further without being more annoyed. Sure the game may look pretty, and may have its moments but it wears thin later on. When I first started playing the game, I noticed some sort of weird jittering movement the protagonist was doing and I tried to find the answer and to no avail there was none. Supposedly, the game doesn't agree with certain video cards despite yours being high end. That, or the game was oddly coded that the ground feels like rugged terrain and Wang is tripping over himself on the floor repeatedly.
Second was the enemies in this game, I didn't mind it at first. In fact I was playing with the sword through the quarter of the game with all the hype in the world dismembering demons, but things started to come into view when I was doing that. The sword isn't that great later on, and the whole 'combinatinos of sword swipes' doesn't really matter at all. If the enemy is blocking, you won't hit them. You can't break their block unless you use a Ki technique, and if you do that enemies will become enraged, zerg rush you, and won't give you much time to react. That's not the worst of it unfortunately, as later on when you keep playing you realize the sword becomes a hinderance late game. An ability that can hit enemies far away isn't reliable at all, so you have to use a gun if you want to progress further. You may ask "Why should that matter?" Well, the guns aren't good either. You're stuck with the pistol for a good while, the shotgun is terrible, and the uzi is just pure garbage.
Nothing shines unless you upgrade them, and all the upgrades are pretty much useless. Yeah you can dual wield Uzis, but that will waste ammo that you need. The only real good weapon is the rocket launcher, and not because it clears faster because it's the only damn weapon that does significant damage to anything. You'll be stuck on a boss for a long time unless you use the rocket launcher. That is if you hit their weak spot to reveal their real weak spot to even do any damage to them at all. Which leads to my third issue with the game. The enemies.
This game loves to test your patience, so be ready to go through every single room and be forced to clear it out everything in there to progress. Because it'll be a lot of them, at first it won't be much but trust me when I tell you that the amounts get larger and more annoying. When you run out of ammo and have to stab at flying enemies with your sword it becomes apparent that this game really wants you to do either three things; use your sword, burn your ammo, use the crappy gun. As I said, the enemies become more annoying in this game as you progress because it will throw these lets call them super demons at you all the time. First not so much, but late in the game there WILL be a lot of them. You might think it's not a problem, but it really is since three of them are made to be the most inconvient time consuming monsters in the damn game.
They have boss like health almost, take forever to take down unless you want to spam rockets or try spamming your Ki attacks. One will always pull you in unless you chop his arm off, and his ranged attack can ignore corners. Another enemie will spam skeletons, which will continue to spawn forever unless you kill him and add more to the twenty demons in the room that you have to kill. Oh and they become invulnrable unless you kill the skeletons sometimes too. Then there is the icing on the cake of annoying super demons, the ones that you have to hit in the back to hurt in a certain spot. The hitboxes for that one spot is so stupid that you have to get it just right. Otherwise, rockets or any explosives will ignore the damage so it's just better to try hitting them in the back with melee or bullets. However, doing so is a huge tedious process since you have to correctly get them to stun themselves or you won't be able to.
Oh, and the puzzles in this game are annoying. Expect door puzzles to increase too, you have to get Shrine A, B, C (Sometimes all three) to open one single door only to be brought to another. Wouldn't be a problem if I didn't have to clear every single damn room to progress to the next one and kill more super demons just to open one damn door only to be introduced to another god damn locked door. Jokes are very mediocre, I don't mind the protagonist's personality or his sidekicks but the whole comedy of the game is very weak and not that hilarious. Nostalgic value? Eh, it's alright but I really can't recommend this unless you can get it for much cheaper.
/endranting

Battlerite is a charming arena fighter with serious substance. The game asks very little to enjoy playing, but will deeply challenge you to master even just one character. The high amount of depth and counterplay is apparent on the surface, and while it may take you time to learn how every character's abilities function, you never feel cheated. There's always a counter or some mindgame around each ability.
The skill to time your abilities, manage your resources, and predict your opponents take precedence over raw stat memorization or mechanics, making Battlerite an accessible game that will remain challenging no matter how much you play. Games are also relatively short, taking only about 5-7 minutes on average for a best of 5 set. Battlerite has a lot in common with the fighting game genre, with unique character designs, EX and Ultimate abilities, short rounds of gameplay, and tons of room for outplay and prediction. This makes it an easy game to get stuck on a "just one more round" loop for hours.
The game's current roster seems small, but the amount of depth designed into each character makes up for the low quantity. The game is also currently short on game modes, only having 2v2 and 3v3 queues in a ranking system. While neither game mode will get boring if you enjoy the gameplay, the lack of an unranked queue for friends of varying skill level to play without obscuring either's rank may turn the uncompetitive players away. Although I imagine this is something that would be address in the future.
All in all, if you're looking for a strategic team based arena brawler to truly test your ability to outplay your opponents, or a curious fighting game fan looking for something new to scratch the fighting itch, Battlerite will fulfill your every need.

Assassin's Creed IV is the game that Assassin's Creed III should have been. You know... like, actually good and stuff. In that way, it's somewhat similar to the drastic change in quality from AC1 to AC2. Assassin's Creed III had some good ideas, including changes to the controls and overall formula, but ultimately just wasn't as good as the previous games (not to mention it was also buggy as all hell). AC4 takes the improvements that AC3 tried to make and actually implements them - with nary a bug in sight. I suppose it also helps that the setting and main character are far more interesting as well. I mean, seriously... who doesn't dig pirates and adventure on the high seas? You play as privateer Edward Kenway - neither Assassin nor Templar - thrust into the middle of both of those worlds. Edward is one of the better protagonists in the series, and is generally quite likeable.
The one huge difference that sets Black Flag apart from previous games in the series is its setting - well over half the game takes place on the ocean. And what an ocean it is... seriously, it is huge. And sailing on it is just so very cool. The closest comparison I can make is to exploring the ocean in the Wind Waker on Gamecube back in the day, only much bigger and more realistic. The exploration element alone is great. However, what really sets AC4 apart is the way it looks and feels. In terms of video game technology, it's just amazing what they were able to pull off. You can almost actually feel like you're out on the ocean, as waves and wind make your ship swerve, sway and dip (and just wait until you see all the gorgeous weather effects). I can't imagine any game ever nailing seafaring better than this... (well, at least not until virtual reality sailing comes along). It just feels great. Naval combat also plays a big part in the game. Unfortunately, as fun as it can be, it does have a few problems. You control your weapons by changing the perspective of the camera (look to the ship's side to fire cannons, or to the rear to drop fire barrels, for example). This is all well and good, in theory, but in the heat of battle with multiple enemies, it can get a bit dodgy. By the end of the game, you should have a good handle on it, but it isn't always the easiest thing to manage. By far, the coolest part of combat is boarding other ships. There are no loading screens on the ocean. Ever. This means that any ship you see (and all of the crew members on it) can be engaged in real time, at any time. If you want to jump off your ship and swim to a frigate and kill every dude on board all by yourself, you can do that. If you want to incapacitate a ship with your cannons, get alongside, board it by swinging on a rope and air-assassinating the captain from one of the masts, you can do that. It is very, very fun. But as with anything, repetition will eventually cool those initial highs and you may start to tire of the whole process by the time the latter parts of the game roll along. This is more an inevitability than a knock on the game itself, but should be mentioned. Rounding out the new additions to the series, Black Flag introduces a set of underwater diving locations. These are mostly optional and don't really make or break the game one way or the other. They are just "meh", mostly due to the horrible controls inherent with underwater segments in every game with underwater segments ever made. Ever. There are some cool bits underwater, but these segments could have easily been excluded and it still would have been a decent game.
The other half of the game takes place in land-based locations, and follows the standard AC series formula. You take on various missions to gather information or assassinate people, which require either stealth, combat, or both. Free-running and climbing also return and are generally OK, though the usual issues (like climbing onto things you aren't trying to climb onto in the heat of the moment) are still ocasionally present. Combat is similar to previous games as well. Mostly all you need to do is button mash and use counters or break enemy defenses at the appropriate moments. As simple as it is, it is still ever so satisfying, due to the insane number of moves you can pull off in various situations - put simply, you are a serious badass. There is also a very limited number of different weapons available (contrary to previous games), which is a welcome change. There's no longer 3 inventory screens' worth of pointless weapons you'll never use. Early on, you'll be able to buy a good set of swords and pistols. Those, along with your hidden blades, are pretty much all you'll ever want or need for the majority of the game. The land-based segments take place in 3 major locations - Havana, Nassau and Kingston. Additionally, there are a number of smaller islands scattered around the ocean that contain fishing villages, ruins, and more. Overall, it's a nice balance between traditional AC and the newer naval bits.
The last part of the package is a sub-plot that continues the goings-on in the modern-day time period. With Desmond out of the picture (mostly), you play as an unnamed employee in the game division of the Abstergo Corporation. I don't mind these sections too much, but for those of you who don't care about these present-day bits, just know that most of these sections are optional, and the parts that are required can be done pretty quickly. The optional activities available involve "hacking" a bunch of computers, which unlocks various bits of lore and info on what has happened since the events of the previous game. If you are into following that part of the series, some of it is pretty interesting. Otherwise, these optional bits can simply be ignored.
Overall, I found this to be a worthy entry in a series I thought was on its last (peg?) legs. The amount of things to do is pretty insane, and I found almost everything to be pretty dang fun. That said, I am also somewhat easy to please, and kind of anal when it comes to games that have any kind of collecting aspect... so take that opinion for what it's worth. A lot of how much you enjoy this game will depend on how much you dig the new seafaring aspect, since it is such a large portion of the experience. I can see how it might be hit or miss for some people. If you liked the naval missions in AC3, then you will most definitely enjoy the improvements Black Flag makes in that area. If you hated those missions, I hesitate to recommend AC4 wholeheartedly (though you very well may still enjoy it). If you've never played an AC game before, or haven't played one in a long time, this is a great one to jump into the series with. It's definitely not perfect, but it's pretty solid overall. I'd rank it up there with the better games in the AC2 era. I'd give it a B+ or A-.

Just starting this thing off by saying this GAME IS GREAT and you should definitely look into it and START PLAYING IT. It comes with it’s flaws, but the game is early access and that is to be expected. The game is extremely polished gameplay-wise and it is sometimes and it is easy to forget this.
Pros
-GAMEPLAY IN GENERAL IS FANTASTIC with tweaks being worked on to improve it
-Short intense games
-Fair in the sense of new players will have access to everything that everyone else has.
-What you pay for this game is great for what you get. I have spent $20 and at this point I have played 2,343 matches and I am not bored by the game at all yet. That equals out to me playing the game for less than a penny per match. $0.0085 per match so for to be a little more precise.
-Replay system to review your games and see what you have done wrong so that you can improve your play as well as share your game’s highlights with your friends and the community.
-GAME BALANCE IS HIGHLY EXCEPTIONAL FOR BEING IN EARLY ACCESS and at high level play during the recent tournament that was held with all of the top players there were only two character that were not used at all. The top 5 lowest picked characters Jumong (whose team won the North American side of the tournament), Ruh Kaan, Pearl, Pestilus (was not played at all), and Raigon (who was not played at all, but to be fair he was released just before this tournament). Link to the dev blog covering these numbers:
***To the reviews saying that the game balance is bad, I’d have to disagree completely seeing that all champions except for two were used among the top players in tournament with money on the line.***
Not As Bad As Negative Reviews Suggest
-Stunlock’s communication with the community is not as bad as the some of the reviews suggest. They are starting to get their stuff together with this and they have been running a weekly dev blog for the past 6 weeks updating.
-The amount of updates that the game gets. Since its release in early access there have been 16 patches to the games since September. On average the games gets 2.6 patches per month and 5 new champions released since early access launch, which is not that bad.
Cons
-Match Making is rough at this point. Needs a few things tweaked with it, but the main issue with it is it doesn’t have the millions of players that games like LoL has to sort through in order make the games even on both sides every time. The game is also not even fully released yet so just keep that in mind. That being said it is number 166 on steam charts at the moment with its peak amount of players in the last month at 3,093 and an average amount of players at 1,327 at the moment which isn’t that bad for a game that has not even been fully released yet.
-Being allowed to play a champion in ranked that you have never played before. Making it so you can’t play a champion in ranked until you’ve reached level 10 with the character would make so much more sense.
-No in game tournament system like their previous game Bloodline Champions had.
-Only has like 4 maps?
-Tutorial does not go over everything that you need to learn about the game. It leaves out way too many key things with the game and an advanced tutorial should be added at the very least to teach players things like using ex abilities and canceling ability casting.
TLDR: Get the game if you like competitive games or you like being able to play on a team with your friend in a game. While the game has its problems, it is still completely worth picking up.

The Stanley Parable demo was intriguing enough to get me play the whole game.
Even if the total play time is quite short (about 2 / 3 hours to reach the supposed end) the game succeeds in proposing an original and unsettling experience.
Starting like a seamingly adventure game, you quickly realize that there are no objects to collect or puzzles to solve - except the whole meaning of game itself. And it's here where it really shines.
One critical aspect of all adventure games is plot and dialogue. Here the plot is as mysterious as you could imagine, and the narrator perplexity in what you do funny as well. After a while, you just enjoy the simple act of doing the opposite of what you are supposed to do, exercing free will, enjoying a strange feeling of agency even if it leads to the brutal death of the brave Stanley.
The game even reach the point of developing beyond the Stranger than Fiction plot (if you happen to know the movie) for a moment of sheer delight.
Really, The Stanley Parable does something powerful in the game world : instead of being a little of everything that works in different genres (like Incredibles Adventures of Van Helsing), it does not try to be strong where it's weak and focuses all its strengh on what it's great at!
And the developers should be praised for that :)

I think its fair to say I recommend this game as not only has it entered my top 5 games ever, it has a good claim on being the best game I've ever played!  It’s a phenomenally rich and detailed pirate sandbox which takes the typical Assassin's Creed formula (of which I am a fan) but adds a twist.
Edward is a different kind of protagonist for this series.  He's instantly likable as a rogue looking to further his own ends.  But there is depth to the man.  He has a conscience and watching him grow as a character makes for a compelling story.
Technically I’m amazed by what the developers have managed to do.  The seamless transition between captaining a ship to the traditional Assassin's Creed free-running is incredible.  The simulation of the sea is a marvel as the rolling waves, the wind and storms look and feel amazing.  Make no mistake, if you have the rig to run it this game looks absolutely beautiful.
There is so much to see and do in this game its almost impossible to get bored, there is such a vast area to explore.  As of right now I think I've clocked 30 hours and I’m just under a third the way through the game.

The exploration in Stanley Parable needs no introduction or enticement. Narration is excellent, both humorous and thought-provoking. Stanley Parable creates boundaries for the sole purpose of breaking them.
Those staunchly against walking simulators should check further into the games content before purchase. The game had a few unexpected, personally-upsetting moments. A few of the achievements are very gimmicky and hard to obtain.
It's probably the best of its kind, but that can hold little value to a person disinterested in this sort of philosophical walking sim style game. This game's worth is definitely dependent on what you like, but it doesn't hurt to know that it sees an occasional sale every other month.
You know when you're willingly spending a couple hours exploring an empty office, the creators have managed to do something pretty awesome.

This isn't a triple A title, but it's no stinker. If you're bored and find this for 5-10 bucks and don't need the money, I'd recommend it. Oh, and there's a new game + sort of thing called EX Mode, and if you raise the difficulty above normal, I can tell this could be quite a challenge.

Unchanged Assassin's Creed-style storyline mission mechanics of stealthily trailing and assassinating various Templars are boosted by a multitude of fun open world activities. Whenever something gets boring, try something else for a while. Sail around and plunder vessels for upgrade materials for your ship, clear a small island of collectibles, harpoon a giant shark in a row boat, hunt an ocelot, or use a diving bell to explore undewater ship wrecks. Actually, don't do the underwater bits - they're probably the worst part of the game. The characters are great fun, including Edward Kenway as the pirate you play as, and the cast features famous pirates like Edward "Blackbeard" Thatch, Anne Bonny, Mary Read, Benjamin Hornigold, John "Calico Jack" Rackham, Charles Vane, and Bartholomew "Black Bart" Roberts. A very welcome return to form and a solid entry in the Assassin's Creed series, although I expect Black Flag to become a franchise of its own in the near future.

Battlerite had what it took to be my game of 2016. It has fun core gameplay, and it comes closer than any other game to filling the void Magicka Wizard Wars left behind. But for it to be my game of 2017, for it to matter to me much past the F2P launch, a couple of things have to happen.
1. We need more players. Believe you me, I can eat my words, and if the developers find a way to focus on 3v3, this becomes less of a concern. But my favorite gamemode is ranked 3v3, and at pre-F2P time of this review it's a gamble whether I'm even be able to play it at peak hours. This CAN be resolved with the F2P launch. 2v2 serves as a capable introduction to the game and I wouldn't discourage playing it, but the long-term health of the game is improved with every person who decides to take 3v3 seriously. What may feel like chaos at first can prove itself to be wildly deeper than 2v2, tactically.
2. We need nicer players. I don't think developing a thick skin is the best way to deal with♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in terms of bettering a community, and it can seriously corrupt your character. If you join the community, just encourage your teammates or maintain a habit of niceties. Every glhf and timely gg/ggwp adds up. Like many online PvP games, lame♥♥♥♥♥bullies are a loud minority but they can have a severe effect in the small lobbies of 2v2 & 3v3.
If this community can round itself out, what we here now, and presumably in a few days or a few weeks, is a solid competitive game that can be healthy for a few years. But, in a slow and sinister way, the game will become a confused, sad mess and die if 2v2 is the ONLY gamemode people play for the indeterminate future.
Keep an eye out for the Discord and I hope you enjoy/enjoyed the F2P launch.

This darn game is a full time experience. You cannot watch a TV show or have a Hearthstone game ongoing at the same time. It will take your full attention and it’s worth it! Here are the reasons why.
As you start to play, you are told by the narrator that you're Stanley, employee number 427, whose job is to press buttons displayed on his monitor. But that day, when you get up from your work station you quickly notice that none of your co-workers are in the office today. You then start to walk in the deserted offices trying to find out what is going on, and the narrator's voice enters to give you directions. There’s a narration system but The Stanley Parable let you choose your own path, each one of your decision will open new choices, your call to obey or disobey to the narrator.
As a gamer, something I enjoy the most in gaming is to choose my way to play. The main thing that differentiates our media from movies is the concept of choice. And this is exactly what The Stanley Parable is about. Choose your path, your experience will not be like any other. One of the greatest moment I lived with the game was after making incoherent choices, a
launched and explained me what a meaningful choice is. What the heck, that game let me choose and then tells me I could do better?!!
The setting chosen, a random office adds a lot of absurdity to the mix. In The Stanley Parable, playing is working. The main character (you) is never happier when being told what to do by others, and you need to press buttons to declare “I love you” to your wife. The thematic visited here are interesting and relate to the AAA video games like
where you need to press a command to perform an action during an impactful moment.
To conclude, The Stanley Parable is about the journey not the destination. If you feel like experiencing something different, give the demo a try. You might like it or hate it, in any case you’d experience a unique game!

Do you take down the giant necromancer who is constantly spawning skeletons and resurrecting the enemies you slay? Do you focus on taking down the horde first so they aren't chewing on your♥♥♥♥♥♥while you fight the big threats? Whatever your choice, you have a spectacular array of weapons, each with secondary fire that alters the functionality of the weapon (such as the crossbow launching bolts with sticky bombs on them).
It is an old-school style shooter in the style of Serious Sam, Duke Nukem, or (obviously) the original Shadow Warrior. Hordes of enemies to chew through and loads of weapons to use. So if you like good, old-fashioned gorey shooter goodness, this is the game for you!

ARMA is a Simulator that focuses on infantry combat, although the focus is on Infantry fights, there is a big armory full of tanks,jets,helicopters and whatever you like to use to advance on the battlefield.
Although many people buy this game to play the succesful mod DayZ, a zombie survival with high focus on PvP, there is alot more to see and expirience in Arma, although this game is already set to be realistic, a Modteam decided to ramp up the realism even more by adding the ACEMOD, a modification that enhances the simulation even further, Weight now plays a role in the game, bullets kill even quicker and teamwork is mostly the only key to succed.
2012, almost 3 years after the war in Chernarus has ended,US forces have been sent to Takistan, a middle eastern country.
The player is part of the "Razor team", the story drags through a series of loosely connected attack, assasination or defend missions with the wide choise of units Arma can offer, this way, the game gives you an overview of what you can do with certain things (UAV's,Helicopters,Jets,Tanks etc.) The story also features multiple endings, which are all based on choises in earlier missions.
The editor is propably the most powerful tool in the ARMA series, with this neat thing,you cannot only create missions, but entire scenarios or campaigns. Allowing scripts, events, waypoint systems, everything you'll ever need, is in this neat feature.
Here, you can put your skills to the test, and use the wide range of armament you unlock through ingame missions, avialable with the stuff you already have.
What would be a Mil-Sim without multiplayer? Through the years the ARMA community has made some gamemodes and missions available to those with and without certain mods, even without such things as DayZ or ACEMod, you can enjoy the milsim in community made missions or popular mods like Warfare and Wasteland.
And if youre pretty new, and dont know what to do, feel free to ask, there are always people helping you getting started.
but although this game is good, and I really enjoy it, there are some flaws, I know most of them are patchable through mods, but were speaking of vanilla here
The main thing is the AI, I cant get my head around it how something that smart as the AI can be that stupid, I mean, theyre able to prettymuch acomplish anything, they spot enemy troops even further than the max Viewdistance of 10 kilometers, they shoot at such precision, you'd call them hackers..but at the same time, they seem to be incapable to drive ANYTHING and I mean ANYTHING, they arent even able to drive down a straight road without crashing into a tree thats waaaay off the roead..
they also seem to be too stupid for CQ fights, once a unit got inside a building, they go blind and deaf, you can even stand right next to them and they dont know where to shoot..maybe its because infantry movement inside buildings is already clunky enough, it feels really akward since your gun is also a physics object and it keeps colliding with every damn part of the building..
and then..there is the performance issues, not only does this game already need higher specs to run smooth, I think even NASA supercomputers wouldnt be able to handle the performance issues inside town areas..framedrops are something completely normal in this game..

This darn game is a full time experience. You cannot watch a TV show or have a Hearthstone game ongoing at the same time. It will take your full attention and it’s worth it! Here are the reasons why.
As you start to play, you are told by the narrator that you're Stanley, employee number 427, whose job is to press buttons displayed on his monitor. But that day, when you get up from your work station you quickly notice that none of your co-workers are in the office today. You then start to walk in the deserted offices trying to find out what is going on, and the narrator's voice enters to give you directions. There’s a narration system but The Stanley Parable let you choose your own path, each one of your decision will open new choices, your call to obey or disobey to the narrator.
As a gamer, something I enjoy the most in gaming is to choose my way to play. The main thing that differentiates our media from movies is the concept of choice. And this is exactly what The Stanley Parable is about. Choose your path, your experience will not be like any other. One of the greatest moment I lived with the game was after making incoherent choices, a
launched and explained me what a meaningful choice is. What the heck, that game let me choose and then tells me I could do better?!!
The setting chosen, a random office adds a lot of absurdity to the mix. In The Stanley Parable, playing is working. The main character (you) is never happier when being told what to do by others, and you need to press buttons to declare “I love you” to your wife. The thematic visited here are interesting and relate to the AAA video games like
where you need to press a command to perform an action during an impactful moment.
To conclude, The Stanley Parable is about the journey not the destination. If you feel like experiencing something different, give the demo a try. You might like it or hate it, in any case you’d experience a unique game!

With the end of the world plot and Demond Miles' story being wrapped up in AC3, Assassin's Creed IV had the freedom to explore and chart new waters and it really does show in this grand adventure. Ubisoft have shown that the Assassin's series is far from running out of ideas as this installment, for me, is easily the most enjoyable and rewarding of them all.
Edward Kenway, a man who is still uncertain of just what kind of man he is, takes up life on the sea in hope to one day be able to live a comfortable and easy life. His ambitions extend to as far as a coin can shimmer and no further. This story isn't one about conspiracy theories or attempts to save the world. It's a personal story of identity, purpose and self realisation that many, including myself, can very much relate to. What truly matters to a man and a woman.
The characrers are easily what make this game so memorable. Each rough pirate and posh kingsman brings with them an equally vast and rich personality that you'll either love to love or love to hate. The voice acting is absolutely incredible and some scenes hold some truly gripping speeches.
Managing to play this on ultra, the game is gorgeous. When you first take control of Edward and you sea the deep blue of the ocean, the lush green vegetation and the warm glow of the sands, it's hard to not take a minute and just observe everything around you. Even free running and chase segments in the jungle, I found myself just admiring the level desging so much.
The music is yet another immersive feature to this game that a great deal of attention has been obviously applied to. The tavern music brings life to the towns you visit and the shanties sang as you explore the west indies makes you feel you're on an adventure for riches.
I think the biggest attraction gameplay wise for most people has to be the naval combat. I personally love pirate games already and found the combat to be fast, intense and very enjoyable. The moment you incap a ship and call your crew to ready to board never gets old! There is enough freedom for you to play as you want. either defensively with fire barrels, up close with heavy shot, or snipe them with mortar fire. As with other Creed games, Black Flag has a A LOT of other activities to take part in, optional lands and towns to explore and mysteries to uncover! If you have an eye for adventure you'll feel right at home on the Jackdaw!
My only problem is that the game is still restricted to the idea you're reliving memories and as such, the 'animus' prevents you from going to certain places at certain times becase "It wasn't available in this sequence" or it'd take you out of the experience of the 1700's to run around in a modern day office doing chores for people you don't know and don't bother questioning why. While Ubisoft DID do a good job in limiting both those things to a minimum, it was still something that didn't need to be there and restricted the experience, for me at least.
Black Flag is a very rich game in character, content and reasons to play. If you want to get lost in the oceans and adventure or be a part of a grand story with grander characters then be sure to pick this gem up!

ARMA II is a spectacular mil-sim that's all about tactics and strategy, running and gunning won't get you far here. This game features a wide variety of firearms, big and small, as well as vehicles and aircaft that can really change the tide of battle. ARMA focuses on representing it's wide assortment of toys accurately, you will find a level of detail here that is uncommon in most other shooters. That being said, it does not achieve full simulation of most things. You could probably find more accurate car characteristics in a racing game, and better aircraft simulation in a dedicated flight-sim game. It doesn't matter though, the combines arms feeling this game creates will make you feel like you're in a real battlefield.
If there was one thing I had to complain about, it would have to be the 'feel' of moving and aiming. To me, everything feels very clunky and tougher than it should be.
If you like a tactical experience of a battlefield, get this game. It really shines, in a small squad with your friends breaching a house, or in a huge battle in a city, this game is great for all aspects of war.
My recommendation: Join/host a game of domination or insurgency with a group of friends, both are very fun experiences that my buddies and I couldn't stop playing for hours.

A slightly revamped version of Bloodline Champions, which was a heavily WoW arena inspired top down arena shooter game with skills.
- Arenas are slightly bigger and you have mounts.
- Resurrection and base channeled healing abilities gone from the game.(thank god)
- Instead of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t itemization that got added in BLC you have Battlerites which you choose every new round.(they are not items you have to collect, they are all unlocked)
- The orb in the middle that give you a chunk of energy is now an actual object that can be damaged,pulled and pushed back and gives your team health and energy if your team can get the last hit on it.
- There are now small health and energy orbs on the sides that spawn on a timer that give you minor health or energy depending on the color.
- The speed of the game is currently slightly slower compared to BLC but still very fast paced, a lot of ranged characters can cast while moving with movement speed reduce during casts.
Overall still as solid with a few minor problems that are surely going to be ironed out during early access,plus the community is great so far so if you are one of the people that quit BLC because of the toxicity, give this one a try.

ArmA II: OA is a great game which when put together with ArmA II to make ArmA II: Combined Operations can cover all the weaknesses OA had when compared to ArmA II.
Though the game takes a bit of dedication to get comfortable with, once you get used to the control system it has a massive amount to offer. It has a massive choice of weapons, vehicles and troops, along with having Combined Operations you have access to two massive maps (Takistan 164 km2 and Chernarus is 225 km2), one desert and one in a forested country.
Apart from the games vanilla mechanics is the massive modding community surrounding ArmA II. These can change the game in massive ways as well as add to them. Everything from DayZ, a zombie survival, to ACE, Adding new sounds, items, vehicles and mechanics to increase the realism and plausibility of game mechanics, such as first aid.
After experiencing the vanilla game and maybe a modded version which is all multiplayer friendly with servers scailing over 100 slots which run smooth, you can go into the games editor which allows you to create fully scripted missions with or without mods, with a user friendly interface that lets you make simple missions, test them and make them instantly multiplayer.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes simulators or squad based shooters, though it would depend on how comfortable with mouse and keyboard they are as a gamepad just wont work with this. make sure to pick it up in a sale as you can buy ArmA II and ArmA II: OA which gives you content from both in one, for a stupidly cheap price for a game which you can easily spend hundreds of hours on.

There's a good chance that if you're interested in the game or have heard of it you at least suspect the game's main conceit and allure. Game may or may not be the right word to describe the Stanley Parable; it's more of a choose your own adventure that shines a light on whether a player really has agency and choice. This isn't a game dependent on skill or developing mastery.
Depending on the path you take, you may be taking a more nightmarish journey, a more slapstick one, or a self-reflective commentary on the nature of modern itself. There's some very clever commentary and widely divergent story threads and ultimately it's those themes and clever gimmicks that make this game worth playing. Once you have found most of the endings and playthroughs, the novelty wears off. That being said, it's more novelty than most games give you in dozens of gameplay hours, and might stick in your craw far longer.
For added fun, make a prediction then see how your friends play the game without any instruction or explanation.

What can I say
This is a game for mature gamers.
The graphics:
The game is beautiful.  Its good to see that they finally optimized the engine. I know some may complain about the "bland" look of the engine, but hey, that what the world looks like, I think this engine truly displays "reality" so to speak better than all the other engines (the Crytek engine is a bit cartoonish for my taste). This is a simulation after all, let's not let COD boys downplay this game and compare it to 2009's biggest run and shoot scam in video game history.
Whats great about the graphics, especially the visibility option, is that even if you set your visibility to low, 1-2 Kilometers, you'd still be able to see the beautiful landscape in the far background, unlike in Arma 2, where the far-stretched landscape disappeared as soon as you lowered your visibility. Here, you'll be able to enjoy the far horizons, hills and mountains - really makes you feel like you're in mid-Asia mountain valley.
They've also added the hot-air effect now, a sort of desert mirage sort of wavy screen.
This game is for PATIENT And MATURE players only, and I rejoice at the fact that it's a PC exclusive.
So anyway. The story is decent enough. Typical American liberation of some CIA installed dictatorship in Mid-Asia I guess. What's weird is that if you play on "Regular" some enemies (i.e. Fundamentalist Muslims) surrender easily. Now here, you can actually kill these POW's without any repercussions. However, killing civilians is a no-no. You get to make big game-altering choices just like in the first two games. It's interesting to see hostiles using old Soviet weaponry and vehicles. You could also encounter some old destroyed weaponry in the countryside, probably from previous conflicts.
The game play.
It's pretty much the same game play as in the first two Arma's. You can roll over now while in prone position. Also, there's a sort of notoriety meter. Its there to ensure that you don't impose your overt American imperialistic aggression on the indigenous population and their property. There's the usual slight general cumbersomeness in moving about, just like in real life, I guess. What's also great is that you aren't tied down to your squad again. I mean it was fun to run around with your buddies in the first two games and kick some a$$. But we know that if one of them died then it was mission over. This time, you are much more free to run around and approach your targets from any direction. In Arma 2 I liked the fact that you played as a black man. In Operation Arrowhead you play as Ben Herrera - probly a Hispanic. So Bohemia Interactive is pretty liberal and reformative I'd have to say. Also, the overall terrain is much more maneuver friendly. But it's not like I didn't enjoy running around the 400 square km of forest in Arma 2.
The bad:
There are still bugs there and there. The enemies disappear and then appear behind your back. The shot up glass windows are really messed up, how could the mess that up? Sometimes, it takes the engine a few seconds to render vehicles correctly. For instance, the wheels are squared before they turn round. Sometimes it takes an extra second for enemies to die after the grenade blast. Also, I'd really like it if the overall physics was improved. Some textures are messed up. Like you can just walk into big rocks and stay inside them.
On a personal note, it's a shame that games like these always get overshadowed by big COD types of blockbusters.
Anyways, it's good to know that there are still good games out there that aren't marred and watered down for the consoles.

This is a re-make done right!
Shadow Warrior is a classic shooter/slasher, health doesn't regenerate and there are tons of secrets hidden in every level, it also manage dto make me laugh out loud several times, and it contains refferences to similar shooters (Duke Nukem, etc..) but also to more serious shooters that shaped the genre (Half Life).
First off, the Sword is THE most satisfying weapon in the game, the amount of detail and efford that went into the sword combat is amazing, you can literally cut enemies in as much pieces as you please, and there are sweet demon-like abilities I won't spoil for you.
The guns may not be all that original, but they sare as hell are a lot of fun, every weapon packs a punch and have interesting addons you can buy, like a laser-guide for your rocket launcher, or a fireball mod for your flamethrower, or my personal favorite; explosive arrows for your crossbow which you can detonate remotely.
Most of the game is mindless fun, but near the end when the story begins to come to a conclusion, it gets surprisingly emotional for a game like this, it left me speechless at the end.
And last, finally a game with those classic boss-fights I like, bosses are HUGE and only a few weak-spots, and since the game doesn't hold your hand like most modern shooters, you'll have to give it several tries before you can beat said bosses.
It's absolutely worth the money if you like classic shooters or are just looking for some fun!

Battlerite had what it took to be my game of 2016. It has fun core gameplay, and it comes closer than any other game to filling the void Magicka Wizard Wars left behind. But for it to be my game of 2017, for it to matter to me much past the F2P launch, a couple of things have to happen.
1. We need more players. Believe you me, I can eat my words, and if the developers find a way to focus on 3v3, this becomes less of a concern. But my favorite gamemode is ranked 3v3, and at pre-F2P time of this review it's a gamble whether I'm even be able to play it at peak hours. This CAN be resolved with the F2P launch. 2v2 serves as a capable introduction to the game and I wouldn't discourage playing it, but the long-term health of the game is improved with every person who decides to take 3v3 seriously. What may feel like chaos at first can prove itself to be wildly deeper than 2v2, tactically.
2. We need nicer players. I don't think developing a thick skin is the best way to deal with♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in terms of bettering a community, and it can seriously corrupt your character. If you join the community, just encourage your teammates or maintain a habit of niceties. Every glhf and timely gg/ggwp adds up. Like many online PvP games, lame♥♥♥♥♥bullies are a loud minority but they can have a severe effect in the small lobbies of 2v2 & 3v3.
If this community can round itself out, what we here now, and presumably in a few days or a few weeks, is a solid competitive game that can be healthy for a few years. But, in a slow and sinister way, the game will become a confused, sad mess and die if 2v2 is the ONLY gamemode people play for the indeterminate future.
Keep an eye out for the Discord and I hope you enjoy/enjoyed the F2P launch.
