This game is really good. I never played the original shadow warrior but after finishing this game I really want to. Shadow Warrior is a Arcade Shooter with some modern elements thrown in. The game is filled with items and secrets that you will need to survive whether you are upgrading your guns and or katana, buying ammo, unlocking ki powers, or unlocking abilities. The greatest strength in Shadow Warrior is without a doubt the katana. Using the katana is the most satisfying portion of the game next to finding secrets, It just feels so satisfying when you are mowing down hundreds of thousands of enemies while feeling the satisfaction of being the ultimate bad***. The guns are pretty good aswell, just not as good as the sword. If you spend your points upgrading your powers correctly you really won't need any of the other guns. But who can say no to wielding a quad-barrel shotgun? Or taking a greater demon's head to use as a beam of death. The voice-acting is pretty good and I really loved Hoji and the banter between him and Lo Wang. The levels are pretty good and well designed. The music is a treat to listen to. The game took me roughly 14 hours to beat, I didn't expect it to be that long, and that was just on normal difficulty. There is tons of replay value in this game. After every fight you'll be graded on a score of 1-5 on how you did and at the end of the game you'll be scored on how many secrets you found, how much damage you took, how much damage you dealt, how many times you died and several other things. Overall Shadow Warrior is a great game and I highly recommend it to anyone who wants to play modern arcade FPS.

"Hard to put down."
For those who haven't played The Stanley Parable yet, I'm sorry. While you will not spend hours upon hours playing this circular game, it is definitely one you will enjoy and should at least play once. You will not be amazed at the graphics, but at the dialogue and the witty humor of the narrator(s). It is a hard game to turn off and you will definitely want to play it again and again.
For those of you that have no idea what The Stanley Parable is, its you. You, Stanley, are trapped in a boring job in a cubicle with no real means to escape. You can fight against the narrator and choose your own path, but it has already been chosen for you... even if you think you've chosen a different path the second/third/forth/etc time around. Although you can get different outcomes based on your choices, you will always end up back to the beginning: your office. The game openly challenges the ideas of freedom, choice, and reality again and again.
The Stanley Parable is an amazing game and one you must have in your Steam library. I would recommend it to anyone, regardless of what style of game you normally play, because your gaming experience will be enriched from it and your mind boggled.
In short, there is a reason why this game has been nominated for so many awards.

(ArmA II: Combined Operations review)
Not for everyone, since it's a realistic military shooter. The maps this game offers are MASSIVE, good for combined arms battles. From the grasslands of Chernarus to the sands of Takistan, the environments are well detailed, and they feel huge.
Make no mistake: This is a tough game to get into. Conventional FPS tactics will not apply, and you need to make sure you don't get hit in the first place while killing the enemy. You have to take account of trajectories and distances of your targets. If there is one gripe I have with this game, it's the controls, especially with helicopters and planes. They feel cumbersome at first, but you'll get used to it after some training. (I recommend the tutorials that Operation Arrowhead has to offer and the Armory to get a good feel on the weapons and vehicles you're using.) While the main campaigns (Harvest Red and Arrowhead) are good, the multiplayer, the editor, and the community are fantastic.
The multiplayer is a lot of fun, and combined with the robust editor and an awesome community (And mods!), ArmA II + Operation Arrowhead is one of my favorite nth person shooter games by far.
Oh, and just a reminder: There's more to ArmA II + OA than DayZ. I can list you some examples: Takistan Life, Wasteland, Invasion 44, and ACE.

A really engaging and active tower defense game. While you don't get many toys to play with (5 "towers" per character plus 2 skills), the character depth comes from how you upgrade your stats. Most of the difficulty comes from tower placement and is easier to read than most tower defense games. Thankfully since there are fewer turrets than normal when you lose a map you aren't left thinking "should I have used the flamethrower turret or the spinning blades?" Although it seems simple/boring at first, there is always something to do on later maps; whether you are upgrading/replacing/repairing turrets or tanking/sniping/aoeing waves of mobs down, everyone is always doing something.
I would recommend this over similar titles (like Sanctum) because of the large amount of maps, diversity of game modes, hero flexibility and customization, and non-rage inducing difficulty.

Bohemia Interactive really made a breakthrough with Arma 2 and this expansion, Operation Arrowhead. Arma 2 features huge battlefields to fight on, with maps like Chernarus being over 200km squared. The ability to be modified through custom made scenarios and missions makes this game's experience ever changing. Four different teams to play on and a wide variety of weapons and vehicles brings huge diversity to the game, and unlimited ammounts of fun. Operation Arrowhead also opens up the opportunity to play the award winning zombie survival mod DayZ.
However, a few cons come with this massive game. The large scale of the game along with seemingly poor optimization can bring about poor and sometimes confusing performance, and it is quite difficult to get to 60 frames per second without some tweaking. Cheating is a huge issue, with any popular server having a very high chance of someone with malicious scripts joining and blowing everything up. Servers tend to have, sometimes, a huge ammount of delay due to the large scale of the game. People you shoot 10+ rounds into might not drop dead for 5 seconds, giving them plenty of time to shoot you back even after you have unloaded a clip into them, bringing about a modest ammount of stalemates. This game is also sort of past it's glory time, as people have moved on to Arma 3 or stick to DayZ.
Granted, this game is still fun as hell. Roleplay in a Takistan Life server, commence in a huge survival warzone on Wasteland servers, or play DayZ. The possibilities to this game are near endless.

ARMA II has had plenty of time to be optimised as an engine, have a large amount of DLC content added to an already pretty substantial game and drop to quite an affordable price. It will also play well on most any mid/top level gaming rig. Even if you only enjoy the single player content this will eat up hours and hours of your lifetime, however, where this game really shines is played with a group of other ARMA enthusiasts who all share the one common denominator which I think is essential to enjoy ARMA II... patience!
This is not a run and gun game like COD 4, Battlefield 3 or those sort of adrenaline fuelled shoot em ups, this rather, is a game about positioning: you and your team/s must co-ordinate your efforts to first of all recon, and then influence the battlefield, not only mustering manpower but also resources: ammo, vehicles etc. If you're not careful the first thing you know about bullets flying is lying in the dirt incapacitated, groaning for a medic. You make as best certain you and your allies are in a good positions, then call fire.
I won't go into the open sandbox editor, which I have not used, but I have been lucky enough to have been able to play with several people who put an enormous amount of time into creating extra content, the possibilities are almost endless, and though the gameplay is severe, the satisfaction of a carefully executed mission is great.
Patience though.... if you're impatient, you will probably get frustrated moving around the map, crawling on your belly, returning your apache to base for fuel and ammo, waiting to see the enemy, waiting for reinforcements when you're pinned down. If you have patience though, you will open up an immersive and somewhat frightningly tangible battlefield simulator.

Let's start this out by saying, I never write reviews for games as in -- I've never written a review for anygame.
Battlerite is simply amazing. I was a huge fan of BLC and sadly the fanbase died due to lack of publicity etc. But the rebirth, Battlerite is just so polished, so much more accessible and so well done. This is a 100% skill based game, literally zero RNG (not even crit chance) no grinding for anything, you just pick who you'd like to play and you queue. If you lose, it's because you got outplayed, if you win -- it's because you played better than the other team. There's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t here, it's all 100% skill.
You decide the outcome of every single match and it's so incredibly addicting. Especially because, even if you are in a 1v2/1v3 situation. You know there's a chance you can win if you play it right. You have to try this game, it's face paced, intense, top-down arena action and quite honestly, the best game I've played in a long time. There's no hidden OP characters, everything can be countered, everyone can be outplayed and you are only limited by your own skill cieling.
Let alone the community is amazing, the community in BLC was never toxic and as of now, it's the same here. If someone in BLC disconnected during the match, everyone would simply wait for them to reconnect, or just decide on a 2v2 match up. It's amazing and so rare to find nowadays.
10/10 -- I see nothing wrong here.

"Old school" is a term that gets thrown around a lot these days, by publishers and developers alike, and more often then not these so called "throwbacks" are nothing more than a cheap cash-in on nostalgia, rater than a real homage to the "good old days", completely missing the point of what made these games great. The most prominent case in recent history that comes to mind would be Bioshock Infinite, or rather its "1999 Mode", which was advertised to be a throwback to the unforgiving difficulty of System Shock 2. But instead of adding inventory or item management it just turns the enemies into bulletspongy death machines. So it goes.
But I digress. After all, I am trying to review Shadow Warrior 2013 here.
So, is this game true to its claim of being a throwback to the days of Doom and Build Engine games?
If you are expecting complex maze like levels, ala Doom or Duke3D, you are out of luck. While Shadow Warrior 2013 gives you plenty of crates to loot for ammo and money as well as keys to hunt for in order to advance to the next area, it still feels like a streamlined version of 90's FPS level. This is not an issue for me however, since I usually got lost once the levels got too complex in later episodes of these types of games. Though I do have to point out, that I still managed to get lost in these rather simplistic levels, because I got stuck more then often without knowing what I had to do. This was mostly due to the fact that SW2013 Highlights usable items with an incredibly obnoxious glow effect that makes it easy to differentiate between geometry and usable entities. Since I am not a fan of these types of mechanics I played the game with the effect off, which unfortunately resulted in me sometimes not being able to figure out what to do because the switch I was supposed to press just blended in with the scenery. That's the issue with these types of helpers. Even if you have the option to disable them, game game is still designed with them in mind, making it unnecessarily complicated to discard them even if you want to.
You are equipped with an arsenal of firearms as well as a Katana and an endless supply of underpowered Shurikens that drain your regenerating stamina meter as you throw them. Speaking of regeneration, your health does not automatically regenerate. Instead there are medipacks and armor vets scattered throughout the levels. Despite that fact that there is no auto health regen, you still have the ability to heal yourself in form of a Ki Power. Ki Powers are combos that you can pull of as a player by completing a sequence of actions. For instance, to initiate your healing ability you press D twice in a row and then press Mouse2, holding it down. Most KI Powers either give you crowd control over enemies, or new moves with your Katana.
Throughout the game the play can find KI Crystals that allow him to upgrade or unlock powers. Speaking of Upgrading there are two other kinds of progression. The first one is the Karma system. If you use a wide variety of skills and weapons to kill of enemies, you are rewarded with Karma points that you can spend to level up various stats, such as your maximum health as well as the amount of damage you deal to certain types of enemies. How ever, by doing so you will cause some enemies to enter their rage form which makes them more aggressive and dangerous.
If we are talking about damage dealing, we need to talk about the weapons as well. Throughout the levels you will find money which you can either spend on ammo (don't ever do this!) or on weapon upgrades. Each weapon has an essential upgrade that will turn it into a great DPS dealer, you will have to resort to in case you get overwhelmed by hoards of enemies. Unfortunately this means that all wepaons are utter trash unless you spend money to upgrade them.
The core shooter mechanics however, is where this games shines. 95% of all enemies either use a projectile or melee attacks in order to deal damage to you. This means that there is no need to ever take any cover, allowing you do keep track of all projectiles and dodging them accordingly. To help you with this, the game allows you to jump in all four directions which adds a refreshing dynamic to the combat. To add to the challenge all enemies use a rather modern hit box system, that allows you to shoot off limps in order to immobilize them. You need to stand still trying to aim for a the head of the on coming enemies, pull the trigger and then do a quick jump to the left or right, to avoid the amount of stuff that comes flying towards you, ready to explode in your face. That being said, the shooting has its weaknesses though, especially concerning the stronger enemy types. There is one in particular that really grind me gears: The Shaman is a so called "greater demon" or mini boss that frequently shows up raising an infinite army of undead enemies, as well as shooting projectiles towards you. He is a real bulletsponge and fighting him is the very antithesis of fun. This gets issue grows less and less important as your weapons grow more powerful and your skill increases. Keep in mind that I was playing on the "Hard" difficulty setting. The bigger problem are the bossfights. They stink. All of them use the same mechanic, which is extremely tiresome and boring. Even though all bosses use a slightly different attack pattern, you feel like you are fighting the same boss over and over again. This is no different concerning the final boss, which was a major letdown for me.
SW 2013 tries to get rid of the "racist and misogynistic" humor of the original game, replacing it with an emotional story. While the game manages to pull of the plot quite well, you should under no circumstances except something like Bastion or The Walking Dead which leave you completely emotionally destroyed, if you get emotionally invested with their respective characters. Shadow Warrior doesn't do this and leaves you indifferent at best towards the whole tragedy in which the games ends. Speaking of ending, the more you advance the more unpolished and untested the game feels. The game builds up an epic confrontation with Zilla, a Faustian villian who caused the invasion of the shadow realm onto the human word for his own needs. But instead of fighting him and adding some much needed variety to the bossfights, you just face him (twice!) in a first person cutscene. The same applies to the leader of the shadow beings. How overwhelmingly disappointing. Heck, the final boss fight doesn't even have music like the others with makes it even more boring.
The games is extremely resource demanding even on my 4770k/GTX 780 rig and does not look good enough in order to justify this. Instead it makes about every other object in a level explosive which unleashes a storm of death and physics across the screen. I also had some issue with the vsync, that caused the FPS to drop to 30 once it went below 60, which was extremely annoying, up to the point where I just disabled it end endured the screen tearing instead.
Overall Shadow Warrior 2013 is a great indie shooter with solid gameplay and a disappointingly weak presentation that completely falls flat on its face near the end of the game. If you are a fan of games like Serious Sam or Painkiller, this game is a must buy for you. But don't except a real 90's shooter, because it just isn't one.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Solid and fun gameplay
-Combat based on projectile avoidance and strafing
-Story and presentation fall completely flat towards the end.
-Resource intensive
-Terrible bossfights

This game is superb.
I had my doubts, as I always do about games that try to revive the classics like Duke Nukem 3D, that there would be too many fingerprints of modern gaming on this for it to turn out decently.
I was wrong.
The graphics are definitely up to par to AAA game titles, especially in the environments.
The audio in the game is stellar as well, delivering both pounding and atmospheric music when the situation calls for it, as well as brutal audio feedback from the swords and guns, making headshots and decapitations feel visceral and rewarding.
The level design is about what you'd expect from a Painkiller, Serious Sam, or the likes. Its fairly obvious where large encounters will happen due to most areas either looking like corridors or arenas, but to be honest, the beauty of the environments and the fact that you're constantly tossed into new environments keeps it fairly fresh.
The gameplay is pretty easy to pick up, in my opinion, and a wide variety of powers, skills, and combos lets you fight the way you'd like. Balance is key to combat, and your score and enemy behaviors will change depending on how much you spam powers or balance gun and swordplay.
The only issue I've had with this game thus far is that it does seem to favor swordplay over gunplay. The sword is just awesome to use, with its combos, unlimited ammo (melee, obviously), and feeling of being a ninja badass, and often overshadows the weapons, which is a shame because the guns are all pretty cool and seem to be balanced pretty well, its just that there's really no downside to using the katana. Then whenever you encounter bosses, it seems like the only option is unloading all of your guns into them, as in a couple encounters, the boss' hitbox kept you physically far enough away that your sword didn't seem to connect half the time.
Either way, I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good action FPS, a fast paced arcade experience, or just some good old-fashioned gibby fun.
I will definitively say it is a must-have for fans of the original, or of any similar BUILD titles.

Devolver Digital and Flying Wild-Hog have brought what Duke Nukem Forever should have been to the Shadow Warrior franchise. The swordplay makes melee combat much more fun than the gunplay; but the over the top 4-in-1 shot quad-barrel shotgun and the laser guided 3-in-1 shot rocker launcher really make a strong effort for attention. Tons of unlockable abilities and skills, and the ability to carry every weapon in the game simultaneously mean your arsenal never runs dry. From channeled shields, and healing spells; to spinning blade attacks, and one-shot charge stabs, no one playstyle is going to be "the best" really leaving you open to play the way you feel most comfortable. The level's are designed well, and there are tons of secrets to find in each one. The characters are all likable, and the dialogue is the perfect mixture of over-the-top action movie and video game/comic book nerd humor. The story is fine, no complaints, it's deep but never goes 2deep4u, it unfolds at a good pace and could be skipped entirely if you just want to cut more demons and dudes up with your Katana. Shadow Warrior is a fantastic game that all FPS fans should play, let the post 2005 gamers see why the retro FPS players always talk about how great the genre used to be. An utterly peculiar game. I haven’t played the original Shadow Warrior, so it’s hard to say how much of the game’s madness is from the original game and how many are new innovations for this edition.
Perhaps the main draw for this game is protagonists Lo Wang and Ogi. Lo Wang is the playable character, a hitman who fancies himself to be a badass comic book hero. Wang frequently cracks cheesy one-liners and actively plays to common action hero tropes; he shaves his head at one point the game simply for dramatic effect. He even has a large secret lair underneath his house which he has dubbed the ‘Wangcave’, full of his secret weaponry which he had prepared for a zombie apocalypse as well as his collection of vintage comic books. Wang reminds me very distinctly of No More Heroes protagonist Travis Touchdown; their mannerisms and hobbies are almost exactly the same. It is possible Wang was an inspiration for Travis or vice versa depending on what Wang was like in the original Shadow Warrior game. In turn, Wang’s demonic partner, Ogi, serves as Wang’s foil and frequently plays the straight man to Wang’s antics. Whereas Wang will fall into common tropes willingly and at times actively seeking to fulfill common tropes, Ogi tries to defy them at every turn simply to irritate Wang. The two have an excellent chemistry and stay interesting and amusing to listen to for the game. Honestly, the game is almost worth picking up alone just to listen to these two characters talk, both to each other and by themselves.
That being said, the gameplay of Shadow Warrior is no slouch either. It’s an interesting hybrid of old-school FPS shooting with additions of current gen depth; you can get classic weapons such as pistols and machine guns, but by collecting money found around each level you can upgrade your weapons to do be more efficient in accuracy or damage, or perhaps unlock new firing modes. The upgrade system adds to the game and helps make each gun feel unique and worthwhile outside of different levels of fire speed. Not only this, but you also have two other venues of character customization; you have a series of demon powers and trees of passive abilities. The demon powers can include things like radius stuns, defense abilities, and healing, while the passive skills cover a wide range of things like finding more money around the level or doing more damage to common demon enemies. All of this character customization makes the gameplay feel very deep and meaningful, and helps set it apart from other FPS games.
One last important note about Shadow Warrior’s gameplay is that alongside the guns, you get a katana for melee attacks. I am of the opinion that melee attacks in first person games never work out very well; it’s almost impossible to keep track of enemies in first person to keep the melee attacks on target. However, Shadow Warrior’s melee system feels good and works well against the enemies who primarily use melee themselves.
Despite these things, Shadow Warrior is not a perfect game by any stretch of the imagination. Perhaps my machine was not up to snuff, but even on the lowest graphics quality I often found the game’s framerate to drop dramatically when a lot of enemies came on-screen. This proved to a problem at times when precise aiming was needed, and I found myself having to play sections over due to failing to framerate issues. The story is also very uninteresting, but this isn’t a game you come to for the story.
Overall very bizarre and not the best optimized, but a game that’s quirky enough and solid enough in gameplay that I can easily recommend it.

Back in the day I very much liked Duke Nuk'em 3D and its engine (i.e. building levels for it). I was quite surprised to find Shadow Warrior Classic Redux, a game I had never heard of at the time, used the same engine. So is played it and pretty much liked it. A nice trip down nostalgia lane.
When the modern remake Shadow Warrior (2013) came up in the bargain bin, I gave that a try, not expecting too much because the advertised "splatter" gameplay is not really my thing. But when playing the game I was really surprised how much fun it was to explore the beautiful levels, looking for secrets (there is one pixeled retro secret, reminiscent of the original game in almost every level), and luckily the splattering was so over the top, to not disturb all too much.
I really enjoyed playing the game, especially since with the most recent patches in place it simply works, so no stress there. Things I very much appreciated:
- You can quicksave at any time, even during combat.
- There is a lot to loot and the looting is worth the effort.
- Nice set of weapons with a twist, upgrading them with money you collect in the game.
- Special powers and skills, again by collecting certain items, or performing intricate attacks for Ki, are a welcome gameplay additions.
- Difficulty (normal) is challenging enough but not frustrating. I am playing on Hardcore using a trainer now, and that is mildly annoying, the weapons are simply too weak.
- Tons of Achievements you may want to get.
- The devs actually did put quite a bit of effort into telling a story. I appreciate them for going that extra mile... after all shooters usually don't have much of a story.
- Over all, very beautiful outdoors levels in Japanesque setting. A few quite epic vistas also await the player. Wonderful lighting too.
- At first the main character, Lo Wang, was a bit of a let-down, but his comments, and those of his cynical sidekick (from the Demon realm) are quite entertaining.
- The only thing I would have loved to have had in the game is the option to bind a key to letting you turn on/off the HUD for clean screenshots.
- Holstering the weapon would have been another thing on my preferred list.
Other than that, a very polished gaming experience.
So if you like shooters, with some degree of exploration and tons of secrets, slightly retro, I would very much recommend getting the game from the bargain bin.

My favourite game this year.
Shadow Warrior is a first person shooter, but the real fun and satisfaction comes from weilding the katana. As Lo Wang you get to chop, dice, slice and dismember your way through hordes of demons and sending body parts flying. A particular favourite move of mine being the 360 degree slash that timed right results in multiple beheadings..
If you like Gore, gibs and general slaughter..think old school fps style, Unreal, Quake... then this game will scratch that itch.  It also recalls Doom in many ways; Its use of keycards, finding secrets and the way that the demons appear and run towards you definitely has a Doomesque quality to it.

Its quite a lengthy game and i'm tempted to play through again on a harder setting and see how far i get.  Normal is fairly easy with only one Demon type giving me much trouble.   It does run out of ideas a little towards the end where you just see more and more waves of the same enemies, but it was never less than fun to slaugter them all.

Graphically the game is absolutely gorgeous, with beautiful Japanese backdrops and atmosphere.  Framerate did tank for me quite a bit in places, particularly in larger open areas. I was playing on Ultra with a less than tip-top graphics card, so ymmv as always with pc gaming.
The humor is just kind of a mix of being goofy and genuinely quite funny. They certainly get a lot of mileage out of his name.  "Wang, are you in yet...? I can't tell..'  etc etc.
I only have a few minor gripes. Sometimes the puzzle aspects can be a bit obtuse and frustrating running around checking for what you've missed.  Also if the game doesn't want you to go somewhere then Lo Wang will be defeated by the mighty knee-high box, whereas in other places the exact same boxes are easily jumped over.  Level loading times are a little slow too, but well... bring a book.

TL:DR: Great game, well worth the money. If you liked Doom, Unreal, Wolfenstein, Hard Target ;) then I can't think of any reason why you won't love this.

Turned out to be one of my all-time favorites. Operation Arrowhead patches so many bugs of the basic Arma II and essentially makes it a new game.
While the game is still riddled with flaws, it is just awesome. A fantastic tool for tactical war-sim gameplay if you're so inclined and you bring a bit of brain matter into the equation.
Grab your friends and roll in a tank, build up an outpost, dominate a crowd of kids in a plane or ditch the whole public domain, install ACE and ACRE, find a platoon and immerse in tactical infantry gameplay the way you did when you were still in boot camp many moons ago.
Be a leet sniper and parachute into the action in hopes of quickscope headshots just to get mauled by enemy fire every two minutes or learn about the range of firearms and proper range estimation and use camouflage to your advantage as you work your way from one objective to the next under the cover of friendly surveillance.
Shout into Voice-Over-Net because mommy doesn't understand you or join an ACRE server, learn about the use of radios and broadcast your grid reference to your platoon commander on VHF, over.
The choices are yours to make once you realize that no two servers are the same and you don't actually have to play with toddlers.
I will love this game forever and for always.

This positive review comes as no surprise. I remember playing the original Shadow Warrior years ago and I even purchased the Redux version on Steam. It's basically another Duke Nukem 3d with different monsters and weapons, sorta like Blood. This "reboot" is different, and you could even say it has nothing to do with the original, despite some common names. But this is a good reboot.
Everything is satisfying about this game when it comes to the combat. Hell, even the Katana is fun to use. Plus, the game is very, very graphic, unlike Hard Reset, and is very, very, VERY satisfying. I gotta emphasis that. Every weapon feels like a weapon when you blast a demon away. There are also secrets and some minor item hunting for money or ammo, which puts pace into the game between the massive fights. Enemies get varied and crowd management is key.
As for the story, it is sorta there, but Wang and the rest of the characters are a neat fit. Oddly enough, the voice acting is good.
Graphics compliment all the locations and the demons have that classic Chinese folklore look about them. There are LOTS of slow downs, but it wasn't ever enough to break the game. The game loads VERY slow. I installed this game on an SSD drive and it still takes forever to load. Keep in mind, this SSD can load any multiplayer level in BF4 in 30 seconds or less, so Shadow Warrior has too much compression for the design. So, when you buy, don't think there's something wrong with your computer, the game loads slow.
I purchased this game for $10 during the sale and I can safely say I would have purchased it at $30.00. As for the $40 tag, it's up to you.

This game...... is terrible. When you first start out it seems pretty fun. The sword combat is solid, the movement is pretty great, and the voice acting is bearable as long as it's short. About midway through the game you start wondering if they're going to introduce other enemy types, and wondering if you've already been through the level you're on. The answers are no and  probably yes because everything is pretty much copy-pasted over and over to lengthen game time, and even when that's not in play, you're going to have to backtrack through the whole goddamn map to look for some keys. The gunplay is terrible and consists of frantically swapping over most of the useless weapons for your staples of handgun, shotgun, bullethose, long-range-rifle-substitute-of-crossbow. When you're tired of strafing and pressing left trigger, you can take out your sword and light or heavy attack. This remains fun for about 10 seconds. I found myself yelling "This isn't fun!" as another load of baddies spawned after I had cleared a few waves in the arena styled room.
What little variety there is of the combat comes off as annoying as you shoot balls that are rolling towards you, circle around enemies with shields, circle and dodge enemies with a weakpoint in their back, and wait for a necromancer to put down their invincible shield. It's awful, unvaried, and annoying as you sprint through the levels. There's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of collectibles that you'll mostly just skip over, a power system that you'll probably forget exists beyond the various sword strikes you can learn, and enough one-liners to give Bruce Campbell a nostalgia induced seizure.
The only, and I do mean only, interesting thing in this game once the novelty wears off 1/8th of the way through is the shadow-world mythology and drama. I would recommend just going on youtube and seeing that if you want to enjoy yourself. On the other hand, if you like bad lines delivered flat, bad jokes delivered with malevolent glee, and repetive action, enemies, levels, and puzzles in the medium of a game that who's idea of fun is searching a room for stuff, and then want to do that over and over and over and over and over and over and over, I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

Grade: B-
Summary Review:
Good - Creativity on steroids. Great humor. Unique.
Bad - Hard to define. A bit too cerebral borderline completely confusing.
Description:
Wow where to do I begin... You are Stanley. You work at a company where you type into your computer every day. But one day you notice that all of your co-workers are not at the office and you adventure begins. What follows is as much a study of the method of story telling and game design as an actual story about Stanley.
Review:
When I bought The Stanley Parable I had heard that it was exceptional innovative game that, while short, was very memorable. After completing the game (which only took about 1 hour) this description is true albeit giving a bit of the hyped review of the game. The only game that could be described as similar to Parable is Portal (which is not surprising as both are Valve games). Like Portal Parable has a sharp level design and narrative writing. And also like Portal the humor is top notch. What makes it different is that Parable then goes and detonates the 4th wall. (SPOILERS) The game quite literally ends with you in a museum of the games design and artifacts/levels that were cut during its design. I would really want to give this game a higher grade/review but unfortunately with so much of the game about game design/story telling it is hard to actual define what the game was about per se. I sometimes felt that I was unsure what the creators were trying to say with the game or narration. In summary the Stanley Parable is a short game that will make you laugh and make you think but may seem confusing and/or straight up bizarre to some.

This is quite simply the most enjoyable gaming experience I can ever recall, and I had a Commodore 64 with, like, a billion games.
This isn't an RPG with an amazing story, nor a story-driven game with RPG elements.  It's not a pirate sandbox in the same way it's not a 3D action platformer.  It's more than any of these things.
The attention to detail, superb writing and genuinely surprising voice acting make it the first game to take the title of "OMG Favourite Game of All Time, Like Seriously, You Guys Should Play This" without a hint of sarcasm.  AC IV: BF is, in my worthless opinion, a masterpiece.  It's the Heath Ledger of Jokers.  It's the double brie of cheeses.
Audio.
This gleaming piece of gaming magic has shanties - Shantii? A Yaaaarrr of shanties?  Whatever the collective noun, if you're anything like me, you'll eschew the money/upgrade/unlockable item side quests, choosing instead to spend two hours chasing down sheet music.  I actually spent an embarrassing amount of time sailing around in circles listening to the crew sing to the accompanyment of thunderstorms and waves.  Aside from the brilliance of the male choir that is your crew (who are just pirating to pay the bills until they're discovered) the music is astounding.  The contextual fade-in/out is perfect - wait until you get into your first major ship to ship combat and see.  Essentially, the sound design and direction is so good it could be used for a feature length film and not feel out of place.
Visuals.
Just...wow.  Imagine having 30g of fairy dust shot into your eyes.  This game is *gorgeous*.  Again, the attention to detail shines through.  Spray crashes over the bow of your ship as you breach a wave. Water ripples in the shallows so beautifully, it will actually make you want to go for a swim (and I *hate* the beach).  In point of fact, the water is the real star here.  It's amazing.  Beyond amazing.  It's easily the best looking fluid model I've seen in a game.  (Two words: Rogue wave. Are water-boners a thing?)
Controls & Gameplay
The controls are intuitive and easy to pick up (note: I played with an xbox 360 controller) across the ship combat, free running and melee combat sections.  My only frustration was due to getting stuck in an climbable-but-blocked area due to a tight chase-camera.  This typically results in Edward, our protagonist, hanging ineffectually like a suave, tattooed pinata whilst angry people whack at him with a variety of sharp things.  This happened to me a lot in the first 30 minutes, but once you get used to the controls it's almost never an issue.
As for the gameplay itself?  It's frankly amazing that the ship-to-ship combat and melee combat mesh together so well.  I was expecting the water-side biffo to feel 'tacked on', but it's no more a hasty addition than the cars are an afterthought in GTA.  Ship-Biff is a central part of the game that feels polish, well balanced and - above all - fun.  Relentlessly fun.  Don't expect simulation levels of detail and accurate phyics (Train Simulator 2013 is over there), because you can't fit that stuff into a package that is jammed to the gills with fun, kay?  You fire various types of ship munitions (all of which are upgradeable, as is your ship) at each other until the other guys catch fire.  Then you can scuttle them, netting half the loot) or board them for all the loot and a touch of hand-to-hand combat.  I can't stress how well the transition between these two areas is designed...  Let go of the wheel and you're back in edwards boots; boots which, in short order, are landing on the enemys deck, neck and pile of booty - in that order.  There are no loading screens to be seen.  AMAZE.
Summary
BUY THIS GAME. YOU NEED THIS GAME IN YOUR LIFE. THIS GAME IS REALLY, REALLY, REALLY QUITE GOOD.

Shadow Warrior 2013 is a reboot of the 1997 classic by 3-D Realms developed by Flying Wild Hog and published by Devolver Digital. The game has you take the role of Lo Wang, a sarcastic and awesome protagonist who is told by the head of Zilla Industries to retrieve an ancient sword that goes by the name "Nobitsura Kage" which is a weapon that is said to have connections with ancient Gods and possess power unlike anything mankind has ever seen. Along the way Lo Wang will meet a spirit known as "Hoji", who helps Wang on his quest to retrieve the Nobitsura Kage.
The gameplay is a mix between an old school first person shooter and a Hack-and-slash, the game starts you off with a Katana as your first weapon which is probably the best weapon in the game, with it you can slice enemie's limbs off, perform moves such as a 360 spin, power attacks and even press reload to clean your Katana from blood, which I gotta say is a pretty cool touch. As you progress in the game's 14 hour single player campaign you will gain upgrades for your katana, one being the ability to drain health from an enemy,Wang can also perform moves with the power of KI, moves include shockwaves, healing, levitation, push, etc. These moves are essential if you want to beat the game on it's higher difficulties.
Along the way you will pick up a vast array of weapons ranging from Revolvers and SMGS, to the more heavy stuff like flame throwers and a rocket launcher at some stage. You can even use a demon's head to unleash a powerful beam which totally destroys enemies and even a demon's heart to instant kill a smaller demon. Some of these weapons may seem weak at first but stick with it and you will find them extremely useful in situtations. Each weapon also has their own description on it's original use, who manufactured it, and it's history which is quite an awesome touch. Each weapon has their own upgrades in the menu which can be bought using money found in the games 18 chapters (Including the prologue), upgrades can range from more damage, a bigger clip size, explosive ammunition, and akimbo for the SMGS.
Speaking of upgrades, Lo Wang himself can be upgraded with more moves, health, KI, stamina, endurace, etc. These upgrades can be bought using Ki Crystals found within the chapters and earning KARMA, which is this game's equivalent to experience points. Then finally you have the games boss fights, which are all giant monsters whose weakpoint is the crystal behind their armour, these fights are definatly fun, but begin to grow repetitive, but are made a bit more interesting with new attack patterns and the upgrades you obtain on the way. Speaking of enemies, there is a large variety of enemies ranging from shield enemies, explosive enemies, winged enemies, golem enemies, shamen enemies and many more off the top of my head and each enemy provides a fair and balanced challenge to the player. This game is by no means an easy game, I had myself dying at certain points which made me angry, but enough to make me continue.
Each Chapter is filled to the brim with med kits, ammo, money, fortune cookies, secrets, Karma pools, KI crystals, easter eggs which all make exploration a key factor in Shadow Warrior.
The graphics in this game makes this one of the most beautiful games I've ever played with stunning vistas, crisp textures, lighting, models and animation. I could sit here for days saying how beatiful this game is.
The sound design is also excellent, with well done voice acting, ambiant sounds, gun sounds, katana sounds and a superb soundtrack which help set the atmosphere.
Lastly, Lo wang himself is an excellent character who let's out witty and sarcastic dialouge which makes the character in my opinion very loveable and full of personality, my favourite line from him was "Where did you demons learn Kung-Fu? Kung-Fu r us?" which had me cracking up.  Hoji is probably my favourite character, he also let's out witty and sarcastic dialouge and creates hilarious banter between him and Lo wang, such as the moment when they chat about Eye of the Tiger which made me laugh pretty damn hard.
Shadow Warrior is no means a short game, each level can take from 25 minutes upwards to an hour and a half which resulted in a 14 hour single player, even longer if you want to find all the secrets and get perfect scores. After you beat the game you unlock Heroic and EX mode, EX is basically new game+ and Heroic has you beat each level with only 1 checkpoint at the start of each level that is apparently harder than Insane (The hardest difficulty).
RECENTLY ADDED: Also, when you're done with the campiagn there is also a survival mode where you fight waves upon waves of enemies while buying upgrades along the way while trying to get on top of the leaderboards, this mode is definatly not one to be missed.
After beating Shadow Warrior, I then took a big drink of water, then started the game all over again on Heroic I did this because Shadow Warrior 2013 is to me is a near-perfect game, and I can happily say that Shadow Warrior 2013 is by far one of my favourite games of all time, which ended on an unforgettable ending.
Flying Wild Hog, I salute you, because this game, is bloody brilliant.

Summary Review:
Good - Creativity on steroids. Great humor. Unique.
Bad - Hard to define. A bit too cerebral borderline completely confusing.
Description:
Wow where to do I begin... You are Stanley. You work at a company where you type into your computer every day. But one day you notice that all of your co-workers are not at the office and you adventure begins. What follows is as much a study of the method of story telling and game design as an actual story about Stanley.
Review:
When I bought The Stanley Parable I had heard that it was exceptional innovative game that, while short, was very memorable. After completing the game (which only took about 1 hour) this description is true albeit giving a bit of the hyped review of the game. The only game that could be described as similar to Parable is Portal (which is not surprising as both are Valve games). Like Portal Parable has a sharp level design and narrative writing. And also like Portal the humor is top notch. What makes it different is that Parable then goes and detonates the 4th wall. (SPOILERS) The game quite literally ends with you in a museum of the games design and artifacts/levels that were cut during its design. I would really want to give this game a higher grade/review but unfortunately with so much of the game about game design/story telling it is hard to actual define what the game was about per se. I sometimes felt that I was unsure what the creators were trying to say with the game or narration. In summary the Stanley Parable is a short game that will make you laugh and make you think but may seem confusing and/or straight up bizarre to some.

Shadow Warrior is an ultra-fast hack 'n slash FPS game propelled forward in a blinding pace with action packed combat using guns, explosives, magic and a deadly katana in an incredibly varied setting with some of the most stunning visuals I have seen to date. Add on top of that a deep and compelling story garnished with tons of humor and cliché catch-phrases that could make you wonder if the game was not taking itself very serious; an assumption you will soon come to realize is as false as false can be.
The new Shadow Warrior is not so much a remake of the original, but rather a re-envisioning of the old 1997 release. The zaney humor, the slice-and-dice gamplay and Lo Wang the protagonist is still the main drive of the game, but the experience  of this latest incarnation as a whole is a much more greater, better and more enthralling undertaking.
You still play as the not-so-subtle Lo Wang, a martial arts expert with an ego of some considerable size. Very early on, due to some minor complications with a powerful japanese entrepreneur (or mafia boss, basically), you get hitched up with a demonic spirit named Hoji, who gifts you with magical powers and guides you through a trail-blazing adventure to collect 3 pieces of an ancient and powerful sword - the Nobitsura Kage. Your agenda for this undertaking is to retrieve the sword for your boss, who will pay a handsome reward for the blade. Hoji's agenda, however, is an entirely different one, and you are getting more and more involved in it with every (quick) step.
Shadow Warrior is one of the rare FPS games with an actual story worth listening to. In fact, it tells a story that one would have expected from a grand role playing game, or an adventure game. Every level brings gives you a little extra story and background lore, and every bit of information you uncover about Hoji's story and the legend of the Nobitsura Kage makes you realize that this game is something special. I can tell you this much; the number of FPS games that have moved me so deeply that I was in tears and goosebumps at the end are few and far inbetween. But Shadow Warrior is one such.
The gameplay features a decent arsenal of deadly weapons, from handguns and shotguns, dual uzis to flame throwers, a high-powered crossbow and even a rocket launcher. Each weapon can be upgraded for extra functionality or alternate fire modes through an upgrade menu that is accessible ay any time. Purchasing an upgrade costs money, which can be found throughout the games by looting chests and cabinets or simply lying around the environment. As such, exploring each level is recommended.
But the staple weapon of the game is no doubt the Katana. The melee combat in Shadow Warrior is eminent. It it fast, fun, spectacular and very skill-based. You can perform fast and precise dodges while chaining multiple different slashes and powerful magical attacks to create devastating combos on your opponents who you will literally be slicing and dicing into little bits. Heads, arms, legs and even torsos will fly in sprays of blood. Killing enemies in specatular and varied ways will reward you with Karma (and you can dispatch of them in truly varied ways once you unlock and master the many different attacks) which you can spend in the upgrade menu to improve Lo Wang's many different attributes. Deal more damage, move faster, increased health, chance of finding more and better loot and so on and so forth.
Again, exploration is a key word. The more you explore, the more currency for your various upgrades you will find. Not to mention many funny and wacky easter eggs, such as hidden rooms created in the old 1997 style graphics with flat and boxy textures. The game is packed with secrets and hidden areas, usually containing extra Karma points. By use of Ki Crystals, which are found throughout the game, you unlock new special powers and magical abilities, which will not only make combat more crazy and fun, but also enhance your options of creating rewarding combos for added Karma rewards. This does, however, mean that if you do not perform too well in combat and don't explore much, the game will get increasingly difficult since you will be missing out on many of those vital upgrades.
Another strong point of Shadow Warrior are the visuals. They are positively mind blowing! It is, without a doubt, one of the visually most stunningly beautiful games I have ever played. The game takes you through a multitude of different environments, from pink cherry blossom gardens to great bamboo forests, to underground caverns littered with stalagmites and stalagtites and even into the Shadow Realm, a strange and mysterious plane of existence that is arguably even more gorgeous than the afore mentioned areas. Through and through the game is sugary-sweet eye candy that actually leaves you time and opportunity to walk around and enjoy it to the fullest.
Do not be mislead by the story, exploration and RPG-like upgrades though, Shadow Warrior is still a true arcade "twitch" FPS game at heart. It is fast, relentless and brutal. There is no emphasis on realism or tactics what-so-ever. More often than not you are swarmed by 10, 15 or even 20 enemies all at once. It is a pure-breed hack 'n slash, shoot 'n scoot powerhouse based on a completely liniar level progression, and nearly all combat scenarios are triggered events. You walk into a designated area, and portals will spawn to spill forth throngs of enemies. Chop them up and move to the next area, then rinse and repeat. Luckily, doing this is SO MUCH FUN!
I really am struggling to think of any downsides to this game. It has just been an enjoyment from start to finish.
Synopsis:
+ Excellent arcade FPS action with many weapons and superb controls
+ Some of the best melee sword combat I've experienced
+ Rewards exploration; easter eggs and  secrets aplenty
+ Lots of humor and nods to the old 1997 game
+ Incredible graphics and varied level design
+ Deep and enthralling story
+ Hoji

- Needs a fairly strong computer to run well with graphics on high

Shadow Warrior came out of nowhere and blew my mind. It is the best single player FPS game I have played in a long time. The gameplay itself might get repetitive toward the end of the game, but the well written dialogue and great characters kept me interested.
Shadow Warrior is a reimagining of the 1997 game of the same name. Some things connecting this new game to the 1997 original is some similar naming of locations, the main character and the heavy use of katana as a melee weapon, but basically you are not missing anything if you haven't played the original or even know nothing about it.
Here are some additional scrabled thoughts about the game
What I liked
-The story, characters, voice acting, visuals and soundtrack.
-The story is a mix between drama and comedy. Usually this is a bad idea, but somehow Shadow Warrior makes the mood shifts enjoyable. One of the most important reasons as to why Shadow Warrior has such good characters is that they are a mix of dramatic and comedic traits, which makes them very approachable and human.
-Good enemy variety. Different weapons/techniques are also required to beat some of the harder enemies.
-Good weapon variety, and you can carry all the weapons at once without needing to swap. There's also a weapon upgrade system in place. The upgrades are kind of scarse, so it's always interesting to get one and the upgrades have real impact, and most of them are not like "+5% accuracy", but alternative firing modes and such.
-Flow of the game. There's a good rhythm with the story bits, enemy encounters, humour, serious moments, exploration. It is aslo separated into chapters that range from about 20 minutes to 40 minutes, so it is nicely paced in terms of when you can just shut the game and take a break or do something else entirely.
-Melee combat. It has a melee combat system with some executable special moves. The moves are always just double tap a directional key and press LMB or RMB, but still it's fun to execute them.
-It has this kind of (but not quite) hint system where you need to always use objects or doors that glow yellow. I thought it was much more pleasant than the reqular arrow or path that shows you exactly where you need to go. Top-down arena battler. Fast-paced, but still deliberative: to really do well you have to keep track of opponents' cooldowns as well as your own, along with managing distance and zoning. It's more like a fighting game, really. Fully skill-based, there's no grinding or stat customization or any of that garbage. You pick your champion, you know exactly what it'll do, how much, and for how long. You can choose one battlerite (basically talents) per round in a match to adjust to the compositions of your team/enemy's team.
With 2v2 and 3v3 modes, you can easily split up your groups and no one will be left out. The game is free of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, you just boot it up and go straight into a match, no garbage to wade through before the "real game" begins. Graphics are slightly cartoonish, but are very clear and it's very easy to understand what's going on. When a champion is using a channeled ability or is under a duration, the name of the ability/effect is spelled out in clear text above the model.
The game is somewhat poorly optimized at time of writing this (early access) but that's improving. The chat interface, especially outside a match, is terrible and needs a lot of improvement.
Edit/Update: It is over a year later, I've revisited it with the Free To Play release. The developers have fixed almost everything wrong with the game back when it was Early Access only. Many champions have had their kits revamped and streamlined, the game is significantly easier to understand now, and there have been model updates across the board. On top of that, there is an actual existing playerbase now, making it easy to matchmake and discuss the game with others.
The drawback is the menu system is unnecessarily convoluted. Fortunately that is overlookable since it's such a small portion of the overall experience.

A incredible fun game, with a lot of focus on Sword fighting and just gernerally murdering stuff.
You get a Katana as your first weapon, and i personally found it to be the most fun to use. You get a lot of the normal old-school FPS weapons (SMG, Pistol, Rocket launcher, Crossbow etc.) But they all felt very stiff. But they're not the interesting part of this gime.
You have 3 things you can upgrade, your skills, powers, and weapons. Skils are for stuf like more health, faster run speed, new katana abilities, Something that a normal person would be able to develop generally. Then there is the powers. 4 different in total. They are all executed by doing a movement key twice then right-click (Movement key twice + left click is for the katana skills). This might seem difficult at first, but it actually works really well, and gives you easy access to all your abilities. My favorite personally, was the flux. By Pressing S twice, and then right-click, you would charge up your first. When you released right-click, it would throw a long line into the ground, that would lift enemies up in the air for several seconds. Its amazing using the flux, then blowing someones head off with a shotgun.
The enemies are a bit weird though.
They're mostly Demons.
Not a concept i enjoyed too much, but you find a few human enemies in some sections too. The demons all have specific abilities, and there are major and minor.
The minor are the ones you might be able to slash to pieces in one or few hits, while the major can take a while to kill.
Of the minor demons, we have your usual run and hit you zombie. The radioactive that explode when you get near or shoot them. The shielders and the invisibles.
The shielders has to be the enemy i dreaded the most, not only do they block your attacks, they keep looking in your direction and you have to either throw them down, or hit the shield until it breaks. It can take a while and really breaks the flow of the game, when you're spinning around and killing litearlly everybody around you, except for them.
Of the major enemies, there are 3: The Warlord, The Charger, and the Shaman. The major are a bit more interesting, so i'll talk about them.
The shaman will summon and resurrect nearby enemies, and just keep doing this until you kill him. After hes around halfway dead, he will create a green unbreakable barrier, and summon some skeletons that flash with green colors. After you kill the skeletons, the shield breaks and you can finish him off.
The Warlord will enrage nearby eneies (Which is, make them darker, and make them more powerful. Enemies can also be enraged if you use abilities or powers near them, even if there isin't a warlord there) He will also try to smash you, a lot. So every few seconds, he will throw a really fast red line, and if you touch it, he will pull you to him, and he will smash the ground.
The final one is the charger. Hes simple, and kind of boring to be honest. He will charge you, you evade it near a wall. He hits the wall. You slice his back a few times. Rinse and repeat. It just takes so long to kill these guys, that the fun quickly dies from fighting them.
But of all enemies, the most interesting one is the bosses. There are a total of 3 Demon bosses, and they're all amazing to fight. They're HUGE, and the shadow realm is just right-out eyecandy. They are all very Zelda-ish, and its very fun.
All in all, if you have ever played Red steel 1 or 2, and enjoyed it. Or just want to enjoy a throwback to the old FPS with a mix of very interesting sword fighting, you should pick this game up.

My advice: PACE YOURSELF. Learn to control your sessions and it'll be a great game for you for a long time.

Don't get this game if you want an "oldie FPS." I think the game is really, really far off from anything that the original Shadow Warrior was about. In this regard, the game is horrible and disappointing, and I really did not find it enjoyable in a way that I'd find old FPS'es enjoyable.
The game feels like a modern shooter in one too many ways. Health is never an issue, maps are painfully linear with only the secrets (that 90% of the time only give boring EXP points instead of say, rare ammo or a neat, shiny gun) diverging for a few brief moments before you're back on the straight conga line. The design gets only just slightly more lively near the end of it, but I'd still call it nothing but a straightforward, plot point > stop in this room to fight > plot point game, more like a Serious Sam game than anything. There is never a lack of ammo or health either, so the game never feels like it's challenging the player in any way other than how well he can sidestep when he needs to run to heal.
The game suffers from the same issue the original had; After a certain point, it starts to repeat itself cheap and bad (the first episode in the original.) The redeeming thing about the new Shadow Warrior is that it actually feels quite a lot more playable past that "breaking point" (and I think the breaking point in the new SW is when you buy a certain upgrade for a certain weapon + upgrade a few talents and skills, resulting in only ever using the katana and that one specific gun; Guns past that point feel useless and powerless as well, the rocket launcher I only seriously used in one fight. ) That, plus a plot that I actually followed through (that's saying something seeing as I was expecting an old school FPS) makes this a game I actually enjoyed well enough to justify owning it.
Another thing I wanted to address was the humor; It has its moments, but I think that what Shadow Warrior did 20 years ago was still something that was new and fresh in everyones eyes compared to the influx of internet meme's polluting video games for a cheap workaround to having actual creative thought devoted to it. The new Shadow Warrior does not pitfall into abusing chewed up internet jokes, but the humor has a pretty obvious rhyme and reason that is only entertaining once in a while. The game would neither gain anything nor lose anything if it had the jokes removed.
Overall, the game is not going to satisfy your craving for an old school FPS. It will also not stand out as the most polished thing, what with most weapons and talents/skills/upgrades being plain out useless compared to others, some plot holes (a certain promise that never happened). It will give you a good, albeit rough around the edges story and modern gameplay that is still enjoyable, albeit very, VERY forgiving on the player.
A jolly good, swashbuckling good time.... but in all seriousness, buy it.

The gameplay feels fresh and its very enjoyable. The narrator tells you what to do and you follow his directions, or try to change the story by taking a different route. The narrator adapts to what you do through his dialouge as well as makes snarky hilarious comments towards you for not following him in the beginning. The more you change the narration the more he becomes frustrated and the more its noticable in the dialouge. No matter what you do, it seems the deveopers were planning on you being able to do that. In one instance you can glitch through a window to where you thought you had broke the game and exited the level, but nope. The narrator picks right up telling you "I bet you thought you could get out of here" "is this what you really want? is to leave?".
The game is however a little short but there are so many different endings some more complicated than others and some very hard to produce. This can keep you playing for long after, trying to see all the different endings and experience all the hilarious and clever lines the narrator has.
The graphics are average, but nothing to special. Its built on the Source Game Engine so think other source games such as half life 2, counter strike, etc.. Levels are well designed and their are lots of different areas to explore and check out, but first you must figure out how to get to them :).
The audio in this game is by far the best part. The narrator is hilarious and clever and will keep you smiling and laughing while you try to trip him up. The actor chosen to voice the narrator was a perfect pick in my opinion. His voice stuck in my head for days after.
The stanley parable filled my need for a fresh game. The clever game design allows for so many different endings that will keep it feeling enjoyable as you listen to the hilarious narrator try to keep up with you as you try to trip him up. If your looking for something that feels a little fresh and will give you a good laugh then this will satisfy that.

Feels more like a reskinned and -- to a degree -- watered down Hard Reset than successor to Shadow Warrior: enemies being bullet sponges and often thrown at you in hordes but their actual threat is pretty low, perhaps mostly due to the very useful and spammable quick dodge. I can't really fault it, though, Hard Reset was actually a pain to play without something similar since then it was a simple race to kill anything before it got to you. But I digress. Most enemies are melee-orientated, so as long as you dance around them you can quite easily slaughter them off without a knick and those that are ranged are, thankfully, projectile-based so you can also dodge them. The problem is that this is all there is to it. There isn't much variation to go on. Avoid the main of the horde and simply slash the edges to whittle them down because lord knows the guns you get are slow,♥♥♥♥♥♥weak and simply not suited to dealing with anything smaller than a barn due to horrendous inaccuracy. Exception to the crossbow since its practically the game-saving railgun.
And then you get the bosses which take all this and just ♥♥♥♥ it all up. You spend most of the game devoting points and crystals and money and whatever else to help deal with the hordes and then you're dropped into a room with a big bad mother with no choice but to keep your distance and chip away. Try your luck and all you get is the taste of your own ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as its forcefully pulled backwards up your oesophagus.
And those that have played/completed Hard Reset probably remember the fun-filled fight that was Atlas. Well, he is now a minotaur. Which you get to fight with a sword. Wonderful.
Arr..

Shadow Warrior stands as a testament to the fps genre that just because a series is old doesnt mean a person cant fill it with nice things and make a damn respectable game. this isnt your big brothers shaodw warrior, or your daddies. this is a modern take on what shadow warrior can be if given the tools and accessibility we have available in current era fps's and its the nail in the coffin for mainstream fps sp experiences. i shudder to think about picking up another call of duty or battlefield for their singleplayer or any other franchise that gets totted around a lot.
you play lo wang. a comic book collector hired by a rich buisnessman to claim an old sword from another collector. however things quickly fall apart as the demons from another plane of existence start spilling through the gaps in soace and time. and very quickly you are left to pickup the pieces, complete the sword, defeat those who would use the blade for evil, and close their path to the human world
visually the game is done well enough that their is little to complain, though i felt that at times lighting was relatively poor and your flashlight was not suited well for the task of illuminating anything. shadows on water, and destructible environments and enemies are awesome. other things like cloth and glass are also good. simply put flying wild hogs have made an above average visual game considering this is an old cryengine revision they are dealing with here.
the audio is also good. this feels lively and banter between the main characters can be funny or make u stop and comment yourself at times. but there are some parts where it falls a little flat or dull and their are some cliche moments but for everyone one of those their is normally a stereotype breaker and those often elft me feeling that maybe those down moments werent so bad after all. i can look past these faults, you might not.
combat.. where should i start. to put an analogy out there if CoD and battlefield are considered the pinnacle of fps combat; this is a cut above. simply put their is few games released on pc that have the other qualities this game does that do combat as well or slightly worse. the list is small i could probably riddle them off with one hand after thinking about it. the katana is your melee weapon and you have a variety of ranged weapons as well. all of which feel fun and exciting and encourage experimentation and have something for everyone. i myself found a lot to like in the sub machine guns and flamethrower. but others may enjoy the shotgun or rocket launcher more. to each their own and their is enough to spread the love.
level design is flawless, this is where shadow warrior feels the msot true to self with homages and references to the origional game by 3d realms, and lots of multi-pathing around areas, this makes the corridor shooter aspects of the game feel less confined and encourage you to go back and grab extra ammo or search for secret rooms or collectibles. and for this it gets an applause.
no for some downsides. at launch this game had lots of crash bugs. these have since been msotly rectified and for that the developers have my thanks, made the game more enjoyable. the games weapons also feel very udnerpowered at times. you will be left wanting more from your guns relying more on your sword to kill foes and this after a while takes the fun out of using what is perhaps its most novel weapon. furthermore some may see their use of rooms again and again in alter levels as lazy or poor taste. i dont see it that way but your welcome to think what you want.
all in all i highly recommend this game and strongly suggest that if you want to feel like your playing a first person shooter again and not having your hand held through a corridor while you grip an M4 with tired franchise one liners and cliche fight sequences passing by you. BUY THIS GAME, dont wait for a sale BUY IT NOW! lo wang reaches out and touches 5 hearts.. out of 5 XXXXX/XXXXX

There was a lot of skepticism surrounding the news that 3D Realms' 1997 shooter Shadow Warrior would be re-imagined for 2013, not least because the original game faded into obscurity compared with other Build engine games and was really remembered only for its often tasteless humour. Happily, Polish developer Flying Wild Hog went back to the original and rather than slavishly remaking it, did a wonderful job in taking from it what worked and removing or radically re-imagining what didn't. The end result is a hectic, gorgeous-looking shooter in a classic style with just enough of a modern sensibility to make it feel fresh. The most crucial aspect of the game's success? It has what the classic '90s shooters had and what modern ones very rarely possess - personality.

Although 2009's Arma II set a high standard for the all-purpose military simulator, its buggy single-player campaign held it back from achieving its full potential. In contrast, Arma II: Operation Arrowhead, its stand-alone expansion, boasts all the beauty, realism, and action of the original and none of the game-breaking bugs. Improving upon its predecessor in almost every way, Arrowhead introduces a new setting, new weapons, and new adventures to a great military sandbox
Much like its predecessor, the primary selling point of Operation Arrowhead is its setting, which swaps the thick forests of Chernarus in favor of the vast mountain ranges, boundless steppes, and parched deserts of the fictitious Central Asian country of Takistan. Both the natural landscapes and the various human settlements, including the teeming capital city of Zargabad that notably boasts a gorgeous Persian-style mosque decorated with mosaic tiles, are characterized by meticulous attention to detail that reveals the story of the place. For instance, the mountains are filled with quaint, well-worn trails, while outside the prayer room of the mosque, you'll find the shoes of the worshippers within. However, the tranquil beauty of Takistan hides a nation in turmoil. The Saddam Hussein-esque Colonel Aziz (who has a penchant for gaudy artwork and carries a golden gun) and his military junta have launched an invasion of their oil-rich neighbors in Karzeghistan. Not amused by Aziz's tomfoolery, the United States has vowed to overthrow the adventurous junta and has sent in the military to do the job. You take on the role of several different US soldiers during the course of the campaign, whose combined efforts will ultimately lead you to victory. Along the way, you'll encounter Takistani military forces operating T-34 tanks and other aging Russian military hardware; hostile, pro-government militias; UN peacekeepers; and antigovernment rebels who will join your cause.
While Arrowhead's campaign can't match the play time, freedom, and decision-making possibilities in Arma II, it surpasses the original by providing a refined, bug-free experience. And, although it loses a bit of the historical backstory of Arma II, Arrowhead makes up for it by leaving out the boring exposition and dropping you straight into the action. Right from the beginning, you'll be occupied with a diverse array of missions and objectives. For example, in one mission, you get to capture a mine with the aid of a friendly militia, search for missing hostages, find and disarm a bomb (using a code with exotic Takistani numerals), transfer control of the mine to the United Nations, and, finally, man a dilapidated Soviet antiaircraft battery to stop enemy MiGs from bombing a rebel village. Other missions range from classic, brutally difficult Arma infantry combat to sequences where you command infantry fighting vehicles, armored personnel carriers, tanks, and helicopters.
In contrast to the punishing realism of even the easiest difficulty levels in Arma II, Arrowhead offers a more approachable point of entry for new players, with its easier "regular" difficulty (veteran and expert difficulties are as hard as ever) and thorough tutorials. However, if you're a newbie, the coddling ends quickly because unlike in Arma II, where you spend several missions as a grunt, Arrowhead puts you in command of a mechanized squad in the second mission. Even after playing the tutorials, it can be hard to remember all the controls, and nothing is more frustrating than accidentally ordering your platoon to exit its vehicles in the midst of a tank battle. Thankfully, with time and practice, you'll improve your leadership skills, but even great tutorials and diligent attempts to practice will turn only a select few players into master helicopter pilots. It's difficult to stay airborne for more than a limited time before crashing unceremoniously into a minaret. Mercifully, you don't have to complete the campaign's helicopter mission to continue. Even after failing, in the next mission, you get the option to rescue the pilot, who apparently survived a 200mph collision with an unfortunate mountain goat or whatever gruesome end you inevitably caused him to suffer.
You'll find an abundance of novel weapons, vehicles, and equipment throughout the game, which provide exciting new ways to liberate (or terrorize) Takistan. These include World War II-era relics, such as Soviet T-34 tanks and British Lee Enfield bolt-action rifles, as well as modern, cutting-edge toys like unmanned aerial vehicles and thermal weapon sights. These are particularly awesome because they use infrared radiation to help you identify potential threats, such as vehicles, human beings, and rabbits. Since pro-US militiamen give off the same amount of heat as Takistani soldiers, it is ill advised to shoot at every human-shaped target you stumble across using this tool.
If you don't get your fill of gadgets and guns in the campaign, every weapon, vehicle, item, and character is available in both the editor and the armory. And, if you have Arma II as well, its content is also available. In the editor, your opportunities for mayhem are infinite, ranging from detailed scenarios with objectives and triggers for the experts to simple skirmishes that are quickly concocted by laymen. Meanwhile, Arrowhead's armory offers up challenges to test your skill with the new equipment, vehicles, and characters. Although putting Eurowoman1 through an obstacle course or trying to set speed records in a T-34 can be mildly amusing, these diversions don't have the editor's lasting appeal.
Stand-alone single-player missions are another highlight in Arrowhead. One of the most exhilarating missions puts you in command of a sniper team charged with eliminating a high-ranking Takistani officer while he visits a military base. With only 10 minutes before his arrival by helicopter, you have to cover a kilometer's distance, sneak past enemy patrols, identify the target (hint: the man everyone salutes) using only thermal sights as a guide, "neutralize" him, and escape. With several varied operations to choose from, these missions even further extend the single-player experience.
Although Arrowhead inherits a few annoyances from the original, even those are much improved. Most notably, the artificial intelligence still has some driving issues and can cause traffic jams and bizarre wrecks, but AI drivers are now much more conscientious about flattening friendlies. This is a major improvement over Arma II, in which it wasn't uncommon to be run over by an allied tank that would brake for a clutch of chickens but not for you. Arma's characteristic arrested, monotone chatter returns in Arrowhead, but it sounds a bit more natural this time. Anyway, how can you be angry at your stuttering ally for warning you about that "tank…T72…at…3 o'clock…50 meters?"
Multiplayer in Arrowhead can be great fun, but little has changed here from Arma II. Whether you are playing a cooperative scenario, engaging in conventional deathmatches, or playing the real-time-strategy-reminiscent warfare mode, hopping into a random Internet game is like being plunged into an unpredictable maelstrom. Some servers feature crazy original scenarios with unclear objectives, some are role-playing servers where you are apparently just supposed to explore the level and will be kicked if you kill someone, and some still are cooperative matches populated by uncooperative people too busy scurrying about the map without any discernable purpose to bother communicating with you. However, when you actually get a group together that halfway knows what it's doing and coordinates via voice chat, then you are in for an exceptional experience. Game Showcase-
