This game is an absolute must.
Actually, no. To call it a mere game would be an insult. This can be better likened to literature in game form.
Despite its minimalist mechanic construction, it is captivating and utterly hilarious, and at the same time, a meaningful commentary on the nature of gaming.
Or it could just be a really funny walking simulator.
GET IT.
EDIT: Actually, no. Allow me to amend this review. Or just skip all the way to the end. Makes no difference to me.
From the very moment you reach the menu, you are greeted with a curious view - a double of what you see on your monitor, on another monitor. What you do is mirrored in that monitor, telling you that you ARE that unseen person behind the monitor at that computer.
Much like many who play MMOs or FPSs online, until they decide to reveal themselves to their friends or the community.
It is both a commentary, parody, satire, and visual essay.
I believe this game should be put forth for consideration on every gamer's list for "Must play" status. Oh sure, you could simply watch someone else play, but then you're not really making a choice, are you? You're watching someone else make choices, which detracts from the game experience itself.
Or does it? Does knowing what will happen change the decisions you will make in the game? Well, if the game is to be believed, no - indicating either curiousity, or a need to rebel against a seemingly omnipotent voice telling you to do things.
Not unlike religion. Listen to the voice, and good things happen. Disobey at your own risk.
Hell, this is probably a game that might, with enough prodding, even be featured as a game to be taught in classes.
For me to write about all the things it comments on here would simply be a waste. (That too, is touched upon hilariously.)
TL;DR: A bunch of literary analysis of a video game mumo jumbo. STILL, GET THE GAME.

If it's artsy you're looking for, this is the best it gets. It's really interesting for a game to question itself so much, and to make you question the game in the process. While this does lead to some jokes said by the narrarator, it's anything but mere humor. While playing a video game, are you choosing to, say, shoot a portal at the wall, or is it simply because the game tells you that the portal goes there? This whole idea of "free will" has been thrown around a lot, but this game stretches it like dough- what freedom does a video game actually give you? Are you bound to doing only what the game tells you to, and are you, Stanley, really doing what you want to do in your life? Can you simply resist the narrarator, or the commands that pop up on your screen?
Play The Stanley Parable, and you will find out.

A parable is defined as a succinct story which illustrates one or more
instructive lessons or principles using analogy. The Stanley Parable is a
narration based game told from a first person perspective .  Through the eyes
of the main character, Stanley, you are taken on many bizarre, twisting
adventures  narrated by sarcastic, hilarious inner dialogue that explore the
meaning of life, and ferns though parables.
The gameplay is fairly basic.  As you progress through the levels, it
offers choices that affect your current and future playthroughs. The level
design is layer upon layer of rooms that seem to twist in on themselves to
confuse your sense of direction and add to the story.  The story never truly
ends, until the player decides it does.
There is not a lot of depth in the game, but there is a lot of choice.
The story plus the narrations is entertaining, amusing, and charming, and worth
a few hours of play through.  It plays on our natural curiosity, making us
wonder what there is yet to discover.  The end is not the end

A parable is defined as a succinct story which illustrates one or more
instructive lessons or principles using analogy. The Stanley Parable is a
narration based game told from a first person perspective .  Through the eyes
of the main character, Stanley, you are taken on many bizarre, twisting
adventures  narrated by sarcastic, hilarious inner dialogue that explore the
meaning of life, and ferns though parables.
The gameplay is fairly basic.  As you progress through the levels, it
offers choices that affect your current and future playthroughs. The level
design is layer upon layer of rooms that seem to twist in on themselves to
confuse your sense of direction and add to the story.  The story never truly
ends, until the player decides it does.
There is not a lot of depth in the game, but there is a lot of choice.
The story plus the narrations is entertaining, amusing, and charming, and worth
a few hours of play through.  It plays on our natural curiosity, making us
wonder what there is yet to discover.  The end is not the end

The game can be "beaten" in five to ten minutes but you could play for hours exploring every choice and ending possible, including a few which are ridiculously hard to find. Maybe $15 dollars seems like a lot for a game of this length but, as a comparison, you could buy a good novel or movie for the same price, spend the same time reading or watching it and get the same kind of artistic value.

THE STANLEY PARABLE is essentially a mod, so as long as you know what you're getting yourself into ahead of time, you shouldn't encounter much frustration. Like DEAR ESTHER and GONE HOME before it, whether or not THE STANLEY PARABLE can be called a "game" is open to interpretation, but what makes TSP different from the aforementioned titles is the humor. The narrator is really the only reason to "play" the "game", but for me, it was reason enough. I laughed a lot while taking my (extremely short) way through the sterile corporate environment, so I definitely enjoyed it. I would, however, suggest you wait until it's discounted to $5 or less before taking it for a spin.

A game of complete parody, the Stanley Parable is something different.
This game was something I didn't know what would happen first starting it up. Trying the demo before initaially buying the game, it didn't clarify what exatly this game's theme was, what you did in it. I watched the trailer for it, still was completely lost on the premise of this game. But me even trying to understand this game was the real problem: it's not a game meant to be understood.
Rather, it is a game that makes you see the unexpected. This game is to deviate from what a video game's norm usually is, and makes you see a new reality of what a game is to an extent. Being a huge part of the game, the Narrorator, he instructs what the game is supposed to be, the path that you follow, what you can do, but at the same time letting you make small decisions along the way. And that's how a game usually is, following the rules, doing what you're told by that narrortor floating in some sort of devolper limbo. But that's what makes this game so intriguing. You CAN break the set path.
Not entirely break the set path, but explore from trial and error. Seeing what happens, how the enviornment around you reacts, and progressing from there. But what also makes this game interesting is how not only it's different from the meta established by video games today, it makes fun of it. It's witty humor and fascinating story it tells is why I'd recommend it to anyone interested in something they haven't experienced before.

The game is derisive commentary on game design and why things are built the way they are. Can be a bit prententious, but it seems to be intentional and ironic as it mocks "art games" that set out to be games after art, and not the other way around. The incredibly limited gameplay (which I usually hate and find unneccessarily crippling) is coupled with a narrator that consistently talks about choice. If it isn't clear that the design of the game mechanics and the narration are supposed to be linked at first (I did not initially see them to be), there are a few segments which are really eye opening to what the game is trying to convey. In essence: it clubs you in the kneecap then talks to you about it so you can understand what having legs really means in other games. Worth a try, but maybe not worth the price tag. I got it on sale for less than $10, though, so I was incredibly satisfied with my purchase.

You’re sitting in your office, doing nothing in particular, when you realize there’s nobody around. You walk down the hall, all the other cubicles are empty. There is a Narrator doing the narration thing, talking about how you’re looking around and don’t see anyone, and thus you decide to go to the meeting room just in case everyone is there. But you didn’t decide that, as a player. The Narrator simply provided a context for why you would continue down the hall. You reach a set of doors you must choose between. The Narrator informs you that the left one goes to the meeting room, and it’s obviously the one you will take. The one to the right isn’t important.
Which one do you choose? Why do you choose it? Let’s see what happens when you do pick one and follow through.
This simple opening to The Stanley Parable is the heart of the game. It’s all about the choices you make, but that’s a gross oversimplification. It’s difficult to talk about the game without spoiling anything, since most of what makes the Stanley Parable a parable, lay in your own interactions with it. You’ll come across many choices. The Narrator will talk about a great many things. Like a complex movie with many plot threads, the Stanley Parable needs to be replayed several times for full effect.

Perhaps this isn't often described as a terrifying experience, however, that is certainly what it was to me after a time. Like a sort of House of Leaves of games. It touches on some very deep existential question in regard to what free will is and what it is to even exist. Impressive stuff indeed.

The Stanley Parable is something of an experiment with a heavy theme sorrounding personal choice and narrative that is cleverly written and often has ways of making the player experience different emotions, but as a video game itself, your money may be better spent elsewhere.
Essentially, you are Stanley, someone who leads a boring life in a boring office, and the story is about you essentially breaking the routine. The story is narrated by Kevan Brighting, who does a stellar job bringing personality to the story and can really turn the wheels with his ability to evoke emotion and the way he speaks is like it really is him talking to the player, which can often bring some hilarious results. The Stanley Parable does offer some interesting things to say about life, and making the most of it. Stanley seems to represent our own disatisfaction with life, or our accomodation to the hum-drum of life, working for cash, eating, sleeping, and perhaps even social expectations. The game challenges us to ignore the rules presented to us, but you also have the choice to follow the narrator's story teling.
The office you walk through will sometimes change depending on the path you follow, and will sometimes (but not always) lead to a new path to discover.
However, while all of this is going on, the gameplay itself is fairly shallow. Your only objective is to walk and choose to follow/unfollow directions, and sometimes the end of the path is fairly disatisfactory. The more play throughs with this game also means you become aware of paths that offer some choices, but there's also some that offer no actual choice-they lock you into one of the endings.
The game is essentially a choose your own adventure storybook-at first it will wow and dazzle us with the sense of adventure, but once you've chosen the option you didn't choose before, the game's charm really dissipitates into a dulling walkathon with a funny voice.

The Stanley Parable is something of an experiment with a heavy theme sorrounding personal choice and narrative that is cleverly written and often has ways of making the player experience different emotions, but as a video game itself, your money may be better spent elsewhere.
Essentially, you are Stanley, someone who leads a boring life in a boring office, and the story is about you essentially breaking the routine. The story is narrated by Kevan Brighting, who does a stellar job bringing personality to the story and can really turn the wheels with his ability to evoke emotion and the way he speaks is like it really is him talking to the player, which can often bring some hilarious results. The Stanley Parable does offer some interesting things to say about life, and making the most of it. Stanley seems to represent our own disatisfaction with life, or our accomodation to the hum-drum of life, working for cash, eating, sleeping, and perhaps even social expectations. The game challenges us to ignore the rules presented to us, but you also have the choice to follow the narrator's story teling.
The office you walk through will sometimes change depending on the path you follow, and will sometimes (but not always) lead to a new path to discover.
However, while all of this is going on, the gameplay itself is fairly shallow. Your only objective is to walk and choose to follow/unfollow directions, and sometimes the end of the path is fairly disatisfactory. The more play throughs with this game also means you become aware of paths that offer some choices, but there's also some that offer no actual choice-they lock you into one of the endings.
The game is essentially a choose your own adventure storybook-at first it will wow and dazzle us with the sense of adventure, but once you've chosen the option you didn't choose before, the game's charm really dissipitates into a dulling walkathon with a funny voice.
I can't tell you what to do with your money, but three hours was about as much as I could take from this experience before I let it collect digital dust in my library. But for $14.99, you are bound to find something much more worth your while.

"This is the story of a man named Stanley. Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was employee number 427. Employee Number 427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in room 427, and he pushed buttons on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what Employee 427 did every day of every month and every year, and although others might have considered it soul-rending, Stanley relished every moment that the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Stanley. Something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No-one had showed up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say Hi. Never in all his years at the company had this happened - this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong. Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office."

I had a lot of expectations going into the Stanley Parable; left and right I was seeing praise about how this game was a flawless parody on the state of the game industry and it's approach to game narrative etc. etc. When I first started it up and began "playing" I definitely enjoyed it. Just in the first 30-45 minutes of play I was genuinely laughing at the commentary and observations of typical video game tropes and I can't remember the last time a game actually made me laugh.
That being said, I don't think the praise was entirely merited; I think the bigger draw to this game is the fact that someone has FINALLY done something interesting, unique and that naturally draws you into playing more through shear enjoyment rather than levels/achievements/leader boards. I do think everyone who enjoys games should give The Stanley Parable a go, not because it's a flawless 10/10, 99 metacritic, GOTY masterpiece, but because The Stanley Parable pulls out a primal, inner child-like curiosity from deep inside you and let's you have a type of fun that somehow feels like an experience we all had lost in gaming long ago.
A perfect game? No. An experience to remember as the gaming industry continues to grow an evolve? Without a doubt, absolutely.

A very interesting take on dynamic storytelling. A first person storytelling game about an office worker following (or completely defying) an obvervant narrator. Taking a silly but creative spin on adventure game narration, this game gets multiple story options right. The choices you make in this game are not explicit, and become very creative. Your moments of choice range from two open doors to refusing to leave a broom closet. With so many choices, you play through the game more times than you care to count, to the point where the narrator even takes notice of your repetitious playing. Every time you play you'll discover a new ending or voice clip, making it worthwhile to play with friends or on your own. The only downside is that once you've gotten most of the endings, you'll grow bored with going through the opening segment over and over. Still, an interesting indie title that rewards creative play with brilliant and hilarious narration.

The Stanley Parabe isn't so much a 'game' as it is an experience. Most games have storylines with gradually ramping mechanics and new enemy types introduced as you progress. You won't find any of that here. Instead, you are simply a man named Stanley listening to the disembodied voice of the narrator telling a story about what you're doing. Many people have expressed concerns with the game being scary, having jump scares, creepy environments, etc, but this game isn't focused on any of those things. This game is focused on the experience of walking around in an office building wondering where your coworkers went. There are no real jump scares, or intentionally creepy environments, and the narrator isn't really out to kill you. Instead, this game is a witty and interactive commentary on gaming, and lots of different cliches and commonalities we see within them, and ourselves. While some parts of the game can be unsettling (only ever so slightly in my opinion) it remains fairly lighthearted and sometimes intentionally irritating. It is true that this game has multiple endings depending on what combination of choices and pathways you decide to take, but it's more about the journey then it is the destination.

If I told you exactly why you should play this game, I would be ruining most of the point.
Just, if you're into story and exploration, and you want to play something unique, play The Stanley Parable.
If you're not sure, play the demo. It's an experience all its own.

How to describe the Stanely Parable?
'Worthy attempt', is one way to put it.
Now, don't get me wrong -- I quite enjoyed the Stanley Parable, and I still like puttering around the office and seeing what I can get up to 'this time'.  The Narrator (with a voice that's
reminiscent of Steven Fry) will guide you on your chosen path, or fall into despair as Stanley forges his own destiny and totally de-rails his storytelling efforts.
Unforunately, every positive experience must, by definition, have a downside; here, then, are what I consider the two largest downsides of
:
1) It's woefully brief.  While I enjoyed following the various paths through the various rooms, none of the paths were more than ten or twenty minutes long, and they all played out in essentally the same way.  The layout of the map only changes superficially, and (since the game only opens certain doors at key points in a particular path) the game's explorable area is quite limited in size.
2) There's simply not very much to
beyond following the pre-determined story paths.  There are very few props to interact with, and once you've set yourself on a particular course, you're shepherded down a (relatively) fixed path to your fate.  There are precious few points where the player's decisions have any tangible impact beyond going up the stairs or down the stairs, or through one of two doors.
If you're the type of person that would understand what the authors were trying to achieve with
, you'll definitely enjoy it; it has some snappy dialogue, an intriguing premise, and just enough variety to kill a lazy Saturday morning.
If you're looking for a deep, thought-provoking experience...unfortunately, you probably won't find it here.  While it makes a worthy effort at deconstructing the narrative process, and gleefully thumbs its nose at literary tropes in general,
simply doesn't dig deep enough or long enough to produce any fresh insights into the nature of the genre.

A uniquely psychological deconstruction of story telling, but too slight on content to really warrant a full-price purchase.
---
The Stanley Parable is Alice's rabbit hole into the weirder side of video game narrative, so tightly scripted that it feels as if the story is actually being created uniquely to your playthrough. The Stanley Parable (PC)
In Synchronex’s own, confusing words…
Is this a review? Is this not a review? Is this simply words written on a page that you have chosen to read? If you answered any of these questions then it is my honour to welcome you to The Stanley Parable from Galactic Cafe.
Enter employee number 427, otherwise known as Stanley. Stanley is for the most part an unknown, although we do know (or can at least assume) he is a human working in a mysteriously empty office pushing buttons, that’s about it. The story itself is driven by the Narrator, who is constantly trying to move the game along by means of story telling (duh) and peculiar commentary. The fourth wall of cinema is completely ripped apart and a fifth wall is created in it’s place. The Stanley Parable takes one look at “non-linear” and completely laughs it’s own♥♥♥♥♥off while still pulling off the illusion of a non-linear feel.  The “game” as it were is more of a visual narrative playing out and you’re kind of just there for the ride, so there’s not much in the way of “gameplay”. The only influence the player has is by means of choice. Do you take the recommended door? or do you rebel and take the other one? Each and every choice brings drastic consequence and immediate alterations to the game. Choice is your powerful and only tool.
But is it all for nothing? Here’s a minor spoiler, the game has a heck of alot of pathways to multiple endings as a result of all these choices you make. Each and every one is brilliantly written and an absolute joy to experience. The set-out of the game as a whole is crazy-level complicated, you will find yourself thinking you’ve somehow been dropped in Groundhog Day with Bill Murray.
The Stanley Parable is a smart game. It will provide a set narrative for you to unknowingly alter at every single turn. You can play the game, you can break the game, you can be the game. It will have you laughing in delight at the slightly dark humour, it will have you gasping in sheer awe at the wonders hidden inside, it will even have you question your very being, and you will be left with one last burning question…Is it all just a Parable?
Story: 10/10. Perfect.
Gameplay: 8/10. - Very few actual “interactive” sequences but overall very good.
Audio: 9/10. Brilliant, the Narrator is perfectly portrayed and small musical sections complete the set.
Graphics: 9/10. The Source engine, simple and crisp.
Overall: 9/10.
Similar to: Portal (PC).
Personal comment: “Rips apart the fourth wall”.

It's for the kind of person who likes talking about philosophy with their friends - and you'll want to talk about the Stanley Parable with your friends, too, if you're that kind of person.
All of this makes the Stanley Parable sound very dry, but more often, it's hilarious, or confusing, or provocative. Sometimes, the Stanley Parable will make you feel bad about yourself for playing the Stanley Parable. Different people will find that different parts of the game affect them more personally, but any way you slice it, it's something special.

Clever satire-No.  Engaging game play-No.  Some transcendent philosophical experience-No.  A money grab fueled by wide spread marketing and fanboy media coverage-yes.  The illusion of choice programmed in such a tiny closed loop of a game is not any type of meaninful choice at all.  The gamer has nothing invested, no time, no community, no purpose or goals.  If you've played any type of sand box game there's really absolutely no need to buy this thing...your gaming experiences have already evolved past any of the cute little points the story is aimed at without even trying.  Try again when enough development effort is spent on this theme to make players spend more than  single digit hours playing it.  Seriously, go see a movie it's more memorable and a better value for your money.  There's no surprises here.

Well, first of all I have quite a few thoughts about this game that should come to be noticed - Wait...oh boy...
SECRETS FOR PRESIDENT 2016
It was real in my mind.
If Stephen Fry and that guy with the crazy hair from the Ancient Aliens show had a baby, and that baby then made a game, it would be this game. The Stanley Parable.

I rate this game 8/8. This game is simultaneously the best game I've played in a very long time, and not a game at all. It is an interactive novel of the highest calibre. Whatever you expect going into this... this... experience, you'll be wrong.
Depending on your choices - and believe me, there are lots of those - the game can end in one of a dozen different ways. From the instant Whiteboard Ending to the lengthy Countdown Ending.
It's a game you will have to restart a number of times to experience to its full. I've played it for five hours straight and I'm nowhere near experiencing the whole story, let alone starting to explore and finding other things. Each restart, things change: sometimes subtly, sometimes entirely. Mugs changing colour, cubicles becoming offices, computers becoming pencil sharpeners, clues to extra bits appearing and disappearing, a weird screen that says "awaiting input"... things can and do change, every time.
A playthrough video isn't going to cut it with this one. Play it for yourself. And play the demo too, it's really funny!

This is not a game, it is a philosophy with an interface and a narrator-- an experience masked as a game.  More experiences could use narrators, especially one as genuinely caring as this one.  Perhaps there would be less misery in the world if we each had a caring narrator guiding us through the trevails of life, even with the ultimate knowledge that each choice remains ours.  I cannot recommend this experience more highly, just as I cannot recommend life more highly.  Life is awesome, just as non-conformity is conformity.

The graphics and sound are mediocre, the narrative is long and up to tedious levels, and the gameplay is underwhelming. Can it even be called a game? Some say it's a meta game or a piece of art, I just think it's smart at times but not very intellectual. Does it teach a moral, a truth or a spiritual lesson, as per definition of the word "parable"? I did not learn anything myself, other than that this Parable is not for me. At least Kevan Brighting's voice is soothing.
3/10 and yes 24 hours of my "played" hours are for getting the last achievement (of course I was doing something else). I figured out most endings by myself.
Weird game. The voice acting is superb. Had a lot of fun discovering the different endings.

The Stanley Parable advertises itself on the basis of choice, but players will very quickly find that it contains very little choice. It is, however, quirky, witty, and self-referential in its style. It's a game one plays for 2-3 hours (enjoying the humour of the narrator, its art style, etc.) before becoming bored with it and realising its distinct lack of any replay value once the majority of its endings have been discovered. I do intend to keep playing it, but only in order to unlock all the endings. The Stanley Parable is a game one should play, but only buy if it is on offer.

If you enjoy thought-provoking games, please get The Stanley Parable: it is a remarkable masterpiece.
In terms of superficial appeal, The Stanley Parable has little to offer. The game environment is a bleak, plain office setting. Your character explores the office without much direct interaction with items. You are alone; there are no NPCs. There are no quests. There is no levelling up, and no action.
On the surface.
Beyond that unremarkable shell lies a truly amazing tale of self-examination, driven by a narrator that is at times funny, at times rude or aloof, at others heart-breakingly pitiful and endearing.
Playing The Stanley Parable is ultimately like enjoying a fine wine: it is a layered, subtle progression towards an end that is different with every taste. It's like slogging through a long book only to discover a marvellous conclusion that redefines your views.
The Stanley Parable is the only game I have ever played that made me seriously question whether I should stop gaming or continue. And I love it whole-heartedly for leading me down that weird and wonderful path.

And then Stanley wrote a review of the game, to tell the world just how much he liked it.
And Stanley was happy.

Verdict: there are two doors, Buy and Don't Buy. You already picked the Buy one, you just don't know it yet.
I'm not sure what I can say about The Stanley Parable that hasn't somehow been said already. It's... different.
No cutting-edge GPU-frying sparkly shiny graphics here: it's a pretty standard Source-engine FPS type environment, minus the S. No need for the S, since there is no enemies trying to dispatch you or in need of dispatching. No enemies, other than your own choices that is. And maybe the Narrator. Or not?
If you ever find yourself watching a movie and desperately yelling at the characters to do something different than what they are about to do, to avoid the cliché choices, to ignore the obvious plots... Stanley is here to actually let you steer away from what he is 'expected' to do. A multitude of paths to follow, each with their own result.
Whether that is in his favour or not is for you and Stanley to find out. Together. Take that Buy door. Go mash some buttons now.
DISCLAIMER: there is no cake here. No arrows in the knee either. We have Endings though. Gotta try them all.

The Stanley Parable is an interesting hybrid of satire, philosophy, and narratology which pokes fun at everything from games to storytelling to The Stanley Parable itself. It is layered with references to other games and pop culture, both subtle and obvious, and is a textbook example of what "meta" entertainment looks like.
The writing and voice acting are quite humorous, of course, but can also be surprisingly thought-provoking, and even sad. The game walks a fine tonal line between absurdist humor and dystopian despair, but ultimately succeeds because it manages never to take itself too seriously. Fans of films like "Brazil" will be right at home playing this game.
The gameplay boils down to a series of mostly binary choices (left or right, up or down, flee or stand your ground, etc.) which result in radically different outcomes. After experiencing a given outcome, you generally restart in the same place and try again. The controls are limited to the movement keys and an "interact" key. The game even has an achievement which emphasizes the fact that you can't jump. Once you've explored all the different outcomes the game has to offer, the replay value is limited, and even before that point, you're bound to get a little tired of restarting in the same area over and over again, try as the developers might to keep it fresh.
Nonetheless, The Stanley Parable left a good taste in my mouth, so to speak. I'm still thinking about some of the philosophical questions it posed, and I felt compelled to share it with others to see how they would react to it and what choices they would make. I firmly believe this game will (and probably already has) make an excellent teaching aid for courses on Game Design, Philosophy, and Narratology. It's also a lot of fun to play!
Pros:
- Excellent writing
- Excellent voice acting
- Thought-provoking
- Funny, at times even Hilarious
Cons:
- Very short (took me about 3 hours)
- Very simple controls
- Repetition can get tedious

For those suspicious that there is more to life than being a drone among a colony of worker-bee's, this game might be for you. That is, of course, assuming you think the missing splendor of your life is a videogame. Whatever might be the case, from life affirmations to an important shift in perspective, The Stanley Parable will make you laugh and then make you cry when you realize it's content mirrors the nightmarish existence shared by so many. Playing as Stanley, you'll be forcing him out of his accepted routine into foreign and beautiful landscapes such as the office break room, thrusting him into such great heights as his bosses office where yet even more surprises await. Expect the unexpected, the outlandish and the sobering. This has to be one of my favourite games I've ever played. The mod was brilliant, and this only improves on the formula. A game unlike any other, and probably unlike any game to come. If there ever is a game that replicates this one it will most likely be terrible because of the absolutely unique nature of this game.
It's funny, charming, sometimes creepy and most of all intriguing. You can sprint to the simplest ending in about 5 minutes, but there is actually about 5 hours of content here. There are so many endings and secrets; even after exploring everything I could possibly think of, the wiki revealed I had still completely missed quite a few.
I'm tired of hearing this refereed to as a “non-game” or a “walking simulator.” There are games that could reasonably argued to deserve such a title (Dear Esther, for example) but games like Proteus and The Stanley Parable are defiantly undeserving of this label. Exploration, discovery and the choices you make are far more important then actual mechanics of moving around. And The Stanley Parable in particular actually has distinct narratives you can follow. It's a game.
This game isn't for everyone, but it's definitely for me. As long as you know what kind this game ISN'T (puzzle, adventure, shooter etc.) before playing, you'll have a wonderful and memorable experience.

This game feels incomplete. In fact this is a selling point of the game- the fact that ‘it never ends.’ But that’s just the problem.
Games simulate achievement, the more you achieve in VR the more you enjoy the game. In the Stanley parable, this entire premise is made fun of in an ironic satire on gaming in general.
The art of game design allows real choices to be taken within the flow of a well told story, this game had no real story and no real choices! Play through after play though I felt unsatisfied and was actually made to feel uncomfortable by the game’s ‘loose ends’ and chaotic nature. It seems this is what the game creator wanted to achieve.
In all fairness, my brother seemed to find the game very entertaining, and he enjoyed the ‘unique’ nature of the game. I can understand why this will be appealing to gamers who are looking for something radically different, but I must say that after giving this game a fair shot it just didn’t work for me, and it may not work for you.

Another interesting "experience", rather than a proper game. My definition of a philosophical deconstruction of a video game. You play as Stanley, a hapless office worker, left alone in his rather eerie workplace. The main aim of the game, is that there is no aim.
Rather you do what you want, pushed only by the dry witted tongue of a sharp commentator, Follow his command, or don't. The choice is yours. With over two dozen endings, the sheer enjoyment of this game is trying to find them all, whether making a left turn, or right, going upstairs or down, or locking yourself in a small room just to see what happens. In the Stanley Parable, the choice is yours.

Despite playing for little over and hour, I have completed the game several times (a single session might take 20-40 minutes depending on how much you wander, aimlessly reading the clever writing on the walls). The game is the "This is Spinal Tap" of its genre, a mockumentary in a sense, plus the narrators British so there that in common as well.
Well worth the price.

I have maintained the notion for a number of years that video games are pieces of art, just as viable as books, paintings, and sculptures--in some ways more so.  There are games that are eyeball-poppingly beautiful, of course, and games that make your brain cells implode--looking at you, Crysis 3 and Bioshock Infinite--but I have never before found a game that really made the player delve into their own psyche, a game that surpassed the boundaries of common narative functions and made the player the true star of the show.
Thus enters this little game.  What can you do?  Walk around.  Sometimes, you interact with an object or two.  The only other being present is the brilliantly voiced narator.   Mostly, you walk, listen, walk some more, and listen some more.
But, oh, that's the beauty of it.  Forget "gaming" mechanics, forget all the bells and whistles.  This game exists to get in your mind, where all the real action occurs.  It is a stunningly deep and riotously funny condiut for some of the most incredible glimpses of human nature I've had the pleasure of witnessing--via game or other media.  The Stanley Parable is a wonderful play for anyone with a sense of humor and a pension for self-examination.  This is a game about you--your importance, and your dispensibility, but even more so, about... well, I can't really say, lest I run the risk of spoiling the fun.  Pick this gem up.  10/10.

The Stanley Parable is a game about possibilities. Every time you restart the game, you enter a parallel universe where everything is (almost) the same except for which actions the player takes, among a few other random variables (I.E. whether the floor is covered in papers). The game's sole purpose is to examine the very nature of storytelling in video games, pointing out just how "fake" the illusion of choice is, and laughing at the player for thinking they have some semblance of control over each predefined story branch.
It's literally impossible to go into further detail without spoiling
about the game. There's no real gameplay to spoil - hell, the player can't even jump. The only thing you can do is walk around, push buttons, and choose whether to go left or right based on the narrator's dialogue. Everything else that matters about this game is the ways in which the game sets up certain expectations and then subverts the hell out of them in some spectacularily ballsy ways. I'm honestly amazed that there
an ending where the game crashes to desktop.
I don't care who you are or what you're interested in. All I know is that if you call yourself a gamer, you need to play this game. For the love of whatever-your-diety-of-choice-is, just play this game. You won't regret it.

If you ever read books you may have heard of a "choose your own adventure" style of books in which the reader is the main character. As the reader progresses through the book they will come across decisions on how to continue in the story, and then be prompted to turn to a specific page in order to make that particular decision.
The Stanley Parable is a lot like that. It's a choose your own adventure story with a series of potentially interconnecting stories. The amount of effort put in to creating a lot of dialogue for the narrator grants the potential to hear different narration even on playthroughs of the same story path. Just like the choose your own adventure books, this game is simply what you make of the story you're presented with.
If you like decisions and interconnected stories with different outcomes, this is certainly a great game along this exact genre.

I think this is one of those few titles that really make you start to think about what a game actually is. And to be quite honest, I think that's a beautiful thing. With terms like "Triple-A" starting to define the success of a game before it even comes out, and stellar games like Thief getting unwarranted mediocre reviews, it's great to see a title be all like, "nah brah, I'm gonna do my thing."
The Stanley Parable really makes you think, and not in a "I must solve this puzzle to advance the story" kind of thinking. The Stanley Parable is trying to teach you something. Hell, a lot of things. It's a game for the philosophical types who want to learn more about themselves and what they value. And the replayability is phenomenal; there are numerous "endings" (play the game to see why I put endings in quotation marks).
The only thing frustrating about this game is the achievements. Made to mock achievements in general, the achievements themselves choose to gravitate to the polar ends of the difficulty spectrum. Some of them are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly easy. Some of them are nearly impossible, which forces you to cheat. But as frustrating as the achievements may seem, even the achievements are teaching you something. It's your job to figure out what.
I think there needs to be more games like this. It's as if they've defined the early stages of a new genre that seeks to teach and inspire instead of tell the same ♥♥♥♥ing story you've heard in every other game in history, instead of 20,000 DLC's, instead of polishing gameplay feature turds.
You will laugh, and you will be speechless.

I think this is one of those few titles that really make you start to think about what a game actually is. And to be quite honest, I think that's a beautiful thing. With terms like "Triple-A" starting to define the success of a game before it even comes out, and stellar games like Thief getting unwarranted mediocre reviews, it's great to see a title be all like, "nah brah, I'm gonna do my thing."
The Stanley Parable really makes you think, and not in a "I must solve this puzzle to advance the story" kind of thinking. The Stanley Parable is trying to teach you something. Hell, a lot of things. It's a game for the philosophical types who want to learn more about themselves and what they value. And the replayability is phenomenal; there are numerous "endings" (play the game to see why I put endings in quotation marks).
The only thing frustrating about this game is the achievements. Made to mock achievements in general, the achievements themselves choose to gravitate to the polar ends of the difficulty spectrum. Some of them are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly easy. Some of them are nearly impossible, which forces you to cheat. But as frustrating as the achievements may seem, even the achievements are teaching you something. It's your job to figure out what.
I think there needs to be more games like this. It's as if they've defined the early stages of a new genre that seeks to teach and inspire instead of tell the same ♥♥♥♥ing story you've heard in every other game in history, instead of 20,000 DLC's, instead of polishing gameplay feature turds.
You will laugh, and you will be speechless.

In this game you play Stanley.  Stanley is a simple person, with a simple job: follow the instructions fed to you by the computer on your desk.  But one day, that changes.  And you get to shake Stanley's little world to its core.
I typically prefer games with ridiculous amounts of content, a never-ending stream of tasks to complete, and a completely immersive experience.  The Stanley Parable is none of these things.  The game is simple: listen to the narrator and do as he says, or do whatever you like.
There's a lot that makes this game great, but a key feature is the narrator.  Not only does he issue instructions on your journey, he also has the reset button on the game - so you find yourself restarting the game in the same little cubicle, in the same deserted office, over and over again.  But it never feels repetitive, and you'll laugh yourself stupid.

Cleverly written, very cleverly written. This game is an amusing diversion that succeeds at being interesting right up until you run out of choices to make and and you start having to replay content looking for elusive hidden endings. Because that's esentially all this game is, a bunch of hidden endings that you access by making different choices (choices that are typically as simplified as right vs left door.)
The game is clever enough to convice you for a time that it is constantly changing and evolving, but once you finally start to see repeated content it quickly loses its charm. It's a modern find your own adventure, but once you see the majority of the branching paths, you are essentially done.
This is worth a look if you are bored with typical games and catch it on sale. In my case I got three to four hours of gameplay for about six bucks, which is a little subpar compared with the entertainment value you can get from other titles at a similar pricepoint.

Originating as a Mod for Half Life (I think it's Half Life?) the Stanley Parable was able to recieve its own standalone with the help of a Kickstarter. That being said, the price of the game is much too expensive to be willing to pay for just a walk-around hililarious point and click adventure. Don't get me wrong, the Stanley Parable is absolutely amazing when it comes to it's wittiness, creativity and narration without spoiling anything! But I found myself quickly growing tired of the humor and trying to find a new story path to go down after about two hours of exploration, but maybe that's because I suffer from depression or something. Essentially I did enjoy the Stanley Parable in the short time that I played it but for a game like this with such a varied gameplay time for each individual gamer (even with maybe five hours to do EVERYTHING) it should be no more than $4.99 at regular price. This game really only has a lasting affect on the player once and maybe again if a significant amount of time has passed so that one does not remember the same paths they took and funny endings they witnessed in the game. I reccommend getting a group of friends together to pay and play this game since it is not worth the full asking price of $14.99 for one person.

This game is a thought experiment. It's an electronic Skinner Box and you are the test subject. In a way, it's a long shaggy dog joke about fate, destiny, and choice especially when you finally figure out the only way to truly win the game.
Don't buy this game if you're looking for a shooter or a platformer or even a puzzle game. It's none of those. It's a philosophy game, a mental exercise, maybe even a personality test . You really can't pin down what it is. But as long as you accept what it's not, you'll enjoy it.

When I first heard about this game, I was curious about the style of gameplay it offered so I placed it on my wishlist. Now having played it for roughly 3-4 hours, I can say with confidence that this is the first time I've had an experience with a game where the entire playthrough was entertaining for reasons entirely not associated with playing games.
You have a narrator. This guy has a pleasant english accent and routinely comments on what you are doing and the choices you make. The start of the game essentially boils down to a choice of two doors, those of which expand into more choices. HAVING SAID THAT, I LOVE THIS GAME.

I finished this game in a few hours, but I spent those hours happily involved, unable to stop playing, and generally giggling like a loon. I truly hope it gathered enough attention from the right people to potentially embrace this choice-making concept and branch it out further - rather than 20 or so endings, could a game be made with hundreds?

The Narrator is what really makes this game. His deep rich voice and non-sense dialogue make for a hilarious game. I would highly suggest this game. I love showing this game to friends and have them wonder what's going on. However, this game does fall short in a few areas. First off, the games loses its luster after you have played for a few hours. After playing it for awhile, you start to get the hang of what's going and how the game works. I got to a certain point where when I found a new ending, I just felt like "Oh, another ending?" Second off, this game only has true value when you first start to play it. After playing for a bit, it gets kinda boring and almost predictable.
All in all, this a great game, but only for the first couple of hours. I don't think it's worth $15, but it's probably worth half-off or less.

A very nice change of pace from every other game out there. Excellent narrator and programming - they have prepared dialogue for almost everything. And I like the subtle weird phenomenons they added... like going through a corridor gets you back where you started almost without you noticing, but the second time around you don't get back to where you started.. and if you try to go back and check if there where 2 corridors it wasn't - messes with your mind! But not in an "in your face" kind of way which is really nice. That said, don't expect more than 3-5 hours of time killed by this game. On my 3.4 hours I tried most endings (I think so anyways, didn't google to get them all). Still well worth the cash.

The breakdown of the barrier between in-game elements and the story being told makes this game very unique, and very interesting. The choice is up to you.

The Stanley Parable is a hilariously narrated walking simulator about choice - what a worker, Stanley, decides to do after he stops receiving instructions from his illusive office superiors.  It has something like 18 different endings, all depending on the decisions you make from the very beginning:  whether or not you follow the narrator's directions, what items you click on, the order in which you generate different endings, and so forth.  It's not the longest game, but it (obviously) lends itself well to repeat playing.  Existential themes shrouded in a delightfully irreverant context, this game is a great (and seriously meta) introduction to the simplest of gaming platforms.  I definitely recommend it!

I don't get the criticisms that this has "no gameplay" or isn't a "real game" or whatever (see some other reviews). Obviously people are playing it and enjoying it, we're not pretending to. You could certainly argue that there's little mechanical depth to it (ie. people's play experiences will be largely the same as each other's, albeit in different sequences) but that's probably true of, say, P'n'C adventure games as well, and people are happy to call those "games", spend a tenner on them and rate them highly.
The Stanley Parable has made me laugh, smile and think. It's subversive, intelligent and feels incredibly reactive for such a scripted adventure. It has the funniest set of achievements I've ever seen. It won't be for everyone but it's the most entertaining three-and-a-half hours I've spent playing a game since... Portal, probably. I'd recommend it whole-heartedly.

No matter what you do, there is no real "winning" in The Stanley Parable. Instead, you have a plethora of decisions you can make through each playthrough and Stanley (you) usually gets screwed in the end by the narrator!
The narrator is possibly the icing on the cake in this game. The proper, soothing, and partly dark voice of the narrator as he tries to dictate your every move immediately reminds you of invisible walls and other impassible objects that hinder our exploration in games. As he tries to lead you through the linear storyline, he becomes annoyed with you if you deviate from the path. During one of my playthroughs, he was so mad at me that he actually restarted the game. Either that, or he'll just kill you off without a second thought xD
As a final verdict, GET THIS GAME! IT'S AWESOME!

This an...interesting game. Oh who am I kidding, it's pure genius. You start this game off as a man named Stanley, who was content with his overly boring job of pushing buttons on a keyboard when he was told to. One day, though, his work environment becomes vacant. What could this mean?
That's about all you can say without spoiling anything about the game. Reading any more reviews will tell you pretty much the same thing. Now, the concept of this game sounds really stupid when you first hear of it; it starts off beign pretty on-rails, until you come up to two doors. The narrator will say Stanley entered the door on his left, but that doesn't mean you HAVE to take the door on the left. Here's where it gets interesting -- the more you deviate from what the narrator wants, the more you deviate from the plot. There are many different endings to the game depending on the path you take, and some of them have to be seen to be believed. The results end up getting laugh-out-loud worthy at times. What truly sells this game though is the narrator himself. He is the perfect mix of sophisticated and snarky that makes him so perfect for the role, especially when you begin disobeying him. Of course, there's the famous broom closet scene, but that's only a small glimpse of the hilarity in the game. You really have to play it for yourself to find out how hilarious it is.
If I had to come up with one downside to this game, it's the shortness relative to its price tag. I got everything I wanted out of this game in about two hours, which makes me question its $15 price tag. I got it at $6, which I think was a good deal. If you can get it while it's on sale, I say go for it. You will not regret it.

This an...interesting game. Oh who am I kidding, it's pure genius. You start this game off as a man named Stanley, who was content with his overly boring job of pushing buttons on a keyboard when he was told to. One day, though, his work environment becomes vacant. What could this mean?
That's about all you can say without spoiling anything about the game. Reading any more reviews will tell you pretty much the same thing. Now, the concept of this game sounds really stupid when you first hear of it; it starts off beign pretty on-rails, until you come up to two doors. The narrator will say Stanley entered the door on his left, but that doesn't mean you HAVE to take the door on the left. Here's where it gets interesting -- the more you deviate from what the narrator wants, the more you deviate from the plot. There are many different endings to the game depending on the path you take, and some of them have to be seen to be believed. The results end up getting laugh-out-loud worthy at times. What truly sells this game though is the narrator himself. He is the perfect mix of sophisticated and snarky that makes him so perfect for the role, especially when you begin disobeying him. Of course, there's the famous broom closet scene, but that's only a small glimpse of the hilarity in the game. You really have to play it for yourself to find out how hilarious it is.
If I had to come up with one downside to this game, it's the shortness relative to its price tag. I got everything I wanted out of this game in about two hours, which makes me question its $15 price tag. I got it at $6, which I think was a good deal. If you can get it while it's on sale, I say go for it. You will not regret it.

When I started this game I had high expectations because of all the good reviews I read. After the first 10 minutes or so, I was feeling rather disappointed, and I left the game. The next day I figured, what the hell, I'll give it another go. 5 Hours later I am writing this review. However short lived the game was for me thus far, I can with confidence say it is one of the best games I have ever played.

If you are like me, you are likely annoyed by all the cryptic reviews and descriptions.  So let me actually explain the game so you can make an educated decision whether it is worth your time and money.
First of, this is not a game like anything you have likely played before, there are no puzzles and no action.  It is the spiritual successor of a text based adventure game on a 5 1/4 inch floppy disk I used to play on my Apple IIe.  Put another way, it is like playing a "chose your own adventure novel."  There are dozens of endings (most of which involve death or worse), and nearly all of them can be achieved in 2 hours.  But like reading a novel, it is the journey not the destination that matters.  The primary story mechanic is the relationship between you (Stanly) and the narrator, and while this might sound limiting, the developer’s ability to truly make you feel like Stanley by using the narrator to tie your actions and choices into the narrative is compelling.  Furthermore, the narrator's dialogue is equal parts satirical, profound, and hilarious, presented in the spirit of Douglas Adams and Monty Python.
I hope you can decide for yourself if this is worth your money, Personally I paid 5.99 on sale and have no regrets, I compared it to purchasing a good graphic novel.  That said, I would have been disappointed if I'd paid $15 for it.
I hope this review helps.  In the timeless words of Obi Wan Kenobi,
"You must do what you feel is right of course."

The Stanley Parable is the most clever and giggle-inciting game I've played since Portal 2. I had only been playing for thirty minutes, and I could tell right away that it was going to be a fantastic experience. If you want a good laugh, get the game right away. The game is constantly aware of your actions and decisions, narrating them and sometimes mocking you for the ultimate futility of your endeavors. Occasionally the velvety-voiced narrator will suggest where your character is SUPPOSED to go, while the game also presents a different path. If you "disobey" your narration, things start to get wacky, and you may question your existence and the purpose of life. The game has no combat, no challenge, difficulty, or penalty for making the wrong decisions about where to go. Your every action is rewarded with funny dialogue and interesting commentary on you as a player, the character you control, and the world the game takes place in. It's the kind of game that even someone who wouldn't consider themselves a gamer would definitely enjoy.
Funny..... Just Funny

From what everyone is stating, it would seem that your opinion varies depending on your disposition towards games.  I personally don't play that many, but I still ended up loving this game, despite it apparently having some deeper message about games themselves.  Does it have a message?  I would have said yes if it wasn't for the uncertainty of the entire experience.  You can take many messages from this experience, much like any interpretive work of art.
I took away that this is a story about the relationship between the player and their own discretion.  You are introduced to three main characters: the protagonist, the Narrator, and the story itself.  As a player, you typically conform to creating chaos, causing all three of these characters to viciously attack each other, trying desperately to come out on top.  But in the end, it is purely up to the player to decide how best to lead them to true harmony, whether it be choosing an appropriate ending or simply turning the game off.
And that to me is the beauty of the game.  That despite its most likely real intent of parodying the basic concepts of video game narratives, there was still room left to interpret something that is more about the game itself rather than what it's trying to say.

I had this game on my wishlist for a long time.. To me, the Stanley Parable was a kind of an unknown title - quirky, different, and I didn't know much of it aside from funny trailers and obscure reviews. I bought it when it went on sale.
After about 6 hours, maybe much less, I'm kinda done with it. If's an interesting exercise, not much of a game. I mean, there is an idea of a game there - but that game is "try to see something different by doing things you haven't done yet." As weird as it sounds, that's basically what this game comes down to.
I chuckled a few times, sat puzzled a few times, became unsettled a few times - and as interesting and as good as those few experiences are, once you've had them theres no need to go back and have them again. The game isn't a never-ending list of endings or choices - there are a variety of ways to play (plots to see) but the list is finite. I don't see any free additions coming any time soon. (I could be wrong on this point)
At the end of the day there are worse titles you could spend your money on. The Stanley Parable is an interesting diversion, to be sure. For a cheap price it's probably worth the experience, but do yourself a favour - if you do get tSP don't read spoilers, or walkthroughs, etc. If you do, the experience will be weakened and yes you will get to experience everything, but once you do you'll have no reason to go back. It's the feeling that there may be a different way to play that will keep you coming back. But once you know the endings, and the choices you need to make to get there, then that feeling will very likely go as will be your desire to keep playing.

If you want to have an exciting adventure, actually it isn't proper one.
But if you are tired about all those breathtaking, spectacular blinks of the games nowadays, it would refresh your brain. literally.

I don't really write reviews because most people will already know how the game will be just by doing a little research on the internet. But with the Stanley parable, it is a bit deceiving, which is why I am writing a review.
First of all, there is not enough content to justify $6 I paid for the game during the 2014 Summer sale. I got the game at 60% off the retail price. If you are REALLY dying to play the game wait till a 75% discount.
Secondly, there is no real gameplay here. Its basically a simple walking simulator, which gives you one other choice each time the narrator asks you to something. You are just locked to a linear path. All doors are locked, there is no sense of random exploration through a deserted office.  I would like more ways to defy the narrator, more hidden pathways, more easter eggs. After 30 minutes playing, the narrator that was really funny at the beginning seems like a complete drag and it gets to the point you just want him to shut the ♥♥♥♥ up (downstairs repeating loop, for the people who have played the game).
I would overlook the lack of content, if the 2.5 hrs I spent completing every ending the game had to offer, was something revolutionary or atleast breath takingly unique , for example a game such as Journey. This game has recieved a lot of love from players and journalists alike. But all this game does is make a point (albeit a good point), but here is the kicker, you can get what I got out of the game just by watching a playthrough of the game. You wouldn't feel any different about the game if you had or had not interacted (played or watched) with the game. Overall, I am not sour about losing $6 although I admit they could have been better spent, but the fact that this game was hyped and praised by alot of people. But what I got was a game from a which I expected MUCH MUCH more and never got it because there never anything to be had outside of a few jokes and some quirky dialogue. Overall, a disappointment.

EXA sat there beginning to question how to write a review of The Stanley Parable. "Was it a good game" he asked. He did enjoy his experience of The Stanley Parable, I mean he played two straight hours of it, non stop, and only had to stop, to write the review. But he questioned would others like to have the same experience, would others enjoy the game, would others read his review and based on his review, make a purchase. Was it important that he wrote a review. Then he began to realize, why was there a narration, its as if he was in The Stanley Parable himself, and the narrator began making his choices. EXA tried to deviate from the review. As he became conscious of the narrator, the narrator decided it was time to restart the review, again.
EXA sat there beginning to question how to write a review of The Stanley Parable.

Stanley opened up his Steam account and began to write a review. "That's odd," thought Stanley, "I'm not really the type of person to write a review am I?"  Of course he wasn't. Stanley hadn't written a review for anything in his life, so why should he start now? Were his actions controlled by a greater force? Some divine being for whom the illusion of free will was just a plaything?
The reality of course was that Stanley's brain was host to a terrible arachnid horror which had bored into his skull while sleeping and was currently driving him around like a Dodge Dart.

The are two questions to be answered: 1. Should you play this game? 2. How much should you pay to play this game (i.e. is it worth it if not on sale)
The first question is easy: YES! It is amazeballs! Do not expect a game in the normal sense of the word though. Expect an experience. I found it funny, sad, depressing, uplifting and (mildly) insulting at some times and I loved it. When faced with choices and when you wonder what to do ask "what does your heart tell you" - (Amanda Bynes in She's the man).
The second question is not easy. If you equate value to time spent enjoyably (I do usually), and if you get annoyed if a relatively expensive game is over in 4 hours (I'm looking at you Kane & Lynch and Homefront) it is probably better to buy it on sale. It has replay value for sure, but in the same way that you can read and re-read a book. If you equate value to the richness of experience then you are more than justified in paying full price for it. It is worth every cent.

Why do you not have this already?
The Stanley Parable is a First-Person walking simulator.  The core of the game is the relationship between Stanley - that's you - and the Narrator - the fancy sounding male voice who will respond to your actions and choices with a wide variety of emotions, reactions, and conclusions.  Sometimes he's your best friend. Sometimes he's your mortal enemy. Sometimes you accidentally do things you don't intend to do and surprise everyone involved.
This game does not take a lot of skill to play, and it's open-ended narrative makes it a joy to play. Normally I say you absolutely 100% should have a mouse to play a game on the computer - especially first person stuff. But the Stanley Parable is a very slow and relaxing game that can be played at your own pace - even to the annoyance of the Narrator.
I'm ashamed I did not get this sooner. If there's anything BAD that can be said about this game, it's that it's not a very deep game. Gameplay-wise. It's very intellectually stimulating actually, but the depth of content is a bit shallow. The Stanley Parable is a wide, branching game with a dozen different endings from obvious but important choices and has good incentive to try and see them all; but each playthrough is rather quick. It is not bothersome at all while playing, but now that I've seen it all I can't help but wish for more.

I've been playing computer games for over 32 years.  After all that time, it takes a really special, unique, new game to pique my interest. I still buy games, and play them, but many are extremely formulaic.   Valve have managed to sidestep a lot of the train-tracks that many of the enabling technologies seem to force game designers down, and have been handsomely rewarded for their ingenuity.
Along came The Stanley Parable.   I've resisted buying it, because it looked like a mod.  For the same reason I avoided Portal.  I made a mistake in both cases.  Both share a wonderful self-awareness and a fantastic interplay with the player that really breaks that 'fourth wall'.   Narration reminiscent of the amazing work of Tony Jay in countless other games and films.
I actually found myself, while playing TSP, saying "Touché" when the game foiled my own attempts at cleverness, and seemed to mock me for thinking I was thinking outside the box.    The main thing that really REALLY experienced gamers have to remember:  This is NOT Half Life.  Normal game mechanic rules DO NOT APPLY.
If you've played every game out there, and think you've seen it all.  If you're fed up with the same old drudge, and are looking for something short, fresh, and extremely humourous, this is a good choice for you.
If you're looking for something with guns and all the depth of a puddle, this is not for you.  You will play this game the way it wants you to play it. You will play it your own way.     Well worth it at £8 or £9, an absolute STEAL when on offer.

I would write a review for The Stanley Parable, but doing so will spoil the whole game. I can't tell you much about, but I will tell you this:
The less you know about the game, the better. This game is not recommended to anyone who is expecting a first person puzzle like Portal. If you want a game that deals with choices and how they affect you (or you're a sucker for Postmodernism and anything 'meta'), play The Stanley Parable. The downside is that it's short, but it's worth the money.

Do not play this game. It is a game with no setting nor ending.
Its significance is only in metaphor meaning that your interpretation won't likey result in a benefit to you. You will find yourself questioning a life of mediocrity and pushing buttons. You'll be on board right up until you realize that it is your life being described in this story.
You will enter Stanley's life and learn a lot of things about him throughout his adventure. You will follow him through until the end. Whether it be through this hallway or the next doorway you will find yourself at the edge of his consciousness left with only a keyboard and mouse to fight off the truth that the parable presents.
The truth that when there is no longer a hope for purpose there is no longer significance in death, nor in life. The Stanley Parable teaches that there is no meaning in the path that is defined for you. That if you continue onward with life for the mere potential of meaning at the end of the journey, you agree to let time make your choices for you.
Meaning is of your making and your's alone. This game will teach you the hard fact of your own existance and force disconent down your throat. You will realize just how much time you have wasted, just how similar you are to Stanley, and how truthfully mentally pathetic each of you are - even up until the last moments of the game.
This parable gives you infinite choices and retries. Reality does not.
If you are not ready to face that, then you are not ready for this video game.

This is, of course, is extended out to the point where it becomes a vaguely explored metaphor for the nature of life itself, before the now irksome nature of its ham-fisted attempts at satire are too irritable to endure much longer.
This may sound critical - that's because it is. It's an honest review from someone who bought it for £4 on a sale and still wouldn't recommend it. With basically all potential endings explored within an hour, my time with this game ended before my time with most other games would be considered even begun. You could argue length doesn't matter, but for something that is too pretentious to really be artistic, it leaves me wanting far more.
If you like the works of George Orwell, you might like this. It's about the same level of ham-fistedness in its approach towards expressing its ideas.

This game is another charming example of modern gaming that bucks conventionality. Rather than providing the player with anything he or she might expect, the game provides a meta-commentary on the nature of expectations and gaming, skillfully satirizing players and designers alike. The game's narrator is your only opponent, in so far as he is an omnipresent omniscient commentator on your behavior that seems to have Matrix-like powers to reshape reality to his will. He's a mix between GlaDos and the narrator from Stranger Than Fiction. As Stanley, the mostly faceless, personality-free protagonist, you encounter a series of choices and have to live (or die) with the outcomes, much to the narrator's chagrin. In terms of enjoyment, this game is akin to watching a really clever and hilarious half-hour pilot of an animated series that will never be picked up. You partially feel sad that you're investing your time in a concept with no real longevity, but you won't regret the experience itself. There are moments when I had to stifle my laughter late at night so as not to wake my neighbors.
The actual experience of playing The Stanley Parable can be best described as a waking dream. You feel simultaneously powerless and rebellious, intrigued but unsure. You might find yourself asking, "Is there any way to beat this game? Is beating this game even a reasonable objective considering the circumstances? Am I stuck in an infinite loop, the mindless plaything of a sadistic god?" You'll alternate between laughing at the narration and cursing your own predicament, hoping you can outsmart a system that tells you from moment one, you're incapable of outsmarting anything. With cleverness (or perhaps a guide) you'll find nooks and crannies buried in this one, and if it's offered on a Steam Sale or discount, it's a hard game to pass up. In terms of replayability, it has that dream-like quality where you enjoy the trippy feeling of interacting with the universe, even when it feels contained and stacked against you. You might pick it up from time to time just to experience it again or to share it with your friends, even though the content itself is not very extensive.
A game that can actually make me laugh goes a long way in my book, and this game is very funny. I greatly prefer it's tongue-in-cheek insecurity, philosophical and self-referential musings to the sort of redundant broad humor as Stick it to the Man, another game I tried recently whose laughs rarely match up to its ambitious artwork. Stick It To The Man is the exact inverse of this game, where you're compelled to keep playing because of the gameplay itself, rather than the jokey narrative that strings it together. The Stanley Parable is about losing yourself down a rabbit hole where there is so little interactivity, it's like one of those dreams where you try to punch someone but your hands feel like they're stuck in molasses. There's layered meta-satire here: Stanley is a put-upon seemingly purposeless office worker whose life's work is a cog in someone else's design. Similarly, the Narrator's seemingly straightforward lifework, a basic narrative, is continually undermined by the player/Stanley. The game reiterates that they both need each other to survive, yet their relationship is by its nature antagonistic and oppositional. Haven't we been programmed by games and movies to rebel against conventionality for the sake of cliche: a lone wolf hero's noble quest for individual freedom? There are more than a few nods to Portal in this vein, but The Stanley Parable prefers that you reconsider your instinctual gaming behavior rather than simply mockings its peers.
The most startling thing about this philosophical and introspective journey is not just that it manages to be consistently funny, creative and inventive all while looking intensely drab and having very little interactive content. It's the fact that it manages to perceptively boil down the crux of modern gaming conventions into easily digestible doses. When we play Bioware games, we crave the choices and branching decision trees because it seems like for one brief instant, our decisions have lasting impact on this vibrant fictional world. Stanley is constantly vying for that type of freedom and power, and the narrator is constantly squashing him under his thumb to remind him that sometimes a story needs a focused narrative to find its beginning, middle and end. Yet the real story and sensation of playing The Stanley Parable is found between the lines of the narrative, in the existential Groundhog Day-like hell of being Stanley, and the Narrator's lonely, vengeful and ennui-based behavior. These two characters are at their best when they're at their worst, and in that way, they truly do belong together.

One of the greatest examples of video game art making use of its interactive element to enhance its message. In The Stanley Parable, a narrator announces choices the player will make, and the player is free to defy the narrator and make their own choices instead. The Stanley Parable questions concepts such as the identity, the importance of choice, the relationship between the developer and player agency, and the notion of free will. The Stanley Parable is clever, self aware, and hilarious, I absolutely recommend it.

It's quite short and cerebral with essentially zero action; gameplay basically consists of "walk around, listen to the narrator, make choices". If you're the kind of person who doesn't like short or slow-paced games it might not be worth the full $15, but for the enjoyment I personally got out of it, I actually regret buying it on sale because I'd rather have given the developers more money.

I'll be quite happy.

As much as I enjoyed the The Stanley Parable mod, the paid version just doesn't feel like enough content to warrent ten dollars, reguardless how many smarmy-liberal-art-school-reject journalists think this is gaming's equivalent to Andy Warhol. I do consider this a game; the challenge comes from, ostensibly, finding all the endings. Or getting the best ending. Or getting the worst. Really, each playthrough you'll want to try something different from the last, and thankfully the game rewards you with wit, humor, and a heavy dosage of metacommentary (each of varying quality; more on that later) reguardless of what path you take. To get through all the endings takes about 3 hours, exluding the secret endings which require a bit more patence and know-how. And to me, that's all there is to the game.
HOWEVER - there has been much talk about how The Stanley Parable is a brilliant peice of gaming commentary, one that questions the very nature of player-game interaction. While it certainly DOES question these sorts of things (and will please those who think that commentary means that a game "doesn't have to be fun" and is not allowed to be criticized), it's certainly not the first game to --- and honestly, there are games that have done it much better and are much more fun to play. At some points, The Stanley Parable itself feels as arrogant as it's narrarator, who, when not talking in a condecendingly controlling voice, outright spills his utter disgust at the player's disreguard for his story (the latter sounds like the TSP Steam Community, doesn't it?). There isn't enough actual story to The Stanley Parable to make me care about any commentary within it - the game's story soley exists to reflect upon how clever it is. Now that's meta.
The Stanley Parable can be fun, even clever, but both the game and it's adamant followers suffer from a severe case of pretentiousness. The fresh idea it has grows stale very quickly. This flower might not just be a flower, but it certainly isn't a metaphor for the plight of middle-eastern dirt farmers.

It's like the guy tells you what you're doing, but then you don't do it.
