Its a funny little game based on a Half-Life 2 mod. You play as a guy named Stanley who works in an office. The narrator tells you what Stanley does and what he encounters. You can choose to disobey him, follow the story, or anything in between. The game has 15 or so endings, which depend on what you choose to do. It is kind of like a choose your own adventure story, but with a narrator that you can disregard if you want.
It's hilarious and witty, and the guy doing the voice of the narrator is extremely talented and funny. The game is essentially one big experiement with storytelling that aims to explore the ideas of free will and narrator vs. character. The game is a big mind game with trippy implications. I won't spoil it for you. Just go play it if you're interested in how storytelling works or if you just want to laugh.
For people who playd the mod: the difference between this and the original mod is huge. Almost 4x the endings, tons more choices, and many lines of dialouge.

This game should take about three hours at most to get through. It gives the impression of astounding depth just because of how simple it all is. The narrative and the numerous different points where you can make a choice make it seem like there's always something more. That of course is the charm and main idea after all "the end is never the end is never the end, etc.." I'm not afraid to say this is one of the only games that made me laugh rather than inwardly chuckle a little. Having this experience with the narrator led to some great funny moments. As to how that whole narrator mechanic works as a whole....well it's hard to describe because the game will explore different ways the Narrator, the player and Stanley could of interacted and all of the possibilities are sepperate from eachother. The narrator is motivated by telling a story, the player is motivated by choice, and Stanley by pushing buttons for the most part. How these three interact changes as the possibilities branch out. There are many ways the game tries to get the player to think about freedom of choice, reality, and the nature of games. The appeal of this game is none of the singular branch paths you could of taken but rather a point in the middle of the game where you are astounded at where a certain set of decisiions took you and you now are motivated to try another set.
Perhaps one of the best games I've ever played. The narration is what makes the game worth playing over and over again.

Well well well, a game without combat? What's the point then, right? I mean, what good is a video game if we can't live out a not-so-deeply buried desire to murder people with a wide array of weapons, vehicles, and vehicles with weapons? I mean come on, nothing else is fun. I just simply cannot fathom how a game could possibly be called a game without shoving a sharp object into something squishy or sticking C4 and blasting with rockets what isn't squishy. I also don't know why people insist on playing games that make you think, and not with mind bending puzzles, but provocative subject matter. I don't play games to ponder the nature of existence! I play to mindlessly press as many buttons as I can, and to do so in a better order and timing than another player miles away that I'll never meet. I play to prove that I'm better than you!
......what's this? This game is actually entertaining? No way. There is no way that a game set in an office building could possibly be fun until it catches fire and the aliens attack after I headshot all the zombies. And why am I playing as a white-collar nobody? I can't do anything but...push buttons.....push buttons........buuuuuuuttoooooonnnnnnssssss.........
So, you made it through my horrid rant of satire, as you can probably guess, I LOVE THIS GAME. I'm so relieved to know that there are still devs out there who are trying new things without packaging it with something tired and overused. Every aspect of this game is the antithesis of what the big-wig empty suits in the mainstream developers' table think a good game makes. This game reminded me why I play games, to be ENTERTAINED, and by the gods above, does this game deliver.
Okay okay, I'll be fair. The gameplay is almost non-existant. You walk, push buttons, and can crouch for seemingly no reason other than maybe another camera control. You can't even jump. But, are we here for action? Not really, we're here for comedy, we're here for surrealism (that doesn't reference a certain girl with a blue dress and a rabbit), and we're here for some new perspective. This perspective, however, can honestly hit a little too close to home. The game almost doesn't want you to play it, the main character speaks volumes of this. His job is pushing buttons, just like yours is while you play ANY game. His path is up to you, but the game loves pointing out that no matter what you choose to do, everything you decide on has been mapped out long beforehand, teaching the player that these notions of "freedom and choice" within games is essentially a delusional fantasy, that no matter what you choose, your options are predetermined, your actions well anticipated. Every game has walls, visible or no, they are there. And the narrator eats that up. Indeed, a game that subtley reminds you that you're deriving pleasure and a misplaced sense of achievement from some light thumb excercise is like a girlfriend casually bringing up her horse-hung/body-builder/rocket-scientist/senator ex-boyfriend while you're trying to get intimate. But somehow, I don't mind because that guy ended up in the electric chair for war crimes and hey, she's with me now, so win!
Bottom line: There will be plenty of people who just won't understand this game, or what's supposed to be fun about it. These people have a poor sense of humor/irony, no self-awareness, and are xenophobic to mind-blowing proportions. It would be one thing to say it costs too much, or it's too short, or it's too repetitive, all these things are true to varying degrees. BUT! Anyone who says this game is "bad, horrible, boring, stupid, gay, pointless" or any other dismissively cynical criticism should be ignored. Only idiots will not enjoy this game, because idiots do not like being reminded that they are idiots. No, The Stanley Parable isn't very long, or lasting in replay value, but it's a great way to feel like somebody spiked the coffee in the employee lounge with a mild dose of LSD and Stephen Fry-esque wit.

Picked this up during one of the numerous Steam sales for 50% off... Despite playing for under five hours, I am more than satisfied after my short tryst with the Stanley Parable. An interesting way of storytelling in itself, the game has multiple endings, each brought about by seemingly inconsequential decisions. There are these brilliant moments were you ask yourself - "Can I do X?" - and find yourself plesantly surprised to see you can.
Now, no game can offer unlimited choice. TSP's limitations are painfully clear after a few playthroughs (which average around 20 minutes a piece). But for what it's worth, this game is worth your time. It's short and sweet, but doesn't leave a bad aftertaste in your mouth.

Firstly, I don't understand why some of the endings are unobtainable, i.e. after following a certain path the screen either goes black or glitches to an earlier spot where a different path must be followed.  I've checked online with guides and this does seem to be a problem, that is to say that following the guides leads to the glitches I'm experiencing without the ending the guide predicts.  Reinstalling doesn't fix this (specifically I'm thinking of what's called the 'good ending' (by most guides at any rate), in case you're interested).
Aside from this, The Stanley Parable is very clever, and any dedicated gamer will appreciate the metahumor directed against choice in video games.  The narrator is cast perfectly and the whole thing is very stylish and original.  It does seem to draw quite a bit of inspiration from Portal, and at times approaches being snarky as opposed to insightful, but it is still definitely worth the experience.
Worth the experience, that is, if the length didn't preclude any sane informed individual from forking over $15 for it; all of the endings (at least the working ones) can easily be experienced within 3 hours.  That being said, The Stanley Parable is an awesome game (despite the length), and, if it's on sale, buy it (otherwise wait).

I have always adored the original Stanley Parable modification, and this new version certainly stands up if not exceeds expectations and its brief legacy. Of course I recommend playing the original first, but I believe everyone should play this game. It is one of the most brilliant programs I've ever had the pleasure to experience, full of witty dialogue, ingenious game design, insightful commentary and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic voice acting.
Seriously, the range of Kevin Brighting surprised me here. He hits so many different marks, with tones of humorous companionship, striking, powerful, bordering on terrifying command and one particular ending that went in the complete opposite direction and had him deliver dialogue like a broken puppy that genuinely made me feel sorry for the disembodied voice.
There is what seems like a near infinite vast of secrets, and I was mildly surprised to find so many small changes from load to load, even where I made the same decisions.
I have always been a proponent of the ideal that games are art---to be honest, I've always found the "debate" quite silly. If images are art, and music is art, and writing is art, how could games not be art? They're composed of those very things! They're a collection of art; a film, simply interactive and typically longer, although of course there are exceptions on every one of those accounts. But ... I digress. The Stanley Parable is art. If you disagree, I mean, I could take the accepting path and just let you have your opinion, but on this issue I'd rather just fight you. If you do not think The Stanley Parable is art I will literally fight you. Pick the time and place. Just please prepare some form of wavers and documentation to absolve either party of legal responsibility.

You cannot play another game like The Stanley Parable. Yes, it is linear, and yes, you eventually get tired of the narration, but there is a certain kind of personal connection that you get from each experience. It's like a choose-your-own adventure book, signed lovingly by the authors in one super-secret ending. Your library is not complete without this.

Some of this game makes you think about humanity and what is really real, some of this game makes you think about the structure of conventional video games, but most of this game is just pure nonsensical fun. If you love the satirical humor of the Portal series, this is absolutely one to snap up.

While you could just watch playthroughs on YouTube, playing it yourself and exploring all the endings and secrets is a lot fun. Buy this game when it's on sale though, becuase it the novelty of it isn't worth full price.

I cannot recommend this game enough. It is simply one of the best games released in the last few years. The Stanley Parable puts you in the shoes of an office worker who suddenly finds everyone has disappeared. A narrator begins to set up the plot, and from there everything goes wild. I cannot say too much without ruining the first-time experience you *desperately* deserve for a game like this, so I'll try to stick to the mechanical aspects. The control system is your typical WASD/mouse navigation. Your character, unlike many FPS games, has no jump function (try it anyways and see what happens) because you're walking a linear (HA!) path the entire time.
Your interactivity with the environment is limited. There aren't very many objects you can physically manipulate besides those necessary for progression. The narrator, on the other hand, will have something to say about almost everything. The graphics are pleasing to the eye, and the game is well optimized, running perfectly fine even on integrated laptop graphics cards. The environment has a soft, clean feel to it. Don't come here for realism.
Lot's of fun passive background humor and gags. Take the time to stop and read notes and examine documents and pictures. You'll notice something new every time.
I will say that this game has endless replay and exploration value. No two playthroughs will be the same. Expect dark humor, dry wit, complete lunacy, tranquility, hostility, happiness, and fear. This game will take you from laughing your♥♥♥♥♥off to a sobering, thought-provoking state. It's a beautiful demonstration of the concepts of free will, causality, fate, and sense of individuality. Just how much are you in control of your life? TSP has some interesting thoughts on the matter.
Buy it. You won't regret it.
And for the love of God, DON'T go to the community page if you haven't bought it yet or if you're just starting. Spoilers everywhere, and spoilers are the exact last thing you could possibly want in this game. You have been warned...

Having explored the branchs and laughed out loud at times I still am not sure if this game was worth the time I sank into it. The game was funny but didn't really have any strong narrative. mostly more a game about going off the rails then getting to any real destination. Basically I am left thinking well, that was fun, but was it WORTH it? which arguably is the point of the game anyway.

I love this game, and since it is on sale this weekend (5/18/14) I highly reccomend buying it and playing it for 2 or three hours.

But is it art?
Well, it's certainly arty, but it's the kind of art I like. It's consistently funny, both mocking and exploiting the mechanics and tropes of games, not to mention the nature of choice. It doesn't so much break the fourth wall as never build it in the first place, and its slow pace and sardonic narration give it a relaxing, surreal, decidedly weird air.
It's not so much a game as it is an experience, and it certainly isn't for everyone. But the demo - itself really more a separate chapter than a demo of the game - gives a good (though as far as I can tell non-branching) indication of the game proper. Try the demo. If you like that, you'll like the game.

Whether or not you feel you have gained anything from the Stanley Parable will depend on how much you value a minor metaphorical critique on ‘gaming choices’ and if so, whether or not that is worth it in direct relation to the amount you spent. In a nutshell, this ‘game’ is essentially an attempt by you, Stanley, to discover what has happened to your co-workers and bosses, all of whom have completely disappeared.
That’s the game in its entirety on a superficial level without giving away any spoilers. The underlying message is regarding the choice, or the illusion of choice, that modern video games allude to offer. The developers seem to be responding to games such as Mass Effect, that suggest they offer the gamer real choice in the outcome of the narrative yet in reality the gamer only has a couple of options dressed up in different clothing. There is a clear critique here regarding the nature of ‘choice’ in the video game industry and while it is welcomed change for video games to include a metaphorical message (beyond the simplistic), these messages and critiques should not exist in a vacuum, devoid of any gameplay. The point being that, there is a thought provoking message here, but this is not a game.
Stripped down, the Stanley Parable is a game of ‘walk and listen’. Yes there are some interesting points mentioned by the narrator relating to conscious decision making, but this same message could have been offered through or alongside gameplay features that stretched beyond walking around a corridor. Quite simply, this is a lecture, a chore of a lecture that unfortunately lasts for 2-3 hours before you realise you could have just read the same underlying message in a free online article in about 10 minutes without being subjected to this gaming con artistry.
Clearly there is a sense that the Stanley Parable is offering some ‘high art’ by not including actual gameplay, or that this ‘genius indie title’ will have your head scratching. There is a suggestion that if you ‘don’t get’ intelligent games that you won’t appreciate the Stanley Parable, that you can’t grasp its deeper message. Well, that is quite frankly a gross lie and yet a master stroke in marketing. People are desperately scrabbling to offer rave reviews of this new form of game, eager to show they are not cut from the COD cloth of gaming, that they can enjoy this intellectual critique. Do not be fooled. This is a totally unsatisfactory experience especially considering the price charged.
Do you want a thought provoking experience about the intricacies of the mind and the illusion of choice? Read a book. This is just pseudo-philosophical gaming at its very worst, conning the masses into feeling like an intellectual giant for a couple hours at the small price of being tricked by the illusion of gameplay. Who’s more of a sucker in this scenario, Stanley? Or us?
'The game will end, the game will never end'. Sold to us as an interesting game of uncertainty. Well, there is at least one certainty about the Stanley Parable; you will never see the cash you spent again.

This is the story of a game called The Stanley Parable. The Stanley Parable was originally released as a Half-Life 2 mod by a small team using mostly Half-Life 2 assets in 2011. The Stanley Parable's gameplay was simple, guide a man named Stanley, who works as employee number 427 in a big company located in a big office building, to one of 7 endings. The paths were pre-defined and, other than that, there wasn't much to do. Regardless, the game was well-received by gamers and critics alike, and while one may consider a game like that soul-rending, those who did indeed play The Stanley Parable enjoyable and savored every moment of it, as though it had been made exactly for them. And everyone was happy.
And then one day, the developers of the original mod announced they were remaking it in a more modern Source engine, using more original assets and containing more endings as well as a more fleshed out office for Stanley to explore in. You have also read this entire thing in the narrator's voice.

I have played through this game almost completely, yet every once in a while I feel compelled to come back, to take one last stroll through the abandoned office space, and to taunt the game's orchestrator one last time. The game is never over.
This game is about Stanley. Stanley is an office worker who spends life mindlessly pushing buttons on a computer. One day he realizes that all of his coworkers have disappeared. From that moment on, you traverse the sprawling office building trying to find out where they have gone. But as you find cracks in the walls, never-ending hallways, and a strange feeling of helplessness, you may question your own sanity.
The sole purpose of this game is to take every expectation you have of what a video game is, burn them down in front of you, and mock you for having them. the game will challenge you, frustrate you, amuse you. You have total control of your free will, and yet you have no choice. At some point along your journey you may even finish the game. It won't be enough. You'll come crawling back to the sterile office to throw yourself at the whim of your devious overseer.
Is Stanley real? Is he insane? Is he being watched? Is he truly alone? Where has everyone gone? Were they ever really there in the first place? The player is thrust into a world of doubt and confusion. Perhaps if you keep exploring these winding corridors you will discover the truth... everything else is just a carrot on a stick.
WARNING: Do not look up cheat codes, gameplay footage, walkthroughs, or spoilers for The Stanley Parable. This is a game in which the unknown plays a crucial role. Explore, seek alternate routes, keep trying, but NEVER go to the internet for help. This is a game that should be played through personally for the most emotional impact. I can still log in and discover something new about this world. Spoilers and walkthroughs ruin that. This is for your own good.

In what delusional world is a game you complete in 15 minutes a good one? People pretending that having multiple endings makes up for such a short game. Sure, it would, if the game was 1. long enough to have enough variations to make it entertaining and worth going back to and 2. if the game was interesting enough to repeat the same thing over and over. It's neither of those things.
The first play through is one of the best gaming experiences I've had. It's clever, witty, fun, interesting and unique. Then the game restarts - you're confused but it was entertaining so you figure there's a good reason to do it all again. Once you play through it again you notice that it isn't 'a different story every time you play, it's the same story except the narrator said some things differently. The game gives you the illusion of control but really provides you with completely linear paths where you either listen to the game or you don't and that's literally the entire game. It's not a game becuase that implies there's some sort of skill involved, this is a choose your own adventure book without that pesky narrative to keep you interested.
Overall, brilliant idea that's executed creatively... for about 5 minutes. This is a demo for a far better and more interesting game.

In the game, the game-makers show us an interesting story with their inspirational thinking through the endless loop of our protagnist, Stanley's fate. It trys to discuss the probabilities that derive from obedience and rebellion, and to achieve a high-level of interaction between players and the game. I cannot allege it is successful, but this attempt is praisable.
Various endings is an attraction of the game. Among those endings, my favoriate one is the 'Crazy Ending', which will be achieved by walking down the stairs instead of up. The final narration is so good that it makes me feel I am Stanley, and being assisted by repetitive rooms, description of thinking and the style of stream-of-consciousness, it gives players an intense atomsphere and great immersive. Every ending is so distictive and interesting that can inspire players to try every choice over and over again. Under those circunstances, I think, it is as a metapher, instead of as a simple character, that should Stanley be defined.
The narrator is the most important role in the game. It is he who continuously pushs the story forward and guides Stanley into different endings. He can be regarded as a highlight and also a drawback of the game. His words and tone contribute to game's style and atmosphere, but also undermine it's reality. If most of the narration can be replaced by text and make it focus on pushing the climax(just like what he does in the Crazy Ending), it would be more splendid.

The Stanley Parable is a unique exploration game that challenges you to explore the concept of choices within video games. Taking the role of the titular Stanley, the player must explore their office complex after all of their co-workers have disappeared. Accompanying the player is the Narrator who frequently discusses the situation and gives the player instructions.
It is when the player is given the opportunity to go against the Narrator's will that the Stanley Parable's charm begins to shine. The Narrator is a witty, humerous and occasionally meanacing force that makes the game stand out. When discussing the Stanley Parable, it is the Narrator that people first talk about.
The gameplay is uncomplicated, requiring the player to explore the office complex from a first person perspective. Other than that, the only other gameplay mechanic is choice: do you listen to the Narrator or do you ignore him? There are several choices to be made with many different combinations which all equate to a game with multiple endings, each more polarising than the last. The time it can take to reach one of these endings varies but no matter which one you have, the game is incredibly short.
Most of the Stanley Parable's endings could be witnessed through just over an hour of gameplay. If you are a player who wants to rack up a lot of time played for their money then you may question whether the Stanley Parable is worth the asking price. In this case you are presented with a choice: if you want a lengthy game filled with action then the Stanley Parable may leave you disappointed. If you want a game that is intricate in design, full of charm and highly replayable then the Stanley Parable will most likely suit you. It is a matter of quality over quantity.
If you enjoy a solid story, a strong narrative, and dont require combat to enjoy a game this is something you absolutely must buy!

A quirky, clever, first-person office crawler where your every action is narrated just might be what your library has been missing!

Stanley this, Stanley that. Stanley this, Stanley that. Stanley this, Stanley that.
When I set down to play this game, I didn't expect it to be the other way around. From the moment the reins of control, or the illusion of it, are handed to you, the masterpiece known as The Stanley Parable spins into motion. I've always tested video games, going back to where I started, finding a way out of maps, and generally screwing with whatever the devs have come up.
But The Stanley Parable stood ready to accept what I had coming for it. When I was able to take my first tentative steps into this game that I knew almost nothing about, my first choice in this game about choices was to stay put where I started, and the results impressed both me and the rest of my house at 2 AM as I found myself unable to breathe for the next 30 seconds.
Remember how I said that this game is about choice? Well it is, and isn't. There is no choice system like a Bethesda game, instead the choice system can be more or less described in the first evident fork in the road you encounter in this maze of a game. Two open doors in front of you, with a narrator expecting you to go through one of them. From there all hell can break loose, resulting in one of my favorite games of all time.
-Gameplay: Walking Simulator 2013 best Simulator. 5/5
-World: The omnipresent narrator is a delight to indulge and anger and having the game itself react and warp around you is an unparalleled experience. 5/5
-Story: What story? Ah, that story. The writing and subtle jokes and references may fly over most people, but for those who understand then The Stanley Parable will prove to have one of the greatest story-shaped holes in existance. 5/5

I don't recommend The Stanley Parable, but I do admire what it's trying to do.
I'm going to ignore the fact that the game is a "walking simulator", because you probably can see that from the trailers and from the demo that's available. At the core, it is a meta-narrative about the linear nature of video games, and how interactive experiences are shaped by the simulation of choice and freedom. Unfortunately, it fails to meet even that criteria, as its self-deprecating humour cripples it from ever making a bold statement on the way games should be designed. The game openly admits that The Stanley Parable is a bad game, when it could be asking the audience to be self-aware about the manipulative nature of their favourite games.
That aside, this game is drastically overrated by professional game designers and critics, who hail this as one of the best games of the year, and an example for big companies. To me, this is outrageous. It's not because the game is boring; if anything, The Stanley Parable is supposed prove how games are inherently boring. The worst part of The Stanley Parable is how forgetable it is. And considering how small the game is for $15, that's just unacceptable. Don't buy it.

A must "play"! This is a game that is really not a game but more of a philosophical study of what a game is. What is narrative? What makes a game a game? What choices does a player have in a game and how do those choices affect the outcome of the game? Are we fooling ourselves when we think we have control in a game? This "game" will have you pondering these sorts of questions with a self-aware wink and a nod. Great voice acting from the narrator and a subversive sense of humor help the overall experience. This is definitely an example of "video games as art". Oh, and by the way, I suggest you download and play the demo first because the demo contains content that is not in the full game. It's not like many other demos that simply show you the first level or two. In other words, there is nothing conventional about this "game"; even with the presentation of the demo.

The Stanley Parable, the recent HD re-release of a Half-Life mod of the same name, is one of the most exciting and hilarious interactive stories of the year, and is the only game you ever need play again. At least, that’s what the narrator would say.
You are Stanley, a lovable every-man, who arrives at his place of work – a standard office complex – and after a full hour of waiting, not a single command has appeared on his computer monitor telling him what to do. Incidentally, all of his co-workers are gone. And then things get a little strange.
The kindly narrator guides Stanley down the corridors and halls of the office building while Stanley tries to locate his missing colleagues. On this path, Stanley comes to a very special room, which is where the plot spoilers in this review end. Suffice to say, things then get a little strange.
The Stanley Parable’s hook is repetition. After a plot arc has been completed – or gets hopelessly stuck in a paradox – the game restarts itself, sometimes very jarringly. The ‘main storyline’ takes a surprisingly short amount of time to complete on your first run-through, and feels incredibly lacklustre. That is, until it becomes apparent that the main story has nothing to do with the game. And then things get a little strange.
The Stanley Parable is a game based wholly on the story, and how your actions change the game around you. Every decision the player makes diverts the story down a different plotline, with immediate and very satisfying feedback from the world you inhabit. Every decision creates such a strong and noticeable difference to the gameplay that even in such a self-referential game the sense of immersion is fantastically held throughout.
Stanley’s primary interaction with the world is through the Narrator, via the honeyed tones of Kevan Brighting. The writing in The Stanley Parable is rock solid – shoulder to shoulder with titans of interactive storytelling such as Bastion and Silent Hill 2. The tone is consistently entertaining, funny and totally engaging – unless you ever have to kill Stanley in which the narration understandably switches to sad and surprisingly gut-wrenching. The voice-acting, combined with such strong writing, is the main reason you’ll come back to this game again and again.
Much of the original hype for The Stanley Parable came from the demo, still freely available on Steam. The demo contains absolutely zero plot content but instead takes you on a tour of the metaphorical factory in which the game was built, introducing you to the very tongue-in-cheek humour the games does so well. Spoiling nothing in the main game, it boasts 100 percent of the feel and comedic tone of the actual game.
The Stanley Parable is a mind-blowing addition to the interactive-storytelling genre, and with over seven hours of play, the game is still engaging, funny and well worth checking out if you have an hour to spare.

The Stanley Parable is a game that uses ways of paradox thoughts and meaningless chaos to confuse the player and let him feel uncomfortable. Yet it tells the player a story, or better, many stories, that teach the player about human society and its paradoxa in a very, very criticising tone. I might have given the impression, that The Stanley Parable is serious or even sad. That is not the case. The Stanley Parable is very ironically funny, sometimes also a bit scary through confusion, and very beautifully made. The decisions you make always have consequences in this game, and very often I stumble across a decision which I have to think through several minutes. And yet the game always restarts itself, so there is no choice that you cant try out sooner or later. Long story short: The Stanley Parable gives you social criticism and media criticism, wrapped in beautiful ironical humor, innuendos, many, many paradoxa and a very small, yet fascinating game world, that leaves you stunned every single time.  The Stanley Parable is not a regular game. It is a parable. If I was a game magazine that gave away points on a scale of 1 to 100, I would add 20 more points to the scale, just for this game.
To call this game unique would be an understatement... then again it isn't really a game but then again it is many games 10/10

I bought this game after much research and views of previous players reviews. In my own personal Opinion it is worth your $15 for the game, maximum game time I spent doing all 18 endings was 4.30hrs. It is a pretty short game, but with a lot of comedic value as well as repeatable gameplay. I would recommend to a friend, and If I would recommend it to a friend, then that should be clear to you the value considering those who may read this, I don't know. The game itself is indepth and thought provoking. I found myself wrapping my mind around the meta-physics revolving around time & space. The inter-dimensional moments in the game really trip your mind up as you play. It was really well made considering how simplistic the enviroments are. There are a bunch of easter eggs in the game you will be able to find with a little work (or google) I found the achievements to be worth while, although few there were enough for me to enjoy and difficult enough for me to gain enjoyment. This is a very user-friendly game, although if you don't have patience for the game that "Repeats itself" then I would suggest not getting it. But, if you do have patience to learn the game while you play and pay attention you will deffinitely find the enjoyment that I did.
TL;DR: Great game, worth the money you pay. Be patient and learn it first don't rush into it.

A funny and cleverly written game.
BUT this is made for certain people, this is made for people who can take narrative over challenge AND for people who can take repetitiveness.
If you enjoy games like Thomas Was Alone or Journey than you'll absolutely LOVE this game.
If you're one who enjoys a challenge and dose not enjoy narrative and artsy games, you're not going to enjoy this.
If you're also one who dose not like a repeated story just to see all endings you will most likely not enjoy this as well.
However, if you're one like me who loves these types of game and can take a repeated story, you're going to have a great time! Each ending is funny or unique in its own way, that narrator's voice, my god I love it. There will be many parts where you will chuckle as well.
At times like this I wish there was a "maybe" or "depends on your taste" button, but sadly there is not.
I recommend this game absolutely for the examples I have listed above.
However, if you're not a fan of artsy games, this is not for you.

The Stanley Parable addresses many issues that gamers are too hesistant to look into because it's "part of the game". It allows for the player to make choices in this labyrinthian maze that is the office building...but these choices (and the narrator's reactions) are scripted to be played exactly that way. You may feel like a rebel, but ultimately you are still playing the game the exact way it is expected to be ran within its system. Even when you "break the game"; it's intended to happen as it does. The Stanley Parable is a refreshing arthouse experience in the gaming world that is an excellent critique on the flaws of gamers and flaws of game developers as a whole and looks to address in this excellent first-person-walker. I definitely recommend checking this game out if you want to expand your library with something a little more stimulating!

The Stanley Parable is a unique game, as it is entirely a game about playing games. Through the twists and turns you take either following or defying the ever-present narrator you explore the oddity of gaming tropes, particularly those of first person games.
The writing provides some of the finest humor in gaming, and I was often caught off guard by how precisely the narrative anticipated my actions at every turn.
Finally, if you are a game designer or writer, this is a must play. To understand the way players work their way through a game and how they react to a quest and level design in game, really dig into Stanley Parable. Tear it apart, find its limits, and take notes. I've learned a number of things from multiple playthroughs, and I'm sure other developers can agree.

I've always been of the opinion that if a game doesn't contain or focus very heavily on gameplay and mechanics, it's not a game. But the Stanley Parable is something which, ironically, EVERY gamer should at least consider, even though it's a very controversial one. No, you're not going to get some super-amazing all-in-one experience. Nor are you going to get the longest or most exciting "game". Nor is there any notion of GAMEPLAY. However, this piece of art illustrates the problem of having no gameplay altogether. It's weird and wonderful. It's repetitive yet different every time. It's easy to understand yet infinitely complex. The game can be interpretted in so many ways, and there is so much to discover behind its seemingly shallow exterior, I can't recommend it enough if you're looking for something that will entertain you in ways you couldn't have imagined. What is perhaps most commendable about The Stanley Parable isn't the whole "game within a game within a game" concept, but its presentation. The slick narration combined with sharp graphics and incredible attention to detail as well as a whole host of secrets, twists, pathways and endings to discover make it feel longer than it actually is. You might get bored of it after a few hours, but those first few crucial moments are something that can't be experienced anywhere else. It's a rich experience but one that isn't so muddled that it's difficult to make progress. Exploration of what seems to be an extremely linear game is very rewarding because the narrator speaks to you personally. The comedy value as well as the unique concept make The Stanley Parable a stand-out piece of entertainment that can't be expressed through any other medium.

Personally, I enjoyed The Stanley Parable immensly and highly recommend it to any player who is above playing just blood and guts games.  Although the plot is very linear and repetative, the plot lines are mostly a funny and sometimes sinister, made all the better by the Narrator's witty commentary and surprising reactions.  Although it is worth playing, the game can become a little stale after a while; the creator even said it's possible for a player to beat all the endings within an hour.  I still love it however and would give it an 8/10 for the superb audio track, graphics and gameplay, only underscored by the linearness and once-and-done mentality of the game. While playing, always remeber; let's begin again.

Stanley pushed the buttons, unwittingly writing a marvelous review for a game that made him hate all his choices.
Not the choice to get the game mind you, just the choices whilst playing it.
Oh how he endlessly and aimlessly tried to find the ultimate way to win the game, but Stanley started to know all too well that; as in life, not all choices lead to the correct path. Nor was the correct path always the right choice.

The subjective analysis of the choices would lead to the correct assumption that all choices had meaning in their meaningless repetition. The same path traveled twice leads to the same end, though not always the same path.
However pointless the choice might be, how often the path was traveled, those were inconsequential. The main point of the story was the story. So listen to the narator, for he will tell you the story untill there is nothing left to tell.
But even then the question will always remain:
Did Stanley discover the true ending, or was there something left unpushed, unexplored, unfinished.
Only one way to find out.

Stanley pushed the buttons, unwittingly writing a marvelous review for a game that made him hate all his choices.
Not the choice to get the game mind you, just the choices whilst playing it.
Oh how he endlessly and aimlessly tried to find the ultimate way to win the game, but Stanley started to know all too well that; as in life, not all choices lead to the correct path. Nor was the correct path always the right choice.

The subjective analysis of the choices would lead to the correct assumption that all choices had meaning in their meaningless repetition. The same path traveled twice leads to the same end, though not always the same path.
However pointless the choice might be, how often the path was traveled, those were inconsequential. The main point of the story was the story. So listen to the narator, for he will tell you the story untill there is nothing left to tell.
But even then the question will always remain:
Did Stanley discover the true ending, or was there something left unpushed, unexplored, unfinished.
Only one way to find out.

The game is made up of atmosphere and very intelligent writing delivered by some spectacular voice acting. Everything is incredibly out of the box, in complete disregard of the 4th wall, and extremely original.
The overall theme of the game kind of jabs at video gaming, working, and the illusion of choice as a whole. Stanley sits and follows the rules (the same way that we do with many games) until he's confused because he stops being told what to do (which coincidentally reminds me of League of Legends players). He also focuses so hard on his job every single day that he lacks the awareness around him to see that everyone has long since gone, which can refer to friends or family or even your other sources of happiness in life when you marry your job.
The last major theme of the game with the illusion of choice kind of embodies the 2 doors to the same room idea. The choice doesn't matter if the outcome is the same, and people can be so predictable that they can be given the illusion of choice when the maker of the choice knows the outcome. Also, people tend to crave choice, even if it is only an illusion. It can all be read very deeply.
The original Half-Life 2 mod version of this game can be found on ModDB, though it only has 8 endings (21 endings exist in this version).
15 bucks is a bit much for the dollar per time metric. However, each little bit of time spent in this game will be very enjoyable. $7 or below is a reasonable price, imo.

The Stanley Parable is a game that is an exploration of gaming.  It is funny and thought-provoking, and you cannot see everything in a single run (or even a few runs.)  I found no bugs.  The notions here are not tied to any particular genre; if you've played enough games to understand how a conversation about the way we play games is even possible, you are the target audience.  There is a free demo which is completely separate, so there are no spoilers but you can see exactly what this title is about and whether you are interested, making this review (and all other reviews) somewhat pointless.
Be aware that, if the length of a game is, by itself, very important to you, you will almost certainly not get more than a few hours out of this title, as the game is highly replayable but we're talking about replaying a sequence that only takes about 20 minutes to complete.
Highly recommended.  More games should reward us so richly for failing to follow simple instructions.

The Stanley Parable transcends the concept of a traditional game.  There are many endings, yet there is no real ending at all.  You will make choices, yet you will have no real choice at all.  Sound confusing?  Well it should.  The Stanley Parable will make you question reality, the notion of free will, and the meaning of life itself through its witty, cynical sense of humor.  The narration is top-notch, keeping you entertained throughout this unpredictable journey.  There is never a dull moment.  You will always be discovering new things, adding to the replayability factor of the game. This is not a game for everybody.  You will likely either love it or absolutely hate it.  I would suggest trying out the demo.  If you enjoy that, consider purchasing the full version.  If not, this probably isn't the game for you.

After having played the demo of this game, which isn't really a demo, I had high hopes for this.
This is a puzzle game unlike any other out there. Basically, it's about being given some choices where the path you take results in an ending or other. There are several endings to this game, and there are several paths to walk, some less obvious than others. So, it's pretty much about exploring all the possibilities. Taking one path may change something the next time you try.
To help, or confuse you along the way, is the narrator. He is at times quite hilarious to listen to. So much of the atmosphere is thanks to the narrator. The other side of it is the cleverly made locations that are surprsingly unremarkable. In fact, a lot of things in the game are unremarkable. There were a few "easter eggs" however. Then there are things that don't make much sense. Oh, and who said an ending had to be good? Expect moments of confusion and uncertainty.
What disappointed me about this game was that it's really short. It took me about 4 hours to see nearly every ending. True, I have some achievements left, but there's not anything more to see. Also, the "puzzles" themselves weren't all that interesting. I thought the demo was actually more fun and better made.
I do recommend this game, but honestly I think you'll find more fun in the demo. Note that the demo really doesn't have anything to do with the game. If you want the game, play the demo first in any case. Consider getting it on sale. Otherwise the price is too steep if you ask me.
Note: It did captivate me enough to play those 4 hours in one single sitting.

One of the most clever, thought-provoking deconstruction of common video game narratives and tropes in recent years. This is not a typical video game in the most common sense. Instead, it is an effective vehicle for some of the most important subjects pertaining to video games and their narrative. Where Dear Esther failed by wasting the video game medium for its narrative, The Stanley Parable succeeded by making full use of video game mechanics, and then subverts them in a humourous, and yet elegant way.
This game is designed to be played several times, and the real value of this game is to see what happens when you stray from the narrative that the game sets the player out to follow.
I will not discuss the specifics of this game, as doing so will ruin the sense of discovery so vital to keeping the experience effective, Instead, I will tell you to go pick it up and experience it, several times. You will not regret it.

The Stanley Parable is a diffucult game to review.  At heart, it is a "pick-a-path" adventure book with a series of completely unrelated endings, that follows the unseen protagonist Stanley through a deserted office building as a narrator (sometimes philosophical, sometimes absurd) tells the story of Stanley's wanderings. Repeated play-throughs offer different endings based on the "choices" Stanley makes (much of the point of the game centers around the illusion of choice in videogames). It has many great qualities . . . it is a unique experience unlike most games you have played, sometimes funny, sometimes clever, sometimes surprising, and mostly non-sensical.  The reason I can't recommend it is the list-price.  At $19.99, it is simply way too expensive for what is essentially a half-life mod with no characters, and just a voice-over.  The game becomes repetitive very quickly, as the player exhausts the posible endings, and essentially walks through the same corridors over and over.  Even the voice narration begins to repeat too soon for a twenty-dollar game.  I would feel satisfied if this had a list-price of $4.99.  That would be five bucks well spent.  It feels like this game was intentionally overpriced, with the anticipation that "Steam Sales" would generate "Steam fever" (wow...Stanley Parable is 75% off...I must act now!) to generate sales.  I can't recommend such a short (even if clever and unique) game for such a high price.

Is it worth playing The Stanley Parable?
Yes, yes, indeed it is. The Stanley Parable should be traslated to every language, and distributed freely across the world.
Is it worth buying The Stanley Parable?
Well, as of now, it's the only possible way to play it, so yeah, you should buy, why not? That being said, the experience feels more like "watching" an episode of some TV show. A very, very, very especial episode that will reach into the fabric of your being, stir up all that is contained there, and then leave gracefully, leaving behind exactly what was there before, only not. It is an experience which should be in a less restricted medium, it is something that the everyday man should experience, regardless of whatever circumstances he is up to. Is something my grandfather should "play".
Yet it is something that can not be accessed from any less interactive medium. An experience which could not be in any other form. Yet there is something "alien" to the product, some elusive quality wich distinguish The Stanley Parable from the rest of works which populates the medium. The Stanley Parable is a work which couldn't be anything other than a videogame, yet it does not feel like a videogame.
So, have I enjoyed The Stanley Parable?
♥♥♥♥ yeah.
Will I play it again?
Yes, yes I will. Only not as I play again with others videogames, but rather more like I will be re-watching some episode of Twin Peaks.

This is one of the coolest games I've ever played. Don't worry, no spoilers.
The first time you boot up this game, you're going to feel like a kid in a candy aisle. You're going to be presented with so many choices and things to do, and so many things to see. You're going to be overstimulated and probably spend five minutes in the starting area, poking around for hidden things. Then you'll make your first choice. That was easy. And then your second takes a little more time. Maybe you won't have a third. Then it ends...and you start again.
The narration is brilliantly executed; a real five star job. The setting is familair but unnerving. There's even a strange force that becomes a new character, in a way, and it's all so intriguing. It reminds me so much of Portal 2, in how they can take something as unassuming as an office, give it incredible detail, and subvert your expectations. And, wow, how the different paths can vary...even something so minute that you don't even realize that it's a possible choice can lead you in such an incredible new direction. There was a point where I thought "Hey, is that...can I maybe just...I CAN!" and the current path was unforeseeably diverted. Maybe you'll know it when you see it, too. Probably not.
Even if you've played the mod, this standalone is not only a fresh coat of paint, but there are a few things I don't remember from the mod (although, that may just be me). Either way, the developers deserve to be rewarded for an AMAZING journey into game design. I may buy this game twice, if I can. It's a brilliant gem.
My complaint is that some of the objects have really poor textures, and the render distance is pretty bad. I really wish that they had HD textures available. You'll squint your eyes to read what's written on a mug, for instance, and sometimes computer screens and documents are completely illegible. That's a real shame, as vicarious detail (even for inconsequential things) is something I LOVE in video games. There are secrets and easter eggs in here, but the small details aren't too important. Still, that's a small scratch in an otherwise gigantic diamond.

The unfortunate thing about talking about this game is that you can't say anything without spoiling what makes the game spectacular. With nothing short of a fascinating, thought-provoking twist on game narrative and storytelling, The Stanley Parable stands as a pinnacle of game narration, utilizing the power of choice and agency in ways that leave you pondering your existence well after you've "finished" the game. You can finish this game in 4 minutes, you can finish it in 3 days, it's entirely up to you. But the amount on content that can be found in this game is astounding, and will leave you wanting more as you explore Stanley's world, thus making the "finish the game in 4 minutes" option the least rewarding option possible. If you ever get the chance to buy this game, BUY IT IMMEDIATELY.

When you now think, "The game just restarted. Everything is same as last time." you completly do not looked what you are buying, because this is The Stanley Parable. And one of the most annoying and strange things about the game is, that your earlier plays affect the world later. One of the next core ideas of the game: You restart it very often and find new ways to annoy the narrator or follow his instructions simply for seeing which other ends this game has. For the great but strange ideas the game is very uncommon, which is clearly a positive point if you are annoyed from common games. The negative point is the extremly limited playtime so you play like 4 hours and nearly have all endings.

A lot of my friends have asked why I play video games at my age and with my job...
Well, The Stanley Parable is one of the reasons.
This game epitomises what gaming is about for me: it doesn't follow the usual formula at all, was made cheaply, easily and quickly, and features oodles of surprises and treats that aren't thrown in your face.
Games like these represent what is so powerful about Steam and PC gaming in general: we don't have to put up with generics.  We have a slew of (cheap) unique games at our fingertips, and we would be foolish not to take full advantage of that.
But, onto the game itself.  How to describe it? Imagine Fight Club, I suppose, if instead of Tyler Durden, the Narrator met Milton (from Office Space).  And then took acid.  And this was all narrated by the Monty Python crew.
See, that's the real beauty of this game: the banality of the concept (an office worker) is offset by a message not unlike Fight Club (minus - mostly - the violence) and painted with a distinctly meta feel to it.
It's the juxtaposition that really makes the concept of this game shine: our protaganist's apparently choiceless, linear line is thrown wide open (with, well, bizzare scenarios at times) by telling us we are not free to choose his ending...and then giving us the opportunity to do the exact opposite.
I had moments where I was chuckling for a while, shaking my head at the absurdity of it all. Other times I burst out laughing.  Still other situations had me stopping to pause, genuinely questioning the implications of an event and how it related to my life.
"Ah, but the cons," you say, and rightly so.  Well, it does feel short.  Which is a concern when it's so easy to pick up cheaper games that last (a lot) longer.  I would very much recommend that you wait for a big sale for this game, particularly if your budget is constrained. To put it into perspective: I reckon (without giving away spoilers) that I've discovered more or less everything there is, and I don't have much time invested into the game.
TL;DR: a recommended game, a brilliant story, but not a game that will keep you coming back for more hours later.

Actually, it has several endings, but none of them are truly the end.  The beauty of this game is that it's nearly impossible to convey the experience of playing the game to another person.  Which is why I'm going to have a great time attempting to write a review of it without ruining some of the better reveals.
Technically, The Stanley Parable is an FPS, but you don't have any weapons.  Placing this game into a genre is almost an insult to its wit.  The closest comparison I could make would be a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book written by Douglas Adams, and even that is an admittedly poor characterization.  I can honestly say that I've never played a game quite like it.
In the beginning of the game, a narrator explains that you are playing as Stanley, office worker number 427, who sits at his desk and pushes buttons on his keyboard.  Already I can relate to this character. One day, the narrator says, Stanley realizes that nobody has shown up for work.  Stanley steps out of his office and begins exploring the building.  While exploring, the narrator continues to narrate the story.  It's as though someone is reading a book while you are playing through it.  One of the first things that happens is you come to two open doors, and the narrator says "Stanley took the door on his left."  However, the player is not required to take the door on the left.  The player has a choice, or at least the illusion of one.  It's the relationship between the narrator and the player that makes this game so unique, and it's the depth and dynamics of this relationship that make the game so much fun to play.
The Stanley Parable doesn't take itself seriously, either.  It knows it's a game about a person sitting at a keyboard pushing buttons, and it knows that the player is also a person sitting at a keyboard pushing buttons.  Every time you click the mouse, you can hear a few keystrokes click on a keyboard.  You, the player, are playing as Stanley, who in turn is playing as himself in a fantasy of sorts.  This theme is used to great effect, and the meta humor piles up.  There is even one point where Stanley becomes aware of the narrator as a voice in his head, and then the narrator describes how Stanley can hear the voice describing itself and how strange it all is.
The illusion of choice is another big theme.  Every adventure game tries to give the player choices, but really all those choices are predetermined.  All the paths have been mapped out and you are merely a rat running in a maze of someones design by your own will.  You implicitly trust that the maze creator has created an exit somewhere, and you set out to find it.  The Stanley Parable understands this, and the narrator resents you when you don't choose the path he suggested.
I could go on about this ending or that one, but really I can't convey the essence of the experience.  I can't distill The Stanley Parable to mere words on a page.  The best way to play this game is with no knowledge of what you're getting in to.  To date, I have inflicted the experience upon at least 5 people and it never gets old.  As the narrator says, "(I) then praised the game for it's witty commentary and examinations of structural narrative tropes."
It might not be for everyone, but it's easy to pick up and play and will keep you coming back to explore another path or try something new.  I highly recommend you try it, and then sit your friends down and say, "Here, play this."

The only "bad" thing I could say about this game is that it's quite self-referential; in order to get anything meaningful out of the experience, you need to be somewhat familiar with video game tropes or, at the very least, storytelling tropes.  Aside from that, the ingenius, Kaufman-esque narrative within a narrative the game presents you is both side-splittingly hilarious and spine-chillingly poignant.  Crisp graphics, immersive sound design and a FANTASTIC voice-over job from the Narrator all contribute to what is essentially a thought-provoking work of interactive art.  This is the direction that video games need to go in for the medium to transcend its story-starved misogynistic miasma of bullets and blood (alliteration makes me sound smart!).

It is a game of what would happened if The Matrix was created by the Truman Show guys. It is a meta experience yet it makes fun of anything that is meta. It laughs in your face for trying out different approach but than it follows your game. This game took some serious effort and is meant to be consumed first hand.
I would recommend this game to everyone who likes a new challange but doesn't want to leave his or her comportable zone. It makes fun of it's own rules and mechanics but wants you so badly to follow them that even when you think that you break the rules you realie that you do not.

Never before have I played a game quite like this.
At first, I was skeptical. Having not played the Half-Life 2 mod of the same name, I wasn't really sure what I was getting into. In retrospect, the game which I was expecting would have had somewhat of a branching story with a few mechanics. As such, like any reasonable buyer, I played the avaliable demo. From then on, I knew this was going to be unique.
Now I could say that Galactic Cafe's, 'The Stanley Parable', is a story about a man named Stanley, and his sudden discovery that no-one in his office was in fact there, but there is so much more to say. One find quite rapidly that the fourth wall is shattered, or much more likely, never existed in the first place. Here is a game which forces the player to look at themself and their actions, and then comments on how utterly rediculous they actually are. A game which messes with the psyche of the player, never forcing them down a certain path, but criticising illogical descisions, like, say, jumping to ones death for no particular purpose other than to contradict the narrator.
This is by no means a long game (One can expect about 2-4 hours of playtime), nor does it really have any mechanics to speak of, but don't let that distract you from it.The Stanley Parable is an absolutely hilarious, frustrating, introspective, unique game, and I recommend it to all. If you don't believe me, or want to try it for yourself, play the demo to get a snippet of the whole experience.

There's no real way to describe this game without spoiling it... This is a meta-game. A game about playing games. The designers understand how gamers have adapted to playing games, how gamers think and react. They made a game designed specifically to exploit all the things we already know about games.
This is a seriously unique experience. There's a reason it was the #1 game on a bunch of year's end lists.
This game will make you question just about everything about the game.  This is an experience unlike any other video game and you would be foolish to not try it.

To be utterly and completely honest and sincere, this game is hilarious, thought-provoking, mind-boggling, and revelation-enducing. The experience is one where you'd have to see it for yourself to experience the true wonder; where you yourself would form your own thoughts about the game whilst playing it. You can't get the full experience just by watching a YouTube commentary. Hands down, this game was an incredible ride and I've been looking forward to it ever since the release of the original Half-Life 2 Mod. BUT, once it's over, the magic is kind of gone. I know you're discovering new stuff every minute and when you least expect it, the game takes another turn to a road you haven't been down before, but despite the slogan, there really is an end. While there's no true definite ending for the Stanley Parable (that's for you to decide), the end of the content comes rather quickly. My suggestion is to not binge this game, or else you'd be getting closer to having nothing left. Unless there's an update, I cannot truly experience the same things in the same ways I did the first time. My verdict: Buy it and play it. However, buy it whenever this game is on sale. That is all.

I'm not sure I should be writing this review yet, because I'm not sure I've reached every ending yet. I think I've broken double digits? Whatever, not running a game into the ground hasn't stopped me before, so here it is!
Buy it. Boom. Done. You need this game in your life. Because it's not just a game, but a story. And not a story like most first person shooters are stories, but it's a story that's 100% about player choice. Some of these choices are hilarious (the Confusion Ending, the Whiteboard Ending) while other result in your death (the Escape Ending, the Downstairs Ending); many of them find a way to re-route you to the beginning of the game, with minor cosmetic changes that leave you uncertain as to whether or not you're truly restarting.
The game's primary draw has to be the narration. The VO is soothing, witty, full of emotion; it's also surprisingly complete, with many dialogues going on much longer than one would expect. The game is all about the joy of discovery, and the narration encapsulates this perfectly, as you can't wait to hear what he says next.
Because of the nature of The Stanley Parable, it does get repetitive after a while. This is why it's best to set aside a full day (preferably a Tuesday) to play through everything at once, so the game can continuously update itself for you. It'll be a good day, I promise.

WHAT THE STANLEY PARABLE IS - NO SPOILERS
TL;DR: Play the demo avaliable on Steam to quickly see exactly "what the game is about".
The Stanley Parable is a game about making choices that is simple in terms of mechanics (WASD/arrow keys to move, E to interact with objects, mouse to look around, that's it)  but it is very unconventional in other aspects such as plot development or character presentation.
You play in first person view as an unsettlingly ordinary office worker named Stanley, in a story that begins with him realizing that all his coworkers have suddenly vanished. What really enriches the story is the omnipresent, amusing narrator (voiced by Kevan Brighting) who eventually contributes to the story much more than simply narrating it.
This story branches out to multiple, very different endings depending on what the player chooses to do. The brilliance of the game is how these choices change much more than just the plot, because the game does not proceed with conventional video game logic, sometimes even criticizing it. For example, the narrator's personality changes according to how you play and sometimes he breaks the fourth wall to comment on your decisions as the player. The achievement system and how "glitches" are handled are other examples of this. The game is also sprinkled with secrets and easter eggs for the more curious players to search for.
I find The Stanley Parable to be a thought-provoking and insightful on matters like the power of choices, the illusion of free choice, and what a video game really is or could be.
Despite its brilliance The Stanley Parable is a short experience, although it is still likely to stick around in your mind for a long time, even after you found all of the endings.

The Stanley Parable isn't a bad game, that is, if you could call it a game.
I'd call it a showcase of what it means to create a game, and what it means to play a game and contemplate the various choices you make as a player, all wrapped up in somethingthat's not really a game. Sure, there's interaction. Minimalistic, but I suppose being able to go from walking in one straight line to another straight line is indeed a form of "playing". Unfortunately, I don't think there's any thoughts or valuable insights that I recieved from this walking simulator that I couldn't have gotten from a well-informed and witty TedTalks video. Was it interesting? Yes, but so is a vast variety of actual games that don't get boring and overly repetative, and don't eventually amount to having spent fifteen dollars for two hours of
gameplay. "
And that's what it boils down to. Walking down the same halls fifteen or so times, and making a slight variations to hear different quips from the Narrator, which in all honesty, if not for his talent The Stanley Parable would have been unbearable for more than three runs. And that's what's sad. It loses it's artistic meaning after a few times, what with the sensation that maybe you do have power (only to have in wrenched away from you in an attempt to get you to look at your decisions from a critical point of view regarding existentialism and all that critical thinking jargo), and the sole motivation was "What's the narrator going to say this time?" It's sad, and you're being charged 15 dollars for something that was made... with a half-life mod. I bought this because I was told it was deeply insightful to the human condition and was a pleasure to play. Then again, the person who reckomended The Stanley Parable to me is infamous for cutting the neighbor's lawns for free because he finds it "theraputic". Whatever that means.

The Stanley Parable is an amazingly funny exploration game, with many different endings. It continually breaks the rules of video games in the most creative ways, and it manages to do this without becoming tedious or boring.
Every individual ending is a completely different experience, from trying to defuse a bomb, to being lectured about the importance of your choices, to playing through different video games, all leaving you shocked and surprised as you play. You can never truly see what is going to happen.
This, along with the excellent voice acting of the narrator makes an experience you wouldn't want to miss!
The only downside, is that the game does not have much replay value, as once you have experienced an ending, you will never get the same feeling of surprise.
Final Score: 9/10

The game started as mysteriously as one would expect after playing the demo.  There are quite a few different ways to play The Stanley Parable, yet only a few of them are interesting or rewarding.  After about 2 hours, playing this game felt like chewing old gum; it's not new and it feels like a chore.  The player suffers through never-changing audio they've heard a million times before to try to get the last bit of flavor they can.  More often than not the end is not the end, nor is it a welcome "new" beginning.
For $4.99 I wouldn't feel as if I got a bad deal, but $14.99 is too much for two hours of gameplay, maybe 1.5 of that being enjoyable.

Again, after Gone Home, I'm here trying to understand if this is a game or not. Whenever the computer told him to, Stanley pushed the designated buttons on his keyboard. And while others (who?) found this to be soul-wrenching, Stanley enjoyed every moment of it.
I am quite jealous of Stanley's job, as I do enjoy following mundane orders. I mean, look at all those white textures! Surely, whoever thought through making windows should get a review in their honour. Or at least a comment.
But is it ever enough? A game, with finite paths and finite randomization, with endings denied by the very fabric of the code? Why yes. Why would you ever question such an authority?
Oh, and by the way, Stanley, employee 432 got a call from your wife. She wants you to remember to pick up that romance novel from the book store after grocery shopping. But don't take too long, employee 427; you know how difficult it is for your wife to make dinner.
Simply wonderful.

This is the story of a gamer named John. One day, John was feeling quite bored. He wanted to play a game but didn't feel like playing anything he owned. "Gee," he thought, "I would sure like to play something new, original, and fresh. Maybe it could have witty comentary, jokes, and easter eggs too. Oh, and it can have tons of endings!" Then John remembered he had heard of a game that souned quite fun. He struggled to remember its name, but at last rembered. John typed the game's name into the Steam seach bar: The Stanley Parable. He clicked on its page, and looked at the confusing screanshots and the strange trailers, and finally glanced at the price: $14.99. Luckly, John was bored enough and had a big enough wallet to give the game a chance. But you see, this where the story ends, for now anyway, because John is not John, nor, if you had easily understood from prior knowledge of the game's narative, Stanley. No, John is you. And you have arrived at the game's first choice: will you listen to what I say, choose the left door and find out what awaits you on this path? Or will you turn right, and continue on playing your dull, run-of-the-mill AAA FPSMMORPGRTS-thingy? If only I knew, I'm not some omni-present Narrator. No, this choice belongs to you. Choose wisely, Stanley.

There there. There there.

Just a sense that maybe you might have missed something important like a niggling in the back of your skull. So you play it again. But you don't find anything and that is clearly not the game's fault. So you play it again. And this time you're absolutely positive that you quite probably missed something and maybe if you play it one more time then you will find it...
Eventually though you hit that realization that there really is nothing more. This is it. Oh sure... there might be more achievements but you're not sure exactly what they might be. You could look them up online but that would be cheating wouldn't it? Of course it would! But maybe if you played it one more time...
No! No! That is it. There is nothing else. I'm really going to stop playing it now and go back to something not so minimalist with better graphics and more explosions. I'm sure Borderlands 2 would be more satisfying at this point. I'm pretty positive I have gone everywhere I can possibly go. 6 hours in and there really does appear to be nothing else left to do.

The concept was not as interesting as I was expecting. Instead of being a game that continuously builds on itself, it is instead a game that just progresses the game by sending you back to the beginning to go down a scripted path that changes if you then take another path. It does not branch too heavily though, maybe 4-5 branches maximum. This game is literally like opening a folder, then making folders with different names inside of other folders inside of the folders inside the folders (inception pls), but just because you can see a different folder with slightly different contents and another slightly different folder in the left folder than the right one doesn't make it interesting. The concept is not even new actually, I have seen free games before on Kongregate that did the same thing (and in some individuals' opinions; done better). The comedy was meh; only giving me a few chuckles here and there. The plot was non-existant and filled with holes, which might have been the point, but was still nonetheless unsatisfactory, due to not really making any progress at all through anything. There was also not enough "game" in the game. The whole game played like being pulled through an art gallery to see what the maker wanted you to  see; like "Hey, you went down the right path? Look at my ducky, now keep walking. Choose a path, left path this time? Look at my donkey. It is very artistic is it not? Oh wait, you wanted to actually be able to do more in the game than just navigate a linear path that seems split until the end (which rarely ever changes dramatically to give anyone any real surprise) and listen to prescripted events that we pretend weren't? Tough luck."
The only fulfillment in the game is collecting all of the endings and Easter eggs, but there isn't any challenge in getting them. Playing this game is like being told to pick up MnMs or Skittles, or if they try to be really edgy and creative; chopped up Twix bars. Wow, so fun. But seriously, no matter what it is literally just you doing the same action over and over (in the example given, bending over and picking up little pieces of candy). You know the general idea of what is going to be waiting for you in the next action or corridor you take and you know that it will end in "now restart". There isn't any twist that keeps it interesting. It is not a game. It is a walk through some guy's art museum project. He tries to keep it interesting, but for the most part it wasn't. Too much repitiveness, not enough plot twists to keep it interesting, once you have seen 3 endings, you have seen 'em all. I could keep going, but I think you get the gist of what I am saying.
4/10; it had its funny moments and was interesting in the beginning, but that feeling quickly died out after the third restart and the comedy and jokes were too similar to keep getting such a positive response out of me as it did in the beginning, no real gameplay inside of this game killed it also. The idea has also been done before, which in my opinion a free game I played before with this concept did it much better. Waste of $15 dollars, would not recommend.

It provides an experience no medium other than a video game could. The Stanely Parable couldn't be a film, a book or a radio drama because no matter how good they are, they lack two key things - participation, and the ability to restart. Only in games does restarting change anything. In The Stanely Parable, it has the potential to change everything, and keep changing everything, right up to the point where you realise that you are in fact changing nothing. This constant feeling of 'it's about this...wait...actually it's about that' is what this game centres around. You will feel trapped, liberated, antagonistic, companiable, satisfaction, guilt, unease and serenity, sometimes all within the same playthrough. It's not something that demands anything technical of you, but it is a game. It's quintessentially a game, and in a medium that often seems envious of film, The Stanely Parable uses the format to deliver something unique, and is one of my favourite experiences in a very long time.

I'll try to review this game without giving too much away (which is more difficult than it sounds). The Stanley Parable is a mod turned expensive indie game about a man named Stanley and his important self discovery about the sinister reality of his job, and the reasons behind his love for his impossibly mundane job. That is the game in a nutshell. It's a very linear, thought through plot and setup. However, what makes this game so special is that you don't HAVE to follow the pre-determined plot. You have multiple choices in everything, and the game can only follow your every move. In fact, the more you deviate from the game, the more the story's narrator will break the fourth wall and berate you. That's another interesting aspect about this game: the Narrator and your relationship with him. You can turn him into anything you want to. He can be your rival, your villain, your friend, or simply your narrator. The appeal in this game is simply exploring the many choices you can make, and the many alternate endings you can seek out, and there are many (there seems to be more than Heavy Rain). I liked this game alot simply for the concept and the reactions with the narrator. I don't think it's worth $14.99 (there are much bigger, better games for less), but I do think the challenging the sensibilites of traditional gaming attitudes alone is worth a couple of playthroughs. Overall, I'd say it's worth playing, but don't pay more than $9.99 for it, unless they release a "Gold Edtion" with even more endings.
