The Stanley Parable is strange. The Stanley Parable is smart, calculated chaos. The Stanley Parable is about many, many things - at least, until it decides it isn't about anything at all. Quite often in the same moment. The Stanley Parable gives you power, and then it takes that power away without a second thought or a moment’s notice or hesitation. The Stanley Parable is a game made up of little moments.
Let's begin again.
The Stanley Parable is a first-person game. It fits into no other genre beyond that. It gives you the trappings you need to play, and no more. You can walk, you can crouch, and you can interact with what is required of you. You cannot jump, there is no action to speak of, and you have no weapons. Except, perhaps, for the choices you make. The Stanley Parable then takes away all of your perceived power, and taunts you mercilessly as you helplessly flail around an endless loop of rooms with no hope of ever escaping. And then you wake up.
Let's begin again.
The Stanley Parable is a game about story. The Stanley Parable winks and giggles and points and laughs at you from behind the screens. It never lets you forget that you are experiencing a story, a contrivance, a wild flight of fancy. Yet there is no story. It never lets you forget that, while you are the player, it is the puppet master pulling your strings. Every choice you make, The Stanley Parable changes. Every deviation, every action against what has been planned out for you, and every act of rebellion alters something. You can go against the designated path, but you will pay the consequences. They may be a simple change in path, a painted line leading you back towards the intended direction, or a fatal meeting with a bottomless pit. There is no way of knowing for sure what will happen when you choose to go your own way.
Let's begin again.
The Stanley Parable is about Stanley. Stanley. ...Stanley. .....Stanley.. Stanley....Stanley..
Let's begin again.
The Stanley Parable is a giant, combat-free choose-your-own-adventure book. There are countless choices and secrets to be found that branch the story off into unseen directions at any given moment. A faceless narrator guides your path the entire trip. An omniscient conductor for the ride you're currently on. He is a prankster, guide, villain, victim, and all other roles that need to be played. He is simultaneously your greatest friend and your worst enemy. Whatever role he embodies, he's fantastic. He'll make you feel rage, sadness, joy, wonder, excitement, and so much more. He'll even cause you to pause and take a moment to think. At one point, he tasked me with answering a phone. I subsequently tripped over the cord, unplugging the phone and altering the outcome of the choice and the story. As a result, the narrator was heartbroken that I interrupted his tale and he made me feel very sorry for him with his reaction to it. He is a main driving force behind the entire game. He is the man behind the curtain. The many, many curtains.
Let’s begin again.
The Stanley Parable is never-ending, but always over. Each time you reach a new ending, or a thread unravels with you starting back at the beginning, you may feel like you’re moving closer to seeing everything the game has to offer. But you would be wrong. There is always something more to be found, and that’s the beauty of the game. You will stumble across secrets so entirely accidentally that you may not even notice anything has changed. Yet everything will have changed. While treading familiar ground can get tiresome, that moment of discovery when you notice something is different is a wonderful feeling. Suddenly the narration is given in different words. A new door suddenly opens before you. Excitement grows, the path moves into new territory, you begin to feel joy at having made a new discovery – and then it’s over. Perhaps you meet a brutal end at the hands of a conveyor belt leading to bone-pulverizing crushers, or perhaps you have found freedom in a sudden path that opens up into a bright, sunny - Minecraft?! Oh dear. Well, by now you know what happens next.
Let’s begin again.
What you are experiencing with this review is the very heart of The Stanley Parable. And it’s just the beginning. It’s hope that you are reaching an ending, and then being thrust back to the beginning. It’s annoyance that you keep encountering another new instance that thrusts you back to another beginning. It’s hidden meanings, subtleties, irritation, and joy. It’s suffering, but rewarding. The Stanley Parable is contrast, and it is uniformity. The one constant is entertainment. If you enjoy it, you will continue to enjoy it. If you don’t? Well, it’s understandable. It’s not a game for everyone and it doesn’t pretend to be. You’ll move on and never look back, and no one would ever blame you. Least of all The Stanley Parable itself.
Let’s begin again.
This is a game that enthralled my entire family while playing. A five year old, a twelve year old, and a 28 year old were completely engrossed in watching the game being played. It is hard to describe how rare it is that this family sits still long enough to watch a movie together, let alone to watch a game such as this being played. The Stanley Parable bridges the divide between generational gaps as effortlessly as it crawls into the deepest recesses of your brain and sticks there until you can’t help but return again, and again, and again.. The Stanley Parable loves you, and The Stanley Parable hates you. But most of all? The Stanley Parable needs you to make a choice. That’s all The Stanley Parable will ever ask of you. It’s friendly like that.

Put
,
, Terry Gilliam's
, and a Douglas Adams text adventure in a blender and you'll get something like this.  The Stanley Parable is a game that asks questions about choice and agency and narrative structure in games, the kind of reality-bending shenanigans popular in movies in the late 1990s (think
,
,
and
), shot through with a dry wit and a college-student sense of philosophical questioning.
I played it through, saw all the major and most of the minor endings, had a good time and chuckled, but it's not going to change the world.  It's fine to ask these kind of philosophical questions but it's important not to confuse this with depth.   Despite all its narrative trickery (and plotting out all those branching possibilities can't have been easy) I found it to be fairly surface, with a cynical attitude about the nature of work that it didn't earn.  I understand it was conceived and written by a 19-year-old originally and it displays a young-adult's view of what it means to hold an office job and be an everyday Working Stiff.   Working in an office isn't death and doesn't mean you become a button-pressing robot known only as a number.  it hasn't since the Fifties, if it ever really did.  Any job, even at a menial level, involves a lot more engagement than what The Stanley Parable thinks it does.  Nobody is entering numbers on a computer without thinking, and if they are, they're soon going to be unemployed.
All that said, I enjoyed the game quite a bit and it was definitely different.  My favorite ending was the Museum ending, where I got a look at the design process and the early stages of the game.  That was really unique and fun.

The overall game is fairly short, and all the endings can be completed within a few hours.  However, the dialogue and storytelling aspects make this game fantastic from start to finish.  Fans of the Portal series will feel right at home, but if you are looking for something to sink days of gameplay into, this is not it.

*SPOILERS FOLLOW*
On the surface, this game seemed to be right up my alley.  A fourth-wall breaking deconstruction of narrative choice and consequence in video games? Yes please!  And at a first play, it lives up to its promise; mechanically it's very smooth, the narration is well done and never feels forced, and the interaction between you and the narrator feels surprisingly organic.
Alas, it has (in my opinion) two major problems.
First, it's rather short; you can find the majority of the endings in a few hours of playtime, and once you've found them there's almost zero replay value in going back through any of them.  Once you're through the easy ones, finding the rest can be a bit of tedious guesswork, and it can quickly turn into a repetitious slog.  The narration becomes robotic and rote, the jokes run thin, and generally the 'fun' factor very rapidly falls off a cliff.  There are very few surprises left after maybe four hours of playtime, and the cracks in the artifice become obvious.  This is, one begins to suspect, part of the point; but more on that in a moment.
The shortness and lack of replay value could be forgiven, if the ideas it played with were big enough or interesting enough to offset the small of fun.  Unfortunately, they aren't.  Yes, narrative choice in most games is a lie, and yes it's funny that even when we violate the dictates of the narrator we're nevertheless almost incapable of doing anything that hasn't been planned in advance by the game designers, and yes the only real free and spontaneous choice we have in the game is to turn it off, stand up, and go do something else, but this is nothing new.  The presentation in a video game is (somewhat) novel, but at the same time there's a certain amount of battering you upside the head with the point that goes on, and it ultimately deconstructs itself; it's a game that tells you that it's ultimately pointless to play games, that the entire experience is artificial and preplanned with zero true sponteneity, that the natural-seeming interaction between you and the narrator in the beginning was nothing more than a monument to your own predictability.  But the only way it can do that is by *not* being entertaining past a point, and *not* having any replay value.
So; interesting?  Yes.  A nice change of pace from the usual FPS?  Definitely.  Briefly entertaining?  Most certainly.  Worth $15?  Not at all, in my opinion.  Ultimately it's a game that's hamstrung by its own key idea: a game that you pay $15 for just so it can tell you that you wasted $15.
(Note: I have no idea why steam says I only have 2 hours of playtime; it's closer to 6 or 7, though honestly the last 3 weren't worth it.)

Put
,
, Terry Gilliam's
, and a Douglas Adams text adventure in a blender and you'll get something like this.  The Stanley Parable is a game that asks questions about choice and agency and narrative structure in games, the kind of reality-bending shenanigans popular in movies in the late 1990s (think
,
,
and
), shot through with a dry wit and a college-student sense of philosophical questioning.
I played it through, saw all the major and most of the minor endings, had a good time and chuckled, but it's not going to change the world.  It's fine to ask these kind of philosophical questions but it's important not to confuse this with depth.   Despite all its narrative trickery (and plotting out all those branching possibilities can't have been easy) I found it to be fairly surface, with a cynical attitude about the nature of work that it didn't earn.  I understand it was conceived and written by a 19-year-old originally and it displays a young-adult's view of what it means to hold an office job and be an everyday Working Stiff.   Working in an office isn't death and doesn't mean you become a button-pressing robot known only as a number.  it hasn't since the Fifties, if it ever really did.  Any job, even at a menial level, involves a lot more engagement than what The Stanley Parable thinks it does.  Nobody is entering numbers on a computer without thinking, and if they are, they're soon going to be unemployed.
All that said, I enjoyed the game quite a bit and it was definitely different.  My favorite ending was the Museum ending, where I got a look at the design process and the early stages of the game.  That was really unique and fun.

The overall game is fairly short, and all the endings can be completed within a few hours.  However, the dialogue and storytelling aspects make this game fantastic from start to finish.  Fans of the Portal series will feel right at home, but if you are looking for something to sink days of gameplay into, this is not it.

This game has a very unique sense of humor that is a blend of both American and British humor.  In this game you play as Stanley, a grossly typical office worker, who's job is to push buttons.  When Stanley finds that one day, all of his coworkers are gone, it is up to the player to investigate just what's going on.
There are many endings that provide an entertaining conclusion to Stanley's incredibly repeatable story.  If you do not wish to simply look up the endings, you are entitled to hours of fun, searching for all the endings.
The game is very short, but the it loves to reset itself once you run into one of the many comical roadblocks that you'll eventually find.  The omniscient narrator provides interesting commentary, as well as playing the role of a partner of sorts.  He'll comment on your decisions, (or lack thereof, in some cases) and will also give you certain ideas as to what comes next.
The game is immensly enjoyable, but has one flaw: this is simply an hd re-release.  Instead of paying fifteen dollars, you can quite easily install the mod as long as you own half-life 2.  This version features nothing in terms of additions, save for the narrator.  You are essentially paying fifteen dollars for some mp3 files.  While he does add some flavor to the game, he can be rather arbitrary at times, and ruin one's immersion.  On a side note, some of the achievements are quite confusing and annoying, where others are hilarous to take part in.

This is not a game, it is an activity. I bought it because of gushing reviews in the gaming press; "groundbreaking", "innovative", "we don't want to spoil the surprise", etc. Well, the surprise is that there is nothing to see here whatsoever. From end to end, this activity can be "played" in a few minutes. There is very little interaction and practically no exploration. This is the gaming equivalent of arthouse cinema - you need to be a hipster with a goatee and a PBR in your hand to even have a chance of appreciating it. The same money could buy you three actual games on Steam.
At $0.99, this collection of assets stuffed into an engine and mislabeled "game" would be merely overpriced. At $14.99 it is rampant theft. Under no circumstances waste your time downloading the demo, and there should be no drugs or threats powerful enough to make you actually pay money for the full version.
AVOID. VIGOROUSLY.

The more I think about it, the more I like it. Is it weird? Yeah. But it's undeniably clever, and presents you with some alarmingly grand ideas in a tiny, ironically narrated package. It's one of those trojan horse pieces of fiction: you think it's about one thing, and it is on a surface level, but the meat of the matter actually reveals itself to be something utterly unexpected, and quite different from what you initially perceived it to be. All of this, conveyed and executed with a sense of verve and assuredness that some games can't achieve in dozens of hours, in a play session that clocked in at just over thirty minutes. I can't stop thinking about it. And even if a fancy-sounding fellow told me to, I would just keep on doing it anyway.

The Stanley Parable is less of a game and more of a lot of really bad Meta Humor. The developers have this entire concept that a game never offers you choices, simply doors to take and instead enforces the idea you never actually make any of the choices you think you are, instead using predetermined paths from developers.
The biggest flaw in the game is though that developers present you with decisions you are allowed to make on your own and the direct results of those decisions. The Stanley Parable takes that varaible away. The game ignores deciisions you make when the narrartor isn't happy with the decisions you made, predetermined or not.
But in that very act, the developers are still delivering on what every other game does. Which are decisions. And the only one you can really choose is to simply turn off the game. The reality is Stanley Parable isn't really much of a game and it's my personal opinion that it shouldn't be classifed as a game, instead more of a social comment on the gaming industry.
Even with this being taken into consideration I bought the game on sale because I thought it'd at least be funny. What you see in the videos is the very extent to how funny the game is. The reality is a lot of the game is spent forced into listening to the incoherent ramblings of the narrator, much of which is very dry and very non-funny.
I don't recommend this game to anyone. Anyone saying this game is "fun" or "funny" or even "intelligent" are only trying to fit in with the rest of the crowd who somehow have been brainwashed into the idea that this is a game in any sense.

The stages you will go through when playing through the Stanley Parable: What is this game? What is this? What is game? What? I never thought I could have so much fun from a game based on a simple choice: do I follow what the voice in my head says or not? The voice in your head is the Narrator, an amazingly voice-acted, deep, and complex character. This isn't like the narrator in Bastion. This is a far more sinister/benign/antagonistic/sympathetic character. This is a wonderful exploration and expansion of the gaming medium without a drop of pretention. In fact, it's played very tongue-in-cheek, and it will be a while before you realize what exactly this game means. And chances are, it won't mean the same thing to you that it does to me, or your friends. Before you spend money on this game, however, I highly suggest you play the demo first. If you don't like what the demo has you doing, then chances are you won't like this game. If you've already bought this game, I still suggest you play the demo, because it's just as exciting (and dare I say, brilliant) as this game.

Speaking of enjoying the journey rather than the destination, this axiom applies even further in The Stanley parable.  I'm honestly not quite sure how to describe this game without spoiling anything, but it basically reminds me of Antichamber without the mind bending puzzles and with better narration.  I felt like I was an unwilling partiicpant in the Truman Show, and you can "beat" the game in 15 minutes or so, but the true joy and payback in The Stanley Parable is by finding just how you can break the narration and go in different paths.  I think I found over 10 endings, each sillier than the last, and I'm not even sure I've found them all yet.  It's surprising to hear just how pretty much every small thing incites some monologue from the narrator; even the same break room that you walk through a dozen times will trigger new narration each time.  There's no real gameplay here, and honestly it seems to buck trends of the video game industry in a very self-referential way, but unlike some games lower on my list (such as Evoland and DLC quest), the winking is clever enough and has enough substance to say that it feels intelligent rather than pandering.  If you think about much of the structure of this game after the fact, you'll realize that there is a very meta form of commentary on current video game design and player expectation overall.  But even without any of that pretentious jibber-jabber, The Stanley Parable was truly enjoyable for the few hours it held my attention :)

Although there are many admirable qualities about this game, there is not enough content to make it worth $15 ($14.99) Now the narrator is fun to listen to, and there are many funny parts, but the lack of variation is high, and you will find yourself to have exposed most of the content in roughly 5 hours. It is one of those games where if you are easy to make laugh, then you will love it, and those are the people some of you may have watched play this game on Youtube. If you did not watch these people, then you may have shared the same opinion. Ultimately what I can conclude with this game is that I have gotten more laughs and enjoyment for $15 in other games, than this one by a long shot. They had very good ideas with this one, but if there were let us just say, more doors to open, item interaction, more variations after each choice, then I could say more. The narrator was the only thing that made me buy this game.
If you chose to buy this game, just be prepared to start over quite often. It is not a savable game, and it is meant to restart with your different choices made. Understand that you will spend quite a bit of time repeating parts to get to a certain point, and change your course of action there. Most of your time will be spent repeating parts. IF you were to cut out all the parts you repeat, I would guess that the game is really only 1.5 hours long. Maybe 2. 3 hours MAX. Think of it this way. This game (in terms of value) is 1/4 the price of a high dollar game that is $60 that has been worked on for 5 years.

One of the best games of this decade, "The Stanley Parable" brilliantly makes of self reflection a raison d'être.
More than introspection we should probably talk about what we can call "self extrospection".
The game's self extrospection is favored by making the player bring up and reflect over all of those things that he (or she) considers being implicitly existing in some formats (that a videogame can be beaten, that there are good and bad choices to make, that enviromental interaction gives positive feedbacks, et cetera), and, on the base of those reflections, pushes him to consider the meaning of such conventions, their real value and, with a more distant perspective, his own relation to them and his acceptance of rules in general.
One of the central arguing points of the game is that the player, by systematically trying to apply the same mechanics he is usually applying to videogames in order to achieve the results he is used to achieve, is substantially growing accustomed to mechanically do the same thing over and over, without demanding anything extra-ordinary (uncommon) of himself nor leaving any space for free reflection. "Stanley [...] has a job that demands nothing of him, and every button that he pushes is a reminder of the inconsequential nature of his existence. Look at him there: pushing buttons, doing exactly what he's told to do. Now, he's pushing a button. Now, he's eating lunch. Now, he's going home; now, he's coming back to work. One might even feel sorry for him, except that he's chosen this life." As Stanley is not questioning the repetitiveness of his job so the player might not be questioning certain patterns that he is automatically following in his gameplay sessions; in The Stanley Parable these patterns are usually bringing the player to look for something that he's used to get in other games, only to end up getting it in a very ridiculing form (
).
In most of the cases, by giving the players exactly the contrary to what they wanted from the game, The Stanley Parable pushes the player to obtain a sort of third person self analytical perspective (even intensified in one of the endings in which
), the so called (by me) "self extrospection", in which he is asked to reflect on the nature of his impulsive attractions or behaviours. The arising questions and the following thoughts are many: is what the players are looking for something really worth to look for, or are they just grown accustomed to have it and therefore they're feeling its absence when it's not given to them? But it is only when this perspective is moved to other entertainment forms, which are also demanding nothing of people and just drench them with a shower of positive or shocking stimuli, that we can really start to question the level of free will that we possess; as Gustave Le Bon writes in his book "The Crowd – A Study of the Popular Mind": ”It is only by obtaining some sort of insight into the psychology of crowds that it can be understood [...] how powerless they are to hold any opinions other than those which are imposed upon them, and that is not with rules based on theories of pure equity that they are to be led, but by seeking what produces an impression on them and what seduces them.”
How much are we automatically doing because we've been pushed to grow accustomed to it? Are we laughing at a video where someone crashes with a motorbike because it is really funny and not at all unethical, or are we doing that to relief some of our personal frustrations by watching someone else failing? "Yes, it's all very amusing. And we laugh and we call our friends over and they laugh too and soon the whole world laughs and laughs and laughs at the man who failed. [...] But [...] you, sitting there: what have you gained watching this video? What have you learned?" And if we do it because of the frustrating monotony of our life, why are we then allowing the frustration to latently exist? Are we so accustomed to our life as it is that we're scared of doing any changes? How many non-influenced choices are we making? What's the worth of those choices?
Stanley might be starting to understand all of this: "in and amongst his aimless meandering, I think he is actually beginning to discover something: he is getting closer to  an answer, an explaination, an exit. He is beginning to earn his freedom", but he is a videogame character bound to narrative limits and cannot escape his own story. He is Stanley and can only be Stanley.
But what about us?
"Now, if I could truly put you in his shoes, to show you the paths he walked and the choices he made.. [...] soon you will be the one to walk: the controls will be in your hands. [...] Oh, I think I'm going to enjoy this. When you find out how alone you truly are.. I will be laughing more than anyone."
Is this a time in which we should break the old entertaining clichés of the videogame medium
and release some of its pedagogical potential? Afterall "men never shape their conduct upon the teaching of pure reason" as Le Bon writes, and we can deduce that they learn by empirically experiencing reality. But if the virtuality is empirically making them experience and hate their own reality, isn't that potentially a formative experience?
Is this then a case in which "ludus est magister vitae"?
Well, it's certainly worth a thought.
The Stanley Parable Personal Review
Renzo "Stermayer" Arcuri

It is hard to talk about The Stanley Parable without spoiling the plot. And that is neither a good or a bad thing, because as it turns out, the plot is secondary to the experience. It might even be tertiary. Fact is, the plot can go a number of ways. You are in control. And you are not.
The Stanley Parable is a game that is designed at its core to challange the notion of narrative storytelling in games. Particularely, the element of "choice". Is it always binary (good vs bad)? How far can the consequeces branch? How deep does the rabbit-hole go? Suffice it to say, I played and then replayed the game a LOT of times - constantly mixing up my choices - trying to locate the "seams" of the games limitation. Eventually, I conclude that the game is both razor sharp in its wit, spot-on in its satire, and fiercly intelligent in how it presents itself.
Not bad for a game where you basically just walk through a mundane office-building.
Never thought I'd be so entrenched and absorbed in a game. Fantastic idea and executed with a beautiful eloquence. Simply AMAZING!

A lot of players have described this game as a piece of art. I cannot agree. Having a narrator constantly make fun of the game, the player, and talking absurd nonsense, does seem like a dadaist concept, unfortunately this form of art being 100 years old nothing in this game feels particularly original nor revolutionary... neither is satire about office workers with a dull job.
Applied to a game well... it just isn't very much fun. There is no gameplay per se, you just move the character as you wait for the story to unfold, so you may as well watch somebody else play it on yootoob.
There was a section (the Museum) which I enjoyed visiting, as well as the first ending I got (the parody one) which I have genuinely enjoyed. But that is pretty much it.
With most the other endings being dull and repetitive, and with only 2-3 hours of play inside, the high price at which its sold is perhaps the most absurd about the whole thing.

The Stanley Parable is great... if you love filing cabinets. Staring at filing cabinets for an hour whilst an unseen voice drones on about how futile it all is. I did enjoy this game, but only for the first twenty minutes. The multiple endings become a repetitive, fruitless labour, with only a few button presses and basic mobility for the player to perform.
The Stanley Parable clearly wants to be a critic's darling and a clever poke at the structure and rationale of video games, but after the originality is tempered by yet more filing cabinets, I started to feel like the joke was on me. No doubt, the developers intend for you to realise just how well they mock the genre, but they achieve this by giving you a game which is fundamentally very thin and boring beyond its air of (unresolved) mystery. There is little actual narrative, there are basically only three or four levels.
Overall, the game might be worth £4 max, but you'll be left feeling mocked and shortchanged at full sale price. It would make a great change of pace chapter in a bigger, better game; but falls flat as a standalone.

The Stanley Parable started as a Half Life 2 Mod years ago, but has recently been remade into its own game. TSP is an exploration game with no action or violence whatsoever; It is driven by the narrator, and how he wants the story to go. If the player does as the narrator says, the game technically will end very shortly (took me 5 min). But that’s not what this game is. When the player “beats the game” the player hasn’t actually beat the game, because it is impossible to beat this game. TSP is called an exploration game. The player is supposed to disobey the narrator and explore the story; Find out what happened to Stanley’s co-workers, wife, and job.
The game is called The Stanley Parable for a reason. It is a parable. By definition, a parable means – A simple story used to illustrate a moral or spiritual lesson. This game does exactly that. TSP has a much deeper meaning than you may think. In my personal opinion, the game tries to teach us that we need to decide how we live our life, and not let others manipulate us into how they want us to think. The game is all about choices. The player has a choice to explore the story or simply do as he/she is told.

I love to read reviews before I play a game; and in return, I love writing reviews back, to help people in making a decision before getting a game.  But for some odd reason, I hope that this review will help you lower your expectation a bit, so you can enjoy the game more than I did.  I still recommend this though, but I felt that I read too many positive reviews of this before I played this game.  So I had the highest expectation when I started playing this.
Yes, I was expecting a lot more from this game.  This game didn't quite meet my expectations.  I was expecting something more profound, more enlightening, inspirational, life changing, soul searching kind of...umm...stuff.  Maybe it did have a little bit of everything that I was looking for.
"To be or not to be, that is the question".  This game reminds me of this famous Shakespeare quote.  It seems like it presents many questions about existence and reality, but there really isn't any answer(there really isn't any definitive answers for these type of abstract questions anyways). But they seem to present all these questions in a very subtle way for you to think about.  Personally I'm used to thinking about these existential questions… maybe this is the reason the game didn't quite meet my expectation...maybe for a person who never think about this type of thing will find the game more refreshing?
The game is all about replayability(which is not a real word).  I usually dislike replaying a game; but this game is so short, it almost seem mandatory to replay over and over again to go through all the different paths and endings.  But I didn't mind it, all of these multiple endings are all very interesting.
I guess what I love the most about this game is the humor, it actually made me laughed out loud a few times.  Perhaps the game is saved by this charming and yet sometimes annoying narrator. The Stanley Parable is a game about Stanley. Except it isn’t really, and it’s not categorically a game in the true sense of the word. It’s more like a parody, except sometimes it’s intentionally not comical; it’s introspective, so I suppose it’s more like an evolving interactive narrative based around first person exploration. Except you don’t really explore that much. The path you take is very linear aside from when it’s completely open. There is a narrative to follow though! Unless you choose to ignore it. Wait, wait, let’s start again.
The Stanley Parable is certainly first person based, and is sometimes seen through the eyes of Stanley, a man working a dull office job in some corner office somewhere who arrives at work one day to find his workplace completely removed of his colleagues. Sometimes, this is a story about his search for his missing workmates and the dangerous secrets behind their disappearance. Only sometimes it’s not. It’s sometimes something completely different. It’s dependent on you. Sometimes. I can’t stop saying sometimes. Let’s start again. Again.
The Stanley Parable is a direct attack on the genre tropes that first person exploration and linear gameplay presents. Upon discovering the empty interior of his office block, Stanley can move through the building, following the subtle prompts of the narrator, except that he’s free to ignore this and just wander off on his own. The narrator might scramble to tie Stanley’s erratic actions into his narrative, or he might attack you, the player, for your lack of discipline. Or he might do something else. For instance, should you stop to try to gain achievements, he may lead you on a merry dance for his own amusement. Perhaps it’s sufficient to say that the real driving force is the narrator and his reactions. Maybe it’s all about all the eventual and multiple outcomes your behaviour might garner. Except, no, that’s not quite right either.
The Stanley Parable is ultimately undefinable, aside from the many aspects of the game that are easy to define. That’s just gibberish, isn’t it? Disregard that. Except, hang on, that’s kind of right. Indeed, the game can be as simple as you let it; do as you’re told, and it’s a fairly linear tale about discovery and freedom. Is that the tale it wants to tell? Maybe? Probably? No, actually, I don’t think it is. Most of the time, you can find conclusion in about 10-15 minutes, and multiple replays are needed to see the outcome of various choices you’re sometimes free to make. The game itself changes along with this; various pathways are boarded up if you abuse them too often; numerous restarts are chastised and long winded exposition mercilessly cut short with exacerbated sighs should the narrator be forced to re-tread old ground too often. It doesn’t so much as drive you towards one big true path as challenge you to pervert its most basic outcome as much as you can. Is that a mission statement? Enjoy messing up your tale? I think so. Why would anyone do that?
Full Review //

Game studies (authors such as Espen Aarseth) explain that videogames are "ergodic literature": ergodic is a text that is generated by the one who read it. The Stanley Parable is not properly a game, or at least it is not a common videogame; when you play it, you do nothing except moving, exploring and interacting with a limited number of objects. The core of the game are the choices you make, that could be consistent with what an omnipresent narrator say or not, leading you to different finales.
It can be sayed that Stanley parable is not a game but an ergodic, meta-narrative experience that functions in virtue of the doubt it generates in the player: am I in control of my character, or the game controls my actions?
For the limited longevity (you can finish it in a couple of hours) and the limited interaction possibilities, Stanley parable has some issues as a game. Despite this, it is a fascinating experiment about the powers of pure (ergodic) narration.
8/10

If I had to sum up The Stanley Parable in a sentence, I would say:
"This is a game that challenges what a game is, how games should be played, and why we play them, all the while questioning whether or not what you are playing can even be called a game in itself."
And what a great job it does of it, too.
As much as I would love to go into detail about the nature of the plot, this is the sort of game that loses too much of its precious value if spoiled. You really do just need to see it for yourself. Resist the urge to look it up on YouTube. Go play it! Buy it, steal it, go to your friends house, I don't really care. You just need to sit down, and play. Your results may vary, but that's the best part.
At the very least, play the free demo. If that doesn't make you shell out the cash, I'll eat my hat.

The Stanley Parable is a simple enough game. In order to win, all you need to do is follow the directions of the narrator. If you choose to be punk rock like myself though, things get real meta real fast. All because you chose one door over the other or went up instead of down. This interactive story is truly entertaining and thought provoking. Do we ever really have control of anything? Are we just pawns in an overall plot? That much is uncertain, but one thing is certain: It's really fun to make this narrator mad.
If you come to a set of two open doors, don't enter the door on your right!

I have a cat, and our favorite game together is "whack the stick". This game consists of me wiggling a small stick and the cat leaping, pouncing, biting and whacking at the stick with her paws. Sometimes I drag the stick in front of the cat, other times I gently beat a tattoo on her forehead. Sometimes I prod her belly or make the stick poke out from beneath a towel.  My cat is equally confused, annoyed, amused and overjoyed by all these interactions, never quite sure what the stick is going to do next but quite happy for me to keep confusing, annoying, amusing and pleasing her with my magical, unpredictable, always-exciting stick.
Which brings me to the Stanley Parable. This game is "whack the stick" for humans. What is the goal of the game? What is the message the developers are trying to convey? How do I win (or, for that matter, lose)? None of this is explained. Or it is explained, and then immediately contradicted. Or perhaps it is not explainable at all. But, like my cat, I can't help but keep whacking at the game exploring all the possibilities.
With its simple graphics and uncomplicated gameplay (the latter is little more than walking around and occasionally pushing a button), the Stanley Parable is less "game" than interactive experience. There is no challenge to this title; no monsters to vanquish or puzzles to solve. Judged on that basis, the game is a total failure and those looking for a game that tests their reflexes or mental acuity will be sorely disappointed. Rather, this is a game, like "Gone Home" or "Dear Esther", that is more about wandering about and soaking in the atmosphere. But unlike those more pretentious and serious minded titles,  The Stanley Parable is far more tongue-in-cheek, greatly aided by its surreal architecture and the awesomely droll narration by Kevan Brighting, resulting in a game that can be as unexpectedly thought-provoking as it is rip-roaringly funny (no computer game has ever made me laugh as much as did Brighting's laid-back narrative responses to my actions). If the game has any fault, it is in how short it is; you can reach any one of its endings in ten or fifteen minutes, and - with some effort - can probably see all the game has to offer in three or four hours. But every minute of those four hours will be an enjoyable treat.
Clever, unexpected, funny and sometimes twisted, the Stanley Parable is a welcome change from the trite and overused cliches common to most other games, and every gamer should play it at least once.

First of all, before purchasing the Stanley Parable, you should understand that this is only a "game" in the loosest sense, and you'll probably either love it or you just won't "get" it. You walk around, you occasionally press the "use" button on buttons and doors, and that's just about it. If you've tried Dear Esther or Gone Home, you can imagine that kind of experience, but where those games were far more serious and "artsy," The Stanley Parable is... something else. I don't want to spoil anything, and you should play the demo or watch the trailers to get an idea of the game's tone and the outstanding voice work of Kevan Brighting, if nothing else. That said, I loved every minute of the Stanley Parable, and though it is extremely short, there are multiple endings that all take the game in a completely different direction. If you want to laugh out loud, this is the game for you. Once you've seen everything there is to see, the game doesn't offer much replay value, but this is not an experience to be missed.

Originally a source mod, The Stanley Parable is basically a commentary on FPS storyline tropes wrapped onto an entire game. Well, "game" in the same sense that Dear Esther is (debatable), but the lack of gameplay is more than covered by wit and insightful commentary, with quite a lot of "endings" to cover, although if you've played the mod, some of the content ends up being a bit of a retread.

The Stanley Parable is best left unintroduced to the player prior to actually playing it. Thankfully there is a free mod version for those curious in what the Stanley Parable is without making an investment.
As to those wondering if the pretty non-mod version of The Stanley Parable is worth the cash, it's definitely worth cinsidering, especially if you are a fan of the Mod. If you have already played the Mod, you'd be happy to find that while most of the Mod's endings are here, there is more than twice as much new content to discover, and that includes new endings! Without spoiling anything, I'll just tell you that you'll basically be rediscovering the game you thought you knew, but in actuality know very little about.
It's a game that plays with you and you play with it, and in trying to find all the game's secrets both big and small, you'll always find that the Narrator is always aware. This power struggle against the 'system' makes the game come alive in ways most games today don't, and in all the little details you'll find a game much bigger than you have thought of otherwise. It's a Rabbit-hole of secrets, secrets and personality, and I suggest you take the plunge.

The Stanley Parable is a sort of first person adventure game. There are no real puzzles to solve, gameplay is moving, one button to interact, and one button for crouch, which I think is used for only one part of the game. It's also potentially very short, a "playthrough" taking maybe 15 minutes. However this game succeeds by virtue of being incredibly funny, with great dialogue from the narrator whom you interact with, choosing to follow or disregard his orders, perform other actions against his will or just being non-active at all, all of which will cause the narrator to respond in some fashion, with anger or confusion, furstration or sadness at your inability to follow his orders as the narrator of this game. The games true length comes from all the possible scenarios you can take in responding to the narrator, which drastically changes the "game" you are playing, and at its core, it becomes a game about finding all the possible endings the game has for the player, which for me took somewhere around 5-6 hours, of which I was thoroughly entertained the entire time, and ended up doing in one sitting. I just wanted to keep playing and finding new things. It's a tough "genre" of game to describe, so it's hard to recommend it to a specific type of person, but I think everyone should at least give it a shot, it's great, and I very much recommend it.

There's a lot of high-quality stuff in The Stanley Parable, but ultimately I thought the scope was too small and the game fell short of expectations.  It's not worth the money right now, but perhaps improvements are on the way.  I think that the substance is there already; some changes in form and structure could get a lot more mileage out of it.
I was really drawn in by the attitude of the game's description and by glowing reviews that indicated the game was a multi-layered mind-warp that will have you questioning everything.  Well, that just wasn't true.  The layers are not there.  The questions are not there, and neither are any answers.  The game presents a mystery, but the mystery is never unlocked or even addressed, really.
Also, it's remarkably non-interactive.  There are just a handful of things to mess with, and nearly all doors are locked.  You literally walk different paths to different endings that are not totally cohesive, nor do they build to any interesting revelations.  There is something of an overarching story, but it could not be called a plot or relevant to anything.
I did enjoy being in that beautiful setting for a while, and the work of the narrator was superb.  I just hope the developers take this excellent meat and put it on a better skeleton.

The Stanley Parable is a refreshing experience within the occasionally lackluster indie game scene. You will find no riveting plot or uncover any mysterious consipracies, as screenshots and trailers may suggest. The beauty of The Stanley Parable is that it plays, and perhaps even teases you, on what your expectations of video games are in the 21st century, and the way you interact with the in-game world. It is good to spend a few hours trying to uncover the various paths one can take to progress through the game, and discovering that it might not be fit to hold the title of "game" at all. Overall if you are looking for a short and interesting indie title, you should try out the Stanley Parable.

I was browsing through the
community page, and I inevitably ended up coming across a number of reviews. To be honest, I was actually surprised at how many negative reviews it got, and not just a bit disturbed at how many people found those reviews “helpful.” After reading several of those reviews, I came to the conclusion that many gamers do not really understand
or how to go about playing it.
The first and most important thing I feel like I should address comes from the several reviews I read which stated how they “beat the game” in such a short amount of time, and how that made it not worth the money. The thing is,
is not by any means a normal game. In fact, as many people have pointed out all over the place in a somewhat fanboyish fashion, it is not even really a “game” at all, in the familiar sense of the word. It is, in fact, exactly what it says it is: a parable. For those who don't
know what that is (don't be ashamed: I had to look it up, too), here's the definition, courtesy of the late Ms. Merriam-Webster:
The point is, you can't “beat”
any more than you could beat a movie or a book. You can finish it, true. Once you've found every ending and heard every bit of dialogue, you can safely say that you've finished it; but there's no award at the end, no “Story Progress: 100%,” no achievement for finding all of the endings, nothing at all to say that you've “beaten” it. And besides, “beating” something implies that there was a challenge in the first place. The Stanley Parable isn't about any challenge; it's about exploration and discovery, along with some intriguing and entertaining psychological wizardry.
Now I've talked about the “beat the game” part, I want to discuss the “length” of the game a bit. Basically,
is short for a reason. Each ending probably takes no more than half an hour to reach, often less. If all the endings took even just one hour, let alone the multiple hours most modern game storylines last, nobody would have the patience or curiosity to start over and find out what happens if you do it a different way.
In the end,
may just not be for you. If you enjoy linear plot lines without pesky deviations and multiple endings, don't get it. If you don't have the patience to search for every possibly dialogue trigger, don't bother. If you get frustrated when you have to start something over, try something else. It's as simple as that. Think and research before you buy. If you wasted your money on
, it's not because it failed to live up to your expectations, but because you did not know what to expect.
Finally, here is my personal verdict on
:
An enthusiastic 👍!
★★★★★!
At least 94/100!

is not by any means a normal game. In fact, as many people have pointed out all over the place in a somewhat fanboyish fashion, it is not even really a “game” at all, in the familiar sense of the word. It is, in fact, exactly what it says it is: a parable. For those who don't
know what that is (don't be ashamed: I had to look it up, too), here's the definition, courtesy of the late Ms. Merriam-Webster:
The point is, you can't “beat”
any more than you could beat a movie or a book. You can finish it, true. Once you've found every ending and heard every bit of dialogue, you can safely say that you've finished it; but there's no award at the end, no “Story Progress: 100%,” no achievement for finding all of the endings, nothing at all to say that you've “beaten” it. And besides, “beating” something implies that there was a challenge in the first place. The Stanley Parable isn't about any challenge; it's about exploration and discovery, along with some intriguing and entertaining psychological wizardry.
Now I've talked about the “beat the game” part, I want to discuss the “length” of the game a bit. Basically,
is short for a reason. Each ending probably takes no more than half an hour to reach, often less. If all the endings took even just one hour, let alone the multiple hours most modern game storylines last, nobody would have the patience or curiosity to start over and find out what happens if you do it a different way.
In the end,
may just not be for you. If you enjoy linear plot lines without pesky deviations and multiple endings, don't get it. If you don't have the patience to search for every possibly dialogue trigger, don't bother. If you get frustrated when you have to start something over, try something else. It's as simple as that. Think and research before you buy. If you wasted your money on
, it's not because it failed to live up to your expectations, but because you did not know what to expect.
Finally, here is my personal verdict on

At 40% off from the holiday sale, people who are used to using the $1:1 hour ratio or something like that might be a bit peeved when they purchase this game.  If it's any consolation, 75% in a distant future may sit better with them if it ever comes.  The biggest draw of this game is the narrator who easily reacts to the player's choices whenever the player decides to not listen to the narrator's instructions.
Also, the 2nd trailer is a total lie.  Don't believe that because if you do play this game and uncover a behind-the-scenes location, you'll quickly realize the game is already making fun of the advertisement.  1st trailer's most accurate, but not everything shown in the trailer plays the exact same way in the game.
Without using a guide, I found all but 3 endings in 2 hours.  Doing 2 of the three took an hour (along with messing on the side) and the third I omitted because it would take 4 hours unless you don't mind using a program to take on this task.  To me, it took 3 hours and after that I knew all the endings.  Granted, I did look at Youtube videos to uncover secrets and easter eggs that weren't game-ending.  The theme of the narration revolves around poking fun at the devices of storytelling and the habit of humans always wanting choices or autonomy over their actions.  Finally, I'd recommend playing the demo as well since it acts as a supplement to "The Stanley Parable" with its own content, but does not overlap with the game itself and provides a preview at what kind of narration to expect.

the game was a total letdown. Once you beat it, it has zero replay-ability. And most of the time spent in game is traversing the same environment over and over, which is highly repetitive and boring. The graphics, sound effects, and music were all lackluster.
The narration was the only good thing about this game. It gave me a few cheap laughs, as did some of the art, such as the painting of the panda with a gun pointed to its head. But that's all it was. Cheap laughs.
I also enjoyed the suspense, until I realized that the endings sucked and none of my actions had any real meaning. To elaborate on this statement, at no point during playing the game did I feel like any of the endings actually resulted in a final conclusion to the game/story. No matter what I did I was still trapped in a cycle, unable to break free from it.
I would have liked to see an ending that allows the player to break the cycle. Perhaps only becoming available after the player first finds a minimum of 5 different fake endings. In this final ending, I imagine the gameplay would significantly change: the player wakes up in a tube similar to the matrix movie - a cut scene shows the character ripping electric sensors from their body. The player no longer hears the narrator at all, and there is a real first person camera perspective including the ability to see yourself in a mirror and to see your body, hands and feet if you look down. Perhaps the graphical quality would be increased as well during this part - for the character models at least, to be similar to crysis 2 quality. All of this would help to reinforce to the player that this is reality and not a loop.
There are other people - scientists and security guards, and the player must run away to try to escape the facility. During the escape, the player is presented with a familiar choice: a room with two possible exits. It doesn't matter what door you pick - your character runs into a dark hallway, and then the screen goes entirely black. The game does not restart - the loop ends. The credits roll. It is up to the player to decide if their character really escaped or not. And that, my friends, would be the greatest decision of all. Is the player an optimist or a pessimist? I know this theme is explored somewhat with some of the endings, but I feel the above take on it would be much more powerful and overall a better ending to a game that attempts to be art but ultimately fails to entertain.

From a typical game standpoint, The Stanley Parable would not normally score very high (like, 40% approval); there is little variablility in what goes on and most of the game is the way in which the narrator tells your story.  Each playthrough (except for one ending) is very short, as the game relies on only a few different paths and which ones you choose to determine what ending you get, which is the primary interest of the game; how does this path cause the story to end?
-=SPOILERS BELOW=-
Instead, this game is intended to teach the player something about themselves and the time they spend in games.  You are Stanley, and his 'job' is any game that you might have played.  If you really do listen to what the narrator says and take the time to explore, replay, and experience the different endings for each path it will be hard to come out without understanding their message; a powerful one at that.  I wont disclose more about the experience however, because there is no way to explain it aside from the way Stanley Parable shows you 'your world'.
-=End Spoliers=-
In my opinion however, buying this game is more of an action of funding the individuals who created it; a tribute, if you will.  Otherwise, I would actually recommend finding a friend who has the game to let you observe them playing or let you play it since the gameplay will only last you a few hours; something most games will only charge you <$5 for.
Overall rating however is 100%; everyone should experience this game and its message.  If you don't want to buy it, try to find it on youtube or a friend because anyone who considers themself a gamer truly should experience The Stanley Parable

A lot of hype and a steam sale led me to buy this game, but I've got to say I was pretty dissapointed.  The game is essentially about the agency of the player and the construct of gaming and the illusion of choice.  Problem is it doesn't have much to say on these subjects, despite some well written and performed narration.
This feels like an interactive version of a game design student's theory paper on the agency of the player.  It's initially interesting but quickly gets tiresome, and it never amounts to much in terms of actual gameplay.  I applaud the developers for taking a chance, and certainly it illustrates the continually evolving nature of games, where we've arrived at a point where metatextual commentary and meta-games as a whole are a thing.  That said, when you get right to brass tax, it's more ambitious and daring than it is actually good.
Ambition and daring alone don't make a good game.  I'm hopeful that in the future we might have more games of this nature, with something substantial to say, but this feels like a first draft.

It's initially interesting but quickly gets tiresome, and it never amounts to much in terms of actual gameplay.  I applaud the developers for taking a chance, and certainly it illustrates the continually evolving nature of games, where we've arrived at a point where metatextual commentary and meta-games as a whole are a thing.  That said, when you get right to brass tax, it's more ambitious and daring than it is actually good.
Ambition and daring alone don't make a good game.  I'm hopeful that in the future we might have more games of this nature, with something substantial to say, but this feels like a first draft.

So this is going to be another spoiler-free super-secretive ultra-vague review of The Stanley Parable.
Is the game worth getting? Yes.
Is it as mysterious and thought provoking as it is supposed to be? Yes, not in a bad way either.
I do have to say visually the game was more impressive than I expected, it uses Source pretty well.
The narration is beautiful, but of course that's obvious.
The game works. It really does. It's a pretty far-reaching concept and yet it's a success.
Hell, it even manages to use the loading screen as a plot device.
Bottom line, if you love games, you'll most likely love The Stanley Parable. Is it worth the pretty high asking price? Absolutely.

This game.... It's one of the best I've ever played. And that's saying something. I've played a ton of great games in my time on this Earth, but I find that there are only a select few that profoundly effect a player. Whether that be by immersing them in a deep tale, touching them emotionally, or simply blowing them away with something so mind-blowing that it is permanently imprinted in their memory. This game is a masterpiece. It's not long, in fact, time plays no part in the game. This game is simply, but not simply, a contradiction. Once you experience this, your whole outlook on life will be changed. It's simply mind blowing. The analysis, the theories, the tone, the story; everything you thought you knew about life is now wrong. Pull out the quantum physics textbooks, hire a scientist, and brace yourselves for a game even more complex and convaluted than the ending to Bioshock Infinite. Don't worry, at the end, your brain might hurt a little, but you'll see that this is one game you simply will never forget.

An existentialist commentary on the nature of narrative and storytelling, The Stanley Parable satirizes video games themselves in a metaphysical first-person adventure game. Much like a philosophy text, attempting to condense anything about it would undermine the purpose; play it for yourself. Is it worth it? Absolutely.
Stanley Parable rips down the fourth wall, reaches through the screen, grabs you by the head and plants a big ol' kiss on your funny bone. It's a good thing.

It's so much fun that it's not fun, then it's fun again.
Then confusing.
Then you get it...
Then you're not sure if you get it, but you think you get it.
And you're pretty sure you understand, and then you begin again and wonder if you got it, or maybe you're just laughing because you're scared of it.
And you smile and wonder to yourself if it's a fake smile, or maybe you're just scrunching your face up.

I should also mention this is a game very much centered on environment and atmosphere. You have to explore and let things soak in, not try and blaze through...because that defeats the purpose.

This game makes me question my value as both an employee and as a human being. I choose, or I don't choose, but there is no choice to make. My choices matter, and yet are meaningless. Or are they? Do they matter? I sit at a computer pushing buttons as directed by my boss. What is outside my office? Is this life? This game externalized my internalized contradictions and altered the decision-making matrix I use to synergize my actions and reactions. It is a game, and the game will end, and the game will never end. Is there a story? Is there a path to follow? I must find it. How can I find it?
Am I Stanley? I am Stanley, and I am not Stanley.
Am I talking about the game or about my life? Would it make a difference?
I don't know.

The Stanely Parable is an odd game, but one that really asks some big questions about what it is to be a gamer, and what it means to be a game maker. There isn't much in the way of mechanics in this game, the joy comes from the experience, the interaction with the narrator, and the examination of choice.
If you've ever wondered about how we construct meaning in games, or what is unique about participatory art, The Stanley Parable is made for you. This quirky, well-written, adventure is sure to make you think a little bit about our favorite pass-time, all with impeccably delievered voice acting and a sure sense of wit.

I wasn't sure about this game going into it even though it's garnered rave reviews so I was a bit worried that I wasted 12 bucks.  After only spending roughly 2 hours with The Stanley Parable I can say it was definitely worth the money.  I overlooked it's initial simplicity once I kept discovering multiple avenues and endings and I took great delight in the wonderful dialogue presented by The Narrator(s?).
This game is witty and somewhat slapstick as times which kept me on my toes and laughing the way through.  Though that's not to say it isn't the complete opposite at times. The ambience of environments and surprisingly menacing diallogue from The Narrator served to ratchet up the tension I felt quite a few times. There are certain environments peppered with the sort of humor that anyone familiar with the "corporate business world" would enjoy. I feel somewhat hardpressed to call it a "game" since all thats required on your part is to walk around and press buttons if you deem it necessary but it's still a joy to play nonetheless.
Overall, I think it's worth a try if you're into games that 1) make you laugh, 2) are weird as hell, and 3) are more about making you think or telling you a story rather than giving you some guns and telling you to shoot everything in sight.

They also do a good job or letting you piece together things rather than immediately telling you. The trailer does a good job of sucking you in, but the game is really just a continuation of the trailer. It isn't suddenly going to turn into an exploration game, in the traditional sense of hunting for clues and solving a puzzle to progress. My biggest complaint is that it is very short and after finding one or two endings, my desire to play is gone and I'd just as well look up the other endings on YouTube. I'm going to recommend it, but only if you buy it cheap. Otherwise, spend your money on a game that holds your attention for longer.

So I did every ending of the Stanely Parable (except the one where you press a button for 4 hours). And I have to say, this game is amazing. It's a psychological game made to make you sad, irritated, or confused. Some parts were depressing, some parts made me want to punch a wall and some parts were so confusing that I had to pause the game to just think. In a sense, it's the best game ever...if you only consider games a work of art. It's not my favorite game, per se, but it's in a list of its own. It's too good to be in a list, to be honest. In the beginning it says, Stanley's job is to push buttons he is told to push. And that is exactly what you do in the game. In many games, you don't think. You are told what to do by quest markers, or narrative. In The Stanely Parable, you are given a choice. Maybe your choice is to follow exactly what the game wants you too. But whats the fun in that? Go through the wrong door, go pass the right door, escape out the window. The game won't like that, I guarantee the game will break. But you made a choice. Or maybe your choosing was what the game wanted you to do all along.
It's a weird game, and I love ever second of it.
A ridiculous, loving criticism of "choice" in games. Highly recommended.

This is a game, and then it is not quite a game. Two first-person paths diverged once back in the 90s, one leading to Doom and the other to Myst. Whereas the former led down to a fairly well-known and successful business model only possible through this medium, the other led down to this mod-made-game and odd philosophy sometimes best experienced for oneself, and solely through this medium. This is the most off-the-wall study in level design any gamer and/or would-be developer should undergo, and it is also one of the most interesting, introspective stories to come out of the medium as a whole. Maybe not quite what anyone expects to represent "our medium" as its focus is not addiction, but perhaps a means towards passing wisdom to others, creating spaces to learn and experience things. Absolutely necessary for everybody who's played too many games and for those who haven't played a game at all.

If sarcasm is the lowest form of wit, well-done satire is the highest. At no point does the message of the game seem particularly overbearing, even though it is essentially one big discussion on the gaming industries obsession with choice. The comedy is great, and there were a lot of "No... They couldn't have... Oh my god they did!" moments. It felt almost too good.
But then it ended. And I'm not sure if it has ended. Which probably isn't a very good quality for a game which uses the phrase "The end is not the end" on it's loading screen. I wanted something big, something final, something that tied everything I was presented with up with a little bow on top. Instead I got, "Well I guess it's over now" and I had to escape and click the quit button. And from what I read on the internet, I'm pretty sure I've surgically removed every scrap of fun I could from the game. The use of the word surgically isn't an exageration. I spent good chunks of time sitting, trying to read everything off every white board, piece of paper and monitor that I could. And my playthrough was on the short side of 4 hours.
At many parts of this game I was expecting to recommend this game with a review of "This is my GOTY", and it could be, I don't know. But it depends on how you consume it. My recommendation is, pay under $10 if you can, then sit down with it on a Sunday afternoon with a packet of chips and some diet cola, and treat it like a movie. That way you'd be saving $5 and getting a couple hours extra. Also, AND THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT, when you get to the bit where you have to pick up the phone, don't. Pull out the plug. (Which is what you were probably going to do anyway, I know) BUT SAVE THE ENDING WHERE YOU PICK UP THE PHONE FOR LAST! That way you might have a nicer bow on the top than I did.

The Stanley Parable is easily my favorite game of 2013. The humor is top-notch (whether it's light-hearted like the Adventure Line or one of the many fantastic times it gets dark) and the Narrator is a fantastic and very well-acted character -- the staircase ending is legitimately among the most affecting scenes I've encountered in a videogame. I can't recommend picking this up more.
If you haven't yet, make sure to pick up the demo too - not only is it free but it also has absolutely no content from the full game in it, instead attempting (quite successfully) to show off the humor and style you'll encounter. It's very much worth trying out.

To describe anything about the game, that is to describe any scene that is going on in the game, any moment that stood out to me would be telling you too much. It would be too big a spoiler, no matter how insignificant the scene might seem. For nothing is really insignificant in the Stanley Parable. A butterfly flaps its wings and creates a hurricane, Stanley does something and chaos ensues.
You can follow the narrator, or you can disobey him and watch what happens. What does happen would be a spoiler, however it leads to both hilarious dialogue and at the same time, somehow, without sacrificing comedy, it manages to make you think things over. It manages to question the nature of choice and free will. Are you truly free to do anything in the Stanley Parable? After all, the game has been predetermined, hasn't it? It has been built by a developer, and as such as a finite number of endings... But that's the thing, it never seems to end. Even after playing it for four hours straight, I had only found what, 7 endings? And I'm sure there's more to find, since I only explored the endings from the choices you were given, and I am told there are 18.
Speaking of the narrator, you thought GLaDOS was good? This is basically GLaDOS on steroids. His voice is soothing, he is well written, and he has the right amount of intonation into everything he says, every line is delivered to perfection.
The only complaint I could possibly have about the game is that it's on the short side, but that's good. It's like the original Portal, its length means that it doesn't overstay its welcome and that it keeps everything fresh.
If I had to give it a number, I'd give it a solid 10 out of 10.

The Stanley Parable is one of the most hyped games of the Winter Sale, at least among my friends.  After playing it and viewing a lot of the endings, I have to say that while it is entertaining, it is not worth the hype and definitely not worth purchasing at full price.  It does take gaming into a different dimension, with the game basically bending itself to fit your own decisions.  However, the ways in which the story diverges every time are a little too similar, the only major difference being one specific ending that removes you entirely from the context of The Stanley Parable and instead inserts you into other games.  The rest of the endings, while amusing, were tedious to get to and frustrating, especially when I had to manually restart the level because of a dead-end location.  I appreciate the direction that the developers took with this game, which is basically a hilarious and satirical version of a plot similar to Dear Esther but instead has a lot more choice.  I would still recommend it if you are interested in a game that will change the way you view a linear, narrated plot, but this is certainly not worth $15.  More like $5, if that.

"The Stanley Parable" is an epic example of interactive fiction and Half Life modification. Despite being a "remake" of the original mod, this verson successfully keeps with the spirit and basic layout of the original game while adding new twists, jokes, and story routes with a professional coat of polish, meaning that people who've played the first game can still enjoy and be suprised by the "second". This game's got fantastic writing, fantastic design, fanstastic voice-acting, fantastic ... lots of things! Although each of the game's "paths" are short, the game offers a fair ammount of replayability as you discover new story paths and relive previous favorites. Even if you don't think the $14.99 is worth the handfull of hours (which I feel it is), the demo of "The Stanley Parable"  is still quite amazing, as well as free!

The Stanley Parable is this game where you are given instructions by a narrator on how to find the ending to the Stanley Parable story. Whether you choose to obey his orders or not is up to you and there is a wealth of possible routes through the game depending on your decisions and actions. I will rate this game on the following things:
Story
Narration
Humor
Content
Music/Sound
Story - 10/10
The story is a mystery even after you play through all the endings. It is a very intriguing mystery about what happened to Stanley's co-workers and changes quickly to other plots during different paths.
Narration - 10/10
The narrator fills the space of noise and keeps the game from feeling like a horror game, in my opinion. He is constantly talking and keeping you involved in walking around.
Humor - 10/10
The narrator is constantly making jokes about everything, including a broom closet. The jokes never seem to fall short of amazingly excellent. Many things besides the narrator contain absolutely hilarious moments, as well.
Content - 9/10
There are many different paths to take and many different endings to witness and it will take a long time to play through all of them. But once you end up seeing all the endings in the game, there is nothing else to really do.
Music/Sound - 10/10
The music is ambient and barely noticeable and isn't even present during the whole game. But, it's there when it needs to be and fits the tone of the game very well. There are sounds for most of your interactions and it also fills the space of no noise.
Total - 98/100
I absolutely loved this game when it first came out and had so much content I had yet to witness.

You should play The Stanley Parable.  You should avoid the Stanley Parable.  You will love this game.  This game is terrible.  Go through the door to your left.  No your other left.
The Stanley Parable is a great meta-commentary on gaming and a legitimately funny and unique experiance.  It is a story about free will and following (or not following) a predefined path, but warps into so much more depending on the paths you choose to take.

Do you know how exciting it is to be wanting a game for so so so long, and then getting it and having it exceed your expectations? I have barely been playing this game for 3 hours (which is about four of the... idk... 18 endings?) and I instantly fell in love with this game. It's not the type of game where you can just tell someone what It's about. You just have to play it. This game never fails to keep me on the edge of my seat excited to see what it has to offer me next. This game gives you the freedom to literally make any decision for youreself. Narrator: When Stanely came to a set of two open doors, he entered the door on his left. Player enters the door on the right. Narrator: This was not the correct way, and Stanely knew that perfectly well. Stanely is so bad at following orders, It's a mystery why he wasn't fired years ago. I love this game so much, I'm glued to my chair for every second of it. 9.5 out of 10. Must Have!

This game is hilarious, I really Love playing it, although sometimes it does get a little tiring, there is always a secret change in sarcasm based on how long you have been playing the game. Definatly worth your time, but I would wait until sales, because it is pushing its worth.
an excellent meditation on choice, game-player interaction, on being a character, and on rule constraint
Very clever narration with many endings and secrets that make you want more even when there is nothing left.

Brilliant. Less a FPS and more a curious exploration on what we do when we play games, whether or not we have agency outside of what the programmers intended, and some great surprises and jokes to boot. Subtle humor, smart voice acting, and a brilliant premise. Lots of neat little hidden secrets. Don't use a guide, trust me, half the fun of this title is exploring to see what you can or can not do.

While I'm not absolutely certain this game is worth the amount of money it costs to buy it and it has fairly limited replayability, it is both deep and funny.  I can think of half a dozen minor improvements that would improve the gaming experience but none of them are needed.  Still, for the cost, 2-3 hours of game play is a little light.  Especially since that game play largely consists of repeating tasks in minorly different ways.  However, if you think of this less as a game and more an experience, it works pretty well and the commentary on gaming is appreciated, if a little smug, self-congratulatory, and (I think) misses the point in a lot of ways.  The criticisms it levels at the entire gaming genre are true, but miss the point that while Stanley is depicted as performing a soulless mindless solitary task, most gamers enjoy their gaming without any brainwashing and for many it's a collectivist experience.  Still, give it a try if you're into Meta.

You've never played any game like The Stanley Parable (TSP) before, but I would somewhat hesitate calling it a game. It contains no gameplay beyond navigating branching corridors, it will at no point require reflex action, manual dexterity, logic, planning, multitasking or strategy, and in that regard I find it better likened to a piece of installation art than a video game. The game is completely self-aware of this
. TSP is carried through by its good sense of humor and excellent narration.
You'll go down different paths some 7-12 minutes each exploring alternate versions of the same story about the mysterious disappearance of Stanley's colleagues while the narrator commentates the surroundings and Stanley's presumed state of mind.
And that's pretty much it. A story telling game experiment carried a bit too far, for I don't really think it's worth its price point for what it gives you. After two hours it has worn out its welcome for me, and I can't foresee I'll ever be reinstalling this, but a fun enough novelty after all. Wait for a price drop first if you're at all interested.

Especially since that game play largely consists of repeating tasks in minorly different ways.  However, if you think of this less as a game and more an experience, it works pretty well and the commentary on gaming is appreciated, if a little smug, self-congratulatory, and (I think) misses the point in a lot of ways.  The criticisms it levels at the entire gaming genre are true, but miss the point that while Stanley is depicted as performing a soulless mindless solitary task, most gamers enjoy their gaming without any brainwashing and for many it's a collectivist experience.  Still, give it a try if you're into Meta.
