You've never played any game like The Stanley Parable (TSP) before, but I would somewhat hesitate calling it a game. It contains no gameplay beyond navigating branching corridors, it will at no point require reflex action, manual dexterity, logic, planning, multitasking or strategy, and in that regard I find it better likened to a piece of installation art than a video game. The game is completely self-aware of this
. TSP is carried through by its good sense of humor and excellent narration.
You'll go down different paths some 7-12 minutes each exploring alternate versions of the same story about the mysterious disappearance of Stanley's colleagues while the narrator commentates the surroundings and Stanley's presumed state of mind.
And that's pretty much it. A story telling game experiment carried a bit too far, for I don't really think it's worth its price point for what it gives you. After two hours it has worn out its welcome for me, and I can't foresee I'll ever be reinstalling this, but a fun enough novelty after all. Wait for a price drop first if you're at all interested.

I've played many games that build themselves around questioning the narrative framework of games. Some of those games were too "artsy" - they gloried in their artificial depth, waving their hands as they said, "What is this game REALLY about? This? This? NO ONE KNOWS!" Some of the games were just confusing- what were they trying to DO, anyway? And some of them just felt disappointing- their attempts at breaking down the barriers of narrative failed to satisfy.
The Stanley Parable defies those problems.
It is one of the best explorations of breaking down game narrative I have ever played.
The game is best described as an experience, one that made me think, wonder, laugh, and feel. It is clever, witty, and finely honed. In some ways I thought it was almost too to-the-point- I wished that I could have messed more with the environment. Nonetheless, the game lacks bloat and that is greatly to its credit. This sort of exploration can wear thin very quickly when it goes too long.
This does mean that the game is short- in a couple hours I saw the majority of the known endings to the game. Had the game been $5 or so I likely would not have thought much of it. At $15, though, I felt like it was a bit overpriced. Still, it's cheaper than some movie theaters, and a far better experience than going to watch, say, American Pie 43: Why Are We Still Making Movies? I recommend waiting for a sale if you are worried about getting your money's worth, but I cannot stress enough that this is a game experience I think you should have.

This game is not like any other game you have ever played - and sometime's that's an amazing thing. Other times, it makes you want to pull your hair out.
The true test of this game lies in the simple premise: How far are you willing to go against your own judgement and emotions in order to simply experience more gameplay? Depending on how much you trust the omnipresent narrator and what experiences you bring with you, this game can be a hilarious ride through Inception or a emotionally-scarring trip through hell. The narrator is always trying to lead you to a happy and conclusive story, but unfortunately, the narrator's plans and the game's plans are completely opposite unless you obey his every word.
If you enjoyed the demo, you might not enjoy this game. This game has a much darker and 'sadder', per se, tone than the demo, which is mostly silly and fun.
If you crave deep and thoughtful experiences, this is the game for you. It will draw you into its world and show you just how easy it is to toy with someone's emotions. I have never experienced the same kind of tension when my character is possibly about to die than I did in The Stanley Parable. If you are faint of heart or like being given a choice when your own beliefs are put on the line, this may not be a game for you.

What is there to say about this "Game."
Many of you have heard that this is not a game, but it is a game.  Some people demanded refunds and others loved it.  I fit in the loved it Catagory.
The basic idea is that this First Person Narrative driven story plays out like a strange episode of the Twilight Zone.  Everything you do and everything you don't do is narrated by a funny story telling narrator.
You find yourself in an office all alone with a bunch of places to go and yet you can also end up going no where.  You can go with the story or find several ways to mess it up.
The overall arc of the story is that Stanley is in a conundrum of a never ending story that already ended before he started.  It doesn't make sense unless you mess around in it for a couple of hours.
Anyways - I totally loved finding all these different endings and silly side stories about nothing and everything.  I would recommend to folks who just want to kick back and play/hear a funny set of consequences narrated by a funny fellow.

The Stanley Parable is a first person exploration game. You will play as Stanley and you will not play as Stanley. You will follow a story, you will not follow a story. You will have a choice, you will have no choice. The game will end, the game will never end. Contradiction follows contradiction, the rules of how games should work are broken, then broken again. This world was not made for you to understand.
The above is the official description of The Stanley Parable provided by the developers themselves. And this is actually the best description of the game, making all other descriptions redundant. Explaining it further would mean to ruin it. The Stanley Parable is most effective when players know little to nothing about it. But then how do you proceed to write a review for this game? Honestly, I haven’t figured it out yet, so I’ll just keep typing and see what comes out. And if you haven’t played it yet, just stop reading right now and go play it. Seriously. You’re welcome. Oh, and play the demo as well. It’s basically a completely separate game.
I suppose the only relevant thing to say about The Stanley Parable is that it’s absolutely brilliant in just about everything it sets out to do. The writing is intelligent in its relentless satire of gaming conventions and the game design complements it impeccably. In fact, The Stanley Parable melds game design and narrative in a way unseen in video games, there is literally no distinction between the two. This is heightened even further by the fantastic voice acting.
The Stanley Parable is uncompromisingly witty, modern and relevant. It will react to just about everything you do and you will find yourself second guessing both the game itself and your actions. And just when you think you figured it out, it will turn everything on its head. It’s an irreverent piece of art and social commentary. A revelatory work exposing both game designers and game players. Sort of a gaming equivalent of a Charlie Kaufman film.
The Stanley Parable is not only an absolutely brilliant comedy, but a game worthy of study. It may come off as simple, but upon reflection, it makes you contemplate so much. That might be its greatest achievement. It’s a game that will make you think and contemplate not only The Stanley Parable itself, but other games, gaming as a whole and your role in it. It’s basically an elaborate social experiment for gamers.
I’m running out of superlatives here. So again, just drop whatever you’re doing and play it. It’s just incredible.

Stanely wasn't sure what to do next. He sensed his experience with pushing buttons would help him here, and he felt an urge to press the ones in front of him. The screen told him to review his experiences in the last couple of days, but Stanley had no idea which buttons - or indeed in what order - to press them in. He knew to fill the box with words, but he could'nt decide which words to do it with.
Stanley quickly lost patience. Why was it him that had to judge what other people should play? Surely they weren't mindless zombies? Why should they listen to him? What did his opinions matter? Who knows if the next person to come along would like the things he did? What if they never noticed things Stanley did? What if he had seen things he shouldn't have?
Stanley decided to ignore the commands his screen gave him. Why couldn't they just do the same things he had done and make their own opinions rather than relying on his? Why did they have to do what Stanley told them? Why did Stanley have to press buttons expressing his satisfaction with his experiences? No. He decided he woldn't stand for it any longer. Stanley got up out of his desk, and left.

The Stanley Parable is a first-person exploration game, but in the sense that exploration is linear and you still get to discover all of the different ways to traverse your environment. Your singular objective is to follow the narrator. Sometimes. The unique thing about The Stanley Parable is that you are free to do whatever you wish. Example: The narrator says go through the red door, but there is also a blue door. Do you go through the red or the blue door? The choice is yours. Whatever lies down either path is unknown to you at the time, but once you choose a decision you can't undo it. So where is the fun in The Stanley Parable? The narrator. All of the game is voiced by one of the best narrators I've heard n a while, with a script to match. I would definitely put him as an equal to Bastion's narrator, whom is also fantastic. The lines of dialogue that initiate when you take an action are spirited and amusing. Not to mention brilliant. Each of the endings I have encounter so far has been of a varied mix, all of which are wonderful. I highly recommend this game as a simple amusement tool. Do not attempt to play this game with a grind-heavy goal in mind. Just sit back and enjoy it.

Ever felt like not going where the game tells you to go in order to progress. Well in The Stanley Parable, you can do just that. Depending on how you decided to move through the game, whether you follow the narrators directions or not, you will get a number of increadibly different (and often very hilarious and completely out of the box) endings. If you like the kind of humor you get from the Portal games, The Stanley Parable is definately something you should give a try. Trust me, you will spend hours finding all the unique endings. The only time the game "truely" ends is when you decide to turn it off. The Stanley Parable is a great study on what it truely means to have "choice" within a game (wheather it is an illusion or not).

The original The Stanley Parable is a simple Half Life 2 mod that distills the essence of storytelling and player choice within a FPS format without being a typical FPS. This game is both a remake and a sequel to that game. It is perhaps one of the most creative, humorous and thought-provoking interactive experiences available and by its nature defies what many consider to be a "game". But it is very much a game, a game about a man named Stanley. I wish I could elaborate more about the game without saying too much, but honestly it's one of those games that has to be played ... no, experienced to be believed. To anyone who has questioned whether or not a game can be considered art, look no further than The Stanley Parable.

The Stanley Parable is a game where you play as Stanley, a standard, by-the-numbers, white collar office worker who one day discovers something new in the midst of his boring, but comfortable, job. The game is played from a first-person perspective, and the story unfolds as you make your way through the game world, with the help of a friendly narrator.
I don't want to say too much here, honestly - the story shouldn't be spoiled. I will say however, that if you enjoy games like Gone Home, but want just a little more interactivity (and the dynamic story that can come with it), I'd definitely recommend The Stanley Parable. It's fun, self-aware, and if you're willing to indulge a bit as you try (and retry) to explore the game, there's a lot of great content to discover.

After a tremendous number of glowing reviews, I jumped in -- to my surprise, I found this virtual office corridor explorer to be dull, trying too hard, and generally disappointing. Expect a Half-Life 2 mod with voice over and high ambition -- nothing more. With titles like Dear Esther, Gone Home, and Kentucky Route Zero paving the way for 'art meets narrative,'  this title simply feels like someone trying too hard and ultimately made me feel like I was bamboozled out of my money. I'm not sure why so many love it, but in this rare instance, the majority does not rule.

I've been playing games for many a year now and many of these games have had lines in them. Many games have had truly great lines in them. Who could forget that one to the left of the web on Tempest? The one that stretches out from the explosion in Minestorm? Ah, the beautiful lines that you crash your bike into in a game of Light Cycles. They were good lines. And as time went past, games got more lines. Then one day we decided that lines weren't enough and we had some triangles and we put the triangles together and we made videogames with triangles instead of dots and instead of lines and oh, what did we lose? But it was OK because then lines came back into fashion around 2006 and they sort of glowed too. Glowy lines! We made games with glowy lines and the lines in those games were great too. I didn't like the green ones so much in Geometry Wars but they were trying y'know?
Years and years of great lines and yet, it took until 2013 for us to get THE BEST LINE. Ladies and everyone else out there, The Adventure Line is the best line in all of videogames. Let us take a moment to let that sink in. The. Adventure. Line.
The Adventure Line is the best line. Sing it from the rooftops because this is -the- Oscar worthy line performances, the BAFTA of road markings, the Laurence Olivier award of yellow. Thank you, Adventure Line. You're amazing. Just great.

I'd recommend this game, but only very barely.
This game may be a victim of its own hype, but in my experience, it didn't live up to those expectations.  There is very little action on the viewers part.  You largely go down hallways, listen to the narrator, and constantly make left / right choices.  Depending on which order you choose these, you get the different endings to the game.  There are some neat ideas and endings here, but the paths can become repetitive to get to them, when the only difference is the final left / right after a long string of these choices.
The narrator is a nice touch, and if you told me that the original version of this game came out before Portal, I could see how the narrator was an obvious influence on the much better GLaDOS in Portal.  However, the original version of this game came out 4 years later, and in my experience, barely does enough with the lightly mocking voice leading you through the adventure.
The length of this game is also not much.  After deducing the system, I was quickly able to get nearly every ending in under 2 hours.  I didn't realize these were the different endings, as nothing explains as much, and you are quickly ported back to the beginning of the game to start again.
So, this isn't much of a game.  That seems to be a trend this year.  But is there artistic merit?  A very reluctant yes.  It's clever, but being clever seems to be about all it has going for it.  There are some parallels to be drawn between gaming and mind control, but it's so light that most of the allegory needs to be filled in by the viewer.
One of the hardest endings to get requires the viewer to click a button for 4 hours.  Another difficult achievement is to play the game for an entire Tuesday.  Light, fun, mocking commentary on reaching achievements in video games, but this seems to be about as deep as the rabbit hole goes.  Even then these examples are outliers compared to the much easier achievements and endings.
So why would I recommend it?  Like I mentioned, it's clever and quick.  Not overly clever, but just enough to entertain, and there are some funny moments.  However, keep in mind the length and notable lack of gameplay if / when you acquire this game.  If you're the type of gamer with a small budget that can only get games once in a great while, I'd highly consider checking out other propositions.

This game is a trip. Things won't make a whole lot of sense at first, but the more you play and explore and wander 'off the beaten path' the more you will end up discovering.
You play as Stanley, a drone among a seeming mass of other like-minded drones; only he 'awakens' one day to realize he is all alone. His fellow drones (i.e. co-workers) have seemingly abandoned him... or at the very least disappeared mysteriously. Thus begins Stanley's adventure. Of course, how long said adventure lasts and what it entails is entirely up to you - you the Player, not you the Stanley - and the disembodied narrator who will inevitably try to guide you along his own intended path.
This is a game that's all about choice and it changes on the fly to reflect said choices. Will you mindlessly obey like a good drone, or will you seek your own path? Will you be content with mind-numbing happiness or will you seek out the hard answers left waiting in the dark recesses of your own mind?

But that was the point, wasn't it?

How does the Narrator control the story when the Player has agency to not follow his instructions?  Is a choice between two identical doors actually a choice?  Why can't these people just play my game the way I want them to?  The Stanley Parable is a satire, and an "arty" one at that.

First, that game has hilarious narration.
When looked at from one side, this game tells a short story about desperate worker class employant Stanley, who tries to escape the evil paths that were laid out before him. The narrator tries to help you on your path, and will respond to your choices with often unexpected and witty behaviour. Like, he will go angry at you when you refuse to leave the nice and cozy broom chamber, or get desperate when you try to ruin his narration by doing the opposite he tells you to. Then it also mocks you, either with giving you useless rewards or just offend you for even playing it. Worth a pretty good laugh and also an extremely likeable setting and characters.
When looking at it from the other side, the game offers a deep philosophical discussion about choice, and how it influences our every lives on a daily basis. How it appears to be unique, to be freely available to have, almost a right to everyone. And how different choices in games are compared to choices in real life, and WHY we play the games we play. Why we emphasize on freedom of choice in games so much, even though there is no true freedom in a game ever to be had. But does this really differ from what we face in life, or is it just different approach to it?
If you want to, this game can ask you a lot of question, and maybe also give you some answers. But don't expect them to come to you black in white, as the game is simply a discussion about choice, it doesn't try to answer it but moreso allow you to see it from different angles and then decide for yourself what you really want to believe.
The game IS short, and it emphasizes multiple playthroughs and secret-searching to find the more than a dozen hidden endings and paths. Also it might be frustrating at times or even call you a fool, but it ever does it with a clear intention. It is NOT a game about progress, as you keep starting over and over again at the same place (which for sure is also an intention to reflect on vicious cycles we tend to run into).
But it is a lovely game, and surely made a dent into the history of gaming (and into a few gamers brains), and I can recommend it to anyone willing to have patience with a game that revolves more around yourself and does have probably the most hilarious narration and unique humour a game had in the last few years.
Also, if you decided to play it I suggest you watching this video AFTER you played it:
DON'T watch it before you haven't played at least through the most obvious paths and endings, as it takes away a lot of the charm of trying to find out yourself what something means and also spoils quite a bit.
OH, and PLAY THE DEMO before you play the game or decide to buy it. It offers completely different content but in the same way the original does and is like a chapter on it's own.

I will start by saying that this review contains mild spoilers, so if you haven't played the game yet, I highly suggest that you take caution before reading this review.
I was not familiar with the original Half-Life 2 mod that The Stanley Parable started out with. Heck, I only heard about this game through word of mouth. The Stanley Parable is what happens when you take an interesting concept that you probably wouldn't dare put into a videogame, and actually make it work. The story (if you can call it that) is of a man named Stanley who works at a boring job in an office building, pushing buttons that his boss tells him to push via his monitor. One day, he notices that his boss hasn't given him a single command the entire day, and appears to have gone missing, along with his co-workers.
That's where the gimmick of the game takes place. While there is a narrative telling you what to do throughout the game, you have a choice to follow it or stray from it. Depending on what decisions you make throughout the game, there are a total of 14 different endings in this game. This can range from ]turning off the power in a mind-control facility that has been controlling all of the thoughts and feelings of the workers in the building, including Stanley, to entering a homage of a small string of existing videogames. The thing I like about this game is that there isn't a morality meter. The choices you make aren't necessarily based on thoughts, but actions. Not only that, but some of the endings are based off of bugs, glitches and whatnot that were in the original mod (Try closing the door on yourself as you start the game.)
The Stanley Parable is almost entirely psychological. During the time that it was still just a mod, the creator, Wreden,  thought up the game considering how most games on the market "confine the user to its rules." The dialogue in the game is very thought-provoking at times, and I've even seen some players and journalists state that it made them think about their own lives. The thought that a simple game like this can have so much influential power on someone like that is remarkable, and I applaud Galactic Cafe for this.
The presentation is definetly not anything to turn your head at either. The visuals are vastly different in this game than anything you would see in Half-Life 2 (Go figure). When the developers said they were going to make an HD remake of this game, they weren't screwing around. No hallway nor room looks the same (unless designed intentionally), and everything looks crisp and clear. The music is a nice touch as well, perfectly fitting the locale and scenario that takes place. The voice acting is also a department I have to give major props to. Kevan Brighting does a fantastic job as the voice of the narrator, depicting emotions of happiness, despair, confusion, anger, worry, really the list goes on. He even goes through an evil persona during one of the endings.
As I stated before, 14 endings is a lot for a game, but it is still quite a short game. Is there anything else that might convince you to take a second glance at the fifteen dollar price tag? Perhaps. The Stanley Parable may be a short game at its core, but there are a ton of secrets to be found within the different branching pathways. Extended dialogue, little visual easter eggs, and areas of the map you probably didn't even know existed until you did a little exploration. The developers really thought of everything when making this game. (Try typing sv_cheats 1 in the console. I dare you.)
If you're one of those people who enjoys a non-linear experience in your videogames, as well as comedic and witty dialogue, then I highly reccomend The Stanley Parable for you. However, if you're still not sure about the fifteen dolar price tag, I advise trying out the demo first. It's actually a unique experience from the official game, and you might like what you see.

I'm simply not recommending this game because it just wasn't worth the money in my opinion. If you're interested in game design, humor and a good story this game is perfect for you, but it just didn't deliver in depth for the price. I went through the entire game and every possible outcome only 90 mins into the game, without even speed rushing or trying to go fast. To give you a reference, this game is about 1/4 as long as the first Portal game. There is even an achievement you can unlock for speed rushing one of the multiple endings in under 4 mins and 22 secs. REALLY? 4 MINS TO BEAT THE GAME?!?! I know there's multiple endings, but jesus christ. I'm not trying to bash this game, I thought it was amazing to be frank. I just feel the $15 I paid didn't live up to its expectations, this is also the type of game where once you did all outcomes it just won't be the same going through the game again because there's no puzzle solving, objectives or things to do. Well like I said, I played this game for about 90 mins and I'm pretty damn sure I did every outcome and after about the 4th or 5th time going back it gets to the point of being more of a job rather than a game. The only thing good about this game is the narrator's voice and how he pronounces Stanley's name. To be honest I'm actually glad it's over, it's so repetitive and annoying it practically has a lenny face written all over it. They should call it "The ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) Parable".

Whatever it is, it's art. And it needs to be played by everyone who claims to enjoys video games at all.

"This is the story of a game named The Stanley Parable. The Stanley Parable was developed by a company in a big building where he was game number 427. Orders came to him through the computer on our desk, telling him what doors to pass trough, how long play the game, and in what moment. This is what Game 427 did every day of every month and every year, and although others might have considered it a mind-bending game, The Stanley Parable made us relish every moment that the game was played, as though he had been made exactly for gamers. This was a blast - I found myself giggling incessantly every time I did the opposite of the what the narrator told me to do in this game, wherin you take the role of Stanley, a standard-issue cube drone who's sole job was to do as instructed by the output of a monitor. One day, the monitor doesnt tell him what to do. Confused, Stanely decides to find out what is up. Thus starts a run of the mill computer adventure.
That is, unless you decide to take the wrong door.
THen the fun starts.
Its a short game, or at least this run through was - I imagine there are many more paths to take and ways in which to frustrate the Narrator. Imagine a Choose Your Own Adventure, where the book keeps getting increasingly confused and snippy in its tone as you made "choices" it didnt like. That is The Stanley Parable, and it really just goes to show how arbirary and silly the idea of "choice" in video games really is.
Try the demo first - its free, and gives you an idea of the tone of the game. And seriously - the narrator is exactly what I had in my head in terms of tone and accent as I was reading Hitchikers Guide to the Galaxy many years ago. (He may have even been the one narrating the movie, overriding the memories of my teenage self from the first time I read it. )

The Stanley Parable is less of a "Game" and more of an interactive "Choose Your Own Adventure" story. There are branching paths with their own set of story archs that change the way the "Game" is played and along with them, the excellent narrator follows along with those archs and adjust his commentary to fit whatever is going on. if you go through the wrong door he will chastise you about it. If you so much as stand in one place for far too long he will badger you to get the story moving again. Definetely an improvement both graphically and writing wise over the mod for half life 2. An experience that no other "Game" has been able to replicate yet.

A beautiful take on the philosophy of videogaming.
Without doubt an unforgettable experience in metagaming.

The Stanley Parable is one of the best examples we have for how a gaming narrative should work. This game knows how to properly balance story and gameplay, while seemlessly combining the two. Highly recommended for anyone, this is a unique gaming experience.

In a multi-billion dollar a year industry full of cookie cutter ideas, 'The Stanley Parable', like so few games, follows a different path, or in this case, many different paths. All of these paths being hilarious, especially when you disobey the narrator, but you're left feeling that it was altogether too short. Having completed almost every ending possible, and some multiple times, I still only clocked in at three hours. As a concept game, much like the first 'Portal', 'The Stanley Parable' is pure creative thinking gold, it is my hope that eventually they create a second, and make the branching paths almost nigh infinite, so those of us that enjoyed the first game so much can dive into this world, rather than stick our toesies in the shallow end for a few minutes because we've been told not to get wet by an over-bearing parental unit, "You might drown!" they say, "Other kids pee in there! It isn't sanitary." they whisper. Well guess what, mom and dad (developers)? If you're going to take me to the pool (game world), I'm going to want and expect to swim (play) for no shorter a time than my little heart desires, which is much longer than three hours. I want to look like a prune when I get out of the water (...er...this metaphor doesn't work for gaming...I should have thought this through a little more)!

The Stanley Parable is a funny, creepy game that makes you want to keep doing the same things over and over again.

I'm fairly certain The Stanley Parable is the only game I’ve ever played that forced me to relax and listen to calming new age music for trying to play through it too quickly. This moment of forced reflection is an example of what this game does so well. It forces you to stop and think about your actions and motivations. It forces you to look at yourself and asks you to think about how much control you really have over your own life.
The game essentially plays out as a first-person choose-your-own-adventure story. You play as Stanley, an office-worker who pushes buttons on a keyboard all day according to the instructions given to him on his monitor. Stanley arrives to work one day to find no instructions on his monitor and all of his co-workers missing. The story is presented via an always-present narrator, expertly voiced by Kevan Brighting.  As Stanley, you must move through the office, searching for clues about your missing coworkers. Eventually you will come upon a room with two open doors, and the narrator will tell you which path to take.
This is the essential gameplay mechanic behind The Stanley Parable - you are constantly presented with multiple paths and must choose to either obey the narrator or ignore him entirely. Each decision results in increasingly bizarre commentary from the narrator, who is constantly remarking about your choices. The narration is both humorous and engaging, and as you progress you begin to see the narrator more as a companion than just a disembodied voice there to tell you a story. There’s a moment in the game where the narrator is forced to confront his own lack of freedom in the system that he is confined in, and it's difficult not to genuinely feel bad for him. It’s a rare occurrence when a video game can make you feel true emotions for one of its characters, and the fact that this game does so for a character that is nothing more than a voice is remarkable. The true beauty of the game, however, comes from the fact that it never truly ends.
Each time you reach one of the multiple “endings”, you are returned back to the beginning of the game and must begin again. The narration changes slightly with each playthrough, and, depending on your choices, each playthrough can last from a few minutes to arguably eternity. Each step of the game is a commentary on choice, on player agency in games, on our relationship with technology. It forces you to look at the choices you make in your life and how much control you really have over those choices. Each decision you make becomes a reflection of yourself. You begin to realize that the game is no longer talking to Stanley, but to you. You are no longer playing as Stanley, but as yourself.
The Stanley Parable is a difficult thing to try and explain in words, and truly must be experienced firsthand to fully understand it. It is a shining example of the narrative storytelling power that the video game medium holds. What the game accomplishes would not be possible in any other medium, and more developers would do well to learn from what Galactic Cafe have done here.

Don't play this game. It's a waste of money. You think it will be deep. Maybe in some parts it is - on a surface level. But ultimately, to save you time, here's the underlying message: games are really like real life, so go out and play in real life instead of following the computer's orders in a simulated environment.
'Cept the reason you play videogames isn't to find one that is so downright dull that it is just like real life. And that's what The Stanley Parable really is. A steaming pile of utter garbage straight from the cesspools of mediocre game design and incompetent storytelling.
Some people argue that this game is a work of art. Really? And what was artistically profound about it? The series of linear choices you made? The randomly generated changes when you completed an ending? The amount of metanarrative conceptualization and the hilarious ways in which you would waste your time trying to find entirely pointless developments that offered no insights?
How about that ending that caused you to quit out of the game? Ooh boy, what an exciting ending. I'm sure that really got you going, eh. You got to walk around a museum and see what the game's creation really was like! Wow! Another brilliant narrative development.
How about the time you followed a line for multiple playthroughs and the same boring, hackneyed idea was drilled into your retinas for close to 30 minutes?
But, sure. Maybe that's art. Maybe. For some really hipster kids who don't understand what the word 'art' implies (hint: effort and creativity). Maybe you think wandering around a Halflife 2 mod's simulated version of an office with no gameplay mechanics is fun. Maybe you think Minecraft and Portal references are the peak of ironic allusions to consumerism in the digital world.
Even then, The Stanley Parable is a worthless pile of dung, not fit for the cost nor the measley time it takes to play. By the way, the game lasts about... oh... 20 minutes per playthrough. And at best, you'll play it for 5 hours to find the endings you want by diverging on certain sets of linear paths (and yes, they are highly linear - not complex at all) to find the 10 or so endings the game offers.
No, no countless narrative structures. No endless divulging explanations into games, into existence, into the power of choice. Just several rather typified remarks on life, society, and the digital age we live in. You'd find more entertainment in an Ayn Rand novel.
Now, before you critique my critique, I have played through every ending and literally every variant of decision-making in the game. And that only took 3 hours. Most of the longer plots have interesting commentaries mixed into the heaping feces-filled drivel spouted, but those moments lasted less than 30 seconds and then I would return to the futile hell that is this so-called game. Overall, I could not be more dissatisfied with my purchase.
What really gets me is how this game was presented - this is where some credit is due. It was marketed in such a clever way, as if it held some deep purpose or meaning, and then it literally quite honestly admits that it doesn't have that significance in the game. The narrator then proceeds to subtly mock you on your purchase decisions, all the while critiquing you as being the kind of addicted-to-computers-and-technology person that needs to get outside.
And maybe the game is clever in that sense. It forces you to be so disgusted with its own pitiful mediocrity that you actually want to go outside rather than play it. It makes you feel sorry that you completed the game in almost every ending, as if to say, "why would you ruin the little, terrible machine I've created?" In fact, I think I'm paraphrasing the narrator pretty acurately there.
The saving grace is the voice acting, but even that can't change the lack of ingenuity and utter stupidity that is The Stanley Parable.
Congratulations if you already bought The Stanley Parable. You were suckered in just like I was, and you have officially fallen into the consumer trap that the game figuratively represents.

A mind-bending experience sure to re-ignite the "are video games art" debate. The textures are a little outdated and I had some technical problems at first, but these are very minor flaws. What this game promises, and what it ultimately delivers, is a strong narrative laced with ruminations on the meaning of choice, freedom, and game design. In some respects, it's difficult to even call The Stanley Parable a "game," as there is truly very littly in the way of player input (there's even an achievement awarded for hopelessly pushing the space bar in a vain attempt to jump). Whereas other similar experiences tend to feel overburdened and pretentious, however, The Stanley Parable, its deceptively light tone set by its Portal-esque Narrator (think GLaDOS's cheek with Wheatley's personality), truly manages something special with this structure. It also helps that there was obviously a ton of love and car put into this game. All things considered, this is a great purchase. Note that any given playthrough is rather short, but The Stanley Parable demands many, many replays to experience the full impact.

I heard good things about The Stanley Parable, so when it went on sale, I purchased it. I really wanted to like it.  Unfortunately, I absolutely hated this game.  I don't even think I'd really call it a game.  It's more like a short very short interactive commentary/argument about free will and the state of modern video game development, which produce games that follow a linear narrative that does not allow the player to diverge from the pre-planned linear format.  If that sounds boring it's because it is boring, very boring.
I mentioned that it's short.  It can be completed in under 10 minutes.  That's not a typo--the game can be completed in under 10 minutes.  There multiple endings depending on certain decisions a player makes in-game.  I found about 6 of them and each time I hoped that the game would continue on to a next level or chapter, but no such luck.
In short, if you like having fun when you play games, do not purchase this game.
But if you feel like playing a very short, boring interactive argument/commentary about free will and modern video game development, this game is for you.  Or if you want to save some money, go watch paint dry or grass grow and have just as much fun and excitement.

A hilarious deconstruction of what it means to be playing a video game, and what to expect from a game in turn.  The game plays like a choose-your-own-adventure book in first-person form, and the narrator's attempts to guide, help, interfere, correct, beg, plead, insist, or simply pack up his ball and go home make up the meat of the experience.  Unfortunately, he's not necessarily in any more control of the narrative than you are, and thus comedy abounds.
If you've played a corridor shooter and wished you could interfere with the preconceived narrative, this is the game to let you pursue that impulse to his ridiculously inevitable conclusions.  If you want to run around in a video game while a British man inexplicably responds to your every action no matter how much you're trying to go off the rails, this is that game.
Took 5 minutes to achieve an ending (if that sounds bad, you don't yet understand this game), and 5 hours to systematically explore every possibility I could find... which is probably not quite all of them.

Is The Stanley Parable a game? That is the greatest question of all, since the narrator is doing all the job and what you are doing is merely pressing some buttons and trying to open some doors. You follow instructions (or you don't) and you understand rapidly that you don't have any real choice. A lot of game give you the illusion of choice without telling you. The Stanley Parable do tell to you quite clearly that the choices you are doing are not real and that everything was planned to make you do specific actions. You will try different avenues, die a number of time by different ways, and still it will give you the opportunity to try again some other options you didn't took earlier (just to understand you can die of even more different ways).
Anyway, I will say that The Stanley Parable is great (and not that it is a great game since it's not really a game) because it has a great narration, great ideas behind it and because it makes you think about what is a game.

Be forwarned, if you are going into this expecting a traditional narrative, or a fantastic story, then let it be known that this is not that kind of game, for this game cannot really be beaten. Now there are endings in this game, but each ending just restarts the game and are quickly done and are very amusing. This game is very self aware of itself and knows it is a game; it is a satire on the modern gaming story and linearity and if you are knowledgable of the tropes then you are sure to get a good laugh at it. There are no enemies to kill, no puzzles to solve, no platforming, just walking through doors and exploring the enviroment for easter eggs and alternitive/secret endings; it rewards players who like to explore rather than just follow a path preset by the developers, which if you do follow exactly how the game wants you to, it is the most boring out of all of them. There are approxitmetly 16 endings  discovered(including secret endings), as well as plenty of Easter eggs to get a good chuckle. If you only play games for a definite story and don't like exploring, then do not get this game, for this is not the kind of game for you, but if you are a fan of exploring the enviroment and like finding secrets, then this game is for you. The graphics to some might seem outdated, but graphics have never been a make it or break part of a game for me. The only negative I think is the price tag for it at 15 dollars(at least for people like me), but since it is on sell as of today it is more fair, but if you reading this after the sale, then pick it up if you are not strapped for cash.

You play the role of Stanley, the titular protaganist that seems satisfied with his extremely boring life. But "play" here is more of term for acting out a part than engaging in a game. The Stanley Parable is barely even a game, but instead an interactive fiction that entices you to go down the same doors again and again in the hope that you will see all of the games many endings. There's nothing to collect, no one to kill, and you can't even jump. You just turn down halls and go down doors. On papar, this may sound boring, but the way it's done is the charm of the game. The Narrator is reminiscent of Portal's Glados: you're never quite sure if he's your friend, your enemy, or your master. 40% of the games enjoyability is because of him and the voice actor who plays him. The rest of the enjoyment is deciding what path to go on or just finding new ones. Each of them means something. WHether it's poking fun at mainstream gaming tropes or telling you a sad story that may actually reflect your life, you'll genuinely want to see everything this deceptively complex "game" has to offer.

You feel every emotion that goes through his mind, you actually feel it. What he found there, was an abundance of other people's reviews sounding much, much smarter than anything he ever could have thought of. Most of it, at least.

What had he been playing for the last hours of his life? What did he witness, that gave him this urge to tell the world of his brilliant experiences? As he clicked on the seducingly shiny button, he somehow knew, that these questions would not go unanswered for long…

What to say about The Stanley Parable apart from it is one of the wittiest games I have ever played. The player starts off with an introduction to the game. The Narrator introduces the character, Stanley, of course. After this short but witty introduction, the player is then thrown into Stanley's shoes with only the guidance of the Narrator to help the player on their way.
As said before, the gameplay is fairly low, with only a few commands and inputs the player can do. Including, turning off computers around the office, opening and closing a few doors around the building and general movement. Heck the player cant even jump, though, even this can be funny as they will receive an achievement for at least trying.
I cant really say much about the story without ruining it for everyone. But what I will say is that is has many different paths the player can take. These paths are usually formed when disobeying the Narrator's guidance, leading to some stunning writing. Each time the player feels like they have outsmarted the Narrator but he always seems to be one step ahead.
Although the game is low on features and gameplay in general, it is still addicting and a swell game to play. However, this is another game to wait for the price to drop or for it to be on sale as the price does not truly match the content. Either way, it is a solid 4/5 star game!

Putting aside all the deep philosophical talk about this game, it is quite the quirky and entertaining practice in breaking the conventions of modern video games. There is no linear progression. There is no significant plot or enemy. There isn't really an ending. What you get out of this game depends on what you put into it. That said, if you are looking for a sense of reward, power, or accomplishment, this may not be the game for you.
My biggest complaint with the game is definitely the length. As the achievement suggests, the game can be completed in about 4 minutes. And depending on whether or not you use a guide, it will probably take about 4 or 5 hours to complete all the endings and easter eggs. That said, It is still an entertaining game, but I would wait for it to go on sale before buying it.

I purchased this game since it was on sale and because I had heard a lot about it from the community at large. After playing through it, I have to be honest and say that it felt like an old school text adventure game brought to life. You have many choices, many paths, some of which go to unique places, others which take you on the so-called "right" path. The narrator is an absolute blast, but I cannot help but feel that its inspiration is drawn heavily from Portal 2's Wheatley character with its rhetorical and often sarcastic responses to player actions. It is well acted, well crafted and like other users have mentioned, it is quite artistic. The graphics are decent, and some of the game's humor is brilliant. The homage to a certain mining game in one of the story branches also cracked me up, but that's just me.
On the downside, however, the game is quite short, and it really is only a matter of an hour or two before you start getting into repeat narratives and story branches. The story itself and the environment is quite unimmersive, taking away some of the potential charm I wanted to see. The price when not on sale is a tad on the high side for what you get, but I feel that this is simply a good bare-bones example for what full games can potentially incorporate via a choice system a la Mass Effect.
Positives:
A lot of paths to take
Humorous narration
Full of homages to other games
A showcase of what choice-based games could potentially incorporate in the future
Negatives:
Quite short and no time before narratives repeat
Despite the humorous narration, it's not unlike anything we have seen or heard before
Unless on sale, the price is a tad on the high side
Feels like an art piece or a technical showcase than a game
It's certaInly not bad, the charm certainly is there, and some of the ideas with regards to choosing one's own path feel quite fresh.
I'd say it's a 6.5/10 on the whole and one to check out. Just don't go in expecting a 50 hour experience because it's not there.

Similar Games:
It’s fairly unique, although certain moments are reminiscent of Antichamber.
The Good:
The narrator’s voice acting is excellent; it’s easy to forget that it’s someone reading lines.
Having an invisible narrator delivering an awesome performance has two distinct benefits to the overall game: 1) enabling the player to imagine their own version of the antagonist and 2) sidestepping having to model a visual representation that would live up to the player’s expectations. A clever move from a game design standpoint, whether intentional or not.
Some seriously creepy/unexpected moments, even having played the mod version. One scene left me literally staring at the screen in disbelief.
Triggered animations are perfectly timed – there are no “glitch” moments because you made it to an area before the game thought you would, etc.
The game includes a “Disable Achievements” option! (Ed. note: this may have swayed my entire opinion of the game)
The text on in-game computer screens balances between tongue-in-cheek parodies of corporate jargon and self-aware references to the gaming industry. Somehow, neither of these manage to break the immersion.
The multiple “endings” vary immensely, and manage to pull the curtain back in satisfyingly different ways each time.
The Bad:
The “games are not art” crowd might dislike this game due to sticking with their party platform; they are wrong.
Players who try to speed-run through the game will miss out on the excellent voice acting, and may actually cut off the narrator mid-phrase. This is more of a critique against speed-runners than the game.
The loading screens kinda (barely) give away the concept of the game’s “ending.”
The Writing:
This is one of the most well-written games I have ever played. I was a huge fan of The Stanley Parable when it was “only” a HL2 mod, and the full game hits the same marks and then some.
The game has a “Choose Your Own Adventure” feel, and does a great job of seamlessly adapting to virtually any action the player makes.
The entire game manages to convey a sense of underlying dread, regardless of the choices you make – even the “happy” outcomes are never portrayed as being 100% certain.
Did I make time to complete it:
Many times, although (spoiler alert) that’s kinda “the point.”
Recommended Purchase Price:
If you’re a fan of unconventional games, philosophy, psychology, existentialism, spiritual ennui, fatalism, causality and/or intellectually challenging games that make you think about anything whatsoever, this is a must-buy. $11.99 is a STEAL.

It's hard to write a game review for The Stanley Parable because I'm not sure that it's even a game. At its best, it's a witty - though pedantic - narrative that criticises common video game tropes in an environment that is mildly intriguing. At its worst, (and it is often at its worst) it's a boring walk through a drab office building with an incessant narrator and the only motivation to keep playing comes from the possibility that there -might- be something actually interesting behind the next door. There are times when the game can be genuinely funny, but for the most part, you'll be sitting through the experience (and I use that term lightly) with a straight face. The game is structured around giving you different choices throughout the plot (another term I use lightly) that will drastically change the story depending on what you do, but none of these choices actually feels satisfying and although that's sort of the entire point of the game, it's not worth paying $15 for. If you absolutely HAVE to know what happens, just watch a playthrough on YouTube and save your money.

At its worst, (and it is often at its worst) it's a boring walk through a drab office building with an incessant narrator and the only motivation to keep playing comes from the possibility that there -might- be something actually interesting behind the next door. There are times when the game can be genuinely funny, but for the most part, you'll be sitting through the experience (and I use that term lightly) with a straight face. The game is structured around giving you different choices throughout the plot (another term I use lightly) that will drastically change the story depending on what you do, but none of these choices actually feels satisfying and although that's sort of the entire point of the game, it's not worth paying $15 for. If you absolutely HAVE to know what happens, just watch a playthrough on YouTube and save your money.

It's nearly impossible to explain this game, so I won't try to.
What I'll do instead is explain why it needs to be experienced, rather than read about.
The Stanley Parable Is a game about choice, giving the player a story to roam freely in, but at the same time, taking away the feeling of making a choice that the player expects. Running counter to how choice in most other games works, The Stanley Parable makes you feel as though everything has been planned out- you were always going to make that choice, and the story continues as such, narrating your tries and desperate hopes to thwart the game's removal of the choices that it presents you with.
The effect that this creates is not one that I have the words to describe, but led me to play it again and again, hoping to discover all of the myriad endings that I could.
The Stanley Parable is impossible to explain, but its take on the nature of choice in games is one that I'm glad i had the pleasure to experience.

Toy with the role of narrative in video games, the illusion of choice, and with just how narrow objectives in video games really are while breaking the fourth wall in The Stanley Parable. It's a game for people who spend forever wandering and poking about in games, for people who try to break games, and for people who defy games' orders just to see if they account for it.
That said, it's not without its faults. The most savage review of The Stanley Parable I've seen was by its own head developer and he accurately points out that TSP is complicit in everything it skewers for lack of ability to think of better options. Let's not throw the word "genius" around willy-nilly. "Clever" is more accurate. TSP isn't going to start a revolution in storytelling in games, in addressing the problems inherent in providing choice within pre-constructed environments, or anything of that sort. It's just very clever. For me, it was enough "clever" to be happy with the purchase. Your mileage may vary.

Here's a review I originally wrote for a gaming blog calle No Work, All Play, and I'd recommend you read the formatted version there at:
Anyway, here it is if you'd rather read it here (hope this helps!):
The Tale of a Man Named Stanley - The Stanley Parable Review
I’ve rewritten this review several times already; I just can’t find the words to describe The Stanley Parable. After all the drafts and redrafts, however, I’ve come to the conclusion that it’s probably best not to even attempt to describe The Stanley Parable. It would not only put a strain on my limited abilities as a reviewer, but also it will ruin part of the magic that makes The Stanley Parable so special. Also I’m still not entirely certain what The Stanley Parable is, but I enjoyed it regardless.
The Stanley Parable is a game. Sort of. It’s also a comedy. Sort of. As you’ve probably learnt from the trailer, a dry and cynical, not to mention British, narrator will tell you the story of a man named Stanley. See, he’ll try to tell you a story, but as a player you make decisions that decide what story is told. For instance if you replay the game taking a different decision you don’t get a new ending or variant of a different of the same story, you effectively  get an entirely new playthrough.The decisions normally involve following the narrators 'plan' if you like, or choosing to defy him.
The game not only makes fun of itself, video games in general, but also (rather boldly) you. It’s conscious of how you act (conscious that you’re conscious that you’re playing a video game) and will comment, even scorn you for this; needless to say the results are rather hilarious. Because The Stanley Parable is very, very funny. Never taking itself too seriously it tells a story filled with more jokes than you will ever find. But beyond the distinctive humour that makes this game so lovable it tries to tell you something about videogames and how you play them. It doesn’t fall into the trap of replicating or over exaggerating the mediums short comings (as I believe Deadpool did, though I have yet to play it), instead it points them out to you and let you do the maths. As you’ll probably notice from the trailer even Stanley’s job is a parody of playing a particularly linear video game.
The Narrator is wonderful. With plenty of tongue-in-cheek humour in his monologues and incredible voice-acting, Kevan Brighting’s performance is worthy of a place alongside narrators from Thomas Was Alone or Dear Esther.
Should you buy it? Yes! If you want genuinely funny humour and incredibly original and innovative narrative then dive into the game knowing as little as possible about it. The price may be a bit steep for the 4-hour play time it took me (though I’m sure I’ll replay many endings and some still elude me), but stop moaning and buy it on sale if you must. If you’re not eager to spend £10/$15 on something you know practically nothing about then there’s a great demo that was developed separately and gives you an indication of what to expect without spoiling anything. I’d highly recommend playing this, it’s free so why the hell not? I will, however, say that it’s probably best not to play the original HL2 mod, as although it’s been remade and expanded upon, much remains similar, and I kind of wish I had experienced The Stanley Parable first as the full game instead of the mod (which I played around a year back). But still, there really aren’t any games that are comparable to The Stanley Parable, and it’s refreshingly original. Video games, take note!

This is a review for the Stanley Parable. In this review, I hope to expose you to all the things that make The Stanley Parable enjoyable to play. You see, the point of reviews isn't quite so much to critique games, as otherwise this would be called a 'critique' of The Stanley Parable. From a purely consumeristic point-of-view, a review is there to give a consumer, ie: you, help for a very simple choice - should I (you) purchase and play this game, or should I let it languish on the store page forever, never to experience the spaces of my computer, so filled with games, and videos of various things (only you, the consumer, know what those things are), and maybe pictures of cats, because those always end up on computers.
Generally, the second paragraph is used to extol or castigate the virtues or issues (respectively) that the game contains. This review will focus mostly on the ability of the game to reveal to you the nature of choice in video games while being obvious and not-obvious at the same time, the superb writing, and the multitude of peculiar ways in which the game can reveal your death...or not? You see, that was this review avoiding a spoiler. Very important to do that, in reviews, lest you reveal all the cards in the game's hands before even letting the person play! And wouldn't that be an embarrassment! Yes it would.
A concluding paragraph is sometimes, but not always used, to sum up the review. Generally, it's hard to write something that doesn't sound hokey or cliched, with phrases like 'And in conclusion...' or 'It turns out that in the end...'. But in conclusion, it turns out that in the end the Stanley Parable lends itself quite well to a play through, being fun, unique, interesting, and different from anything else that's come before it, is what this review would say. And at the end, it's all about the final sentence, perhaps some pithy pun on the game's name, or some phrase containing the words 'fans of the genre will...'. The Stanley Parable is a game that exists for two primary reasons: To push the limits of definitions relating to what is and what isn't a video game, and to completely screw with the player in ways that I doubt even the developers fully comprehend.
It is a simple game that only uses a total of six buttons, relying on the player's hunger for exploration and it's own humble brand of psychiatric paradoxical mindtricks to become one of the greatest experiences for 2013. The story, setting and experience are almost impossible to define with the limited vocabulary of the English language as well as the way the game is always changing for no other reason than to simply take your mind and it's capacity of understanding and going anal with it without using lube.
You are told what to do by a narrator, but doing what he says is completely optional and going off to wherever tickles your fancy, and in fact it feels like the game is simply daring you to disobey, making you wonder what to do and where to go. The answer? Wherever you feel like. The narrator will play along with your choices and in some cases will have you sitting in your chair chuckling like a demented chipmunk overdosing on near-apocalyptic laughing gas.
There are unfortunate cases where if you want to experience every possible outcome in the game then you'd have to sit patiently by while the narrator blathers on about the exact same subject previously encountered for no other reason than to witness another conclusion before being thrown right back to the start. This I felt was unecessary and made me ultimately wish for a "skip" button to pass by the long-winded "explanations" (quote-unquote) so I could proceed to the next branch of this massive, tangling jungle of outcomes.
For all it's worth, The Stanley Parable, a humble game made on an outdated engine created a memorable, albeit mind-screwing experience ten times better than all these over-the-top generic tacticool FPS tryhard badass games that pollute the market. This is proven by simply standing in a broom closet and doing nothing.

The Stanley Parable is a hidden-gem of a game that really stands out among the bigger "AAA" game releases of the year such as Battlefield 4 and Call of Duty: Ghosts. While some may write off this game for being an indie title with a smaller budget, I find that the compromises which were made are wholly acceptable. The biggest difference being that instead of having AI companions open all the doors in the game for you, the developers of The Stanley Parable simply could not afford such luxuries and instead introduced the gimmick of "The Narrator"; whose only purpose is to open the doors for the player, and to announce when he is doing so. One could argue that is quite innovative since instead of cluttering up the screen with arrows pointing the player where to go, in The Stanley Parable every action which the player is expected to act out is audibly announced. This innovative reduction of HUD-clutter leaves much more screen real-estate for more useful information such as XP bonuses and level progression.
Sadly, The Stanley Parable cannot keep up with its peers in all facets of game design. Turret sequences are shorter and less numerous than in similar blockbuster titles, and mutliplayer game types include only the standard trite collection of Deathmatch and Capture the Flag. While The Stanley Parable is lacking quite a few features which gamers today expect and take for granted, it does a good job of executing on what it does end up bringing to the table.

Do you enjoy contemplating the space between the game and the gamer? Got a somewhat-off-center sense of humor? Don't mind a little intellect in your exploration?
Buy this. Play it.
However, if you prefer the solid comfort of a guided entertainment ride, where the path is always clear, and there is always a guarantee of purpose...
...then this certainly isn't the game for you.
The Stanley Parable is, in the words of the developer, the exploration of the implications of a single choice given to the player: follow along, or go against the flow. The fractured web of possibilities that sprawl out from that choice are... well, let's just say that after I had convinced myself that I had found them all, I went and found a walkthrough and discovered another four or five endings that I had completely missed.
The game is brilliant, providing both witty critique of traditional adventure narrative *and* an interactive deconstruction of player agency. It isn't perfect - there is a lot of necessary repetition, and there are very few places where the game transcends it's maze-like structure, but these shortcomings are far outweighed by the cleverness of the writing, the world structure itself, and the performance of the narrator.
Check it out, I say!

This isn't a deep game in the traditional sense, but there's way more to explore than I was prepared for initially. Do you enjoy contemplating the space between the game and the gamer? Got a somewhat-off-center sense of humor? Don't mind a little intellect in your exploration?
Buy this. Play it.
However, if you prefer the solid comfort of a guided entertainment ride, where the path is always clear, and there is always a guarantee of purpose...
...then this certainly isn't the game for you.
The Stanley Parable is, in the words of the developer, the exploration of the implications of a single choice given to the player: follow along, or go against the flow. The fractured web of possibilities that sprawl out from that choice are... well, let's just say that after I had convinced myself that I had found them all, I went and found a walkthrough and discovered another four or five endings that I had completely missed.
The game is brilliant, providing both witty critique of traditional adventure narrative *and* an interactive deconstruction of player agency. It isn't perfect - there is a lot of necessary repetition, and there are very few places where the game transcends it's maze-like structure, but these shortcomings are far outweighed by the cleverness of the writing, the world structure itself, and the performance of the narrator.
Check it out, I say!

Stanley played a game about meta-narrative in games. All the while a narrator talked to him in a deep and soothing British voice and gave context for his actions. He made several choices, some explicit, some not. And eventually he reached an ending which reflected those choices and the narrator wrapped up his experience in a big bow and gave it to Stanley to unpack and reflect on.
Then, the game started over.
Stanley wiser for his last playthrough, made some different choices this time and he reached a different ending.
And then Stanley made some more choices.
And he saw some more endings.
Eventually Stanley started making choices he would not have recognized in his earlier playthroughs and was surprised to find they too had endings attached to them.
Stanley was pleased by his wanderings through the game, each ending was interesting and so very different. Stanley explored and explored and marveled at how many small things and details were scripted to be explored. Even when Stanley tried to break the game the narrator was still there to greet him!
Each and every path Stanley chose gave him pause for thought and introspection on the relationship between a player and the game they play. And, by extension to the artists responsible for the game.
And in the end, Stanley was happy.

Why I think Stanley Parable is pretty swell!
The first contact I had with this game was when they released the mod.
I didn't know what to expect at all, and was pleasantly surprised.
I hardly ever find myself laughing out loud at games anymore, the industry is still in a very juvenile stage, that little mod though had me in stitches before I even reached the doors.
There is a lot going on here, and I guess I can respect it all the more because I'm old enough to have grown up and played through almost the entirety of spectrums games have offered.
What I most enjoyed was the fact I felt for the first time in a long time of games about shooting different things, that I could just kick off my shoes, and become involved in a story.
Thats what the Stanley Parable is, its the kind of game that sinks in, that you will want to go back and relive.
On my third or fourth playthrough of the mod, I got an ending that told me it was imperative that I turn the game off, I didn't even go for the menu screen, I literally alt+ctrl+del'd my way out.
Knowing they were working on a HD remake, I left it at that, and it was one of the best gaming experiences of my life.
This is minimalist in terms of mechanics, you can't even jump, yet the amount of story and soul they've been able to convey using SDK(notoriously one of the hardest engines to bend to your will DONT CARVE MAN DONT DO IT) is incredible.
Many people have criticised this as a non-game, and you know what, maybe it isn't. The fact is that 'game' is a definition that is still up in the air, and we refer to these multimedia experiences as such only due to lack of a better term. We've used it since the seventies to define this medium, and everyone is content to agree its a catch all for what is an industry that now encompasses just as many sub-genres as music or film.
This isn't a game for everyone, and not everyone will value it in the same way, in fact some people have been offended by the games narrator and taken personal offence.
Which makes me want to redefine this as art, because it obviously has an effect on people, and has caused massive amounts of conversation around it.
I think that if you are truly going to enjoy this title, you need to not take yourself too seriously, because to be honest the narrators and makers take pot shots at the entire industry, even at themselves.
In this sense it reminds me of great stand up comic, it's a parody, it takes the things we know all too well, boils them down, a pokes fun at them. It does so in a way that is inoffensive, playful, and meant to inspire rather than provoke.
On a technical level I would like to just say that they have done quite a bit of cool stuff within SDK. Hell just getting an asset into Source is a nightmare, and this game is polished.
The presentation of the remake really is consistent, it's diverse and teeters into the surreal as heck quite a bit. The effects on show(loved them particle effects), are subtle, but impressive and really pull it all together.
The real strength of this game/experience is the story though, and this is voice acting at its finest.
The energy, emotion, and believability of the narrator is incredible, and if you want proof of this look no further then at how much controversy it has caused.
People feel a true connection with the narrator, they either laugh along, or get horribly offended. Both signs that they've done a stand up job.
To wrap up I'd like to say that its really hard to quantify this game, really hard to provide examples of why the people who are fans love it so much.
Partly because its really not in any one genre, and partly because you really cant talk about specifics without ruining the experience.
All in all though, this game is going down in my list of all time favourites. I really cant wait to see what they make next, and hope they have nothing but success.
I'd on a personal note like to extend a thank you to the devs also(like they need my praise).
This was one of the games, and changes in the industry that made me take a pipe dream from the shelf, and realise that with enough tenacity and elbow grease it was attainable, and got to work.
I really felt this game spoke to me personally, and inspired me to start on a life journey of poverty, poor nutritional choices, lots of caffiene, late nights, no social life, and constant study.
I'm happier than I have ever been, and live for trial and error, and the eureka moments that come after. :P
I'm pretty sure anyone working toward or within this industry knows what I'm talking about.
So thats what I think about The Stanley Parable, I hope their next game is just as thought provoking, divisive, and surreal.

The Stanley Parable is a game of the story of a man's adventure working on a puzzle found in a labyrinth wrapped in an enigma--and that's just one of the possible outcomes you'll encounter while living the life of a man known as Stanley. A man who is both living and dead, who exists and does not exist, and is the game's protagonist and antagonist. His parable is written in stone, but can be changed or even destroyed outright, much to the chagrin of your hapless yet omnipowerful Narrator. In the end, The Stanley Parable is a game of the illusion of choice. A power you have and lack.
Simply put, the game is enchanting and unbearable. It is beautiful and thought provoking; it will upset you, scare you, even make you laugh. The Narrator's voice complements your actions instead of being obtrusive or annoying, and the minimalist musical accompanyment lets you focus exclusively on the story--wherever you choose to take it. I highly recommend this game.

Truly amazing. I wrote a review of the Demo and the original mod before the full game came out awhile back and never got around to writing a review for this one, but I can say that this was well worth the $15. For those who played the original, know that it is not just an HD remix of the original Source mod. It also adds plenty of new endings, as well as new secrets. The original made it quite obvious to the player the choices available and the amount of endings that could be had, but now they've changed plenty of things around to add more secrets, endings, and oh, the replayability!
Now, every time you finish the game, the game will begin again and sometimes after certain endings certain things will change, and it has some hilarious achievements, such as playing the game for the entire duration of a Tuesday, or not playing for five years, or the "Unacheivable" acheivement (which is apparently somehow acheivable but I'm not sure how to legitly yet).
I definitely recommend this game to EVERYONE.
PS: Don't look up any videos or any information about it. It's best experienced first-hand; there's a reason the Store page tells you nothing about the game. If you aren't prepared to throw your money around without knowing about it, play the Demo. Actually—either way, play the demo first. It has exclusive content from the actual game and is hilarious in its own right–it's the best Demo ever, such a good Demo that I wrote a review of the demo.... yeah.
If that's not enough for you, you can play the original mod if you want. It's on Desura and IndieDB for free–you don't need Half-Life 2, just the Source SDK Base 2007 will do it.
I rate this game 8.8888 Stanleys out of 8.8888

Sure the trailer teases a critic for calling the game 'annoying', but this isn't even annoying in it's cleverness (there are no puzzles to solve, truly) or its social commentary. It's just a choose your own adventure style game with a random level generator. It holds your hand while talking to you.
Despite the branching paths, you still won't play this game for more than five hours without seeing everything, and it will already feel linear by the 60% completion mark.
The narration is grand. I can give it that much. For all the potential Stanley's Parable had, I consistently list it as among the greatest letdowns this year.

Wow, this piece of art is amazing. It may not be a game per se, but it's an amazing critique of gaming in general, how we play games, and what games these days are like. Everything the game does is brilliant. Sometimes it locks you out of places for no reason, comments on games that lock you out of such places, and makes you laugh at yourself for playing games like that. Other times, it directly makes fun of games you're playing, and asks you why in the world you're playing them, when they're "obviously" a terrible experience. At times, it makes you kill yourself or kill children... yeah, this game is unique. It breaks what you thought the rules of games were, then breaks them again, and leaves you laughing your head off at how unreasonable The Stanley Parable is while realizing how much it just makes perfect sense. You find yourself becoming a jerk in how you play the game, and the game doesn't care because it's being a jerk right back at you.
I wouldn't really call it a game, but it's far, far more entertaining than these other stupid creations that call themselves "an experience, not a game." This one actually pulls it off where others have failed. And it's utterly magnificent.

At least now you can explore the limitless possibilities of your own mortality through this wonderful mod turned standalone experience.
You play as Stanley as he realizes that no one else is in his offiice and he decides to figure out why. Based on the choices you make and how well you follow the Narrator, you can end up completing this game in under 5 minutes or just over 30 minutes. I found most of the endings thought provoking and funny, and there were some 4th wall breaking endings that were well worth the full ticket price of the game.
The narrator is really the best part of the game, and listening to the full narration and emotions used will keep you engaged throughout your entire experience.
Game time will vary depending on if you wanna take short bursts or plow through all the endings at once, but there is no denying how great this game will imprint itself upon your imagination. You will be narrating your life for the next few days after playing it.

If you think it's a load of crap and quit after half an hour, the game thinks that's a totally valid response. One of the endings speculates that it's the only way to win.
