Inbetween Land is a weird, but a definitely good hidden object adventure game with a strong emphasis on puzzles, taking place on a floating island above a nameless city and set in an alternative sci-fi world. On second thought I'd rather call it a puzzle game, because it focuses on these and contains only a fair number of hidden object scenes, still it bears all the marks of the genre.
Mary, a friend of ours contacts us in our dream asking for help. There's a mysterious floating island above the city where we live (it's been there for 2 years now, according to the local newspaper) which seems to be connected to her disappearance. Upon visiting the local orphanage, where Mary was working and where a ray was aimed at from the island recently, we discover that Mary is indeed missing. Apparently Mary was trying to solve the mysteries of the strange island before she vanished. Of course it'll be our job to find her.
As in other hidden object games (and as a matter of fact in all point and click adventure games) we have an inventory (at the bottom of the screen) and by combining items and using them at the matching locations, we can advance further.
The main feature of the game however is the wide variety of puzzles and minigames. Even though a hidden object game expert has probably encountered most of these in other games, there are some pretty good ones here. They prove to be quite challenging at times yet they never get really frustrating. There are relatively few hidden object scenes in comparison and they are - just like the game itself - rather unusual: there's no description, we have to match picture with picture, usually reassembling a machinery piece by piece. Unfortunately, most of the difficulty in these scenes comes from the fact that sometimes we have to click more than once on a recognized object in order to get it registered.
The game is strange in more than one way since there are no enemies (but it's still fun) and as a result it means no fighting, no evil powers to stop. The only obstacles are the puzzles.
The achievements are mostly puzzle related, but there was one which I found awkward: 'Like us on social media'. I don't think there should be achievements to be obtained like that as it seems like a rather cheap way to increase one's populartiy and the game doesn't need it at all. It's no big deal, just thought I'd mention it (by the way you don't have to really 'like' them, just clicking on the button should unlock the achievement).
The mechanical imagery may appear repulsive (it did for me), but the outdoor scenery (occasionly looking like as if we were in a landscape from a fantasy world) is in fact quite beautiful. The visuals seem dated compared to recent HOGs, but despite this the game still manages to look good. My problem was the mixed use of realistic looking scenes and the cartoon-like characters and cutscenes. The layout is similar to the ones seen in other hiddens objects games and the notes in our journal really do  look like as if they were diary entries. The music is relaxing and mysterious sounding at the same time and really fits the actual scenes, the voice acting is nicely made as well.
Inbetween Land is a charming little hidden object game and if you are a fan of the genre you'll most certainly enjoy it. It might seem a bit strange at first, it may be a bit shorter than the average (only 2-3 hours long, depending on how fast you can solve the puzzles) but it is a well made game. Give it a try and let it enchant you.
PROS
+ lots of well thought out puzzles
+ very good, relaxing music
+ strange, interesting environment
+ simple but nice graphics
CONS
- slow placed, a bit too simple story
- clicking on an object may not always register at first
RATING
7.5/10

Such a very underrated game and the Metacritic reviews are a joke. The 'God is a Geek' review for instance describes the game as "enjoyable" but then scores it a 40 out of 100, only for reasons by comparison to other games of it's genre. There are a lot of game reproductions on the market (the twin stix genre has to be one of the most reproduced) so its not really a fair reviewing Hexodius by comparison and not seeing it as it's own game. 'Hexodius', with it's own challanges, and characteristics that separate it from all the other twin sticks on the market. I need not remind the real gamers how many of them that are on the market but it's a lot and I'm a fan of everyone of them (well almost...
,ehem.) and Hexodius is not an exception.
The game play is your basic twin stick arena shooter, you do get power ups which gives it a hint of action stratagy. The other part I didn't like about Hex was how stale the "Action" started out. Yes, it started off a little slow but the action eventually starts picking up becoming more challenging to the players skill level, and the arena's start getting a little more tricky to navigate, and enemies a little more stronger and powerful. In turn, you power up as well and there is no shortage to choose from, with 4 large sets that can be upgraded and customized.
Controls are highly programmable, in fact, makes this twin stick even easier to pick up and learn.
Yes, there are minor annoyances in this game... like the text popping up in the middle of the battle and pausing it, then throwing you back in... it kind of isn't kewl and you'll see that complaint on a lot of reviews. A minor design flaw. Really Dev's?! ...this is a robot based game... if you can't/won't hire voice actors, get a text to voice simulator!!!
Geez...
Graphics are okay (screenshots tell that story) but I'm not exactly sure why this will not run on my i5-HD3000 GPU laptop, as I have no problems running Assult Andriod Cactus... ?! (Currently running this on Phenom IIx4 810 w/ R9 280X - no probs)
Sounds are okay but also bring us back to the text issue. So I must note to devs: If you are going to progress a story, or write a book of instructions for the player, don't do it in the middle of the action, very few players will have the patience to read it regardless of the fact that it removes players from the game.
With more worlds beaten, more arcade modes are unlocked, so there is a decent amount replayability here but because this game cleverly infuses hazards in both the enemies and in the environment, it becomes tricky, with it comes frustration. It is sometimes best to experience Hex in smaller doses.
Overall I enjoy this game, I think the Metacritic score killed what should have been a more popular game, because 47 is a ugly number and in my opinion, it should have been in the high 60's or low 70's. Even so, over a year later, I still play and enjoy Hexodius.

Hexodius is a traditional twin stick shooter. Usually games that reccomend the controller before you even start playing, really grind  my gears. However, With this one after trying both settings. I'm glad I got that message for a change, because with keyboard and mouse it was next to impossible to play.
The game is great fun and highly addictive, but from what I can see, not very popular on steam. I don't know why this is as its a fantastic game. You have a story mode, and a traditional arcade mode (with leaderboards everyone. Yes. You can own your friends). The story mode follows a very basic story and has several objectified missions to get to a dimensional portal at the end of the zone. There is plenty to do. And you get rewarded for exploring all the map with bonus unlocks and bonus health items.
Your ship is also fully customisable with whatever powers you desire from the menu, different combinations will give you different pro's and cons of course, but work out whats good for you.
The soundtrack to this game in my opinion is rather good, but gets slightly repetitive when you've been in the same zone for a while.
All in all, Hexodius is a great and addictive twin stick shooter, and there is a lot on offer if you try to give it the time of day. I give hexodius a 8/10.
While the concept is solid and the game inventive, Hexodius unfortunately lacks both the intensity and fun a good twin-stick shooter should provide.

I really do love a good hidden object game and I decided to play
because it was recommended to me. It was a fun game to play, with a decent story and good gameplay along with nice artwork and decent voice acting. Something about the game, to me, felt like it was trying to hard. Some of my issues with the title are nitpicks, and it is, overall, a solid hidden object game that I even played twice for both endings. I will state right now that you can play the game only once and still get a very fulfilling experience.
The story is rather generic, a small child named Sophie is kidnapped and the main character is a detective tasked with finding her. He is never given a name but I liked him alot, he was full of witty lines and humorous observations of the situation he was in. What starts in a modern world some how leads the detective to a mystical castle that, despite being near wherever Sophie lives, looks like it’s straight out of medieval times. This is never actually explained and honestly could have been avoided if the time period that Sophie and the detective were from was changed. What also doesn’t make sense is some of the items you find in the mystical abandoned castle, like modern day lipstick. Nitpicks aside, to save Sophie you must also help the ghosts trapped on our mortal plane, people who died because of the evil sorcerer who has Sophie. The game has a choice system, either good or evil, and promises that you can change the story by picking your own path. But you can’t. Everything is very linear and the ending barely changes at all depending on the path you take. I was very disappointed by this, why offer choices if they barely affect anything?
Because of this “choices matter” feature, I played the game twice. I’ve seen it before and was hoping that in this title the choices would affect something but they don’t. You can choose to decline to help a ghost but they just scold you and you are forced to help them anyway. You can also choose peaceful or violent methods to handle issues, like using a bag to move a snake or a slingshot to hit a bird. In the end, you feel like a jerk for choosing the bad options and little else.  Aside from this, the gameplay is very solid. The hidden object scenes were fun, though I did find some items a bit small to find. Also, you will have to revisit the scenes, thankfully only once, but still wish there were just more scenes instead. The puzzles are for the most part not too challenging but there aren’t many of them. Most of the gameplay is item collecting and backtracking to use said item to then get another item to use, repeated the entire game. The game has a very detailed map making this a lot easier. Also, if two items need to be combined they do it automatically, though they have no initial indication that they can’t be used alone. The game offers four difficulty modes, one being “hardcore” where there is no hint system at all which is pretty interesting.
The game is aesthetically lovely. The artwork is well done as are the animations and cutscenes. My major complaint is that, as mentioned before, some of the items were really small in the hidden object scenes so I did have to squint a bit due to my eyes being not the best. However, nothing was blurry and everything was rendered well. The game also has full voice acting and for the most part everyone does well. The main character talking is always a nice a feature and the actor does a good job bringing the witty detective to life. I will point out, there is an option to turn off the main character’s voice if you want to, but not the other characters. The music in the game is fitting, nothing too amazing but in no way was it bad.
is a fun time and a satisfying entry to your game library if you’re a fan of hidden object games. I will say, there are in-game achievements but there are no Steam achievements if you’re playing the game there which is a shame since it would make playing the game twice for both the “good” and “evil” routes more worthwhile. There are also no Steam trading cards. This game does, however, have a bonus chapter that gives us more backstory on the Unicorn Castle and the mystical unicorn itself. For a game with a main game that you can play twice for a different ending and a bonus chapter, the price point is very reasonable. I recommend this title for hidden object game fans or even new players to the genre.

Mystery of Unicorn Castle 2 is a game that vastly surpasses the sum of its parts. The seemingly stock story, the almost-familiar level design and atmosphere, the carefully crafted hidden object scenes all come together as one of the best hidden object games on the market.
Mysteries of Unicorn castle was a forgettable, old-school hidden object game that only caught interest with the challenge of some of its hidden object scenes. The official sequel, The Beastmaster, is on a whole new level though—a level that surpasses most other hidden object games, even the justly-fabled Artifex Mundi portfolio. Simply put, this is one of the best HOG I ever encountered.
It is strange, because the story combines the two most tired clichés of the genre: a detective is trying to find a missing child, only to end up battling a mostly unexplained evil wizard of evilness.
The game’s strength lies in its individual elements and how they combine into something much greater. Elements like the protagonist’s somewhat cheesy constant narration, the slow build-up as the history of the castle is told, or just the sheer atmosphere created by the combination of scenery and writing style. They result in a quintessential hidden object game that manages to rise above the genre’s limitations.
The only reason I cannot give it an even higher score is that it tends to reuse its hidden object scenes (they are almost perfectly balanced, by the way), and because the puzzles are few and just barely above the interesting level. Still, it is just a small drawback for an otherwise great game.

Bone: The Great Cow Race is the sequal to Bone: From Out of Boneville game by Telltale Games. Based on the second volume of the said title, the game picks up where the last one left off. The Bone cousins are adjusting to their current lives in the valley they all ended up in after being chased down by the swarm of locusts. They have resided at the cottage that's occupied by a kind elderly woman named Grandma Ben & her gorgous granddaughter Thorn. A spring fair was being held in the valley where the villagers and travellers from abroad gather together for import goods, carnival stands, and the yearly "Great Cow Race". Fone Bone who has a secret crush on Thorn will use the spring fair as an oppurtunity to express his love to Thorn. This attempt came to a halt when Thorn develops a relationship with a traveling beekeeper. Will Fone Bone be able to show Thorn how much she means to him is yet to be seen. Meanwhile Phoney Bone and Smiley Bone who are trying to pay their debt at the local pub run by the no-nonsense Lucius are crafting a scheme to get both of them out of debt. Phoney views the cow race as the oppurtunity to strike it rich and become the new owner of Lucius's pub in two swoops. Because Grandma Ben who is the only human contestant who par takes in the all bovine race is the popular choice to bet on. Phoney spreads rumors about Grandma Ben's health and claims to have a cow who is the fastest piece of beef in the whole valley. He goes all the way by making Grandma Ben appear to be ill and getting Smiley Bone to pose as a cow. Is this scam going to help Phoney's ambitions, or will it be as much of a failure as his Boneville election? This game is much more lengthy than the previous game as you play as all three Bone cousins each having a different story path that leads to one finale. There is the option to switch between the Bones in case you want to focus on a different cousin or if you feel stuck. The extra fair contenders weren't from the original comic volume, but they do feel like they originated from the Bone comics and helped made the game slightly longer than the predessor did. Keep in mind that this game wasn't intended as the last Bone game as it was open for a third game that was going to be based on the third volume "Eye of the Storm". The game in question never went into development and Telltale never went on record for the reason. Either due to low sales on the game or a falling out with Bone's creator Jeff Smith. But 10 years since this game's release, Telltale never went back to the Bone series for more games. A real shame too cause the good stuff in the comic series happens in volume 3, as it further develops the relationship between Fone Bone & Thorn, many secrets are revealed including the identity of the mysterious Hooded One of the Locusts. I can totally see all of the Bone comic volumes as episodic adventure games. But with the unlikelihood of more Bone games all we have is the anticipated animated film trilogy that's been in development for years. If it does officially get off the ground, I can see it being on par with the two Bone games which is all we have for now as a Bone related media. So if you have finished this game and are craving to know the rest of the story, read the comic series. It is a creative and wonderful comic series that will delight generations of readers to come. It will be the comic series I will read to my future kids some day as well.

I have been playing this game a lot and dearly loving it.
Drifter is still in "Early Access" at this time, which basically means it's in beta.   I'm playing version 0.6.3.  Even though it's in beta it's surprisingly bug-free, but not every feature intended for the final game is implemented yet.  That's ok, the game is actually quite complete as it is.  More content and additional features are just icing on the cake.  While there are some glitches, most are minor and generally just cosmetic.  Expect subsequent versions of the game to be improved.
A lot of this game's depth isn't obvious on the surface when you first look at it.  While the enemy AI seems overly simplistic at first, eventually you'll see the enemy ships doing other things.  Instead of just performing a slash attack, they'll turn and run if they think they're being overwhelmed, for example.  And while it's easy to fight just one enemy, you can get into situations where you are facing a lot of bad guys at once, which can get pretty challenging.
The game is well balanced, with simple missions to get you started, and more difficult missions after you learn your way around.  These aren't labelled as to which are easy and which are hard, you get a variety of missions from the very start and you'll have to pick and choose what you're comfortable with.
You have a good variety of ships to try out (there are 13 currently in the game) but some are better than others and you'll quickly find your favorites.
There are a lot of weapon and equipment upgrades as well, and sometimes buying even a single upgrade changes the nature of how you fight battles or even just fly around.
Trading is well implemented, with a lot of different types of systems with varying prices of goods, and there is a major metagame involved in finding good items to trade and good trade runs. While trading isn't useful in the early game, once you've made enough money to buy lots of expensive trade goods, you can make more money in trading than you can killing bad guys, even with a smaller ship.
I've written a detailed guide, available in the Guides section, that describes everything I've found that you can do and how to do it.  It has a lot more information than what I could fit into a review.  Check it out.
Be sure to check out the various gameplay videos.  They'll tell you very quickly if Drifter is something you'd like.
Drifter is a fairly simple game, with lots of stuff to do if you go looking for it.  If you want a more complete and complex Space Game experience, check out Elite: Dangerous.  Right now, Drifter is quite enough for me.

Inbetween Land may not look much, but its dated exterior and Verne-like aesthetics hide an incredibly short but surprisingly engaging fragmented object game.
On the store page, Inbetween Land looks like just another cheap casual game. But if you decide to pick it up, you’ll learn the reason behind the current high ratings, because this game has an incredibly gripping atmosphere.
The source of this atmosphere is mostly the visuals. The majority of the game takes place on a strange floating island, where the architecture looks like something out of a Jules Verne inspired movie. The player’s task is to slowly explore this island and uncover the truth behind its mystery. (If you played Return to Mysterious Island, imagine that as a casual game.)
Although most of the play time is spent by exploration, technically Inbetween Land can be classified as a fragmented object game. Don’t expect many puzzles though, as they are mostly there to give a reason to discover new areas. The downside is that since there is little gameplay, the whole game doesn’t really last more than two hours—but at least those will be memorable hours.

I'm recommending this game to anyone who:
1) Understands that it's SHORT (it took me 2 hours).
2) Likes adventure games or hidden object games.
3) Wants a casual game with a decent story.
4) Gets it on sale.
5) Likes puzzles, but doesn't need them to be super difficult.
I'm NOT recommending it for anyone who:
1) Expects a lot of playtime for their money.
2) Wants something fast paced.
3) Needs hardcore puzzles.
That being said, Inbetween Land is not your typical hidden object game (as some reviewers have called it). However, it does have that FEEL of a hidden object game. You do hunt for objects at times, but mostly it's more akin to a point-and-click adventure game where those objects you find get used in other places. Ex. You have to find a key to open that door, but to get that key you need to find a missing part of an object, which is located behind a different door with a key, etc. There are occasional rooms where you need to find a bunch of different pieces to objects, which you then assemble and use to unlock other things. It's not the standard "Here's a room full of random junk, and find two rubber ducks, a shovel and four teacups" that you'll have seen on flash game sites.
As for the story, it's nothing amazing, but there's enough of it to keep you interested. The art is good, but be aware that there's not really a lot of animation. Just "here's a room, isn't it pretty? Go find stuff." It's the kind of art style that's common to hidden object games.
That being said, the two hours I killed with this game were worth the $2 I paid for it. Any more, and I might have felt a little ripped off. If any of what I've said appeals to you, especially the casual nature of the game, I think you'll enjoy it.

I could not reproduce the error by reloading the game and dying to that same enemy, but as soon as I would die to an enemy on a new level the error would reoccur. Even if the bugs were fixed, the game just feels too easy and I can't help but feel like I'm wasting time when I could be playing something else.  I don't recommend purchasing this game, not even if it were on sale.

I'm really not sure whether I should recomend this game or not. On the one hand this platformer-RPG has some cute graphics (although quite a lot of people won't like how simple and "empty" they can be) and a great, relaxing soundtrack. There are plenty of levels with ascending difficulty and a huge variety of enemies and bosses -every world, literally, has its own kind of enemies- that throw away tons of loot to collect which then can be used to upgrade weapons or construct different stuff like some very useful teleporters. If you want a relaxing game to play when you have some free time and you find its graphics appealing, then you can give it a try (since it doesn't cost much), but you have to play it on easy or medium at max, cause hard is irritatingly difficult.
Quite disappointingly, hard is the only way to gain achievements and unfortunately it's very difficult and unfair. Platforms tend to get smaller and smaller as you progress and your jumps have to be more and more accurate every time, thus making the last worlds almost impossible to beat, since the controls lack the precission needed to make these jumps and if you press the button a tiny bit longer you fall into the gap and have to start the level all over again, as there's no sign of a checkpoint even on the biggest levels. God knows how many unnecessary and irritating deaths you will have to suffer on your way to beat the game (if your nerves manage to fight it till the end). And since this isn't enough, even these simple graphics can get confusing at times. For example some enemies can be hidden behind a tree or on a platform that's beneath you and you can't see them properly, so if you don't pay much attention you might get hit and fall, which equals to even more unnecessary deaths.
However, the most annoying thing about this game is that you don't expect this kind of difficulty. There are these cute graphics, made by kids, there's also the sounds that make you relax and the first levels are quite easy, too. So you lossen yourself and sit back and then you get suddenly caught off-guard and smacked hard in your face for being such an unwary fool.
So, finally, if you want to have a little fun for some hours or buy something for your kid, you could give this game a try, if nothing else is on your mind, but if you are an achievement hunter that wants every game completed 100%, you should first double-check that you can handle the irritation caused by this game's unfairness, before playing it.

Ghosts inhabit medieval smithies littered with modern hardware and safety equipment? The magical-meets-modern thing has been done successfully in these games, but there isn't even an attempt at an explanation here. It's just a checklist of themes and puzzles, weirdly mishmashed together.
Worse are the achievements. Some border on unreasonable (five items in five seconds) and others exist solely to pad play-time. To wit, there are a number of utterly meaningless decision points throughout the game: you choose to play nice, and go on your way (and eventually earn an achievement for being nice)... or you act like a jerk to ghosts or solve an environmental puzzle violently... and earn precisely the same result, plus a 'you're a jerk' trophy if you go straight through like that. You still have to do the ghosts' quests and solve the same puzzles. It's completely meaningless.

All that said, Drifter does offer a very interesting take on a tried and true genre of space exploration combined with the open world freedoms that we've come to love with newer games.  There were some nit-picky things that I noted that I felt were rather wierd, like no one would build a mining base in a star system that has nothing to mine. One suce complaint was the ability to tell the difference between different types of star systems at a glance.  Thats easily done by displaying them with different colors on the galaxy view.
Aside from the overbearing development slowness and persistent game issues, I'd give the game an overall 7.5 out of 10.  I would recommend this game for space exploration enthusiasts. This is one of those games I wish I could give a neutral opinion on. It's not inherently bad, yet it's not all that great. Allow me to explain, dear reader.
Planet 1138 is an Action/RTS game where you control a "Command Buggy" that has rockets, a machine gun, a shield and nitrous that captures bases which then produce units and pushes them down the lane towards the enemy base. As the game goes on and you complete levels, you will unlock new upgrades which passively upgrade your buggy to deal more damage or to upgrade the turrets on support bases. Honestly, the game is more of a MOBA like Warshift than it is an Action/RTS like Battlezone or Uprising: Join or Die. There are a ton of levels to play through with super challenging AI and even multiplayer. Overall, the gameplay is solid enough, it works and it is competent.
This all sounds great right? Well, it's more meh than it is good. The core concept is amazing, I'm a huge fan of Uprising: Join or Die and I'd kill to have another one or at the very least an Action/RTS that operates in the same style but that is aside the point. Planet 1138 is meh because of presentation and the cheating nature of the AI opponent.
Presentation you say? Well yes, unfortunately all the menus in the game look as though they were made in
and the game has the barest of aesthetic qualities. While this isn't bad in itself, it makes the game look more like a first time flash game than an actual 9.99 Steam game. While this isn't meant to be a knock on the dev but I'd highly recommend they hire on someone who can redesign the menus or the interface in general. I truly believe that presentation is one of the most important qualities when designing anything and I'd love to see some more work put into the game's aesthetics.
My second problem? The AI is utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Somehow he can lock on to you and shoot at you from every angle while you can only autoaim at opponent's directly in front of you. The AI isn't foolish enough to sit still and let you shoot at him, he will drive circles around you and pummel you into the dirt. It causes the AI to be super aggressive while the player has to fight defensively by standing next to bases and such. This may just be me being a noob but it seems like the AI has a naturally unfair advantage in the game.
In conclusion, not a bad game, not a great game. With some work, I can see this being an amazing first attempt by the studio. For now, I can't recommend it at 9.99. I would at 5.99 though. Seems more reasonable of a price.

Having tried a few games like this (steam marines, space hulk, templar battleforce) I feel safe in saying if you're looking for a turn-based space marines vs aliens game this is the best available on steam. The UI looks a little amateur but there is a very solid game underneath.
The game sells its theme through its gameplay very effectively, with every fight a battle for position to avoid getting surrounded, opening and closing doors to move through cramped corridors safely, enemies breaking down walls and doors to reach you, there is a lot of tension and uncertainty. Your guys have a lot of health and relatively high % chance to hit compared to similar games, which I find helps keep things focused on the tactics and does a pretty good job of avoiding those all too frequent XCOM moments where the success of a mission ultimately comes down to a single dice roll.
Game rules are consistent, and with plenty of actions per turn it always feels like each turn represents a significant change in the state of the game. Enemy AI is pretty good and at its best feels very human-like, attempting to surround you, negate chokepoints and pick off your weakest squadmates.
Graphically the game is a bit of a mixed bag, I love the way the map tiles look like they came straight from a Fantasy Flight board game (as do the procedural map layouts), but on the other hand the marines are servicable but obvious knock-off 40K marines, and I find a few of the alien designs a bit samey. This is really a non-issue for me, but then I play a fair few ASCII games so clearly graphical fidelity is not high on my priority list.
Ultimately, if the theme or genre of this game interest you at all you will almost certainly get a lot of fun out of it, and considering the depth and robustness of the underlying ruleset, at £6.99 its an absolute steal.

I usually wait until I've got at least 30 hours or so on something to review it, but in this case, I think I'm safe writing one earlier.
TL;DR = A tactical combat game very similar to the tac games of the 1990s. Quite a bit of micro, and lots of freedom to do what you want. It's a yes.
Review Proper:
Ultimate Space Commando is a bit deceiving. The name sounds like a weird Japanime crossover thing that's gotta be horribly translated, and the graphics are kinda ugly, even for a retro-esque game like this. That said, the gameplay itself is great, the freedom the mechanics offer is pretty hard to match, and it's certainly addictive.
The concept is pretty simple - you've crashlanded on a far away planet, and need to escape. To do this, you need to fight through enemies, collect materials, and maybe uncover some answers as to what's been happening. You'll upgrade your gear on the way, meet increasingly scary [s]sprites[/s] monsters matched only in their deadly-ness by their ugliness, and uncover little bits of a surprisingly well translated story on the way.
As many have mentioned, it plays a lot like older X-Com, Jagged Alliance, Silent Storm, etc. etc. As of such, there's some great stuff, some stuff you might love or might hate, and some meh stuff.
The Good:
First off, this is currently about the same price of a pack of smokes. That's never bad, particularly when the game is actually good, like this one is.
The combat is interesting, and the "18 distinct weapons" are actually pretty distinct. Even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ starting guns can be upgraded to respectable death machines with their own advantages. That's kinda cool.
The story is good for this kind of game - for one, it actually exists, and for two, it's reasonably coherent.
Dev support is great. Think I waited something like 3 hours to have my question answered. Given that you'll often only hear the words "there's only one dev" followed by some excuse as to why it shouldn't matter that a game sucks, is broken, or what have you, it's actually pretty mindblowing when you consider that this lady has managed to make a game that suffers from none of the above, is more indepth and packed with features than most multi-dev projects in the same genre, and is just genuinely good, while still having time to reply directly to the fanbase in a prompt manner.
It's
. Seriously, why the ♥♥♥♥ are all games like this, not to mention turn based 4x games, not hotseat multiplayer anymore?
The mechanics run deep.
You generally don't die because something utterly unfair has happened. Sometimes you get unlucky, but usually, you just ♥♥♥♥ed up.
There's really alot of good to say about this game, but the store page itself lays most of it out very well, so there's no need for me to do it again.
The Mixed:
You need to buy and manually equip every bullet you fire, every healthpack you use, and literally anything else you might expend in a mission. I don't mind this, because I grew up when games were like this, but some people might.
You have a very limited inventory. Your guys can only carry what they can carry in nine inventory slots, and you can only store nine things at your base. There are some good mechanics to help you not lose out on potential loot during a mission - namely that materials are automatically picked up at the end of most missions, and you can "field salvage" weapons and stuff for a percentage of their value if you don't have room to pack them back - but if you like to hoard stuff, you might find this irritating.
It's a little punishing. The mechanics run deep, but aren't usually very evident. Part of the fun of these kinds of games can come from figuring stuff out, but there's just some things you can't know until something goes wrong, or unless you ask the devs directly. Or read the manual, but who does that?
Similarly, the UI is oldschool. It's not as incomprehensible as some of the games it imitates, but it's not incredibly intuitive either. On the flip side of this, it's actually pretty simple once you get the basics down, and thus the learning curve isn't so bad.
The translation is surprisingly good, but it still seems fairly evident that the writing is either done by a complete amateur, or a non-native english speaker. That really doesn't matter at all to me, since it's still effective in getting the story across, and you're supposed to build your own attachments to your troops in these kinds of games, not have them thrust on you. But it might matter to someone. The only real complaint this causes is that sometimes, instructions are a little unclear.
The Bad:
There's not a lot to say here, but a two things do come to mind.
The fields of fire are messed up. You can only shoot straight, like a rook in chess, unless you're in defensive mode. Then you get a much larger field of fire. I'm guessing there is some reason behind this, but I haven't encountered it yet.
It's ugly. I couldn't design something prettier, but it's basically animation free, overly sterile, and just not pretty. This usually doesn't matter to me in games, and likely wouldn't here if the graphics style was something else, but I just don't like it much.
Conclusion:
All in all, this is really a hidden gem. It's cheap, has hotseat and online multiplayer, great gameplay, and tons of replayability. It's a really good game that catches the feel and style of 1990s turn based games very well, without descending into mediocre mechanics and design flaws.
I should also mention that there's a ton of other features such as an annual tournament, a series of challenge and other game modes, and a bunch of other neat crap I didn't touch on in the review because I haven't played around with them yet. There's a good bit of content I don't even know about, personally.
If this is your type of game, then you may find this is the best ten bucks or so you'll ever spend on Steam.
Wish there were more of these games!

Ultimate Space Commando
Ultimate Space commando is a great game in its own right, but nagging flaws keep it from achieving the truly brilliant mark. It is a game designed for pure strategy fans like myself taking ideas from games like XCOM.
Ultimate Space Commando gives you a squad to play around with just like XCOM. Your squad members have landed in a hostile territory which seems to be crawling around with aliens of all sorts. The story in USC is pretty generic considering the theme and there are few meaningful choices in the midst of the campaign. The campaign itself is pretty lengthy and is a blast to play through. It is told through written dialogues instead of cutscenes which is understandable. Various ways to handle a situation come as a shining star in the gameplay. There are various choices and tactics based on your squad, weapons etc.
It also has a permadeath system for your squad members if you notch the difficulty up a bit. You manage 16 members throughout the campaign from which you can select whom to take on the mission and who will stay back and look after your base. There is even a surprisingly fun Defend your base where you set up a base and try to defend it from the increasingly difficult hoard of aliens.
Another thing USC gets right is the environmental backdrop set up for your battles. It sets the mood right for the one more turn fights and also gives a sense of dread for your squad. Deep customization and depth in characters are all present in USC
The gameplay of USC is very fun but what lets it down is the amount of bugs present throughout the game. Frequent crashes and screen freezes also are very common. The amount of bugs present makes it feel like a  beta test or an unchecked game of some kind. That’s a real same though as the original game present beneath all those bugs is really great.
I am surprised at how a game as good as USC is still not known to the majority of the people even an year after its release. This is what we call a hidden gem in steam libraries.

Ultimate Space Commando is a turn-based tactical rpg/strategy game that is completely old school in both good and bad ways:  unique, intricate game mechanisms with lots of meat, but also extremely slow-moving and unforgiving gameplay.  If you find yourself enjoying it, I believe you could easily get dozens (or hundreds) of hours out of this game.  Conversely, it could easily take you dozens (or hundreds) of hours to try and get your enjoyment out of this game, which modern gamers may not have the patience for.  Likely you will either love it or hate it - this is a niche game to the extreme.
Ultimate Space Commando is a massive game stuffed to the brim with a large campaign and tons of content in the other game modes along with richly complex gameplay mechanisms supporting them.  The developer clearly has put much love and effort into this project, which shows both in the game as well as their online presence - they appear to be extraordinarily active and helpful in the forums as well as the enormous (and necessary) online guide for the game.
In the game, you take your squad of Ultimate Space Commandos into the depths of a harrowing alien world, inhabited by countless hostile aliens that bear a striking resemblance to... well, 'Alien'.  The dark, foreboding atmosphere lit only by your active scanners and field of vision sets a perfect stage for your wary approach into the unknown, where monsters may suddenly swarm you or even start chewing through the walls to get to your tasty team. The gameplay itself is rather enjoyable, with every action needing to be carefully planned out to best make use of your extremely limited action points, ammo, randomly obtained gear, and the uniquely developed skill-sets of your party.
Alas, with all these wonderful things going for it, I still cannot recommend the game in its current state.  As much as I want to like Ultimate Space Commando... the game feels like an Early Access version to me, rather than a fully finished product. This is mainly due to the incredibly slow pacing of the game and the presence of at least one gamebreaking bug.
Turn-based strategy games are usually slow by design, as you must plan out every single movement to efficiently win battles.  However, with 4 separate characters, each with many actions per turn - and dozens of enemies on screen with the same - battles in Ultimate Space Commando can last for aaaages.  The painful inventory management slows down the action even more, as four distinct 9-slot inventories must be carefully arranged and rearranged with all the scraps and items you find.
As for the bugs... let me set the stage.   Imagine that you are a member of an undergeared and overwhelmed elite fighting squad, who has found a brief respite from the action by jamming into a tiny elevator car only big enough for the 4 of you.
Yup.  That happened.
In a very long game that relies on a single auto-save to keep the feeling that your past actions matter (*see edit*), gamebreaking bugs like this can be pretty frustrating.  I also experienced a couple of game crashes on loading levels (although my save files were still fine in those instances).  From the forums, it appears things like crashes and unending levels have happened to others as well, though not frequently and the developer seems very quick to patch them out.
--
*The developer pointed out that players can enable an option that allows an extra backup save.  I would highly recommend this, even with the in-game restriction of having your campaign labeled as a 'training drill'.)
The campaign's narration could also use that final bit of polish that takes it to the level of a $20 game. The story of the game seems rather well done, but... the actual words used to convey the story?  Not so much.  While reading sentences that sometimes lack punctuation or need to be rearranged to make sense does have its own special retro charm, putting the game script into the hands of an editor would probably be a good idea.  This mild lack of editing just adds to the feel that the game hasn't quite made it to the final release (though to be fair, this can easily be overlooked in favor of the incredibly deep gameplay).
In the end... I still see huge potential in this game, and strategy fans may find endless hours of entertainment in USC's immense, immersive world - especially with the outstanding community events the developer has hosted.  If this were an Early Access title I would definitely give it a thumbs up...however, I just can't bring myself to fully recommend it as a finished product.  I wholeheartedly hope that Ultimate Space Commando will do well and keep getting patched to smooth out the experience, but right now you may need to be a very patient gamer to get the most out of this so-close-to-amazing game.

Steamified » Indie Spotlight » Ultimate Space Commando: Turn-based Tactics in Space
Ultimate Space Commando: Turn-based Tactics in Space
BY STEAMIFIED APRIL 12, 2016 INDIE SPOTLIGHT
Indie Spotlight: Ultimate Space Commando
Indie Spotlight: Ultimate Space Commando
Developer	Creatio 49	Publisher	Angry Cat Ltd.
Release Date	13 May, 2015	Genre	Indie, RPG, Strategy, Turn-based Tactics
Official Website	Twitter	Facebook	Steam
STEAMIFIED IN A NUTSHELL
Ultimate Space Commando marks the Steam debut of Creatio 49. It’s a turn-based tactics game that has been set in the era of early interstellar colonization. You’re looking at a small indie team’s attempt to enter the same genre as the XCOM franchise among others. Somewhat surprisingly their take on the genre is more polished and enjoyable than I thought that it was going to be. Similar to other games within the genre, players have the opportunity to customize four-troop squads with weapons, ammunition and tools. While the core of the gameplay is turn-based there is a well implemented RPG-style management system.
There is a lengthy campaign mode which I have yet to complete but I can tell you that it is immersive and is soundly designed. The basis of the campaign is controlling the fate of the crew of the U.S.C. ship Wraith which is a recon vessel stranded on an isolated mining planet. It’s your a typical first contact scenario that, of course, poses the greatest risk to the survival of humanity. There are over thirty missions – of varying length – within the campaign – so to suggest that there are many hours worth of content within the campaign alone would be considered an understatement.
A fantastic touch by the developers was making the combat environment fully interactive. What this feature actually does is enable a superior level of strategy than would otherwise be possible. The interactive environments work hand in hand with the deep combat mechanics and squad management tools. Incorporated into the combat system are four statistics that are all of significant importance – health, morale, action points and armor as well as nine attributes that have essentially been stripped from an RPG game. The amount of weapon types (18) and gadgets (30+) help make the game one of the deepest strategy games that I’ve ever played. It all works exceedingly well and although it may lack the polish of an XCOM it is well and truly worth your time if you are in any way enamored with the genre. If you’re not then the earlier levels will serve as a great learning tool for the game.
Of course, there are further game modes beyond the campaign including defend the base and an almost limitless single mission structure where the size of the map, difficulty, player handicaps, the objectives and more are all able to be customized. My personal favorite game mode, even ranking it ahead of the great campaign, is the defend the base mode. In this mode you have to build your base while incorporating resource management and survive wave after wave of alien attacks.
There are trading cards to be harvested and multiplayer availability. Unfortunately the developers are yet to incorporate Steam achievements into their game but their definitely is the potential of them being added. In regards to the multiplayer game there was a season one competitive mode. Season two is being planned but the developers are hoping to get a larger player base so that they can make that even more challenging and engaging than the exciting first season. I’m certain that Lt. Commander Bozdo will be back to defend his crown.
Ultimate Space Commander is one of the deepest games that we’ve covered to date. I’m certain that I’ve only just scratched the surface of what is available to players and as such Steamified wholeheartedly recommends it.

You can read a compared review with Templar Battleforce here
The single player campaign is about an elite commando-like group of soldiers, stranded in space after a ship breakage, and having to confront an horde of aliens that have taken over the planet on which the ship crashed. The goal, or at least the intention, is to get back to civilization safe and sound. Dialogue mostly happens at the beginning of missions, and is of little importance. 5/10
There are also alternative game modes (defend the base/play random map) the can be played on co-op. The campaign itself is around 30h or more, the replay value is also quite good. 7/10
There aren't different classes, but different ranks based on the experience level. You gain more experience on the field, depending on inflicted damage, and special actions, such as hacking secure doors, closing hatches, etc. When soldiers gain a level of experience, they get skill points to distribute on a number of skills (melee/small arms/heavy weapons, reaction, engineering, biochemistry and all sorts of skills you can expect in a turn based game). Different soldiers have also a specialization, that makes them better in a certain role. New equipment is salvaged from the field, including blueprints for new kinds of ammo, new weapons, new gear or special weapon prototypes. Moreover, on the field you'll be able to salvage special components used to craft prototypes or other gear. This feature is slightly annoying because you have to manually pick everything up, it get tedious especially for screws and other crafting material. Another aspect to ponder is that the gear found on the field can be extremely random. In my first playthrough, I found the automated turret (a very powerful piece of equipment) near the end of the campaign, while in my second run I found it in the second mission. There's a good variety of weapons and ammo types. 7/10
The combat system is indeed the core of the game. The most peculiar aspect is that all weapons have distinct fire modes, that in turn may have different firing patterns (for example 'star' means cardinal direction plus diagonals, 'free' can reach any square that isn't blocked etc.) and different area of effect (single square, 3x3, 5x5, along a line etc.). I was sceptical at first because I wanted to be able to shoot everywhere my line of sight allowed me to, but after a while I can say it's a very good system, it makes all weapons uique and soldiers with different weapons will have to cover different roles. There's also a wide range of ammunition calibres and types (incendiary, armor piercing, marker tranquilizing, etc). You'll often find ammo crates or kerosene barrels, that can catch fire and explode. Morale plays also a big role, there's a morale requirement for anything that isn't shooting (moving, using items, entering defend mode, etc.)
Many lesser aliens leave on death a radioactive substance that will poison you if you enter a square covered with it (you can clear it with fire or moving a crate over the said square). And fire, that can damage you and the aliens. Pathfinding is quite good, dangerous square (with fire or radiation) will be avoided by default, and the UI will warn you if you will take damage in your chosen path.
Another big plus is that there is a real lighting system: aliens in the dark, when they can be seen, are more difficult to hit. Later in the game, a kind of alien appears that projects darkness all around itself, making it and the nearby aliens much more difficult to hit (there's a pistol that can shoot flare ammunition).
Most missions are of the 'seek and destroy' type, only a few have some more interesting goal. 9/10
Graphics are in pure 2D, the alien sprites and the backgrounds are well drawn, your soldiers not as much. Animations are non-existent, except for explosions. The music of the main menu sets the right atmosphere, but the in-game music does everything it can to ruin it. Sound effects on the other hand are very good, again with the exception of the voices of your soldiers when they're wounded. 5/10
Very old-fashioned. There is a total lack of tool-tips, and the tutorial doesn't help you much to understand it. There's no way to know if an alien has been poisoned or suffers damage over time, or its armor. Sometimes you can read its hit points (probably skill-related). There are also some 'undocumented' features, by pure chance I discovered I could split stacks in my inventory right-clicking on an empty square. On the plus side, all keys are customizable. After you get used to it, it's all right, but a less wordy and more to-the-point tutorial would help you understand it better. 5/10
The basic enemy types are not plentiful, but each of them can be seen in a lot of varieties. Some of them may have increased armor, health, action points, life stealing attacks, explode after death and other attributes. They are named in a way that remembers Tales of Maj'Eyal. Interestingly, the most powerful aliens will have their turn split in two phases, the second of which is processed after all other aliens have moved. 6/10
Pretty much everything on the field is destructible, you can also pull or push crates or barrels around to raise a barricade or to clear radiation. You can pick objects from the ground, or pass them from soldier to soldier. I've already mentioned the lighting system. Definitely one of the strong points of the game. 8/10
Immersion isn't too good, mostly because of the lacking music and the thin background story. Also, it takes some time to get used to the interface, the firing patterns and the various gameplay elements. The developer has a sympathy for ducks, and in the maps you'll find some 'vendor machines' that can boost your health, action points or morale. This can take away a bit of the 'seriousness' and/or the immersion, depending on your tastes, but I can't say it bothered me. Could be better, but not too important. 6/10
Unfortunately it hasn't been a bug-free experience for me. There are some CTDs, luckily harmless because the games always saves before crashing. I suggest you don't use the abort/redo mission feature, because it gave me some nuisances. Only start a mission when you're ready. The developer is present in the forum if you need help, but some bugs still have to be fixed. 5/10
It takes time to appreciate it. Very challenging at the highest difficulty setting, there are some multiplayer options (that I didn't test) for those who look for some online co-op fun. I have the impression that a game/campaign editor would greatly benefit the game, but at this time there is none. Rather uneven in its delivery, but tactical combat is definitely brilliant. The price is probably excessive at 20$, maybe reflecting the fact that it's a one-man (woman) project that has been in development for some years. Because of there rare but annoying bugs, you'll also need to be more patient than usual.

Clearly the Dev has put alot of time and thought into this, it very much feels like the product of one persons imagination. While I found the controls a bit wonky and the menus are complex I felt it was worth the learning curve, it has an old-school approach and a ton of detail. The writing is quite good and the story and universe are well crafted and felt real and lived-in. This is not for the casual gamer, it throws you in the deep end and the tutorials such as they are are minimal. No hand holding, no quest markers to follow. I died many times learning to play the game but each time was entirely unique and entertaining, seeing an alien armada warp in and pursue my tiny ship with laser cannons, missiles and drones screaming after me had me laughing through the frustration "I'm just trying to mine a few asteroids! What did I do to incur the wrath of your trading dynasty!?" Sometimes it is a little rough around the edges, there will be bugs but the Dev is very responsive and puts in a lot of work hunting them down and smashing them, great to see someone truly commited to the game they've built.  Lots to do and explore and a compelling and complex story/enviroment, it feels like a labor of love and those that remember the early days of PC gaming when one person/a small team could create a world of their own will find much to enjoy here. It has a punky underdog spirit that is all too rare today even from the likes of many "indie" developers, reminds me a bit of Heavy Metal the movie. Put some Hawkwind on the stereo, crank up the volume and fire up your engines!

This is what I would call a very good turn-based tactical sci-fi squad combat CRPG.
There's a fair amount to absorb at first, and when I first saw the battle maps it took a while to absorb, but it soon became natural and made sense. The combat similarly seemed very chaotic at first (especially when I jumped right into a one-off single mission with hordes of weird aliens - I tried to hide in my elevator but they started eating through the walls and electrocuting me and who knows what. But then I started the campaign and tutorial scenario and it was nice and slow and full of skippable explanations and things made sense from there out. Now there is still often all sorts of chaos, but it makes sense and I get what's going on even when monsters are eating through nearby walls and chain reactions of fuel and ammunition are ripping through a base and setting monsters on fire who go running away while other types come creeping in, etc...
It has most of the things I want in such a game, including many that are fairly hard to find all in one game:
* A campaign where you can manage your squad, trying to keep them alive through many battles, see them improve through experience and adjust their equipment and so on.
* Enough challenge and risk and permadeath, and no expectation to savescum/replay when things go wrong.
* More or less fully destructable environment, where missed shots and violence damage everything - walls and doors and objects, accidental "friendly" fire, etc.
* Tactics that mostly make sense and arise naturally from simulating the situation in ways that mostly make sense, with overwatch, use of cover and doors, a variety of weapon effects and skills, etc.
* Interesting, meaningful, and logical choices both at the tactical level and between missions.
* Freedom to try various approaches, as far as weapons and tactics, but also taking time to rest and repair at the risk the aliens will come after your base, etc.
* In the campaign, you manage 16 men but only use one or two squads per mission, so you can choose who to send on attacks, who to leave behind resting or doing repairs, and whether to try to get experience for the greener people or not.
* Nice relative absence of contrived scenarios and hoops to jump through, compared to some games. More of a chaotic simulation feel, which I like, though also with a fun/gamey/dark-humorous flavor.
* Details of ammo/equipment management, but not too much.
One great thing I didn't expect is the Defend The Base mode, which lets you set up a base and try to defend it against increasingly stronger waves of aliens, with damage details (including spilled fuel and acid and so on) being carried over, and limited resources to repair or re-arrange things, and an option to retreat rather than hold once the position seems untennable. Nice!
Also, the game is still in development and the developer is listening and adding some things that players have asked for, which is awesome, and in my very long experience with games, is what makes for the best games. For example, one thing that was jarring to me was the firing arcs of some weapons, which were limited during one's own turn to firing along straight or diagonal grid lines, which the developer had an interesting intention for doing, but which seemed unnatural to me (in contrast to the way most of the rest of the game works in ways I would expect, in nice detail, in fact). Turns out in response to player comments, they are working for an option to not do that, for players who don't want it, which may be in the next patch. Sweet!
I have a few gripes but nothing major. The odd firing arcs of some weapons was probably my biggest nitpick. The looting and inventory manipulation can be a bit fiddly but it hasn't bothered me too much yet, and I quite appreciate all the detail and choices. I could even wish it were more fiddly, as I find the recycler and manufacturing of new items during the campaign is very generous and I'd be interested to have to make do more with what I find. (Though without the recycler/manufacturer the lack of storage slots would become an issue.) Mainly I'd just like more of the same. I expect I will eventually have had enough for a while and wish for another campaign, but for now I'm happily hooked.
Anyway, I quite recommend Ultimate Space Commando!

Pros:
Meaty, non-casual, action-point based combat like the orig X-com.  The tension and onslaught of Space Hulk, where campaign ending death can occur at any moment.
Rogue-like randomisation, permadeath, one-save, possible to make campaign ending mistakes both tactically and strategically.
Oldschool difficulty.  Normal is hard, hard is Ninja Gaiden/Battletoads sewer difficulty.
Tons of items.  Random unique shiny loot.  Melee weapons.  Lasers, flamethrowers, tranquilizers, rocket launchers, miniguns, and everythig else under the sun.  Each weapon has multiple attack modes, mods, and different types of ammo.  Will you survive long enough to make use of any of it?
Helpful, responsive developer.
Cons:
Tedious, at times infuriating looting system that trolls you and can cause campaign restarts.  Your commandos only have 9 slots, most of which will be filled with essential items, which means you'll spend a lot of time micromanaging inventory space to pick up loot after battle.  Missions will abruptly end before you can reclaim deployed equipment/pick up loot.  I'd kill for an option just to have all discovered/deployed items on the floor automatically looted after a successful mission.. it's all just unnecessary downtime that gets in the way of the tense combat .
Weird, arbitrary firing angle rules on the majority of weapons/firing modes, limiting your shots  to UDLR and diagonals. Granted a token few are simply LOS, but the vast majority use the "star" aiming system.  Overwatch/defend mode and monsters completely ignore these limitations.
The visuals are what you'd expect from a one-person project, but combat/gameplay trumps everything.. and USC has damn good combat.  This is clearly a work of love for the genre.
Gameplay 8.5  (9 if the looting/inventory system is ever improved)
Visuals 6.5  (needs more alien variation/tilesets)
Developer 10

I've been playing USC since Beta and I find it a very complex, elaborated and pleasantly old-school game. My favourite modes are "Single Mission" and "Defend the Base!", because my team can do very well and I can play with it in both modes.  I'm very excited for my team to survive especially when a Wunderwurm attacks us.
And you can distribute skill points to set up your units for different roles (medic, heavy, technician, etc.). You have certain amount of credits, which sometimes makes it a challenge to buy everything you need, but this also makes the game very exciting.
In "Defend the Base!" mode you have to make sure that you use everything you can, because each wave is stronger and stronger (e.g. having turrets is very useful). It is also very good that you can repair your base and build new rooms or walls - between the waves.
I recommend this game for everyone who likes complex tactics with a lot of possibilities and high stakes (and being bullied by a worm, after you survived dozens of reapers).

First I have to say that I really want to like the game. And I certainly want to support the developer. But I make the review for customers like me.
Its really hard to find a game to compare Ceres with. According to the developer it has been inspired by Homeworld. But in Homeworld you just do one fixed mission after the other. In Ceres you have a whole solar system to explore. So its like a mix of Homeworld and Nexus: The Jupiter Incident and a touch of Eve-Online in an Open-World setting. While this is in principle a good thing the execution lacks some basic things which make the game pretty hard to play (at least from my point of view).
I did the tutorial and double clicked on the instrucotrs ship as it requested from me and my ship launched some missiles. The instructor fired back and my "mission" was over. I left the game frustrated for some weeks and came back. Tried the tutorial again. Got stuck somewhere and left again. Tried 3rd time after some weeks and it hung somewhere but I could solve it in the end. So from my point of view the tutorial leaves much to be desired.
Then I tried a normal game. There was a large "level" with coulds, asteroids and stuff. I killed some pirates with my starter ship and followed the mission. After finding a destroyed station I tried to approach it to make the requested scan. The ship flew 3 times around it, collided with an asteroid nearby and it took some minutes until I was finally in the right position to do the scan. Did not know how to proceed so I decided to investigate the wormhole nearby. Accidentally double clicked it and my missiles started to attack it (a wormhole!). When I came close 4 alien ships appeared and quickily ended me.
So you see this game is a bit rough around the edges. Especially the user interface is one of the worst I have seen in a game so far (and I have seen alot).
The controls are unresponsive (giving a flight direction with double right click works 1 out of 10 times).
There is no information about your targets (health bar, faction etc.). So you don't know who you shoot at and why.
I would have liked a list of points of interest (missions, discoveries) where i could quickly navigate to without searching 3d space.
I had no clue how many loot is there to collect by the drones.
I have not tried fleet command since I just had the starter ship but when I can hardly tell one ship what to do how am I supposed to control several of them?
I had never the feeling I know what I do, it was more like try this and that. So I was simply lost in the complexity and had no real guidance.
I'm sure when one learns the ropes and quirks of the game it is fun and interesting. But a game must be accessible from the beginning to investigate the player with it. When it "prevents" the player from playing it does not a good job. I don't know if its just me and wether I'm "spoiled" by easier games or plain silly. But I could not grasp the game to a level where I could be confident with playing and enjoy it. I just fought the UI and thats sad for me. Because I think its a pearl of a game just unecessarily difficult to control and to get into.
So if you are a fan of spacegames or you like to figure things out and can handle a hard UI you should give it a try. But I think most people will be frustrated with the game. Thus a negative review albeit I really like the concept.
Note: I play Steam in offline mode and thus my time played displayed is wrong (it seems to count only when online). I should have played around 4 hours now.

Startide is a strangely boring shoot-'em-up, strongly reminiscent of the 2003 freeware title Warning Forever mechanically but much slower-paced, to its detriment. Essentially the entire game is fighting bosses by destroying them part-by-part from the extremities inward, since only the outermost parts on a limb take any damage, with the scaling falling off such that hitting any part other than the two outermost is almost worthless.
So, it's all about slowly circling enemies, minimizing the amount of hits you take, and slowly wearing them down. Of course, with a system where you both regenerate health and destroy the boss's weapons as you fight, this means that essentially all stages get easier as they go on, which contributes to the tedious feeling. Likewise, there's not all that much difference between stages - some will have time limits, and some will have breaks for asteroid fields (which are to your advantage, since you regenerate health and super bar during this time), and as you go on you fight five different alien races, three of which have their own gimmicks, two of which matter - except for stages where you are attacking supply trains, which are similar (you still destroy armed parts coming off the train, from the outside in, then destroy the "core" that contains the supplies) but involve different enough mechanics that they at least feel like something different.
Startide is also not free of minor issues that I felt dragged the game down. The biggest one is that I felt the 4th alien race was the hardest to fight by far, which made the entire end of the game where you fought the 5th race feel very anticlimactic. Another is that, instead of getting notably harder (except when you fight the 4th race) or more interesting, stages just require you to fight more bosses in a row, which increases both the likelihood that you'll mess up and die sometime during them, and makes you have to replay even more when you die. The least and silliest gripe is that the game gave me a giant laser cannon with only one fight left before the rest of the game was fighting the 5th race, and due to how the mechanics interact, the giant laser cannon is useless against the 5th and final race of aliens.
Ultimately, I don't think I was expecting tedium from a shoot-'em-up. It's a genre with quite a few bad entries, but few boring ones, but Startide somehow managed to be. Check out Warning Forever instead, it's a significantly more fun freeware take on many of the same ideas.
(Postscript: Startide has a workshop functionality, but I felt it was somewhat limited in terms of being able to create interesting things due to fairly low "cost" limits, hopelessly degenerate designs like my Invincible are quite possible, and there's no real ship design community for the game. It's at least fairly easy to use, but I didn't think it was notable in any way.)

As a player of these supposedly 'casual' games for some years, I was initially tricked by the visuals into thinking - "Uh oh, another Flight Control HD/Airport Madness spin-off". One word: wrong.
Yes, the Dev was kind enough to provide a free key but I write only objective reviews, and don't mind flying in the face of public opinion (pardon the pun). If there's a kink, I'll mention it.
Just a word on the visuals and how they may trick - this is not "Flight Control HD". Far from it. In fact this has more in common with "Airport Control Simulator" than the aforementioned casual and a little zany title. In fact "Miniature Golf Course HD" has more in common with "FC HD".
You begin with three tutorials, that are over far too quickly if, like me, you are slow and steady. They set you up with your basic flight and control rules and basically boot you out the door while you're still attaching your flight controller badge, wondering where you left your headset. By the fifth mission, it really is sink and swim.
So what is this game? I mentioned "Airport Control Simulator" which is a top-down flight control game, using real earth images for the maps. You control incoming aircraft coming in to land, as you do with "Airport Madness" and "Flight Control HD". Where this is more like "ACS" is that you control the speed of the aircraft, but not the height that you do in "ACS". In "Flight Control HD" you may do endless loops to slow down or 'park' aircraft in holding patters, but with "Land It!" you alter the speed by stretching the arrow leading from the plane. This affects turning circles, travelling times, and flight plans. The longer the lead you give your arrow, the faster you go in other words, the wiser your turning circle...makes sense. Easy, right....?
Nope! For a start, this is not just a "landing" game. You also control take-off and egress on some maps - no landing at all. Here, it is similar to "Airport Madness" in that you decide when to let the aircraft take off, but beware. Unlike in "Flight Control HD", "Airport Control Simulator and "Airport Madness" you are not just attempting to avoid mid-air collisions with your own controllable inbounds.
No sir!
No, here you have No-Fly Zones (over airports and taxiways) where if you stray into one you have seconds to get out and air lanes with constantly flowing traffic out of your control.
You must seamlessly merge into these flight paths, gingerly altering your lead arrow (IAS) to navigate your flightpath safely into the air lanes just ahead of, or behind NPC aircraft, matching or increasing your speed to keep a safe distance. Trouble is, speeding up will change your turn angle and instead of egressing safely off the map you might find yourself juggling your aircraft's flight path/speed to keep clear of No Fly Zones while still keeping a safe spacing between NPC traffic. It is not easy.
NOW - multiply that by 4-5 aircraft under your control. Getting the picture?
The visuals are excellent: crisp, colourful and with a depth of detail not usually seen in these small titles. Love is in this game, and it's obvious. Sound is not the tinkle, tankle you get in "Flight Control HD", where you'd swear your cutlery drawer fell when planes collide. Here you get red visuals and a "BOOM!" to go with it. There's nothing funny in a mid-air collision.
"Land It!" sticks to the overhead view, which works best in these games. Whereas "Airport Madness" has been fun I think they've over-reached with their latest title "AM 3D", and I find the myriad views are useless as an impending collision doesn't draw your attention, if say in Control Tower view. A "Snap-to" camera would work, or an alert...but these are not to be, so despite the flashy new camera angles you'll end up flying in isometric all the time just to pass each map.
Here, "And It!" sticks with the tried and true and the Dev has thrown his resources into the design and pace of the maps.
I haven't played more than a  few maps past the tutorials, and will adjust my review as time goes on but a word on Difficulty.
This is NOT a casual game unless you have the hand-eye coordination of a fighter pilot. I think a "Casual" setting should be just that. The tutorials are paced well, but after that it's the Deep End....and I dog-paddle.
7/10
