ARENA GODS:
~~~~~~~~~~~
One of the most deadly games ever invented by humans was officially recorded in 264 BC. And yes, you guessed it . . .  it’s the Gladiator Games. The interesting point is some of them actually volunteer to become swordsmen in order to rise to fame and improve their social standing within the state of Rome. But most of the so-called Gladiators were prisoners of war, thieves and slaves. They were trained under harsh conditions in secluded Gladiator schools until they were ready to walk into the Arena for the first, and for a large number of them, the last time. Now, are you going to be our next champion and crowd favourite, and even become a god of the Roman people? That is, if you can survive long enough in Arena Gods!
ARENA GODS is a top down local multiplayer game where you take control of one of four colourful gladiators and aim to be the last man alive in the arena. At the time I write this review, this game is currently under development and listed as an Early Access Game.
Right now, you can play against three of your friends, or against bots. Your goal is to become the last man standing for three rounds to win the contest. As you face three other opponents there is the possibility for you to play up to nine rounds (assuming that each gladiator won two rounds each) before winning the contest.
The game play is pretty simple; competitive, brutal and so much fun! Within the arena, you have four large tiles with circles on them, and several smaller tiles with hexagon motifs on them, scatted around the arena. The gladiators will enter the Lion den via the large tiles at the same time, with bare hands and a helmet. During the fights, about every fifteen seconds or so, one of the hexagon symbols on one of the smaller tiles will glow white and a chest will appear. Hover your character over the chest to discover which weapon it holds. You will have to grab the weapon first by using one of the buttons on your gamepad or keyboard to acquire it. You’ll be able to swing or even throw it to your opponent for the kill. However, you haven’t managed to pick up a weapon, your fist will be doing the talking. Try to get your adversaries on the ground face down, jump on him and his day will be over soon. If you character is the one who is kissing the ground, you might be able to avoid your enemy before he is on top of you and beating you to a pulp!
The game looks ok in regards to the graphics, and the controls are pretty good too. So far, I am enjoying the game. The content is fairly small right now as you have just a few arenas to play in and no character customizations. The good news is that the developers are working on more content in regards to the arena and might even consider an online mode, too.

The good:
- System Designs are well thought out, robust, and add depth to the game.
- Concept is great: Squad/Small Fleet in space (been waiting for something like this for awhile).
The bad:
- The art style falls into that awkward category of games that look old but don't pull it off in some charming way.
- Character portraits look like they were made in EVE Online in 2003.
- It's difficult to get into without going through the tutorial which is bland and more or less like reading a manual.
The ugly:
- Precise navigation feels impossible. I can only guess I'm doing something wrong, whether in map mode or in 3d space, I can't seem to get my ships to arrive at the right x,y,z coordinates without major headaches.
- Interaction with objects is difficult as well. Non-ship interactible objects seem to be the worst offenders.
- NPC Ships can (and will) follow you across the map. While I don't generally mind that idea, it only leads to frustration. One time I was trying to read quest text, and a bunch of little drones were swarming me, so I bolted away, then started reading the text again. They followed and blew me up. Several hours lost since my previous auto save. Another time I had traveled to the main space station. I was docked with it, changing loadouts when I was attacked and destroyed by... Well I have no idea what it was, but it wasn't fun.
Final thoughts:
- I'd be more excited about the game if it were early access so the "ugly" issues could get addressed, I don't feel this game reached the quality level that you would expect for an actually released title. (indy or not)
- If you can get over the old-style art and initial learning curve, there could be dozens of hours of fun.
- If the game were $10 I'd probably give it a thumbs up, but only for those who are system design nerds and/or are into sci-fi ship management.

Even though wondering "What if?" has always been a popular pastime for armchair generals, Paradox Interactive has stayed away from speculation. Franchises such as Europa Universalis and Hearts of Iron feature authenticity so precise that you often feel like you're paging through a textbook. Playing geopolitical sims such as these should earn you credit toward a BA in History due to such a rigid "just the facts, ma'am" design philosophy.
Until now, that is. Doomsday, a stand-alone expansion for World War II uber-simulation Hearts of Iron II, takes Paradox into the world of alternative history for the first time. And it succeeds in a big way, thanks to the seamless transition from a realistic depiction of the conflict between the Allies and the Axis to an imaginative look at how the tense early years of the Cold War could have unfolded. Gameplay feels too familiar to be entirely pleasing, especially if you've spent much of the past year running roughshod over Hitler or slapping around Stalin in the compulsively playable (well, once you ascended past the cliff-like learning curve) original game. But if you're looking for more of the same, this is a winning approach.
There aren't any surprises here. The look and feel of the expansion match the original game right down to the shrill musical score and the lame fixed resolution of 1024x768. Doomsday is a standard expansion with fairly standard accoutrements. It includes a new campaign, along with odds and ends such as updated units, a US/USSR invasion-of-Japan scenario (although it must be said that the Soviets don't seem to help all that much), and a scenario editor. The centerpiece is a revamped grand campaign that lets you set a starting point between 1936 and 1945, and play to January 1, 1954. Choose to start with the Doomsday scenario in October, 1945, and you come onboard as the Allies are forced to defend Western Europe against the swarming Red Army by nuking Moscow. Nothing like getting things going with a bang.
Moving the finish line into the 1950s redresses a problem with Hearts of Iron II. Earlier, campaigns ended abruptly too often. You'd be right in the middle of a big push into France or on the verge of finally deploying the A-bomb, and the game would wrap at the end of 1946 with a dissatisfying tallying of victory points. Wins seemed cheap at times, and losing could be really aggravating, particularly when the calendar, not the enemy, cut off your grand plan for world domination.
Games still end a little brusquely; New Year's Day in 1954 arrives all too soon. But the additional years typically provide enough time to bring the cataclysmic war in Western Europe to a gratifying climax. There isn't quite enough time to wrap things up on a global scale, however. You get a sense of the Cold War's early tension as the race to develop nuclear weapons heats up through the later 1940s and early 1950s, although games usually seem to end before a nation emerges as the clear winner or has at least thoroughly nuked rivals into the Stone Age. Even though an extra few years would have been nice, you don't find yourself thinking "I wonder what would happen six months from now?" nearly as much as before at the end of campaigns.
The additional seven years tacked on to Doomsday are tricked out with enough new units to enhance the feel that you're not quite playing Hearts of Iron II. Much of the advanced military hardware that characterized the Cold War is on offer here, including attack helicopters, nuclear submarines, H-bombs, ICBMs, surface-to-air missiles, advanced rocketry, jet aircraft, and so forth. If you could build it in the real world in the late 1940s and early 1950s, chances are you can research and build it here.
All of the new hardware is overshadowed by the mad rush to split the atom and build an arsenal of nukes, though. Just as in the real Cold War, nuclear power dominates the scene no matter how much in-game alliances and events differ from those in the history books. That said, it's not easy to go all Dr. Strangelove. You need to put serious effort into tech to develop the H-bomb and the ICBMs required to deliver it to enemy cities, and that can be nearly impossible while a conventional war is ravaging Europe and Asia.
Spend too much time on tech and not enough on production while guiding an Allied power such as the US or UK, and the massive Red Army could soon march into Paris. Conversely, while the Soviets can bypass production due to numerical superiority as the campaign gets started, they begin without nuclear technology and must race to acquire it before the clock runs out in 1953. In short, everything is balanced, and there are no simple answers to tactical questions.
Intelligence further adds to the Cold War atmosphere. Oddly omitted from the original Hearts of Iron II, spies play a huge role here. They are crucial when it comes to the nuclear race, as well-placed agents can steal the technology needed to provide an atomic edge. Spies are particularly vital for the Soviets, who need to deploy them to catch up with the Allied ability to make enemy cities glow in the dark.
But espionage isn't easy. Agents actively trying to steal tech, foment rebellion, sabotage industries, or assassinate enemy ministers are at great risk of being detected. The artificial intelligence does an impressive job picking off spies, so it is very difficult to play Julius and Ethel Rosenberg and gather information effectively. Spies can be sent in as sleepers in deep cover, but this limits the information provided, makes intel unreliable (an overrun Berlin taught us not to rely on sleeper intelligence about Soviet armor), and prevents you from pulling off major missions such as swiping tech blueprints.
Basically, if you want more Hearts of Iron II, Doomsday is a great bet. It feels a bit too much like its big brother, but all of the speculative history, nuclear tension, and Cold War spice make it a great addition to Paradox's stable of strategy games. It's also a great bargain when you consider the sheer amount of game you get here for less than $20 and the extra hours you'll get out of what modders will undoubtedly create with the scenario editor.

総評 : 課金モバイルゲー臭がする有料ゲーム
TLDR; Paid game with a feeling of "a Pay to Win mobile game". (English review on bottom)
マッチ3にクラフト要素があるというのを聞いて購入したが、以下の点で「本来これはモバイルでF2P(P2W)形式にするつもりだったのか」と思えて仕方がなかった。
・アイテムのクラフト回数は有限。その回数を補充するには盾を500個消す必要がある(3個マッチのみで計算すると170マッチ近く)。
・クラフト素材自体はマッチ３でランダム入手。土タイルや砂タイルを掘ったり、宝箱を開けたりすると手に入る。いわば運ゲー。
・馬にはヘルスとスタミナがあり、ヘルスはエサを与える(１回ごとに食料を大量に消費)、スタミナはクラフト品を渡すことで補充する。前述の「有限クラフト」と馬の健康度ボーナス(両方が高いと+10手、両方が低いと-10手)との相性が悪い。
・どうみても課金通貨にしか見えない「ゴールド」でキーを買わないと「完全クリア」メダルがもらえない。ゴールドの入手はすさまじい量の資源と交換するかクラフトするのが主だろうがその入手量は需要(キー購入以外にも消耗品補充、復活の羽の購入、スロットのコイン追加購入など)と比べるとはるかに少ない。
・「デイリーログインボーナス」や「３０分で１回復するライフ(最大５つ、リトライ時に消費)」というモバイルゲームお約束の仕様。
・スロットマシンが運ゲーにさらに拍車をかけている。３つ絵柄がそろう気がしない。
マッチ３自体は比較的オーソドックスだが、次の問題点があるため難易度は高め。手数の問題はリラックスモードで遊べばオフにはなるが、オンでプレイしたときの意見をあげる。
・手数が200近く与えられるステージもあるが、多くのステージは複数の盤面にわたって繰り広げられることが多いため「１盤面を３０手ぐらいでクリアしないと無理」というバランス。
・マッチ３ゲームではよくある「シャッフル」が手詰まり時以外で行われない上にヒント表示が遅いため、次の一手がわかりにくい時のストレスに悩まされる。
・パワーアップは「3x3爆破」、「３～４つのブロックを選んで破壊」、「残り手数+20」、「1種のブロックを全消滅」、「盤面にある氷・鎖・箱・土をランダムに現在の50%分吹き飛ばす」、「隣接する同種のタイルかお邪魔ブロックを破壊」といった基本的なものばかりだが、補充はポーションを500個消す必要がある。切らした時に限り、ゴールドを支払うことで補充できる。
・4つ消し/5つ消しで作られる爆弾は初動(1コンボ目)でしか作られず、落下コンボでできた４つ(以上)消しでは爆弾ができない。また、爆弾同士をスワップすることで列爆破も行えるがこれも機会が限られすぎていて扱いに悩まされるし、手数の無駄になりうることもある。そもそも盤面が小さすぎて爆弾を作る余裕もないことも多い。
・画面の上側にある順番どおりにスワップ＋マッチすることで資源を追加で得られるが、手数の少なすぎるこのゲームではそんなことをしている余裕はない。
・手数が少なすぎるためステージ評価の3つ星は案外難しく、メダルは「完全制覇」が条件で、「金銀の宝箱を全オープン」「土/砂タイルを全部取り除く」「資源置き場をすべて枯渇させる」「箱をすべて破壊する」となる。前述の「ゴールドがないと金箱が開けられない」問題や、とても少ない手数とコンボ仕様の厳しさからメダル取得は難しい一方で、ステージ進行にはメダル取得が必須である。
・暗い洞窟を掘って最下層の花を取りに行く面はむしろ手数が多過ぎる。完全に見えない場所でもスワップ対象として扱われるため、光源アップグレードのそろってない序盤では「見える範囲でマッチがなくてもシャッフルされない」のは大問題。
完全に「有料の買いきりで出す」つもりで設計していれば面白いゲームになり得たのだが、中途半端にモバイルゲームの要素を入れたまま課金要素をインゲーム資源に置き換えただけという印象を感じざるを得ない内容かつ、その課金要素(になるはず)であるキーの購入やパワーアップ連発によるゲームプレイはとてもスマートとはいい難い。
------------------------------
I bought the game as I saw a charm with a combination of Match 3 and Crafting, but this game had a feeling of "Supposed to be Freemium but decided to make it a paid game":
- You have limited *times* of crafting, and you need to match and remove 500 Shield tiles to recover one attempt.
- Craft materials are obtained from uncovering dirt/sand tiles or opening chests, but the contents are completely random.
- Your horse has Health and Stamina; feed horses(lots of Foods are used in each process) to recover Health, and use crafted items to recover Stamina. This is a HORRIBLE combination with the forementioned "limited crafting". If you neglect your horse's condition, you get moves penalty or you'll have to spend phoenix feathers.
- GOLD CURRENCY. This obviously look like a paid currency and you must use them to purchase keys for getting Medals(which you receive on 100%'ing a level). Instead of paying real money, you'll have to spend TONS of resources or craft materials to get Gold. Of course, you'll be spending much more Gold than you earn them.
- "Daily Login Bonus" and "Lives that regenerates over time". Only mobile games and online games have them.
- Slot Machines add another layer to "game of pure luck". Give us the exact chance to win ANY matches, and show what each matches will give.
Match-3 part is quite orthodox, but it's generally hard for these problems.
(The moves problem can be ignored with Relaxed mode, but I turned that off) :
- Sometimes you get 200+ moves, but most levels consist of multiple boards, so basically you'll have to solve each boards within 30 moves or so.
- Shuffle is only available when you have no more moves. Other Match-3 games usually let you use it every few minutes.
- The "hint" that appears when you don't make a move for few seconds, takes too much time.
- Powerups are quite common, but you need to match and remove 500 potions to get one. You can pay Gold to buy powerups if you run out of them.(P2W, huh?)
- The bonus bombs on removing 4 or 5 tiles can only be created in first move, unlike other Match-3s where you can get them from combos. Swap two bombs for bigger explosion, but it's much harder to actually do so and there won't be much space to make multiple bombs.
- You can get bonus resources if you swap & match in certian order(shown on the top of screen), though it's nothing but a waste of moves.
- Getting 3-star gets difficult due to very low moves, and Medals require 100%'ing the boards(Open all chests, remove dirt/sand tiles, deplete all resource stockpiles, destroy all crates). This means YOU MUST PAY GOLD TO GET MEDALS, because Gold Chests are also counted for the Medal.
- As for Stars and Medals, you will NEED them to progress.
- The cave levels have TOO MUCH moves available. And in earlier level without light radius upgrades, it irritated me often when I don't "see" any matchable blocks, but the game knows there are matchable blocks IN THE DARKNESS.
The game has potential and could've been great if it focused on "pay for the package, and everything else is free, no currencies ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t".
I can't really understand why they made decisions to make the game less engaging, by adding lots of "Gold contents" that basically slows game down, and ignoring the standards of Match-3 games(such as bombs creation in combos and shuffles).
Good game.

First, I am not a full-time gamer.  Although I have logged a few thousand hours between this game, and a couple others.  You won’t see my play time in winning putt on steam as I log in from BN’s website directly due to the fact that the steam login messes with my screens.
Having said that, as a non-gamer, I have the new player perspective of reviewing games.  i.e. ease of use, player interaction with the game and so on.
Before settling on Winning putt, I played and reviewed most of the top golf games and although I found a couple good ones, this was by far my top pick.
This is a great game with lots of issues that may or may not ever get resolved.  The logistics of this game make it difficult to imagine that things will ever work perfectly.  {but what in life ever does right lol} It's a hate-love relationship between the players and the BN teams.  At the very least, you can have lots of fun with it without ever spending a single cent.  But if you have the disposable income to spend some cash in this game, it’s much more fun to play as you can buy and craft game items that will enhance your toons play.
Another nice feature is you can also chat and play with folks from around the globe making new friends.  There is no pressure to do any task. Anything you play will build up your level and that will improve your abilities. There are tons on missions that will challenge you.
The sad part of this game is the complainers.  No, not just people voicing their issues, the people who will always find something about this game to be unhappy about.  It's not a perfect game but then what game is.  There is lots the company could change and plenty they have changed but it's free so you don't have to spend any money.  It’s up to the individual.
I would suggest starting slow and playing until you get your toon up to a level where you really understand the game, and then investing some money to get the better equipment, cloths etc.  Because if you don’t understand the game, better anything won’t do you any good, and you will just end up frustrated and unhappy with the game.
I have personally taken a break from the game but only because I spend too much money in the game, nevertheless, this game is good enough that it will keep me coming back for a long time.
My three cents.

I have nothced more than 200 hours in this game, mostly in little bits.  You can jump in for 15 minutes, play a quick 6 holes and then get out without having to commit anything else. It's not easy.  I have 2 eagles to my name and one lucky hole in one so you have to make an effort.
You can chat and play with folks from around the globe or just do your own thing.  There is no pressure to do any task.  Anything you play will build up your level and that will improve your abilities.  There are tons on missions, including daily new ones that you can do if you want and plenty of them are very hard.  They will challenge you.
You have to ignore the people complaining about Pay To Win.  For a start, it's just not true,  Sure, you can get better equipement and give yourself some advantage perhaps in distance or control but what actually makes a difference is knowing the courses, knowing your clubs, judging the wind, angle or lie, and how brave you are when putting.  As the say, 'Driving for show, putting for dough.'
It's not perfect but then what game is.  There is lots they could change and plenty they have changed but it's free so you can't waste any money.  I suggest getting it free, playing until you get a character up to a level where you really understand the clubs (about level 25) and then investing some money to get a couple of decent clubs and extras when you know what you want and what will help.
It's going to keep me coming back for a long time.

The sounds are customizable, but most of the built-in samples aren't relaxing as the store page implies. You get random sounds, like dog barks and cat meows. Below that lies a fairly nice speaker orientation system, though. You can move sounds to the left or right of the center icon and they will play in each speaker based on their horizontal position. Unfortunately, the sounds do not play in surround sound like I hoped.
The controls are also very unintuitive, but I figured out the controls fairly easily due to there not being much you can really do in this tool other than drag sound effect icons around and spawn and delete them. The delete key should be used to delete a selected sound effect object, but it doesn't; the right-click does it instead. While this isn't necessarily bad, I was confused and worried for a short period of time about how to delete objects. I wish the dev would give us more than one way to delete these objects. Overall, the interface controls need more work, especially for such a simple tool.
Finally, I'm a little confused why this is even a sequel. What wasn't in the original ASMR Universe that warranted a sequel? I didn't and do not plan to play the original.

A great little app to get started exploring AMSR (Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response).
Using this and listening to the loops as you add sounds and move them around te "sound universe"is like rebooting your mind. Particularly with headphones. And it comes with 7.1 support.
A few minutes toying with this and I'm all chilled out and my three dogs have wandered into the room and gone to sleep.
I'm a pretty "stressy" grumpy sort of old git, and this fixed it. Amazing what effect sounds can have on the mind.
Handy for making sound effects and background sound loops for your games too, you can record output as a WAV file simply by pressing 'R'.
The Dev has made this with unity,and it has a nice feel to it, almost everything is very intuitive.
There is no manual as such, but a useful help tab in the edit screen which covers everything you need to know in a brief clear way.
You can save your "sound universes" to the steam workshop, save them on your pc, or record them as audio tracks. In addition you can import sounds, loops or beats in several audio formats, inclusding OGG into a custom sound library accessed under a separate tab.  (You can't share universes with imported custom sounds to the workshop for legal reasons).

I played it through the end, but I can't recommend it for everyone. Nikopol is an point and click adventure with prerendered backgrounds based on the Nikopol story by Enki Bilal. And to be honest that is it greatest plus, so if you've never heard of any of those two then you probably want to skip this game.
<tl;dr>
Pro:
+ Nice Artwork, inspired by Enki Bilal
+ References to his works
+ Can be beaten in one evening (might want to consult a guide)
Con:
- Some very difficult puzzles
- Timed events that result in your death if you're not quick enough
- Generally not much instructions, more of a trial and error approach
- Though this has not happend to me, players in the forum complained about situations where you run into a dead end, without the game telling you that.
- No movement. You're in a fixed position, where you can rotate 360° and can interact with things and/or travel to the next screen.
- No hotspots, making some things difficult to find (e.g. projector start button)
Two final statements: Go read the comics/graphic novels and consider using a guide to play this game.

Nikopol: Secrets of the Immortals is definitely more enjoyable and understandable for those who are familiar with the graphic novels by Enki Bilal (The Nikopol Trilogy) and/or at least the movie (Immortal, 2004), because the game leaves a lot of things unexplained. However it brings to life quite interesting and gritty sci-fi world. Besides classic puzzles and pixel hunting adventure games are known for the game utilises timed sequences, where you need to think and act swiftly or face consequences (as to be killed or captured which ends the game). It features several cutscenes done in a style close to comic book storytelling - with bordered images, different angles of view and focuses. Music is quite good, voiceacting not as much and the game can be finished in like four hours, making it really a narrative quickie but still... it's nice. I would recommend it for fans or as an experiment for those who are not familiar with the source material but are curious enough and really likes adventures (grab it when discounted). Maybe you will get interested in the movie or books afterwards.

Half Minute Hero is an old-school RPG with one twist: you have to win in 30 seconds. You can pay the incredibly frugal Time Goddess to reset the clock, but you can't do it forever. The result is a fast-paced game that cuts out the fluff and has you figuring out how to best spend your last precious seconds. The story is simple and very goofy, but effectively told. The music and graphics are both very good. Controls are bad, though... this game was ported from consoles poorly. You basically need a controller for some modes (not Hero, thankfully).
The game comes with six modes, but Hero 30 is the big draw: the rest pale in comparison. Evil Lord 30 and Princess 30 are fun distractions and don't take long. Knight 30 was okay once I figured it out. Hero 300 is the big climax, and gives you a big payoff for playing the other modes. Hero 3 is infuriating. I didn't try the multiplayer.
Anyone who has enjoyed 8- or 16-bit RPGs needs to pick up this game. Other RPG and puzzle game fans will probably enjoy it as well. It's definitely worth the money.

Real-time/pause global strategy game, based on the events of the midst of XX century, which resulted in the biggest bloodbath in known history. HoI2 still (like the first HoI) using engine from Europa Universalis 2, but this time, it was actually reworked accordingly to the game's main plan: choose country and prepare it by economical and political means to the oncoming WorldWar. So, major point is - every game of Hearts of Iron series was made with waging wars in mind. Diplomacy... exists, of course, but mostly as a very short intermezzo between Wagner's Valkyries making another fly-by.
So far, the second volume of Hearts of Iron series is still the most successful and respected by all gaming community. I loved Europa Universalis 2, and of course, I was very happy with HoI2 when I first started it.
There are, of course, tech troubles - like flickering screen bug, which kills this game for so many people. Or even if you're lucky one, and haven't met any blink with HoI 2 - there are AI mishaps, questionable features like obtuse air support and spamming pop-up messages... And by all means, the game never looked all fresh and new aesthetically. The visuals are very basic and rigid, obviously.
So, the question: would I recommend the game now? If you're not new with Paradox games - sure, why not? The flickering bug seems fixed at moment (at least, for me). Newer HoI games presents different mechanics, especially the fourth volume - and while some features of the game were improved, others were messed badly. So, if you're up to to win WW2, but can't tolerate neither tons of micromanagement of HoI 3, nor cheating AI at HoI 4 - welcome back to the proven ground of world's nerds beloved warmongering grand strategy, Hearts of Iron, volume two.
However, I wouldn't recommend to buy the game simply to broad your collection - especially if you, like me, wanting every game working and proving satisfaction on every single day. There are too many chances that this game won't start, or will be too difficult to manage.
As of my personal overall rating, I'd say, 8 out of 10. Great game, still very interesting, if you're knowing the drill already. But it looks too plain, and seems too complex for the majority of nowadays players. So come prepared.

First off, this is more about a 6 or 7 out of 10 and not a straight thumbs up.  Again, only play if you like the theme or Adventure games.
The premise of this game is quite neat.  A dystopian Paris mixed with Blade Runner, Ancient Egypt, weird meta religions, totalitarism, and some old school 70s style flying vehicles.  Theme-wise this is my kind of game.  The story is based on the French graphic novel "La Foire aux immortels" [1980], which I have not read.
At heart, it is a traditional FPS rails adventure game.  There is not a ton of pixel hunting (but there are couple hidden ones that are beyond aggravating).  Most of the puzzles are straightforward and not too difficult.  I would have loved to explore the areas in full 3D rather than being stuck to rails.  This was a failing ingredient that the studio White Birds (founded by Benoît Sokal) seemed to stick with for some reason.  There was plenty of 3D modeling in the game and it wasn't half bad but doing a rails adventure game in 2008 is such a bad idea and limits the potential of the title.
The other negative was the voice acting.  The main character was fine but every single other voice was horrendous....detracted very much from the unique/weird story and presentation.  This was probably in part to the translation and inability of the studio to hire good English actors.
Also, the game is way too short for a story that is so strange...it at least needs to be episodic.
White Birds became defunct in 2011.  I think if they had adapted with the community, and market by leveraging existing 3D engines/tools and changed their delivery platform (e.g. episodes or parts) I think this could have been really awesome.  Otherwise, this is just a pretty good attempt but still misses the mark.

Nikopol is another interesting title from Benoit Sokal creator of Amerzone and Syberia. This game is a first person point and click adventure done in the same style as Amerzone. Set in Paris of 2023 A.D. where the city is under marshal law and is being "watched" by a mysterious pyramid that floats above the sky. The length of the game isn't as long as the Syberia games, but you do get enjoyment out of the plot and the presence of the Egpytian gods. If you like the movies Brazil, Blade Runner, 1984, or Fifth Element, then this game is worth your time.

The story is confusing and it feels like there's a lot you aren't told at the end of the game. Many puzzles are quite confusing. In fact, some of them I solved without being very sure what the reasoning was. The first-person perspective is a bit dizzying at the beginning, but actually makes the game much more immersive once you get used to it.

This game has decent graphics and good atmospherics, but that is all it has going for it. I am a big adventure game devotee, but this is among the worst games I have played in that genre.
The puzzles are highly counter-intuitive and often require you to die before getting a hint of what you're supposed to do. Lethal trial and error may sound like impatience, but you have only seconds to figure it out before dying again, and again, and again... That could be excusable if the puzzles where enjoyable, but none of them where.
There is an excessive amount of pixel hunting (that accounts for most of my playtime), further complicated by the fact that many object are only usable if you are holding an item, and some objects are only usable after a specific sequence of events, meaning you could have already gone over the area with a fine tooth comb and still missed the necessary object to escape.
I can not recommend this game under any circumstances.

Nikopol: Secrets of the Immortals could've been a much better game if certain parts of it were changed.  The setting is pretty cool, a sci-fi version of Paris that is controlled by a dictator, but the story suffers due to the game's brevity. Additionally, while many of the puzzles are interesting, they also suffer from unnecessary object hunting that makes them more difficult then they have to be. Overall, the game is recommended only if you are interested in the setting and puzzles, but expect there to be a bit of frustration over game mechanics and a lot of head scratching over the sparse plot.

An excellent sequel to the legendary Fish Fillets. It offers a proper logical challenge on a reasonable curve. You quickly get obsessed with solving the rooms and collecting bonus stars that can raise the difficulty incredibly high.
Compared to the original Fish Fillets, the humour got somewhat tuned down, the rooms are more uneventful (no more talking heads and dancing crabs) and the game is generally less silly. However, it is still funny and lively, as there are more active characters and plenty of dialogue. The 3D videos are not of great quality and look like someone needed to check them off a list, but the in-game 3D graphics is surprisingly good-looking and not too distracting.
The rest is only praise. The game got incredibly improved with completely new and original mechanics. Apart from a big and small fish, you work with crawling crabs, sticky snails, items that float and rise up, deadly lasers and radiation. The authors also cleverly introduced bonus starfish that can be collected for an extra challenge. That way, the puzzles can be impossibly hard for those who want to, but the player does not get stuck in the story progress. Solving the puzzles is also made more efficient with the save and undo system, and you can unlock a square-grid feature that is really helpful. There is a great number of rooms to solve, to many of which you will return to solve them again, but this time collecting starfish on your way out.
The game does not aim to keep up with the current visual trends and may seem mediocre at first sight. However, it has a very catchy and cleverly designed gameplay. It is one the best logical games I have ever played, and you should definitely give it a try.

If you like Minecraft, and Runner games then this is the game for you! Turbo Pug 3D is a hybrid of both elements stated before, accompanied with a feasible unlock system for new characters and hats through grinding for coins. That alone is surely enough to give a player a “run for their money"!
While there is no plot present in this game, the player’s goal is to achieve the highest score (points). This is if you plan on playing competitively. If not, there are the steam achievements there. This is what I ended up going for.
The graphics and effects are like that you would see in Minecraft. I would add that the effects were too overdone, because they could be distracting and there is no option to minimize or turn them off completely. I found myself dying on parts where it is the most hardest to see the obstacles: Such as the bones in the desert, when it is snowing. That is one aspect that I was displeased at, though I can also see it as another unique factor to challenge players.
The audio and music is suitable for the theme of Turbo Pug 3D. There’s nothing too odd about an 8-bit BGM on a game that solely consists of a block-like environment and textures.
Overall, it was a nice experience for me, and can be played both casually or competitively for the high score. The tips I would give to players who want to aim for that 1000 points are:
-Focus on your character’s movements and timing of jumps
-Make sure you look ahead a few times, so you can expect certain obstacles
-Try and try again
Good luck. Turbo Pug 3D is a game that I recommend playing!

TLDR: Best game ever, 11/10.
Longer version:
ArmA Cold War Assault aka Operation Flashpoint Resistance is a game that you must have played when it came out or close to release date to really appreciate. If you played it at a much later date, you likely won't be able to fully appreciate it because all you will see are dated graphics, limited engine (in comparison to later ArmA titles), strange controls and a broken multiplayer mode (which still functions if you download the "OFP Monitor" program made by community).
However, if you played this when it came out or when it was still pretty active, you likely hold it in good memory. Infact, this game was quite groundbreaking when it came out, the first actually realistic (or authentic, if you will) military war game with a proper open world, dynamic AI behaviour (may look stupid in some situations but for a open world game of this age is quite amazing really), the usage of vehicles (a bit more on the arcadey side physics-wise but still very playlable), the ability to create your own missions as well as play user made ones and the quite titanic modding scene that used to surround this title. The mods and modding in particular take this game on another level as there is so much quality content made for the game with a certain following that still mods the game existing.
But for me, this title holds a special place because it is not only most likely my most played and modded game in recent few years (if not all time - do not pay attention to my Steam hours, I play this game since 2001), it's also a game that connects me to other individuals and fans of the game, so it's also a community rather than simply just a game.

This would still be a worthy addition to anyones gaming list.

Have you ever picked up a game from a bargain bin, back in the days before Steam sales, just on a whim? Out of a little pool of obscure titles, picking up one you've never heard of, and giving it a shot just because you can, and it's cheap. And sometimes, it'd be mediocre, or broken. But sometimes, you'd end up with an awesome experience that you'd never have come across otherwise. This game, in my opinion, is the latter case.
It's a budget title, sure. That shows through in quite a few occasions, be it skyscrapers abruptly appearing with a low draw distance, or the hard-to-place voice acting. But as far as outright fun goes, the game only spends the first half pretending at all that the story is anything but an excuse to put you in increasingly preposterous vehicles and doing awesome things.
Many game mechanics are introduced, and some instructions seem to be outright missing from the game (when tailing someone in the open world, for example, you must destroy their car when the timer runs out, despite no hint that you should do so unless you fail to). But overall, this is an arcade racer at the very core of it. Some control issues (those of you using 360 controllers must use the D-Pad to scroll through menus), poor design choices (you must go back to the menus to go back into the open world when you've finished a mission) and strange missions (collecting tickets from cameras to pay off collateral damage costs?) hamper the experience a bit, but the core racing and pursuit is fun.
There is a point where the main story stops taking itself seriously. You will know the exact line where this happens. At that point, it becomes much, much more fun. Treat it like a campy romp through the Autobahn, with the excessive driving of an 80's TV show and the pyrotechnics of a Michael Bay movie, and you'll get exactly that. And a monster truck. You also get a monster truck. So there's that.
You unlock more tracks and cars by playing through the game, and while there are plenty of street races on the open highway, there are also legitimate race courses, which add a nice variety to the overall experience. You can take on races with undercover cop cars, tuners, a Formula 1 car, and armored trucks, so you can make any race as intense or as preposterous as you'd like. I can't vouch for the multiplayer experience, having yet to try this with someone else, but from my single-player look at Single Race mode, it seems pretty solid. Reminds me of the classic NFS games, especially with mods that let you drive firetrucks and such.
In short, a surprisingly intense thrill ride on the cheap, with some design quirks here and there that may strike you as odd, but aren't nearly bad enough to make this game hard at all to recommend. Also, cool original soundtrack.

I've played Drifter for 70+ hours pre-Steam, and while there is a steep learning curve at the moment and a lack of content in some areas, the level of detail and the all around playability already make it one of the better space trading sims out there.
One of the first things you'll notice when starting a new game is that your ship follows the laws of momentum, and doesn't come to a full stop every time you thrust in a different direction. Couple this with projectiles and energy weapons that take time to reach their target, and you get tense and often disorienting battles, fighting as much with the laws of physics as with the pirates that want whatever it is you have.
Outside of a few core systems the galaxy is procedurally populated with star systems and destinations, some friendly and reliable, others viciously hostile teeming with marauders. there's trading opportunities everywhere, and it's up to you how safe you want to play it.
As for the trading, it's a steady if slightly shallow source of income. However the framework for it is in place, with regional price differences and the need to balance what you can carry with what will make you the most money, and with this being Early Access new content is always in the works.
Like with trading, the available missions are steady cash flow but a touch mundane, with patrol missions being the preferred combo of seeing new places and blowing up things.
All in all, the fanatical level of polish and the overall level of detail, combined with the devotion of the devs and the steady stream of new content make Drifter a very highly recommended purchase.

Winning Putt: Golf Online is a golf-based MMO available on Steam.
I will preface this review by saying that, prior to playing this game, I had almost no knowledge of and absolutely no interest in golf. After playing this game, I have more knowledge about golf than I ever expected I would ever have and have a passing interest in golf. This being a game about you playing golf, there’s essentially no plot to be discussed, so I won’t waste any time talking about what little there is. There’s also not a whole lot to be said about the world design, almost all of it just being various golf courses and what little remains being taken up by the hub area.
On the topic of the hub area, and by extension the characters that dwell in it, the whole thing feels a bit hollow and uncanny, for lack of a better term. I’m not sure what exactly I expected, but I just get something of an odd feeling when I see all the NPCs arrayed around the edge of the plaza, each standing stock still and dispassionate until spoken to. There’s also the fact that there’s an semi-anthropomorphic present box standing around in the middle of if. Finally, the fact that there’s an NPC who can enchant your golf clubs strikes me as a bit odd, considering the complete lack of fantasy elements otherwise.
Moving on, the environments are vibrant and nice to look at overall. However, no matter how high I turned up my texture quality in the options menu, there didn’t appear to be any significant improvement in the textures I actually saw. Conversely, no matter how low I turned my graphics settings, there didn’t appear to be any significant improvement in my framerate, though that might have just been my connection. In addition, the game stops to load very frequently. While these loads are pretty short in general, they are irritatingly frequent - with a second or two of downtime each time you try to hit the ball and before and after the game decides to show your character reacting to whatever shot you just took. Additionally, the music in this game is very repetitive. As far as I’m aware, the game only has one music track that plays during gameplay. I say “as far as I’m aware” because I got tired of it very quickly and muted it so I could play my own music. I highly recommend you do the same if you decide to play this game.
As for the gameplay… it’s golf. Though I enjoyed the golfing a lot more than I personally expected, it’s not exactly thrilling, so if golf bores you in real life this game probably won’t change your mind about that. In the beginning of the game the relative lack of precision and control over where your ball goes exactly can be a bit frustrating at times, but the game gives you better gear fairly quickly and I imagine if I’d played longer I would have gotten even better equipment. As you might expect from a free-to-play game, gear can be purchased for in-game currency that can be bought or earned through gameplay. From what little I’ve yet seen, it looks like it takes a fairly long while to be able to buy any gear with currency earned through play. As I recall, most gear is only available for a limited time after purchasing, which requires you to purchase it again after a while.
Pros:
Game looks pretty overall.
Tutorial does a good job of teaching the player about golf.
Overall fun to golf in despite the flaws.
Cons:
Even on high settings, the textures are unimpressive.
Framerate is fairly unstable regardless of graphical settings.
Game stops to load very frequently, especially when showing characters reacting to shots they just took.
Music is very repetitive.
Crafting and enchanting systems feel out of place given the fact that the game appears to take place in a perfectly mundane, modern day Earth.
Not a wide variety of outfits.
TL;DR
This is a pretty good golf game marred by various technical issues. The game’s attempt at emulating an MMO-esque hub area full of NPCs falls as flat as the characters themselves are. I would suggest that the developers spend more time trying to make the game run smoother and less time trying to mimic ordinary MMOs, perhaps making it so the most commonly-used functions NPCs provide are migrated to a menu that one does not have to physically walk to, or outright removing all of them and making it all menu-based.
JSantos approves.
10/10 would fap again.

I'm really glad to have played Chainsaw Warrior, because now whenever someone says a game is "brutal", "unfair", or "punishing" I have the gold standard to measure it against. And I think that perfectly encapsulates the game: It's completely unfair and brutally punishing, to the point where it merits an explanation of each of the three words that defines it. But first, a brief overview.
Chainsaw Warrior is a direct port of a board game I've never played. The core idea of the game is that you make your ultimate chainsaw warrior (chainsaw optional) with a few dice rolls and some tactical clicking then set off to grind through a legion of mobs and traps to defeat the big bad before he can do his big bad thing which, in this case, happens to be exactly one hour. You do this by a repetitive sequence of flipping cards and rolling dice: each card represents an encounter of some sort which you then respond to by choosing an action and rolling a die, or using an item and probably rolling a die. That doesn't sound like a whole lot to work with, but its simplicity belies its depth; the combination of character attributes, equipment, and of course the encounters themselves make each game a unique experience. If Pokemon taught us anything, it's that you can derive surprising depth from shallow systems with a little craft and creativity.
But while the system is solid, I don't think it's sufficient justification to purchase on its own. What really sells the game to me is just how thoroughly nasty it is. This may seem misleading, or even something of a non sequitur so I'll break it down. I previously said three words encapsulate the game: "brutal", "unfair", and "punishing". Let's go through each of them and their appeal.
The game is brutal because it presents itself as itself, and offers the player neither concessions nor quarter. The world it presents is legitimately threatening. Because you can trust the game not to go easy on you, there is a real and authentic sense of danger in every aspect of the proceedings, as
a real and authentic danger in every proceeding. The randomness of the card driven system ensures that. This perfectly segues into the next word...
The game is unfair. Because everything is decided by card draws and dice rolls, your agency is starkly limited. The game is designed very specifically so that you're always in want, but have little control over whether you actually get what you want, even what you need. Except for the small subset of things you control,
is arbitrary. The game has no compunction against casting you in unwinnable situations, and in that sense feels very reminiscent of the old Sierra adventure games.
And that's a large part of why it's punishing. Every mistake prompts a strong penalty, regardless of whether the fault lay with you or the dice. This is compounded by the fact that many things ostensibly under your control are arbitrary in practice because of the opacity of the deck. Bringing that one use excruatingly specific get out jail free card could be the best or worst decision you make, but you won't know until you do or don't encounter the go to jail do not pass go do not collect 200 dollars card. To my mind the most interesting thing about this is that when I remember my games of Chainsaw Warrior, I don't define them by what
, but by what
.
This no doubt sounds infuriating to some of you, but it really is remarkably compelling. The danger makes every step tense, the paucity of supplies makes progress perversely exciting, and sheer randomness makes it compulsively replayable in the same way that slots, pachinko, and opening CS crates are. But most of all, it makes for memorable experiences. This I cannot emphasize enough.
When you sit down to play Chainsaw Warrior, you're going to remember your last game vividly, whether it was a day, a week, or a year ago and there's a good chance the emotions will be just as strong to. If you're like me, you might even build up a whole narrative in your mind. Glory, valor, tragedy, despair, whatever; it'll stick in your mind. I'll close with my last few games from today, which I'm sure will do just that.

Interesting concept, fun at first, but quickly grows easy, dull, and repetitive.  Each board starts you at level 1 and gives you 30 seconds to run around and kill bad guys to level up and get gold which you use to buy equipment, heal up, or reset time.  Fighting happens automatically with your only options being to 1. Increase your attack speed while doing damage to yourself; 2. Run away; or 3. heal yourself during the battle if you've bought an herb.  Boards generally have multiple villages/towns/caves/etc that you can visit to talk to villagers and get various things.  Some boards have splitting paths or side missions/characters you can get for that board only.  You grind up enough levels until it says you're a higher level than the boss, then you go and defeat him at his castle.
The problem with the game is that you're doing all of this for every single board.  Essentially, once you've played 3-4 boards, you've seen the whole game.  Most maps come down to whether you're a high enough level to beat the boss.  If you are, go fight boss, if not, then go grind some more until you are.  Dying in combat doesn't penalize you in any way that I've noticed, you simply go back to the starting village.  At the worst, you might have to run 3 seconds to get back to where you were.  It can actually be helpful to die at times if you're low on time and need to get back to the start village to reset the timer.  Also, for some strange reason, the game shows you what stats equipment increases but doesn't bother telling you what the stats actually mean.  I'm still not sure if weight is supposed to be a helpful or bad stat?  You can replay boards, but in order to do so, you must de-equip any equipment that you received on that board or after it, which is often a hassle.  Also, the inventory system for your equipment is a mess, making it annoying to find what you want to equip.
The main factor in the game is supposed to be the time you have to complete a board, but it's often the least important factor.  This is because every board gives you the ability to reset the timer back up to 30 seconds while keeping all your stuff.  The cost of doing this goes up each time you do it during a board, but the cost is very minimal.  Resetting time once costs 100 gold, 2nd time costs 200 gold, and so on.  The problem is that you can grind out 500-1200 gold during those 30 seconds, so not having enough gold to reset the timer is almost never an issue and you'll have leveled up significantly during that time.  Most boards can be completed resetting the timer just once or twice, as you'll already be stronger than the boss by then.  Being able to reset the timer removes any sort of meaningful challenge from the game.
There's not enough happening in this game to keep it interesting.  Quests often devolve down into fetch quests or go there and kill that thing.  Side characters are almost always useless since you can quickly grind up levels and beat the board without them.  Equipment is nice, but I'm still unsure on what some of the stats mean, and being a higher level negates the need for good equipment anyway.  The only useful equipment I found were the swimming gear to swim around on water boards, or the weapons that allow you to 1 hit kill certain monster types, but those are almost always only useful for killing some otherwise invincible mini-boss to complete a sidequest.  Being able to reset the timer makes the main draw of the game pointless.  They should've set the clock for 2 minutes with no way to reset, called the game 2 Minute Hero, and made players deal with the time limitation.  This would've made exploring boards more tense and actually given some meaning and challenge to the game.  Instead, it's just a pale imitation of the game that it should have been.

Hearts of Iron 2: Doomsday / Armageddon is a grand strategy political war game developed by the grand strategy masters from Paradox Development Studios and published by Paradox Interactive. Unlike its siblings (Europa Universalis, Victoria, Crusader Kings etc.) in this niche genre, the Hearts of Iron franchise covers a more modern timeline by covering the Second World War and the early parts of the Cold War (if playing the expansion Armageddon).
Players can take command of
and rewrite history as it unfolds. The game features major historical events, world situation and military leaders, and most importantly, historically accurate technologies and armies.
+ The World Map is your playground
+ Historical Accuracy on leaders, events, technologies and provinces that allows players to...(see below)
+ Make their own alternate history
+ Very complex and in-depth economy and resource management system
+ Very complex and in-depth technology tree
+ Brutal difficulty levels
+ Extensive replayability (over 175 playable nations)
+ Easy to mod (specially if the player wants the historically accurate flag of 1936 Germany)
- Resolution locked at 1024x768 (No HD support)
- Very steep learning curve
- Tutorial, though extensive, does not cover even half of the game's mechanics (you'll have to learn the other half through trial and error)
- Some historic events sometimes do not trigger properly
- AI can be dodgy
- Hotkeys can't be rebound (you can see a hotkey list from the manual)
GREAT GAME if you're the type of player that likes long term strategic planning and don't mind occasional wars of attrition. The game features a historically accurate 1936-1964 world with appropriate nations, their technologies, economy and historic leaders. The empire management system is very detailed, in-depth and complex that may require some time to learn and master. The graphics of the game are very simple but the easy to install mods that are available will certainly improve your experience.
Grand Strategy games have a very niche audience and even among this audiences, each has their own preference of timeline. Some people like the Victorian age, Feudal Japan, Medieval Europe, Ancient Rome etc. Hearts of Iron 2 caters for those who like to play with the 20th century theme of World War 2 and the Cold War.
This game is best purchased when it is on SALE. Its easier to learn than Hearts of Iron 3 in my opinion and it makes for a good collectors item for Grand Strategy players.

HMH Review 1st draft
An epic RPG... With a deep plot, heart-wrenching drama, and real tension... are all things that this parody throws out the window in favor of pure wackiness and hilarity. Half Minute Hero: Super Mega Neo Climax Ultimate Boy (Which we'll be referring to as HMH or Half Minute Hero) is, rather than simply being as advertised, a series of small genre parodies with a sense of humor. It never takes itself too seriously. For the sake of this review, we'll only be focused on 1 of 6 game modes: Hero 30. It starts simple. Just some level grinding. Then you go back to the castle, and OH DEAR HEAVENS THE WORLD IS ABOUT TO EXPLODE! You have 30 seconds to go defeat the evil lord, as a level 2 no less. You frantically run around the small overworld getting into battle after battle, and winning some if not all of them-! But your efforts are in vain. The world explodes, and we are greeted by an ending screen. Until the goddess of time makes us a deal. She'll rewind time for us as many times as we need, and we become her cash cow-... Er, acolyte/adventuring partner. She rewinds time, and poof! We can kill the evil lord, with time to spare! The game mechanics, you see, are simple and few. The 2 major ones are battle, and donation to the time goddess. The battles, like the rest of the game, are short but surprisingly enjoyable. They're random, but don't happen too often. Before a quest, you choose equipment to your liking.
and you can change out in the middle by buying equipment. Anyways, a random encounter is as such. You have your hp and level, they have theirs. If your stats are better, you win. As aforementioned, it's surprisingly enjoyable. But the goal of this game is to beat the clock. Er, timer. To do that (without dying) you have to pray to the time goddess. Er, pray being a loose term... It's more like you throw money at a statue, and she rewinds time. To get this money, you kill monsters. You need more levels to kill the evil lord of each level. To do that, you need XP. But to do that, you need to kill monsters, but for that you need more time. But to get more time, you need more gold, but you need to kill monsters to have the time to do that. It seems complicated, but you'll get the hang of it. "Why do I neeeeeeeeeeeeed more time, Proto?", I hear you ask. Simple! There's a forbidden spell that will summon the demon overlord, and someone leaked it. Now, every evil wannabe is using it, and it only takes 30 seconds to cast. You need to kill them before they finish casting it. To do that, you need- ... we already did this. Anyways, you travel across the land, killing everyone trying to cast the spell, before they finish. Slowly, a story unfolds. Not one that particularly is normal, but an engaging one. There are also several endings you can get and paths to take depending on how you beat a level. This game is funny, with well-written dialogue, and references that diehard gamers like myself will at least chuckle at. This game, whille still a parody, is a love letter to oldschool RPG's, and the ones who play them. Overall, I give this game a 9/10. I can see it getting boring to a certain audience, but for gamers like myself who want to play in brief, humor-filled bursts, it's pure gold.

This should be called "Quesitionably Programed D6 Simulator: The Game."
After almost two hours, five or six full games, and more than a few dozen restarts at multiple difficulty levels, CW feels like it has a particularaly shoddy RNG. It felt weighted to provide outcomes to the player generally well below expected outcome of a d6. Most player rolls seem oddly to favor 1 & 2, which only works to the player's advantage in a small handful of situations and accounted for mutiple restarts in my nearly in-vain effort to avoid rolling multiple 1 & 2 outcomes for a majority of stats - an alternative name might be "Build an Unplayable Character: The Game." Opposed rolls (player vs Something in the Deck), however, give the SitD outcomes at least of expected outcome but generally better: usually SitD rolls at least 3, but seemed to settle in on 4 & 5 more often than not. I guess it would look too suspicious if it "rolled" too many 6s.
Add to that issue that the trap mechanics have a suspicious inclination to target only the items needed to fulfill the victory condition of the game so that, even on occasions I did reach the final enemy, I never once had any item that would appear to allow a win, makes this an unattractive, uninspired, poorly designed exercise in futility. After reviewing the original scenario, from the tabletop game, I read there's a mechanic that would allow the Warrior to "leave" the dungeon to get a new victory weapon - at a time penalty - and return to the fight. It makes sense that such a mechanic should be built into this computerized version, but, if it was, it was not obviously apparent - especially given how much it over-communicated a few, less critical, aspects of the "tutorial" at the start of the game - and I just don't care enough now to go back, play this game again in the hopes of actually losing the weapon to see if there's an option I missed before. The RNG mechanic is so frustrating, and the basic game design so underwhelming, that I simply don't care anymore.
It's also worth noting that the Hard difficulty level, in addition to severely limiting the number of chances for stat rolls (a 1d6 + 18 at Easy vs 4d6 at Hard, for instance), also hides the identity of the equipment loadout cards so you also have no clue as to your loadout on any specific play. Not that it appeared to matter, really: the game "randomly" seemed to give me the same items from a class of gear (Hand-to-Hand, Gun, Heavy Weapon, Gear, Clothing) regardless of which nameless random card I picked. The "random" nature of equipment selection at the Hard difficulty seems unnecessary: the significantly reduced statistics create sufficient difficulty in a game that is essentially only a more-than-unusually-imperfect RNG. I understand that this probably reflects the Random Card Draw nature of the source game (you pay, for instance 1 resource point to purchase a Hand-to-Hand weapon card, drawn randomly), but that doesn't translate well in this simplistic interface or to a computerized interpretation. Sometimes, 100% adherence to the source material isn't a good idea.
That the game did not go out of its way to explain this, when it made very sure I was aware of the difference in dice allocation between Hard and the other levels, seems inexcusable. That's half of the difficulty spike, there. Not that it took more than ten seconds to realize what was going on after the game actually started. But the lack of the explanation when there was no reason to not explain it just speaks to the slipshod game design.
The flavor of the original game doesn't seem like it has come through very well. None of the "card" designs seem to be particularaly inspired. After reviewing imagery from the source game, it just doesn't seem like a great deal of effort was put into it. While the game seems designed to appeal mostly to people who played its original tabletop incarnation, it is very odd that it doesn't appear to look enough like it at all.
It seems clear to me that this was designed solely for people who actually played the original tabletop incarnation of Chainsaw Warrior, but, even then, I'd advise avoiding it an any price due to the especially shoddy-feeling nature of the RNG and how heavily the game mechanics rely upon the outcome of what, to me, appear to be poorly-simulated d6 rolls.
However, if, no matter how badly anyone else says "The RNG of this game is crap," you are the type of player to be extremely lucky with your rolls, and you also love the original tabletop CW game, then stop reading this review and give the devs your money: you're pretty much the target for whom this game was designed.

You know, I think everything that could be said about Resident Evil 4 has been said about Resident Evil 4, and probably by people better qualified than me, as I played the first three games of the series (or at least parts of them) but never was a huge fan of it.  I still plan on playing the REmake of one and zero, but I have never been a huge fan boy of this series, and in fact the new one scares me enough that while I probably will play it I'm not sure.
Yet I'll try.
Resident Evil 4 is commonly known as "The really good one" especially to people who didn't like the odd tank controls of the original Resident Evils and didn't like how actiony the fifth and the sixth games are.  And while I disagree that this is the only good game (I rather enjoyed 5, and I respect the original trilogy at least from a distance) I can't deny that this is probably the best one of the series with out counting anything after 5. (I know six is worse, but VII does look incredible, though it does look like a bit much)   but I digress.
Resident Evil 4 has you play as Leon Kennedy the wise cracking bad♥♥♥♥♥secret agent who is tasked to protect the president's daughter.... except she's already kidnapped, but somehow not your fault so you now have to go in and find her and protect her.    And while yes Leon isn't a wise cracking guy before or after this mission, he is here, and it works.
Leon walks into a village and basically you know the plot.  Well you can guess it.  There's a zombie virus that is out and about and pretty much everyone is infected, they come at Leon, Leon can kill or run away from then, and rinse and repeat.   What you might not expect is a whole new story that actually never uses the words Umbrella Corp, in fact this game connects to the original game mostly through Leon, which is yet another refreshing change from the original games.
Through the game, there's a remarkably interesting and in fact great story where Leon unravels exactly what's going on and discovers an all new zombie threat, with new characters, new allies and enemies.  I almost feel like the people at Capcom realized how silly it was to be making a fourth game in the series and rather than playing it straight, much of this game is played up for comedy, usually coming from Leon's quips.  So much of this game works in this way that it's hard to take it serious, but it's also impossible to completely dismiss.
And it all works.  A cheesy but mostly serious story works, Leon is an interesting character, the president's daughter (Ashley) is a great character, and then there's the game play that works with it.  Overall though the story works in a different way.  It's the way that five wanted to work but didn't have the charismatic protagonist who just makes fun of the absurdity of it to bring the whole package together.
The game play also delivers while it does feel similar to the original games, the new third person mode changes everything.  No longer do you have awkward angles that fight against the player.  The player is able to use dual sticks to move and aim at the same time, as well as a button to ready the knife or the gun at a moments notice.  There's a little awkwardness of having to ready a gun and then hit X to fire it, the same with a knife, but the steam controller streamlined this process for me, so I was able to bypass that awkwardness.    But the controls are vastly improved from the original games, even if they aren't perfect.
However the game play isn't as fluid as it could be.  It's improved, but the controls to turn around are awkward as it can get, and the player pretty much turns or walks, the controls don't really allow an easy movement, and watching the game you'll notice that the player moves awkwardly.  This is likely to assist the odd game play rules the game wants to make, but while this is a huge improvement for the series by this point, it will feel awkward to anyone who hasn't played the original trilogy and realize this is improved from the tank control.  A lot of people compliment the controls but honestly... Well Spec ops the line has good third person controls, this still has awkward controls at times.  You will get used to them, but you shouldn't have to get used to controls at least not for the reasons that this game requires you to become used to them.
Though the controls rarely got in the way, it did happen but really this game isn't about tight controls but more about resource management, namely bullet.  You can't buy bullets in this game ever, so instead you need to manage how many bullets you get and where you use them.  If you do this successfully in the first half of the game especially managing your money (mostly used for guns and upgrades) in the second half you can start picking up rocket launchers and such for bosses and make the game quite easy.  In fact most of this game is relatively easy as long as you can avoid wasting bullets on most enemies, or only using bullets when necessary.   From that point it's mostly dealing with zombies, using your precious ammo sparingly and then exploring a really great set of locations.
So how is it trying to do this?  It's actually incredibly fun and tense.  Like I said for the first part I honestly kept being afraid I was going to run out of ammo (I don't think I was every very close until the mid point where I should have been switching guns a little more often, and got low on hand gun ammo).  But for difficulty, it's actually a bit easier than I expected.  I admit that I used a rocket launch on a few more bosses than I could have, but overall, this game is more fun than challenging.  However if you do want a challenge, the game does offer a harder difficulty, and at least three additional modes, each of which worth playing for different reasons.
On the other hand after about 20 hours of playtime which I believe is a little slower than average, I was done with this game.   I didn't feel a need to jump into a second playthrough as 20 hours is very long, and the side content was interesting but I didn't want to play that right away.  Yet, 20 hours is well worth the price of admission and you can easily get 30 or more hours just replaying it.  I know a number of people online brag about how many times they beat the game and how they go through the game (the game allows multiple choices of how to go through the game as well as strategies) so you can play multiple times.
So overall how is it?  Honestly it's as good as everyone has said, this is easily one of the best Resident Evils I have ever played (again haven't played VII yet but it won't ruin this game even if it's better) and just a great action game.  It's a zombie game that doesn't take itself too seriously, and it's a action game that doesn't go too off the rails.  I really liked this game.  The controls and fluidity hold it back from being as great as I have heard people calling it (Best game ever?  Guys come on) but still this is such an easy recommend because it's really a fantastic experience.
To finish, I know this is a port and some people have had issues with it, but I've had none, though I believe the game did force close on me a couple times, in over 20 hours I might have only had a couple minutes dealing with it once or twice.  I had a blast with this game and I'm likely to return to try a professional run at some point.  Just not right away.

I got the game through Humble Bundle, so I did not pay the full price, but I still consider it well worth 5 USD.
The game is hard, unforgiving and to some extend you throw yourself at the mercy of the RNG Gods, but with that being said, I have completed the game on all three difficulties in only 4 hours. Admittedly, I was savescumming my way through the hardest difficulty, but easy and normal can be overcome without too much of a fuzz, if you put some thought into you items selections and perhaps reroll your character once or twice. There are times where you will find yourself unequipped to handle a cave-in or an unpassable chasm, but losing is part of the game.
For some reason, I love tormenting myself with these sorts of games, but if you want a more skill-based experience, you should try the Chainsaw Warrior: Lords of the Night. They improved upon a lot of things – especially the influence the player directly has on the game.
Overall, I would say this game is 50/50 on luck and skill with most of the skill being in foresight (choice of equipment) and trial and error (you learn what to fear and how to avoid it).
The only real issue I have is with a feature you are almost always forced to use against the endgame boss who can only be killed with a special weapon (or an implosion vest which – as a pretty cool feature – ends the game in a draw). You get one shot and after that you get some ‘lucky shots’ and those are just annoying. Basically, you roll a die and depending on what you roll, something will happen. You will only win, if you roll a six, but rolling anything else will either waste the shot or something else, like, shooting yourself. Granted, there are things you can do to improve these odds (like mounting a scope on your weapon), but losing the game because your supposedly badass character shot himself in the foot, is a little... disappointing. Still, the game is far from unbeatable.

There are times when Metacritic gets it wrong, and this is most definitely one of those times.  A score of 61 would put this game in the "Meh, it's OK" category, though with Vigil:  Blood Bitterness, that decimal point needs to go about 1 or 2 places to the left.  Even a score of 10 should have triggered a federal investigation of payola over at Metacritic.
The game's one novel feature, the developer's apparent tweaking of the Dark Engine's texture filters until only black and white remains, is a one-trick pony that wears out its welcome within minutes, and becomes simply glaringly, wince-inducingly annoying.
Gameplay is nothing more than an exercise in frustration, as clues are cryptic without being logical, solutions are arbitrary and often linked to timers tuned so short that anything less than following the developer's intended path and timing, without an  angstrom's width of deviation, will result in certain death and banishment back to the last checkpoint.  Bugs are game-breaking and interspersed with the wonky puzzles in such a way that there is no way to tell if you are simply approaching the puzzle "incorrectly", or if the game has broken itself in such a way to make the puzzle unsolveable.
I had played through a section with a long walkway outside and "airlocks" at each end.  If you remained outside on the walkway, you died, suggesting vacuum outside.  If you didn't open, run through, then CLOSE both airlocks, you died.  If you ran through, opened and closed both airlocks, BUT didn't run far ENOUGH into the next room, you died (That's right: if you did it correctly, and were standing inside the safe room -- but too close to the CLOSED airlock -- you died).  If you ran through, opened and closed both airlocks, ran far enough into the next room, BUT didn't do it quickly enough, you died.  Fine.  Except that a few puzzles later, backtracking through this area, one could now stand anywhere on the outside walkway indefinitely.  The airlocks were now open and inoperable, presumably because that section was now "solved" and no longer necessary.  So, really, just suddenly no more vacuum of space?  But as soon as I stepped through the inoperable airlock into the next room, I was immediately killed by asphyxiation, judging from the death cutscene -- a cutscene by now in furiatingly familiar to me in this area.
Finally, giving up after about 36 tries, I looked up the solution on YouTube, only to find that I had done everything correctly, but the game had jiggered itself up so completely that it was now  impossible to "solve" and progress.
I generally make a strong effort to complete every game I begin, but this game had played me like a cheerleader plays a nerd on prom night, and I had had enough.  I never went back.  I swear, as I clicked "Delete local content" I heard myself let out an evil little giggle.
So don't do it.  Just don't.  Browse away from this page and never return.  If I can save just one of you from the torture that I endured trapped inside this♥♥♥♥♥♥of a game, then my suffering will have been worth it.  Look upon my trembling, twitching form and mutter, "Wow, that could've been me".  Now go.
